#81. Wigan pine for FA Cup glory as not even victory can lift them off foot of League One

Gary Caldwell, club captain in 2013 and now manager, needs much more than the weekend win against Reading to disperse the clouds

If the 2013 FA Cup final represented a blip for the Sheikh Mansour-era Manchester City in their quest for total domination of English football, it was a historic moment for their conquerors, Wigan Athletic.

Memories of that famous day at Wembley still endure for Latics supporters despite the relegation from the Premier League that followed. Yet watching the modern‑day Wigan, who remain bottom of League One despite a 1-0 win against Reading on Saturday, makes the toppling of City in a Cup final seem an epoch ago.

The club, perhaps understandably, continue to hark back to their halcyon days. Last season they brought back Gary Caldwell – club captain in 2013 – for his second stint as manager, having led the club to promotion from this division in 2015-16. Choosing to swap Exeter for a return to the Latics was seen as a risky move by Caldwell, considering the shoestring budget imposed upon him by Mike Danson, the owner who is keen to sell.

Finances are ultra-tight at the Greater Manchester club amid dwindling crowds and losses on the pitch and on the balance sheet. The local businessman Danson and his family saved Wigan from liquidation in June 2023 after mismanagement from previous owners brought a points deduction and relegation from the Championship. Three successive mid-table finishes in League One under their stewardship have brought a semblance of stability, but this season they have plummeted.

The problem is the Dansons have been unable to find an ambitious buyer to take the club to the next level. Now the prospect of a first season in the fourth tier since 1996‑97 is a distinct possibility, although victory against Reading – the Latics’ second league win of the campaign, sealed by Scott Hogan’s 71st-minute strike – made the picture a little rosier.

“Some of our play was tremendous,” Caldwell said. “Our spirit, our character, our determination not to let the ball go in the net was fantastic. It was pretty stressful towards the end. We need to try and build on this. You have to keep the players believing and committing. There’s still so many aspects of our game that need to be better, but a result makes you feel better about yourself psychologically.”

The presence of Leam Richardson in the opposition dugout at the Brick Community Stadium gave fans more reason to reminisce about better days. Richardson, who claimed the League One title as Wigan manager in April 2022, was sacked in November of the same year just 16 days after signing a three-year contract.

Caldwell has also found himself under pressure. The former centre‑back has been criticised by fans for his team’s uninspiring style of play, which has produced just six goals in nine games, the fewest in League One. They went 447 minutes without a league goal until Hogan, the veteran forward, converted after Christian Saydee’s cross was parried out by the Reading goalkeeper, Joel Pereira.

And while Wigan’s keeper, Joe Whitworth, was regularly called into action to see out the win, the home team were still good value for three points, allowing Caldwell and his squad to breathe. The manager’s backers will rightly point to the lack of spending by the club in the summer, with the £1.5m generated by the sale of Sam Tickle to Bristol City not yet reinvested on players and an overreliance on young loanees to prop up the squad.

Danson and the club’s hierarchy have issued rallying cries to supporters to return to the stadium in an effort to generate more revenue, thus making the club more appealing to new owners, but why should fans part with hard‑earned cash to watch such insipid football?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Before the game, Caldwell said: “We also recognise the need for points is big, for our supporters to have that feelgood factor, and be able to leave the stadium in a much better frame of mind than they have been.”

The Scot got what he needed against Reading, yet the sense of chaos above Caldwell was evidenced by the abrupt departure of Sarah Guilfoyle from her role as managing director on the eve of the new season, after a 10-year stay at the club. And there are plenty who feel the owners ought to bear the brunt of criticism.

The Wigan Athletic Supporters Action Group is demanding answers from Danson on why selling the club has been such a struggle and the lack of investment. Other fans are more resigned to the idea that some short-term pain may be necessary for long-term gain; most agree a sale would be transformative.

For now, despite a rare victory against a hitherto in-form Reading, the short-term struggles look likely to continue. The hope is that a hero of 2013 can perform miracles on the pitch, despite the constraints off it.

The bombastic former Leyton Orient chairman is back in the game

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Over the past five decades, Barry Hearn has made a habit out of turning sporting outsiders into major attractions.

But for all his success in darts, snooker and boxing, the former Leyton Orient chairman has never been one to settle for past glories.

The former Matchroom supremo is now back in football, having bought a stake in non-league Brentwood Town, relishing the challenge of building something special.

“I’m not the type to sit on his arse all day, you know?" Hearn tells FourFourTwo as he opens up on his latest venture.

"We staged 700 sporting events in the past year alone,” he adds proudly. “I followed them all religiously.

"After every single darts and snooker event, I update my world rankings by hand. I’m a sad, sad bastard. My wife likes to remind me of that.”

Hearn can also be found at Matchroom’s other sporting ventures, from ten-pin bowling to carp fishing.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“If the world was ending in an hour, Geoffrey Boycott would have a turn in the nets, Steve Davis would play one last frame, and Barry Hearn would have a quick glance at his latest spreadsheet,” he adds. “That’s what people like us do.”

Was there a family vote when it came to buying a stake in Brentwood? “No, I just said ‘Bollocks to the lot of you’,” Hearn laughs. “They all think I’m mad, but it’s not a lot of money. It’s a commitment in time that’s much more important than how much money you put in.”

Hearn will be using his time in the short term to drum up interest in the club, but insists that Brentwood will not be getting their own version of Club For A Fiver.

“There’ll be no Netflix series here,” he says. “Wrexham have done that and good luck to them. We need to make our own noise. I shall use what influence I have. I will fight the good cause to my last breath, and I will, in some way, win. I can promise you that.”

It’s hard to imagine otherwise, given the extraordinary energy that Hearn throws at every project he takes on. “I could be drinking champagne on a beach all day, with staff topping my glass up every five minutes,” he winks.

“But where’s the buzz in that? I’ll make a success of Brentwood Town or I’ll die trying.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#85. This is how far ragged Man United have fallen. Anything that isn't a defeat is a good result, they can't control games, are weak in the centre and had to hang on against Leeds, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 16:24 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 17:44 BST, 18 October 2026

It may not have looked, felt or smelled like it, but this was a good result for Manchester United.

It wasn't a performance or an outcome to mask problems or deficiencies that run right through Michael Carrick's squad but in terms of an outcome it was about par.

For this is where United are right now. Anything that isn't a defeat – especially away from home – to a team with ideas and ambition and a good coach represents a decent day out. This, frankly, is how far they have fallen.

Carrick's team took the lead in the first half and had the better of it for a while. But then they lost control of things to the extent that it took them half an hour to have another shot. By then Leeds had equalised and taken a grip of the game.

In fact, by the end, Daniel Farke's energetic and likeable team had mustered 62 per cent of the possession and this is one of the reasons that the other United – the one from along the M62 – are stuck in such a rut. They simply cannot control games.

They have some good players and Bryan Mbeumo is one of them. He scored in the 35th minute. But in the centre of the field where tempo and rhythm are set and territory is won, United are weak.

Manchester United and Leeds played out a hard-fought 1-1 draw at Elland Road on Sunday

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised in the second half after Bryan Mbeumo had put United ahead

Here, with Carrick betraying the look of the team sheet by deploying what looked like a back three, it was new signings Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba who were given the job of securing ball and position. They were okay but that was all they were.

Over time, Leeds won that battle and as the game wore on, it was they who had the loftier ambitions. It was they who sensed a win and Carrick's players who were looking to get out of town with what they had.

They were a little bit all over the place by the end. Three promising counters in the space of five minutes, for example, were halted by utterly needless and brainless offsides.

But United survived and some of the noise around Carrick's position will quieten between now and Wednesday's Champions League game in Como. The pattern seems once again set now, however.

We are seven games in to the new Premier League season and United have won just once – against Ipswich at home.

Here Carrick's formation had a look of Ruben Amorim's back five about it. It was inflexibility – not to mention poor results – that got Amorim the sack last season but at least Carrick appeared to be trying something different.

Mbeumo slid home from close range in the first half after Youri Tielemans' inviting cross

Calvert-Lewin levelled by firing home from close range after the ball broke to him from a corner

Diogo Dalot and Amad Diallo appeared to be playing as wing-backs in a line-up that saw United start without a clear centre forward. Youri Tielemans, Bruno Fernandes and Mbeumo were the front three with Fernandes more often than not occupying the central position. After all the fuss of the week, Lisandro Martinez was in the team but only until half-time, after which the Argentinean failed to appear.

Arguably, United's problems have not been about tactics and formations but about application. Here, against an upwardly mobile Leeds team, Carrick's team seemed for a while to have more about them than they showed in drawing against ten-man Tottenham eight days earlier.

They were more compact but also more energetic and it ensured they initially competed with the home team on the metrics that really mattered. Sadly for United, it wasn't to last. Leeds were honest and spirited but lacked consistent tempo in the first half. They created sporadic half chances but nothing that sufficiently engaged the home crowd. Indeed Elland Road was rather quiet at times and that told part of the early story.

Mbeumo's opening goal didn't arrive until the 35th minute. Up until that point the game had been scrappy and occasionally required the vigilance of referee Darren England.

Leeds captain Ethan Ampadu should have been booked for an early stamp – accidental or not – on Mbeumo while Fernandes was indeed cautioned for a late challenge on Tarik Muharemovic. That offence came after Fernandes applied a heavy touch to the through pass and was perhaps indicative of his recent poor form. Prior to that, the United captain had taken a free-kick from a good position on the far side and delivered it straight out of play.

Leeds were occasionally progressive around this point and United keeper Senne Lammens was sharp enough to touch a header from Nico Elvedi over the bar in the 25th minute. At that stage, it stood as the only chance of the game.

The result slightly eases the pressure on under-fire Red Devils boss Michael Carrick

Lisandro Martinez was subbed off at half-time in the first game since his explosive rant

United always looked as they may carry a threat when they did motor up field, though, and Mbeumo served notice of this almost immediately when he found space to meet a Tielemans cross six yards out only to head the ball six inches wide of James Trafford's left hand post.

As the visiting team grew into the game, so they settled a little. There was nothing haphazard about this performance at this point and after Trafford tore from goal to stop one dangerous attack with a slide tackle on Diallo, United returned again to take the lead.

It was Tielemans again with the cross from the right only this time it was a low one. Mbeumo was under pressure from James Justin with the Leeds defender taking a piece of his shirt. But the United forward was strong and determined and he kept enough of his balance to side foot the ball in from a few yards out.

United just about deserved their lead. They had looked just a little more clinical than their opponents. They held it until half-time – despite half chances for Calvert-Lewin and Jayden Bogle – but it took only six minutes of the second period for the game to change.

With Noussair Mazraoui replacing Martinez at half-time, the Moroccan conceded a corner in the 51st minute. When the kick arrived, however, he was beaten to it in the air by Muharemovic who headed the ball down for Calvert-Lewin to swivel and volley in.

Thereafter United were ragged. All their previous structure and composure had gone and for a period they hung on. There was nothing particularly sophisticated about Leeds' football. It involved width and crosses – not always as accurate as Farke would have liked - and high energy. But it made United look ordinary and uncomfortable. Indeed when Fernandes swivelled and drove a low shot across goal and wide in the 65th minute, it represented United's first effort on goal of note since they scored.

Bruno Fernandes, Carrick and Amad Diallo salute United's fans at the final whistle

Technical director Jason Wilcox, the subject of much of Martinez's ire, was in attendnace

Leeds were not creating lots of chances, either. Just a couple of smashed shots over from Ao Tanaka and Noah Okafor and then another from Anton Stach with 18 minutes left. But the home team did have some momentum and that threatened to be precious.

As they looked to turn the game back their way, United's options from the bench were limited. Mason Mount came on for Carlos Baleba with 15 minutes left but Carrick seemed reluctant to introduce Marcus Rashford or Matheus Cunha. Maybe that was a sign that the United manager valued a point above anything else. Eventually, with six and a half minutes left, Cunha was given his chance.

It was still Leeds who finished the stronger and they could have stolen it in added time. United keeper Lammens applied a weak punch to a cross and watched Stach's shot dribble through his legs. Fortunately for Lammens – and indeed Carrick's emotional wellbeing – Mazraoui was positioned behind him to hack the ball away.

Leeds 1-1 Man United: Bryan Mbeumo opened the scoring in the first half with a sliding finish but Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised for Leeds after the break

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s second-half equaliser extended Manchester United’s winless Premier League run to five matches as they were held 1-1 by rivals Leeds United at Elland Road.

Bryan Mbeumo stole in to fire the visitors into a half-time lead, but Leeds hit back early in the second period through Calvert-Lewin’s thumping finish.

Leeds fans held high hopes of securing their first home win over the Red Devils in 45 years after Michael Carrick’s side had won only one of their previous six league games this season.

There was little in terms of quality on show from either side in a full-blooded derby clash, but Carrick will have no complaints about his players’ application as they matched Leeds’ intensity to earn a deserved point.

Relive all the action from Leeds vs Man Utd with our live blog below:

"We worked on it this week,” he told Sky. “We wanted to match them up without the ball and go quite aggressive.

"We knew we could get a lot of joy in the middle of the pitch with them only playing two in there.

"That's probably the area of the game where we could have done more. We could have been a bit braver with the ball and taken the ball under pressure.

"But we're in a circumstance where we are not as brave as we should be, and we have to get that back because to win games for Manchester United we have to have that bravery and composure."

One visiting midfielder impressed on a day when Bruno Fernandes was not at his best.

"We are slightly disappointed it is just a point,” he told Sky. “Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United.

“Second half, we got the equaliser. We should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

"We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

"We were the dominant side but we couldn't capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

"It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

"It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going."

Dominic Calvert-Lewin, whose goal earned a point, has been speaking to Sky Sports.

"More so just be more confident in possession and choices when to cross and when to keep the ball, I think it was down to that,” he says of the half-time message.

"They tried to [match our formation]. Not really surprised given what happened last season. It took us a little bit to adjust but it was mainly down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.

"They are still a very good team with a lot of quality, regardless of the outside noise. We are so used to it as players.

"I just tried to cause a ruckus. I just make it difficult for the defender. I read the flight of the ball and was quickest to react.

"I feel really comfortable. I feel the support from the club and the fans and it is a great feeling stepping onto the pitch, particularly at Elland Road."

He adds of their overall start to the campaign: "We have to be pleased. I think we could have been better in pivotal moments but it could also gone against us in pivotal moments."

The Manchester United head coach had lost all five of his previous meetings against his Leeds counterpart. At least that has ended.

That could have been the game Manchester United turned a corner. Instead, it wasn't. They lost another lead, conceded another set-piece goal and did too little to win it after Dominic Calvert-Lewin levelled. So United stumble on, six without a win in all competitions.

It ends level, which is about right following a match that saw two committed teams fail to produce a huge amount of top level stuff.

The pressure eases on Carrick, Leeds’ wait to beat their visitors at Elland Road will drag on to another season.

93’ - The set piece is unable to yield an opportunity.

Is there one more chance to come? Probably not.

92’ - Ampadu is finally booked for clattering Amad’s right shin. Santos appears to have been shown a yellow for reacting angrily too.

The result is a chance for Fernandes to pump in a deep free kick.

#91. Another unremarkable win shows Arsenal’s strength is in depth rather than creativity | Jonathan Wilson

Champions so risk-averse Forest were lured into thinking they had a chance, until bench was used to see them off

Pass. Pass. Pass. Pass. Sideways. Square. Backwards. Pass. Pass. Recycle. Pass. It wasn’t much of a spectacle. But in the end, for the second week running, thanks in no small part of their bench, Arsenal won. Fireworks in the autumn are for Bonfire Night; titles require relentless accumulation. Since the international break, Arsenal have won three games out of three despite not being in the lead at half-time in any of them.

Hammered at Brighton and having endured a drab first hour at home to Leeds last week, there has been a rare sense, for the first time really since Manchester City dropped points at Everton at the beginning of May, of Arsenal not being quite at their best, needing to reassert their quality. This was not a performance that would terrify any opponent, but it did highlight Arsenal’s consistency and it did demonstrate just how deep their squad now runs.

There were long periods when they were extremely flat. In the first half the ball was moved too slowly, too risk-aversely, for Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze consistently to isolate their full-backs. There were very few attempts to play the ball in behind an admittedly well-organised Forest backline. It was all very safe, seemingly predicated more on waiting for Forest to make a mistake than on trying to break the game open with a moment of genius.

The breakthrough, ultimately, was delivered by Noni Madueke who, when he got a run at Daniel Múñoz, took full advantage, albeit with a substantial deflection off the thigh of Jair Cunha. It was Arsenal’s only shot on target – and it wasn’t even on the bit of the target it ended up going in.

Arsenal may have been working with Germán Castaños, a creativity coach who has worked in handball, in designing TV gameshows and with his local council. By challenging the players and presenting them with unusual situations during the week, the theory goes, he can help them to come up with innovative solutions at the weekend. It must take a lot of creativity to make a team as unremarkable as this.

Mikel Arteta is a great believer in the sort of team-building techniques that to outsiders might look like high-performance gimmicks but you dread to think how hard a watch his side would be if their collective imagination wasn’t constantly being stimulated.

Castaños got a boxer to fight two opponents and a Japanese football team to play against a side with 16 men. You wonder how a team might prepare to face an Oliver Glasner side in full stifle mode. Running headfirst into a line of three brick walls, perhaps? Or rather, given how Arsenal played for the first two-thirds of the game, running parallel to three walls looking suspiciously at them? For an hour, this was about patience and risk aversion, the only occasional flurries of something approaching unpredictability coming via Saka on the right.

The England winger perhaps suffers the curse of those who emerge young, that consistent excellence seems somehow not quite enough, a betrayal of that teenage potential. Familiarity in football often breeds, if not quite contempt, then at least a sense that there could be more. He is certainly not playing badly, and he has scored three league goals, but equally, at 25, he is not the exhilarating presence he was at 21.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Perhaps that is simply how Arteta wants his wide players to play, prioritising consistency and efficiency over the spectacular. Perhaps the fears of those who felt Saka was being played too consistently are being realised and he is experiencing an element of fatigue. Or perhaps this is just what regular mature performances look like in the modern Premier League.

There was one delightful early turn that drew Neco Williams into a trip that earned him a yellow card, which it might have been thought would encourage Saka to run at the wing-back, but the pattern remained the patient sideways passing. Saka, though, did at least offer more than Eze on the other flank, and it was no great surprise when the former Crystal Palace man was withdrawn at half-time for Madueke. Staying wider more consistently, Madueke did perhaps offer a greater threat but he did have more space for him to exploit as an encouraged Forest began to push forward more.

That, in fact, for a long time seemed Arsenal’s best chance, playing with such an absence of threat that it lured Forest into the thought that there was more for them in the game than a worthy clean sheet and a notable point. Leeds, perhaps, might argue they were suckered by something similar last week. As in that game, what turned things Arsenal’s way was a triple substitution midway through the second half.

The arrival of Jurriën Timber, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyökeres gave Arsenal legs and purpose that Forest could not match. Even as Forest were forced out of their defensive shape to chase an equaliser, the bulk of the game was played in their half. It may not have been especially thrilling, but it was enough and it was, in its own understated way, an expression of Arsenal’s strength. Thrills can come later.

#93. El Clasico’s Merseyside match-up is a tale of two careers on different paths

Trent Alexander-Arnold and Anthony Gordon could go head-to-head in El Clasico - but while one player has kicked on in Spain, the other's career has stalled

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This time next week, two sons of Merseyside could be about to go head-to-head in the biggest club fixture in world football.

Trent Alexander-Arnold and Anthony Gordon were born barely a couple of miles apart, in West Derby and Norris Green respectively, and both joined Liverpool’s academy when they were in primary school.

Of course, Gordon was released by the Reds and ended up coming through at Everton, with the pair facing each other in a Merseyside Derby for the first time in June 2020. They are now on opposite sides of another rivalry, but as Alexander-Arnold’s Real Madrid prepare to face Gordon’s Barcelona in El Clasico, their careers are on different trajectories.

Next Sunday’s meeting between Barcelona and Real Madrid happens to fall on the 10-year anniversary of Alexander-Arnold’s Liverpool debut, which came against Tottenham Hotspur in the Carabao Cup fourth round in October 2016.

He scored his first Reds goal on his Champions League bow 10 months later, curling home a classy free-kick against Hoffenheim that served notice of his outstanding dead-ball ability.

Alexander-Arnold was picked for England’s 2018 World Cup squad when he was just 19 and became a key figure in Jurgen Klopp’s great Liverpool sides, redefining the right-back role with his vision, passing range and technical ability.

As well as winning six major trophies at Anfield, the defender posted some incredible individual numbers, including claiming double figures for assists across all competitions in all but one season between 2018/19 and 2023/24.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

When Alexander-Arnold left his boyhood club for Madrid in summer 2025 - a decision that saw him booed by sections of the Liverpool fanbase during a draw with Arsenal - he was expected to thrive at arguably the biggest club on the planet. But it hasn’t worked out that way.

The England international’s debut season was hampered by injuries, as separate hamstring and thigh issues ruled him out for a total of four months. When he was fit, he struggled to make his mark in an underachieving side that ended the campaign trophyless, not helped by the change of manager from Xabi Alonso to Alvaro Arbeloa in January.

Alexander-Arnold failed to make England’s World Cup 2026 squad and he has been similarly overlooked in two of Madrid’s biggest games this season. He was an unused substitute in last month’s derby defeat by Atletico Madrid in La Liga and Wednesday’s victory over Roma in the Champions League, with head coach Jose Mourinho selecting summer signing Denzel Dumfries instead.

It means there is no guarantee Alexander-Arnold gets on the pitch at the Nou Camp next Sunday, when he could be up against Barcelona left-winger Gordon. In contrast, the former Everton man looks increasingly likely to start after beginning the season in promising form.

Despite starring for Newcastle United in a three-and-a-half year spell after leaving the Toffees in January 2023, eyebrows were raised over the £69.3m fee Barcelona paid for Gordon earlier this summer.

The 25-year-old has responded with an excellent few months individually, starting five of England’s World Cup games and scoring in the semi-final defeat by Argentina. He claimed two assists off the bench on his Barcelona debut, against Elche, and notched his first goals for the club in the wins over Getafe and Galatasaray in the past eight days.

Gordon has become a regular starter for European football’s form team and has risen to the challenge of playing alongside the likes of Lamine Yamal and Rodri every week. Ultimately, he has already kicked on following his move to one of Spain’s superclubs, whereas Alexander-Arnold’s career has stalled.

This is also evident in their international prospects. While Gareth Southgate failed to get the best out of Alexander-Arnold when he was England manager, he did at least continue to select him. Thomas Tuchel has largely ignored the right-back completely.

The defender was recalled for the first time since his Madrid debut for the recent batch of Nations League fixtures, although even that was hardly a ringing endorsement from Tuchel. It is unlikely he would have made the cut if Reece James or Tino Livramento had been fit, while Jarell Quansah started the Three Lions’ biggest game of the international window, against Spain.

Essentially, Alexander-Arnold is further down the pecking order with England now than when he was at Liverpool, which seems crazy for a player of his ability and age, having just turned 28.

The ex-Red did start both matches against Czechia and provided the assist for Gordon’s opener in Prague, one of three goals in as many games scored by the winger in the international window. Gordon appears to have more of a swagger now he is a Barcelona player and looks a certain starter for England when fit.

It is already shaping up to be a hugely important season for both players, but for different reasons. Gordon has made an excellent start to his Barca career and if he maintains that level over a whole campaign, he will establish himself as one of the best wingers in world football.

Meanwhile, Alexander-Arnold is at a crossroads. He certainly has the talent to turn his Madrid career around, but another inconsistent season would amplify the nagging doubts that his move to the Spanish capital may have been a mistake.

His inability to nail down a place with England was arguably a red flag ahead of joining Madrid, who tend to appoint head coaches that take an approach to management often seen in international football. Just look at Carlo Ancelotti and Zinedine Zidane, who would trust the club’s superstars to win them games, rather than leaning on complex tactical plans.

Alexander-Arnold may even have been better suited to Barca, where he could now be linking up with Gordon in the same way that they did for England against Czechia. Instead, they will be El Clasico foes next Sunday - and that night at the Nou Camp will offer a clue as to what is in store for both players, this season and beyond.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#96. Leeds 1-1 Man United PLAYER RATINGS: Who 'still looks short of his best'? Which star was 'a real handful'? And whose performance will have pleased Michael Carrick? Plus, vote for YOUR scores

Published: 16:52 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 17:04 BST, 18 October 2026

Leeds and Manchester United played out a hard-fought 1-1 draw at Elland Road in the Premier League on Sunday afternoon.

Under-fire United boss Michael Carrick saw his side go 1-0 up through Bryan Mbeumo after he turned home Youri Tielemans' cross, before Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised early in the second half when he fired home from close range.

Both sides pushed for a winner but neither could find a breakthrough as they were forced to settle for a point on an intense afternoon.

The result leaves United with seven points from seven league games, while Leeds are up in seventh place after racking up ten points so far this season.

Daily Mail Sport's CHRIS WHEELER was at Elland Road and he has rated both sets of players below...

Manchester United and Leeds played out a hard-fought 1-1 draw at Elland Road on Sunday

JAMES TRAFFORD 6 – Looked solid and showed good anticipation to race 40 yards out of his goal and clear at the feet of Diallo. Had little chance with Mbeumo’s goal from close-range.

JAMES JUSTIN 4 – Will be angry at himself that he lost track of Mbeumo for United’s opener. You can’t afford to switch off in games like this.

NICO ELVEDI 6 – Presented with one of Leeds’ few chances in the first half when his header was saved by Lammens. Had his hands full with Mbeumo as United’s forward line chopped and changed.

TARIK MUHAREMOVIC 6 – The big Bosnia defender was on the end of an ugly challenge from Fernandes early on, but recovered to get the crucial knockdown for Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser.

JAYDEN BOGLE 7 – Got forward to offer a real threat at times and also defended well. Great interception tackle on Dalot in the first half got a huge cheer.

ETHAN AMPADU 7 – Right in the thick of it. Set the tone with a couple of strong tackles early on, and squared up to Fernandes in the second half. Just the kind of approach Leeds fans love to see in this fixture.

Leeds captain Ethan Ampadu was up for the fight on what was an intense afternoon

But James Justin (right) was caught out after switching off for Bryan Mbeumo's opener

AO TANAKA 5 – Had a couple of half chances, including a volley over the bar shortly after Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser. Replaced by Longstaff towards the end.

GABRIEL GUDMUNDSSON 5 – Booked for a challenge on Andrey Santos in the first half and was perhaps fortunate it wasn’t a red. Referee Darren England did well to let the tackles go in a fixture that was never going to be short on intensity.

ANTON STACH 6 – Had two chances to make his mark on this game but volleyed over in the 72nd minute and then side-footed straight at Lammens late on. Got away with a cheap shot on Fernandes but the United captain was never going to have much sympathy here.

NOAH OKAFOR 5 – Leeds’ two-goal hero from the win at Old Trafford in April rarely looked like scoring in this one and was replaced by Nmecha for the final quarter of the game.

DOMINIC CALVERT-LEWIN 8 – Playing with the confidence of a striker who only needs one chance and he took it with a clinical finish early in the second half. A real handful for United’s defenders.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is in the form of his life and was a real handful for United's defence

Subs: Zetterer, Longstaff (for Tanaka 80, 6), Wilson, Aaronson, Nmecha (for Okafor 73, 6), Bijol, Bahoya, Bard, Gruev.

DANIEL FARKE 6 - Will see this as a missed opportunity with Leeds on such a good run and their opponents struggling so far this season.

SENNE LAMMENS 5 – Couldn’t be faulted for the goal but still lacks the composure of last season which is perhaps inevitable in a United side short of confidence.

LENY YORO 6 – Looking more comfortable at right-back with each game he plays there. Took a blow to the face from Calvert-Lewin in the first half, but recovered well and stood strong against Okafor.

HARRY MAGUIRE 7 – His physicality was important here after missing out against Madrid in midweek. Good battle against Calvert-Lewin but wasn’t marking the Leeds striker when he equalised which was odd.

LISANDRO MARTINEZ 6 – Kept his place as expected after the furore over his post-match comments in Madrid and subsequent apology, but went off at half-time. Showed why United needed him here with a solid first-half display.

DIOGO DALOT 6 – Played out of position at left-back in the absence of Luke Shaw again and performed well in his duel with Bogle. Got forward well on occasions.

ANDREY SANTOS 6 – This was a big test for the Brazilian and Carrick chose to keep him on the pitch when he replaced Baleba, which says a lot for what the head coach thought of his performance.

Andrey Santos faced a big test in this game but he impressed and Carrick will be pleased

CARLOS BALEBA 6 – Cool presence in midfield after he was flattened by Ampadu early on. He has brought a calmness and composure to this United team that was needed in the cauldron of Elland Road.

AMAD DIALLO 5 – Returned on the right flank and there is room for improvement after his injury lay-off in the first part of the season. There were concerns Diallo had suffered another one when he needed treatment after a challenge by Tanaka, but he recovered.

YOURI TIELEMANS 6 – Playing at No.10 suits his game better. In a game of very few chances, he created both openings for Mbeumo in the first half.

BRUNO FERNANDES 5 – Switched between the left flank and striker with Mbeumo in a fluid United formation, but still short of his best. Had to be careful after picking up an early yellow card for a lunging tackle on Muharemovic which had the home fans baying for a red.

BRYAN MBEUMO 7 – United’s most dangerous player. Scored the first goal with a simple finish after heading wide unmarked in front of goal. Was outmuscled by Calvert-Lewin for the equaliser, but it’s anyone’s guess why he was marking the big Leeds striker.

Bryan Mbeumo was United's most dangerous player and put them ahead in the first half

But Bruno Fernandes continues to look out of form and had to be careful after an early booking

Subs: Darlow, Amass, De Ligt, Mazraoui (for Martinez 46), Mount (for Baleba 74), Lacey, Cunha (for Tielemans 84), Rashford, Zirkzee.

MICHAEL CARRICK 6 - It’s only two wins in 10 games this season, but the United boss will take a point here after another difficult week.

#97. Man United player ratings vs Leeds: Midfielder earns 8/10 as Bruno Fernandes struggles

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Bryan Mbeumo opened the scoring at Elland Road but Michael Carrick’s side could only draw 1-1 with Leeds

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United’s winless Premier League run continued as they could only secure a 1-1 draw with rivals Leeds at Elland Road in a result that will only ease the pressure on boss Michael Carrick slightly, if at all.

United haven’t won in the league since beating Ipswich 5-2 on 30 August and this cross-Pennine derby came at the end of another volatile week at Old Trafford, with Lisandro Martinez criticising the club hierarchy following a tepid defeat to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday and being forced to subsequently apologise.

There was a much-improved performance from the Red Devils, especially defensively, in the first half and they deservedly led through Bryan Mbeumo’s sliding finish from Youri Tielemans’ low cross.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised early in the second half after some shoddy defending in the box but United strengthened again and were good value for a draw.

Here’s how the Man United players rated at Elland Road:

Was alert to produce a decent save on 25 minutes from Nico Elvedi’s header and there wasn’t anything he could do about Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s smart finish early in the second half, with the defence in front of him letting him down. A poor punch in injury-time could have been costly but Anton Stach’s weak shot was fortunately blocked a couple of yards from the line. Distribution was decent throughout.

Forced to right-back again and quite frankly, he is simply not a right-back. Gamely tried to stride forward and create form the flank but the sooner he is able to return to the heart of defence, the better for all involved. Defensively, he was very, very solid with a number of key interceptions and headers clear, helping United’s back-line look much sturdier than in recent outings, aside from the goal.

A couple of rash moments but United’s defence was much improved, so he has to be given credit for that, and he generally shackled Calvert-Lewin pretty well in the first half. After the break, there was a wobble around the time of the equaliser but the former England international marshalled the troops and steadied the ship from there.

All eyes on the Argentine after his midweek outburst at the Manchester United hierarchy and subsequent apology. A key part of United being much tougher to break down in the first half, reading the game well and making some crucial interventions. Was subbed at half-time, potentially with a slight knock, and United conceded a goal within a few minutes of him going off. Those two facts weren’t completely unconnected.

Another man displaced by the defensive injuries, forced to play at left-back rather than in his preferred position on the right. Bombed forward into dangerous positions but usually failed to produce a decisive final ball and was made to work hard defensively by the lively Jayden Bogle. Brilliantly launched a counter-attack on 75 minutes when he made a tackle on the edge of the box and ran 60 yards with the ball before slipping in Amad for a shot.

Took a bit of a battering in a niggly opening 20 minutes – being fouled on multiple occasions – and never seized control of the game in the engine room. Can’t escape the feeling that Chelsea will have been delighted to get £50m for him this summer and there is no evidence that he is the answer to United’s general midfield woes. Was booked late on.

A first Premier League start and perhaps a bit unlucky to not quite earn a 7. Has generally appeared to be the most impressive of United’s trio of summer midfield signings and again showed composure, drive and a decent range of passing, although Tielemans was the real creative hub in the first half. Made a couple of fouls after the break and couldn’t help the United midfield regain control of the game before being subbed off 15 minutes from time.

Whipped a lovely ball into the box for his side’s first big chance, that Bryan Mbeumo contrived to head wide, and picked out the Cameroon international with another glorious pass to set up a shot shortly afterwards. His creativity was then finally rewarded when Mbeumo slid in to convert another pinpoint low cross for the opening goal 10 minutes before half-time. Quieter after the break before being subbed for Matheus Cunha late on.

Nominally a winger but actually tucked in at points to make a back five, with Carrick setting his side up to be much more structured and tougher to break down, which they were. Used his pace to be an outlet ball at other points, produced a couple of dangerous deliveries from corners and linked up beautifully with Tielemans to create the opening goal for Mbeumo. Looked threatening when on the ball in the Leeds half, although the end product is still sometimes lacking, as proven by a neat cut inside, followed by a wild, wayward shot with 88 minutes on the clock.

When the line-up was posted, it was presumed that the United skipper would be playing out wide again and, while he did spend some time out on the left, he was also almost a false nine at points as Carrick seemed to eschew a traditional frontman. He was again surprisingly subdued in both roles... Set-piece delivery wasn’t great and was rightly booked for an ugly lunge on Tarik Muharemovic early on. Flashed a shot wide on 65 minutes but didn’t offer much else. It’s now five consecutive Premier League games without a goal or an assist for Fernandes – his worst run since May 2025. For years he was the lone bright spot in struggling United teams but at the moment he is simply one of many issues in an inconsistent United team.

Had United’s first big chance on 27 minutes as he drifted into space 12 yards out and powered a free header wide of the left post for a bad miss before producing a tame shot from a decent position a short while later. But his persistence paid off with a great run and sliding finish from six yards out to open the scoring before half-time. Calvert-Lewin got the better of him in the box for Leeds’ equaliser.

Came on for Lisandro Martinez at half-time, who appeared to have picked up a knock, having been an injury doubt during the week. Was promptly outmuscled by Muharemovic in the build-up to Leeds’ equaliser and then started squaring up to Calvert-Lewin. Hardly a vintage display...

Had a shot shortly after coming on after a well-worked corner but skewed it wide. Not hugely involved other than that.

Sent on by Carrick shortly before the end to try and snatch a winner from somewhere but not enough time to really make an impact.

#100. ‘I suffer a lot’: Villarreal owner Fernando Roig on not enjoying games and the prospect of Liverpool | Sid Lowe

It will be a tense time for Europe’s longest serving president, despite the Champions League game at Anfield offering a symbol of how far they have come

The first time Fernando Roig watched Villarreal play as their president, he sat in the stand at a tiny whitewashed ground that had concrete fever and was half empty. It was a Sunday night in the second division, they lost 3-0 against Badajoz, and he didn’t enjoy it much.

But then, he never enjoys it much. Even on Tuesday at Anfield, he will not: into his 30th year, the longest presidency in Europe, that is about the only thing that hasn’t changed. More than 1,000 games and still it happens. “I don’t get nervous,” he says. “It’s worse: I get worried, very anxious. I suffer a lot.

“It’s emotional to play Liverpool. This will be the fifth time we have faced them, the third at Anfield. The other two were European semi-finals. I’ll watch the morning training session, travel with the team. We’ll go and eat; everywhere we go we get treated very well and we treat them well back. The next day I’ll watch the under-19s in the morning, that I do like. And then the game, which I don’t. Then we’ll fly back here very, very late. It’s very stressful.”

It is the morning after Villarreal have beaten Napoli in the Champions League and Roig is in an office at the headquarters of Pamesa, the ceramics company he owns, on the edge of town. He is better now, the tension subsided. They needed that victory, their first in the competition going back to before they last faced Liverpool, in the 2022 semi-final, and, besides, he is always better the next day.

A cabinet holds pictures, mementoes, footballs, a basketball, too. Three paintings by his wife, Elena Negueroles, fill the far wall. He has been talking a short while when two people join him, at the long table, in front of the cabinet. He introduces them as Villarreal’s consejero delegado, chief executive, and Pamesa’s director of communications; they are also his son, Fernando, and daughter, Elena, named after their parents.

“I can enjoy it today, the day after, tomorrow and the day after that,” the 79-year-old says. “Until Elche comes on Saturday and it’s time to suffer again. And then the Liverpool day. It’s very stressful for me.”

So why do it? “Because when the game ends, there’s that satisfaction, that feeling that the town, the province, have enjoyed it, that they admire their team. It’s about community. It costs people money to come to watch a game. What they want is to enjoy it and what we want is to give them that.”

They have done that, come a long way. “I remember that Badajoz match, thinking ‘so this is how it starts’,” he says. “We didn’t have a training ground. We trained on any patch of grass we could find. The stadium held fewer than 4,000 people. The first thing was to try to build a squad that could go up, find a pitch to play on, a decent dressing room, create an academy.”

It was May 1997 and Roig describes the offer to buy the club as an opportunity, but it was more like answering a plea. For survival and stability, not success: asking for Anfield would have been absurd.

Villarreal had spent most of their history in tercera, reaching the regionalised Segunda B nine years earlier, and had never played in primera. In the second division for the first time, they had barely 1500 members, were struggling to stay afloat and the former player and current president Pascual Font de Mora was seriously ill. His family were looking for someone to take on the club and assume a debt near €80m.

The man they entrusted to find a buyer was José Manuel Llaneza. One day, Llaneza came to these offices. Roig had money and experience with sports: Valencia Pamesa basketball club. His brother Paco owned Valencia’s football team.

So why take on another club? And why in Villarreal, an hour up the coast? “All my factories are here: here, in Almassora, Onda, L’Alcora; 98% of all the ceramics made in Spain are made here in a 50km radius around the town. We knew a lot of people in Villarreal, in the province of Castellón. This was our place, where we could give something back.

“And the owner wanted to sell; it was an opportunity. They came to us. I had been at Pamesa Valencia since 1986. We had been in the second tier and taken them to the ACB [the top professional basketball division in Spain], so I had some experience. I still watch them. Yesterday, after the [Napoli] game, I watched them against Olympiacos on the tablet.

“I was president of both for a while, but you couldn’t combine them. I remember winning the Copa del Rey in basketball at the same time as we were playing at Numancia.”

Another of Roig’s brothers, Juan, continued at Pamesa Valencia. Alongside Llaneza, manager general, consejero delegado and vice-president, he began building at Villarreal. “In a city of 52,000 people, we did something we can be proud of,” he says. What they did is barely believable, although investment was heavy and Roig keeps insisting there was never any doubt. This, he says, is exactly as they imagined it.

Well, maybe not exactly. “We went up, probably before we were really ready, then came straight down again. Went back up. We got into Europe, reached a Champions League semi-final in 2006. We’ve been promoted three times, been relegated twice.

“The second relegation in 2012 was terrible: really, really awful. We started that year in the Champions League, but didn’t win a game and went down in the last minute of the final game. We were in the second division for one second all season, but it was the last second. We had to sell players, rebuild. I had to ‘compensate’.”

That was a warning they heeded. Roig sold a 2.4% shareholding of the 9% stake he had in the supermarket Mercadona to balance the books. Villarreal had in effect been part of the Pamesa group, but they were separated, only the sponsorship remaining, the whole model restructured. Now he says the first thing every year is survival – “42 points and it’s time to raise a toast” – even if ambitions, and indeed the model, see Europe as a minimum.

How much have you invested over the years? “I couldn’t say. Maybe about €200m. There has been a lot of investment: the training ground, another training ground, the stadium.” Roig looks at his son. “€180m, maybe? I haven’t calculated it all, but Villarreal is worth more than all of it. We can’t compete economically with the biggest clubs, the state clubs. We can’t have salaries of €10m, €12m, €15m, €20m. Our policy is clear: be sustainable, spend what we can generate. We’re not a selling club, but if someone offers the right amount maybe we sell, for two reasons: one, economics; and two, we won’t curtail a player’s career.

“We keep growing: we’ve extended the stadium: over 23,000. Very nice, very comfortable, very yellow. We’re constantly reforming.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There’s another glance across the table, something Roig does often. “The consejero delagado does everything now: he’s the one that decides, leads and executes,” he says. “He has us on a good path. I don’t do anything any more. All I do is suffer during games. We think we have done something important, but what really matters is what’s next. In 30 years we’ve spent 27 seasons in the first division, 19 in Europe.”

If Anfield offers a symbol of how far they have come, so do Liverpool’s rivals to the east. “When we went to sign Diego Forlán from Manchester United, I said to Llaneza: tell them to come and play a friendly here, make it part of the deal. And they said: “Where? Villarreal?” Roig says. “I said: ‘Don’t worry, they’ll come next year … and they’ll do it for free.’ And then next year, or maybe the year after, they came in the Champions League.

“Diego wasn’t playing much, but we looked after him, gave him affection, and he was a great player. He won the golden boot here. Because he was at Villarreal, no one talked about it much. When he won it again, at Atlético, then they talked about him.

“If you want, you can call us a family club; we admit it. It’s a club with no pressure, not much media attention, none of the toxic surroundings other clubs have. We have to create the pressure ourselves, the demands. Above all, we create an ecosystem.”

It works. It started with investment in established players, particularly from South America. But they searched for emerging footballers as well and, bit by bit, the academy, built on an old orange grove, bore fruit. Mention Santi Cazorla, who joined as a teenager, and Roig’s eyes light up. “An excellent player and an excellent person. He came as a kid. Real Madrid wanted him, but we convinced him to stay.

“He overcame so much with those injuries, then came back at the end. He didn’t know if he would be able to play again, but we welcomed him back, were pleased to give him that opportunity and he gave us three more superb years.

“And we had a Ballon d’Or winner here. Rodri was with us for five years. He wanted to progress and we weren’t going to stop him: he went to Atlético Madrid, from Atlético to Manchester, and won the Ballon d’Or. We have great memories of him, a good relationship. It fills me with pride to see him win the World Cup.

“Not just him: Álex Baena came to Villarreal at 11. He had those first years of melancholy, not being back at home in Almería, but he grew up here. Yéremy [Pino] came very young. Borja Iglesias, too. That’s an example of what we want to be.”

Ask Roig for a player from all those who have been at Villarreal and beyond Juan Román Riquelme or Robert Pires, Marcos Senna, Bruno Soriano and Gerard Moreno it is Pau Torres that comes to mind. “He’s born in the town and triumphed here, won a European title,” he says, “which was the only game I couldn’t go to.”

All those matches and Villarreal’s president missed that one. The 2021 Europa League final, the greatest, most epic victory of all, the one that completed a journey and delivered their first trophy. Football can be cruel.

“I had Covid the week before,” Roig says. “I got certificates from every lab in Villarreal: they all showed I was negative. But as I was in the team bubble, Uefa demanded some other certificate. There was no time. We tried to argue, put some pressure on. It was no good. But it filled me with pride. And when Pau dedicated the win to me, it meant so much. He even came back from Poland and gave me his medal.”

It is here: a simple gold disc on black ribbon, around a match ball in the cabinet behind Roig’s son and daughter. “Pau won it there. As for me, I had to fly back and watch the final calmly at home with my wife. Well, ‘calmly’? I suffered there too, terribly.”

#103. The story of Alfie Conn, Tottenham’s rock ’n’ roll cult hero who crossed the Rangers-Celtic divide

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Tottenham’s answer to George Best, Alfie Conn was a cult hero in North London in the 1970s – before controversially becoming the first post-war player to represent both Rangers and Celtic…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You don’t have to be over 60 to know about Alfie Conn, but one look at any picture of the Scotsman in action will carbon date his heyday firmly to the 1970s.

Long curly hair flowing over his collar, huge sideburns plus a ’tache to die for, shirt hanging outside his shorts – Conn was the epitome of a rock’n’roll footballer in an age when the Bay City Rollers and the Faces were riding high in the charts, and fashion trends on Top of the Pops translated to the terraces.

At Tottenham back then, one fan was seen wearing a white butcher’s coat with “Gilzean is King of White Hart Lane” written in blood, a unique tribute to the club’s Scottish forward Alan Gilzean. In 1974 though, Gilzean was replaced in the affections of Spurs supporters by his compatriot, when Conn arrived from Rangers for £140,000, a huge sum at the time.

“We’ve got our own George Best,” was the sentiment on the Shelf and the Park Lane end at White Hart Lane, and there could be no higher praise. Best was football’s first bad-boy superstar, long before Paul Gascoigne, Eric Cantona and Mario Balotelli.

Conn looked the part too, played in a similar devil-may-care way, and quickly won over Spurs fans who’d grown up during the Bill Nicholson era, when the club won eight major trophies in 12 years playing stylish, attacking football. Nicholson’s final signing before stepping down fitted the bill in terms of what fans loved in a player, but it wasn’t all plain sailing.

Now 72, polite, softly spoken and mostly bald, it’s hard to marry the Conn of today to the image of a player who infamously taunted Billy Bremner and Norman Hunter by sitting on the ball during a game against Leeds, and prompted graffiti that proclaimed “Alfie Conn is God”, still seen in parts of north London long after he’d left Spurs.

“George Best was my idol, although I was never going to reach those heights – if I had an ounce of his ability, I’d have been quite happy,” he tells FFT now. As a youngster, he’d seen the Northern Irishman up close when Best played in a charity match to raise funds for victims of the 1971 Ibrox disaster. Best and Manchester United team-mate Bobby Charlton were guests in a combined Celtic/Rangers team against a Scotland XI, and Conn trained with them. “Just to see him up close was unbelievable,” he says.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

At the time, Conn was still traumatised by the events of January 1971, when 66 Rangers fans died and more than 200 were injured in a crush at the end of an Old Firm game. “I’d just turned 18, played in the game and had no idea what had happened until later that evening, when my mum phoned to check if I was alright,” he explains.

Rangers officials and players spent days and weeks visiting survivors in hospital and attending funerals. “Sometimes we went to three a day – one was for five young brothers, who lived down the road,” Conn says. “It turned out to be one of the worst events in my life. I lost over a stone in weight.”

Conn started his career at Rangers, even though his father Alfie Conn Sr had played more than 400 games for Hearts and once for Scotland. “I was a fan from the first time I went to Ibrox as a kid, seeing the big red brick facade,” Alfie Jr explains.

He was thrown into his Rangers debut in a Fairs Cup game against Dundalk at the age of 16. “I had no nerves, no fear,” he admits. “You don’t at that age.” Conn went on as a substitute for Alex Ferguson, then the Rangers centre-forward. “I had no idea he’d go on to be one of the best managers ever, but you knew he’d succeed in whatever he did because of his nature,” Conn says now. “He was always up for a battle.”

A year after the low of the Ibrox disaster, Conn experienced the club’s greatest success, winning the 1972 European Cup Winners' Cup at Camp Nou. The Barcelona Bears, as they became known, beat Dynamo Moscow 3-2 in front of 35,000 fans. “It was over 34,000 Scots and two Russians,” Conn quips.

Crowd trouble in the city centre and two pitch invasions led to headlines around the world and a chaotic final. “We'd gone 3-0 up soon after half-time, but whether it was the heat or the occasion getting to us, we were shattered, out on our feet,” he says. “Dynamo got two goals back and to be honest the second pitch invasion did us a favour, it gave us a breather.”

The pitch was cleared in time to allow the players back for the final minute, before another invasion. “We were hit by police batons as we tried to get down the tunnel,” he says. “It was chaos.”

UEFA decided not to risk having a trophy presentation on the pitch, so the cup was presented in a small room inside the stadium. “John Greig, our captain, was taken to a wee room by UEFA officials, given the cup and told to get the hell out of there,” Conn says. “That was a real disappointment not to be able to celebrate with our fans, but it was one of the greatest nights of my career.”

The following year, Conn scored as Rangers beat Celtic 3-2 in the Scottish Cup final in front of 122,000, the last time Hampden reached that capacity before being downsized.

A year later he was off to England, having fallen out with manager Jock Wallace, but he was surprised to be joining Tottenham.

“I’d spoken to Tommy Docherty the week before and it was agreed that I’d join Manchester United,” Conn explains. “But then I was told to meet at the airport for a flight south, and thought I was going to meet him again in London. So imagine my surprise when I heard the Cockney voice of Eddie Baily, Bill Nicholson’s assistant, saying ‘Welcome to Tottenham’.

“As soon as I met Bill and he told me what was on offer, I said ‘Where do I sign?’ He was a great manager, one of the few who had that special aura which commanded respect, like Jock Stein, Bill Shankly and Don Revie.”

Conn’s wages more than trebled from £60 to £200 per week, plus a ‘crowd bonus’ for cup games – £3 per thousand fans, once the crowd reached more than 29,000. It was a huge incentive to pull in the punters, and Conn certainly did that once he’d established himself, which took six months.

He had injuries as Spurs struggled at the start of the season, before Nicholson quit and was surprisingly replaced by Terry Neill. The former Arsenal defender lasted less than two years at Spurs, before leaving to manage the Gunners. “The fans all thought he was using Spurs as a springboard to manage Arsenal, and we didn’t see eye to eye, but at least he gave me my chance,” Conn says.

His full debut, in January 1975, couldn’t have gone better. Away to Newcastle and needing a win, Spurs were 4-0 up by half-time and ended up winning 5-2, with Conn scoring a hat-trick. “My dad and grandad came down from Glasgow, and I went back up with them afterwards,” he remembers. “We all had a few drinks on the train back and when the ticket inspector came round, my grandad said we were celebrating my hat-trick, then ended up taking over his duties!”

Conn quickly became a fans’ favourite at Tottenham, taking over the King of White Hart Lane title from Gilzean. “I couldn't believe it the first time I heard it – that sort of thing makes your chest stick out,” he says. “I got on great with the fans, and to this day I still think of Tottenham as my club.”

But that result was an outlier as Spurs went on a run of eight defeats in nine games, and in their final game of the season, needed a win to avoid relegation. They were up against Leeds, a club he’d almost signed for as a teenager, now preparing to face Bayern Munich in the European Cup final.

Inspired by one Conn goal and two assists, Spurs raced into a 3-0 lead. He then, however, decided to sit on the ball and taunt Bremner, Hunter and Co. What was going through his mind? “Nothing!” he laughs now. “I don't know why I did it, but as soon as I looked round and saw big Pat Jennings shaking his head, I thought ‘What have I done?’ The Leeds players suddenly turned it on and within 15 minutes it had gone from 3-0 to 3-2. It was a relegation battle for us and I could have been the villain rather than hero. Fortunately we got a penalty, won 4-2 and stayed up.”

“I thought I'd better apologise to the Leeds players,” he adds. How was it received? “I don’t know – I popped my head round the dressing room door, said ‘Sorry lads’ and got out as quick as I could!”

The incident cemented Conn’s place in Tottenham folklore, but he still couldn’t nail down a regular place. Keith Burkinshaw replaced Neill but also had little time for the maverick Scot. Spurs continued to struggle and by the time they were relegated in 1977, Conn was gone.

“I was playing the reserves and got a call to say someone wanted to see me,” he explains. “It was Jock Stein. It’s fair to say that no-one else could have tempted me away, but he was different. I needed no persuasion, even though it meant going to Celtic, which I knew would be difficult.”

Stein had just one special condition. “He told me all the best players wore their hair short and were clean shaven, so would I mind a haircut?” Conn says. “It wasn’t a problem and he said ‘Good, I’ve got you booked in at the barber’s tomorrow!”

The newly clean-cut Conn went on to experience success at Celtic, winning two titles and the Scottish Cup, but as the first man to cross the Old Firm divide since World War Two, his move was not without trouble. “An old friend, the best man at my wedding, was a diehard Rangers fan and never spoke to me again,” he says. “People would come up to me in pubs and at social occasions, and give me grief. On rare occasions they still do, unfortunately.”

Conn’s career took him from Celtic to America, playing professionally in an indoor seven-a-side league and then for San Jose Earthquakes, before a brief return to British football. He retired to run a bar in Scotland, with his former Rangers team-mate Willie Henderson. On the opening night they promised a special guest, and the locals were stunned when the great Stanley Matthews walked in. “Everyone wanted his autograph, including me,” laughs Conn.

There’s great sadness in his eyes when he talks about losing his wife Sue to motor neurone disease in 2021, and he now raises funds for MND charities through events and royalties from his recent autobiography.

He has few regrets from a colourful career that was blighted by injuries and some managers' mistrust of mavericks like him. He won just two caps for Scotland and wishes he could have featured more for Spurs. “If Bill Nicholson had stayed on, I would have played a lot more and stayed longer,” he says.

Conn appeared just 49 times for Tottenham, scoring 10 goals, yet his impact was about more than just pure statistics. With his swagger, sideburns and long curly hair, for many of the Spurs supporters who watched him play, he’s still the King of White Hart Lane.

Conn’s book What’s It All About? The Alfie Conn Story is available now

He's interviewed Pele, Zlatan and Santa Claus (it's a long story), as well as covering the World Cup, AFCON and the Clasico. He previously spent 10 years as a newspaper journalist, and completed the 92 in 2017.

#105. Texans beat Jags in final seconds of Wembley thriller

CJ Stroud throws three touchdown passes as the Houston Texans beat the Jacksonville Jaguars thanks to a game-winning field goal from Ka'imi Fairbairn in the final seconds at Wembley Stadium; Travis Hunter records touchdown and interception for Jaguars

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Ka'imi Fairbairn kicked a 49-yard field goal as time expired to lift the Houston Texans to a 34-31 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars in a thriller at Wembley Stadium on Sunday.

It was a game that began with referee Larry Smith being carted off with a non-contact injury in the opening seconds. A game that spent its interval staging on-field Corgi races. And a game that concluded with another dose of boot-fuelled drama following Cam Little's last-second winner against the Philadelphia Eagles at Tottenham the previous week.

Texans quarterback CJ Stroud threw for 312 yards and three touchdowns while Jaylin Noel led his side with four receptions for 107 yards and a score as Houston improved to 2-4 on the year.

Stroud's first interception of the season came by way of Travis Hunter as the two-way Jags star became the first player to score a touchdown and record a pick in the same game since Brian Dawkins for the Philadelphia Eagles against the Texans on September 29, 2002.

Trevor Lawrence finished 24 of 41 for 306 yards, four touchdowns and one interception as the Jaguars slipped to 4-2 at the end of their fortnight in the UK.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hunter had derailed Houston's attempt to put the game to bed with four minutes left when he intercepted Stroud in the end zone to halt a 12-play drive.

Last week's hero Little delivered again moments later when he converted a 60-yard field goal to tie the game at 31-31 with two minutes to play.

Stroud proceeded to navigate a game-winning drive that included a 19-yard connection to Woody Marks on third-and-two as Houston reached field goal range to set up Fairbairn's defining moment. He delivered on cue.

Having led 17-14 at the break, Houston pushed their lead out to 24-14 on the opening drive of the second half through Noel's 13-yard touchdown catch on third-and-10.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jacksonville's reply came courtesy of a one-handed one-yard touchdown grab by tight end Nate Boerkircher to pull within 24-21 after Jakobi Meyers had springboarded the drive with two catches for a combined 50 yards.

Jawhar Jordan, elevated from the practice squad for Sunday's game, scurried clear for a 25-yard touchdown on the ensuing possession as Houston opened up a 10-point cushion.

Back came the Jags, Hunter taming a bullet from Lawrence for a seven-yard touchdown to make it 31-28 after the extra point with 11.26 to play in the fourth quarter.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Houston had struck first in the game when Stroud floated a six-yard touchdown pass to tight end Foster Moreau, rewarding Nico Collins for his 42-yard airborne contested catch in direct coverage from Hunter along the sideline.

The Jags were foiled in their immediate response when Bhayshul Tuten's three-yard touchdown run was nullified by a Brenton Strange holding penalty, before Lawrence was intercepted by Calen Bullock in the end zone while targeting Jakobi Meyers on third-and-goal.

Tuten refused to be denied again when he slalomed through two tackle attempts for a 27-yard touchdown catch-and-run mid-way through the second quarter.

The Jags running back struck again when Lawrence peeled out to his right to float a two-yard strike to Tuten for a 14-10 lead with a minute remaining in the half. Houston responded instantly when Moreau hauled in a one-yard touchdown pass with eight seconds left after Noel's 50-yard reception.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jags head coach Liam Coen on Travis Hunter: "He made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football. We've got to continue to get him the ball and keep building off of it and making sure it fits within the rhythm and flow of the game. But he definitely helped put us in a position to win that game today."

Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans on CJ Stroud: "C.J's been hot all year and he's still hot. He's lighting it up, he's dishing the ball around to a lot of different people. It doesn't matter who it is. He's doing an outstanding job of just leading this offense."

Texans quarterback CJ Stroud: "I'm having fun, man. I'm having a joyful energy. My teammates have looked to me. And, man, this all just, really, just a team effort. Special teams played great, defense did their job, and offense came out and got the dub. We got a long season ahead of us, and a lot more football to get played."

#107. Dejan Kulusevski to finally return to Spurs matchday squad after more than 500 days

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Bottom-of-the-table Spurs will be missing seven players for the clash with Coventry

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dejan Kulusevski will return to Tottenham’s matchday squad for the first time in more than 500 days for Monday’s visit of Coventry, but Savio and Lucas Bergvall will be absent.

Spurs have spent the majority of this week in a warm weather training camp in Marbella, but Savio was absent after he reported a “muscular problem” on Tuesday and Bergvall is sidelined for “two weeks” with a knee issue.

Those absences along with Kulusevski’s ever-improving fitness have opened the door for the Swedish playmaker to potentially play on Monday night after a serious knee injury has sidelined the attacker since the end of the 2024-25 season.

“Yes, Kulusevski on the bench. We had a meeting with the medical staff. They gave the OK and it’s great news. I think it’s one of the best news after Everton game last season because Deki he suffered too much. He deserves to feel emotion on the pitch,” boss Roberto De Zerbi told a press conference.

“Unfortunately Savio on Tuesday… before we leave for Marbella, he felt a muscular problem. We lost him for some weeks unfortunately.

“And Lucas Bergvall because he had a problem at the beginning of the game in Manchester.

“The day after Manchester (United), Sunday, he came to (the) training ground to our medical staff. And I think two weeks (out).”

De Zerbi provided a positive update on right-back Pedro Porro, who could be available for the trip to Chelsea next Saturday.

However, bottom-of-the-table Spurs will be missing seven players for the clash with Coventry with Rodrigo Bentancur suspended for a fixture where the hosts will be desperate to end a six-match winless start to the new Premier League campaign.

“Coventry is a good team. They played a fantastic Championship last season,” De Zerbi said.

“But we are Tottenham, keeping humility, keeping what you want, but we want to show to be good enough to win the games, especially if we deserve to win the games.”

Kulusevski could be required to help Spurs get off the mark in the league after a torrid spell on the sidelines with a patella injury, which required a second procedure in March to fix the long-standing problem.

After Kulusevski missed Tottenham’s Europa League triumph in 2025, the whole of last season and this summer’s World Cup, De Zerbi was delighted to tell the 26-year-old on Saturday that he would be in the matchday squad against Coventry.

De Zerbi revealed: “ I said to him, ‘I spoke with the medical staff and they gave me the OK’ and he smiled like this (wide).

“And we are happy. We are very, very happy. It’s not football. I’m not speaking about football. OK, he’s a special player, but we are speaking about different things. He suffered a lot and his reaction was great.”

Richarlison remains unavailable after he was left out of Tottenham’s 25-man Premier League squad following an eventful end to the summer transfer window – but featured and scored for the club’s Under-21s on Tuesday in a Jersey Mike’s Trophy match at Cheltenham.

On Saturday, Richarlison posted on his Instagram story “you are right” alongside a story where ex-Everton forward Duncan Ferguson criticised De Zerbi’s treatment of the Brazil forward.

But De Zerbi insisted: “It’s not my problem any more. You have to ask Vinai (Venkatesham), to Johan (Lange), it’s not my problem.”

#108. Leeds extend Man Utd's winless run to six games
