#109. James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’

The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career

“The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.”

McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.”

But there’s sadness, too, in the way his life and career were scarred by his refusal to wear the poppy when playing games around Remembrance Sunday in England. “It’s completely changed me as a person,” McClean says. “It’s made me a bit of a recluse because I don’t trust a lot of people now. I’ve been stung bad.”

McClean’s autobiography, The Walls, is one of the best sports books of the year. It’s a powerful and sometimes disturbing read elevated by McClean’s willingness to show himself in an unflattering light.

I have written a lot about Derry and boxing, and Bloody Sunday, but it helps to be back here to understand how McClean can respect the millions of soldiers who died in two world wars while refusing to forget how the British army killed so many Irish people in this city.

He comes from Creggan, the estate affected most on Bloody Sunday in 1972 when 14 unarmed civilians were killed by the British army in Derry. Six of the fatalities were from Creggan. In 2010, after the Saville report finally concluded that all the victims posed no threat, the British prime minister David Cameron apologised for the “unjustified and unjustifiable” massacre.

McClean was born in Derry in 1989 and he writes that “learning how to make a petrol bomb was one of my first life lessons. I was 11 before I’d properly mastered it.”

He pauses when asked how he would feel if any of his three daughters or his son, who is 11, ended up making petrol bombs. “I’m very thankful they don’t have to. It’s a different era now. I just want them to be proud to be Irish.”

The 37-year-old spells out the contrast with his youth. “I grew up in a very Republican community still dealing with the effects of the Troubles. You would see gunmen on the street. People got shot, kneecapped. To get access to my street you had to go through a lane where you sometimes saw masked men doing punishment beatings. But you weren’t scared. You knew you’d done nothing wrong. That was the norm … but it’s not normal.”

His biological father, Joe Kelly, was an alcoholic in Creggan and McClean spoke to him only once – when he shouted at him in the street to stay away. But he remembers a happy childhood and, when his professional career began with Derry City, “I was very carefree”.

McClean was 22 when Steve Bruce signed him for Sunderland in August 2011. He made his Premier League debut that December after Bruce was replaced by Martin O’Neill. McClean soon became a regular starter and that first season in English football was full of joy and praise. He was fast, skilful and disciplined. Apart from wasting money his biggest vice was typing his name on Twitter where he would revel in glowing reports of his play.

“It was amazing,” McClean says. “I never thought about the politics when I first got to England so up until November 2012, when the poppy thing started, I never experienced any bother.”

Everything changed when he told Sunderland he wouldn’t wear the poppy because it also represented the British army which had occupied Derry for so long. “There was never a decision for me to make,” he says. “Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen. It was a very difficult year and I felt a lot of that could have been handled better by the club. But Sunderland came out with a statement before the game which drew all eyes on me. It was there to protect the club. They basically said this is James’s personal decision but we, as a club, wholeheartedly support the poppy appeal.

“I wanted to make my own statement but I was constantly told by the club that: ‘No, no, it’ll die over. Just leave it.’ I’d just turned 23 and I thought the club had a duty of care to look after me and that’s what they were doing. I’d won the player of the year the previous season but I felt they hung me out to dry.”

McClean recalls that: “The next game was away to Fulham on a Sunday, on Sky. A threat was made that I would be shot if I came on to the pitch. I remember [his wife] Erin panicking. It sounds extreme and people might say: ‘Oh, wise up, you’re not going to be shot on TV.’ But the night before the game I was assigned two police officers to stand outside my door. So the Met police took it seriously and that made it more real.”

O’Neill brought him on in the second half and his every touch was booed – by the Fulham and Sunderland supporters. The vitriol poisoned his world but McClean kept searching for his name on Twitter. He became furious whenever, after a mutually respectful encounter with a member of the public, the person would go online to abuse him.

Sometimes McClean would track the person down and demand an apology. “Maybe that madness was always there, but it got stronger,” he notes.

McClean moved to Wigan before joining West Brom where, in “the best kind of madness” he earned £42,000 a week while he had his best spell in the Premier League. But as one poppy season blurred into another, the death threats kept coming, as did the warnings that Erin would be raped. McClean says: “My reaction was always to fight fire with fire. I went into some games in the wrong frame of mind. It wasn’t: ‘Can I help the team?’ It was: ‘I hope I score today so I can shush them up.’”

McClean admits: “There were days where I went looking for the conflict.” He posted a photograph of himself listening to his favourite Wolfe Tones song, The Broad Black Brimmer. “I knew exactly what I was doing,” McClean writes. “It was an IRA song – and I was sure it would rile a certain type of person up.”

By the time he reached Stoke, for whom he played 111 games between 2018 and 2021, his problems in English football reached a new low. “Brexit made the idiots louder” and “the poppy season seemed to be getting longer every year”. He had also made a stupid mistake during lockdown when he posted a photograph of himself, wearing a balaclava, with his two eldest children below a caption which read: ‘Today’s school lesson – History.’”

McClean thought he was being funny but his choice not to wear the poppy, in contrast, was heartfelt. “I thought others might have followed suit but it never turned out to be the case.”

Did he feel that a more rounded understating of his stance had emerged by the time he enjoyed his happiest seasons in English football, while playing for a Hollywood-tinged Wrexham from 2023 to earlier this year? “A wee bit, aye. When you explain it to footballers you’ve played with, and to people on a personal level, it opens their eyes and they say: ‘Oh, I understand that.’ But the overall British population? I don’t think so.”

Reflecting on his Premier League years, McClean marvels at the brilliance of Kevin De Bruyne and Eden Hazard. “You had to accept there were lads capable of doing things that were beyond you,” McClean writes. “But there were also games where I thought I was coming up against a physical strength that I found suspicious. Coming back into the Premier League after a break convinced me that some players had to be benefiting from some kind of performance-enhancing support.

“I remember coming up against one player that I’d encountered at Sunderland who I always felt that I’d been able to match in terms of his speed and power. While I’d been away from the Premier League, he’d gone to a bigger club, and now he was a different animal completely.”

These are startling allegations and, while McClean has no concrete evidence to support his doubts, he trusts his gut reaction. “I’ve always been very fanatical about my fitness,” he says. “But when you come against the top Premier League clubs, no matter what height, what size, they’re just faster, they’re stronger, and you’re thinking: ‘How is that possible?’”

After their daughter Willow was diagnosed with global development delay and autism, Erin persuaded him to be tested for autism. He was found to be “at the high-functioning end of the spectrum” but he still struggles with the fact that “I’ve probably got body dysmorphia or some kind of bulimia. Maybe it’s the autism thing, because I’m so strict with my diet 95% of the time. But when I can’t work out I binge. So if I’m travelling and flying, I’ll just eat that much shite to the point where I have to make myself sick. I still feel really guilty, because the next day I’ll punish myself in the gym – which is not healthy.”

Life has become even more complicated since he returned to Derry City in January. “I was meant to be coming home for the fairytale ending. But you quickly realise the promises are just bullshit.”

McClean has not played for the club since July and, asked about the situation, he says: “It’s not good. It’s a player against owner and there’s only one winner. I think that’s it in terms of Derry City. You never think you’ll be betrayed by your own so it’s painful.”

When contacted by the Guardian, a spokesman for Derry City said: “The club cannot speak to, or comment on, how James feels.” He also rejected the suggestion that Derry City had failed to fulfil any promises made to McClean.

Earlier this month, McClean said he couldn’t “understand or accept” the way he was being treated by the club and that he was fit to play despite being left out of the squad by interim manager Mark Connolly. Derry City then released a statement in which they said: “The club has sought to resolve this internal matter privately. Out of respect for confidentiality and the fact that this dispute involves sensitive medical details regarding James’ hip condition, the club have previously refrained from making any public statement on the matter.”

McClean insists he could play football elsewhere but how does he feel if this is the end of his career? “It doesn’t unsettle me because I’ve been boxing off and on for 10 years and in the past 18 months I’ve really thrown myself into it. I’m not going to start a pro boxing career because it’s just not feasible at my age. But I’ve been in contact with Misfits and they want me to fight.”

Misfits Boxing was set up by KSI and the Sauerland brothers, who made their name in the traditional fight game, and it features YouTubers and former athletes who want to become boxers. It is dismissed by boxing purists but McClean sounds enthusiastic about making his debut in the ring once his contract with Derry expires: “Boxing is giving me that purpose to wake up and train hard.”

What kind of boxer would he like to become? “I’m a pressure fighter. I like to be constantly in someone’s face because I’ve got the fitness to maintain that. I’m not saying I’m by any stretch of the imagination a [Gennady] Golovkin or a Canelo [Álvarez], but I love watching them. I’m not looking to have a career in boxing but three or four fights a year is perfect. The dream was always to be a footballer but this is a new excitement, a new challenge.”

As we prepare to step out into a rain-sodden Derry, there seems little chance of any reconciliation for him on the football field. But he looks up and his taut fighter’s face suddenly relaxes into a smile. “It could be a blessing,” McClean says softly. “It could end up a blessing in disguise.”

The Walls by James McClean (Sandycove, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

#114. Zonneveld wins first senior PDC title at Dutch Darts Championship

Niels Zonneveld defeated Danny Noppert 8-5 in the final of the Dutch Darts Championship; Zonneveld and Noppert beat Stephen Bunting and Gian van Veen in their respective semi-finals; watch Grand Slam of Darts live on Sky Sports from November 14-22

Niels Zonneveld won his first senior PDC title with an 8-5 victory over Danny Noppert in the Dutch Darts Championship final on Sunday.

An entertaining all-Dutch final in Maastricht saw a tight contest with the score locked at 2-2 before Zonneveld won three successive legs to pull away.

Noppert responded to close the gap to 5-4 but Zonneveld regained control and won back-to-back legs - including a checkout of 157 - to earn a 7-4 lead.

Despite a tough battle against Noppert, Zonneveld was then able to see the match out with a 81 checkout, hitting double three to seal the title.

The 28-year-old's route to the final saw him beat Stephen Bunting 7-4 in the semi-finals and that match came following a stunning comeback with a final-leg 6-5 victory in the last eight. Up against Wessel Nijman, Zonneveld recovered from trailing 5-3 to level at 5-5 and was able to pounce after his fellow Dutchman missed a match dart.

Noppert also impressed in his run to the final, claiming a 7-5 win over compatriot Gian van Veen in the semi-finals to book his place in the tournament's showpiece.

It followed a comfortable quarter-final showing from Noppert, who recorded another impressive average on his way to reaching the last four, registering 113.42 in his 6-2 win over Luke Woodhouse.

In the quarter-finals, Bunting clinched a 6-3 win over Damon Heta and hit a 148 checkout, while Van Veen beat Ryan Searle 6-3.

Earlier on Sunday, round three provided some upsets as Gerwyn Price was beaten 6-4 by Zonneveld and Nathan Aspinall was thumped 6-1 by Bunting.

#117. Emi Martinez shares injury update from hospital bed after undergoing surgery

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Argentinian goalkeeper collided with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite while challenging for a cross

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Emiliano Martinez has confirmed he expects to be “back in a few weeks” after undergoing successful surgery following a clash of heads during Chelsea’s 2-0 victory at Everton.

The Argentinian goalkeeper collided with Jarrad Branthwaite while challenging for a cross.

After receiving more than eight minutes of on-pitch treatment, he was carried off on a stretcher to a waiting ambulance, with reports suggesting he had suffered a broken jaw.

Sharing an update from his hospital bed on Instagram, Martinez wrote: "Thank you for all the messages, the operation went well." He added: "We’ll be back in a few weeks."

Before the incident, Martinez helped Chelsea claim a 2-0 win, securing their first Premier League clean sheet in nine months.

Speaking to TNT Sports immediately after the match, Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso said: “As far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.

“Right now he’s in the hospital doing precautionary tests. So let’s see, but this is what I know so far.”

Alonso later added: “It was concussion but more than that I saw only one clip. Hopefully it won’t be too bad but we need to wait.”

Martinez was replaced in the 73rd minute by Belgian reserve goalkeeper Mike Penders, who came on to make his Premier League debut with Chelsea leading 1-0.

Branthwaite was cleared to continue for Everton after team physios performed concussion checks on the pitch.

When play resumed, Pedro Neto scored his second goal of the game to double Chelsea’s lead and seal a 2-0 victory on Merseyside for their first away win of the season.

It also meant that Chelsea kept a clean sheet in the Premier League for the first time in nine months, or since a 2-0 win over Brentford on 17 January.

Match-winner Neto dedicated Chelsea’s win and clean sheet to Martinez. The Portuguese forward told TNT Sports: “We are really pleased. It is a shame for Emi but we wish him all the best. This win is for him. We are really happy but of course our thoughts are for him.

“It’s in his honour. We needed a clean sheet. We needed a good game. Emi deserved this. Mike [Penders] who came in deserved this as well. So we are really happy.”

Can you tell us the answer to this quiz question?

Give us a club that could come next in the sequence: Charlton Athletic, Bradford City, Bournemouth, Dagenham & Redbridge, Crystal Palace, Leicester City…

We'll reveal the answer this time next week when we reach the next edition of The Pre-Match Poser – for now, here's the answer to last week's poser…Q. Miroslav Klose is the obvious answer – but Stern John, Angelos Charisteas, Oleksandr Zinchenko and Xherdan Shaqiri are all other examples. What is it?A. They all scored more goals for their country than they did for any club they played for. Klose netted a whopping 71 international goals, including a bunch at the World Cup that you might have heard about.

John, who counts a number of English clubs among his former employers, scored 70 times for Trinidad & Tobago, while Charisteas scored 25 times for Greece and never managed to match that total elsewhere.

Ukraine's Zinchenko isn't a scorer but does have 12 international goals to his name, eight more than the total number of league goals he's scored in his entire club career.

But Shaqiri will drop off this list imminently when he scores a couple more goals for Basel. Indeed, there's an argument his two spells at FCB combined exclude him anyway.

The former Liverpool and England frontman now has a new passion

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Like many retired footballers, the competitive itch remains for Michael Owen.

But rather than drop down the leagues or enter the dugout, the former Ballon d'Or winner has turned away from football to indulge his post-playing competitive instinct.

At Manor House Stables, his training operation in Cheshire, Owen has built a business that combines his love of horse racing with the same drive that saw him become one of English football's most prolific goalscorers.

"I don’t really like just taking part – I want to be at the very top table," Owen tells FourFourTwo when asked about the scale of his ambition for the stables.

"We’re mixing it now but there’s a long way to go to be one of the best. Being the best is possibly an impossible thing when you think of the superpowers, but we’ve definitely got room for improvement.

"What do we need to do? We need more horses, better quality horses. How do you get more horses? You need more owners, wealthier owners I suppose if you want to be brutally honest about it. How do we do that? We need results and a facility to look after people that want to have a good time. And how do we do that? We have to be at the cutting edge of science and get out there when there’s a big event on and there might be potential owners there.

"You’ve got to get your arse off your comfy chair and start pressing flesh. You have to have drive and ambition, you have to be here at the crack of dawn, learning your business, getting the best out of your staff, motivating them. It all starts with a target, which is to be the best in the business.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"If you’d seen us 20 years ago, when I set this place up, and at any stage in between, it’s been constant progress. That can’t stop and won’t stop while I’m here – and I’m going to be here for a very long time hopefully."

Owen's focus at Manor House is on flat racing, which precludes a crack at the Grand National, but does he dream of winning one of the other big races one day?

"The Derby, absolutely, although people ask me what’s the dream, and having this business, employing all these people, in many ways I’m living the dream now," he continues. "And it’s like saying ‘If you win the league or the Ballon d’Or as a footballer, is that the dream, is that it then, you’ve achieved it?’ No it’s bloody not, I want to do it again and again. Who the hell wants to do something that’s so good once and doesn’t want to do it again?

"If I won the Derby, I wouldn’t put ‘For Sale’ signs up. So yes, it is a dream to win it, but this place isn’t stopping regardless of what we achieve. I will die doing this, whereas I had to stop at football at 33. I can continue running this place forever, trying to be successful, and the beauty is you really enjoy it along the way.

"It’s a constant joy – following horses, going to Royal Ascot for a week, Glorious Goodwood, I might go to the Breeders Cup in Kentucky or the Melbourne Cup in Australia, travelling the world seeing your horses running. It’s just the most incredible business.

"I don’t have to run around for 90 minutes any more – blood, sweat and tears. I can just enjoy it."

Liverpool starlet Rio Ngumoha says he has been inspired after watching Bukayo Saka and Anthony Gordon for England – and insists talks over a new Anfield contract are 'going well'.

The 18-year-old played an integral role in the Reds' comeback victory at Brentford on Saturday and is well-trusted by boss Andoni Iraola, also starting in the Champions League midweek game.

Ngumoha has also won three caps for England and said: 'Playing on the right (wing) was good for England but also watching the likes of Anthony Gordon, Bukayo Saka… they are top, top wingers.

'Training with them every day and just seeing what they do, that can really help me and I take some of the stuff they tell me on board and it is really helpful.'

Ngumoha is in talks over a new bumper contract at Liverpool, having signed for the club in 2024 from Chelsea – much to the dismay of the Stamford Bridge club.

He has also been learning a new role at Anfield as Iraola demands all of his wingers can play on either flank.

Rio Ngumoha is in talks to sign a new contract at Liverpool to reward his growing role

Ngumoha added: 'To be fair (the contract) is all with my agent now. I think it is all going well. I am not too sure.

'I just let the football do the talking at the end of the day, so I enjoy playing and all of that stuff is in the back of my mind really. I just play for the club, play for Liverpool and hopefully I can carry on doing well.

'(Playing on both sides) gives me a bit of unpredictability, so if teams see me playing, they might think I am on the left but I can offer something different on the right.

'So it is good, I think at a young age, being able to play off the right or the opposite side and be unpredictable, I think that is something that is really key and I am enjoying it. It is good.

'I can't thank the gaffer much more really for putting me on so early in the game and like I said, whether I start or if I come on, I just have the same mentality.'

Liverpool duo Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong are set for scans, meanwhile, after suffering injuries in the win at Brentford.

#134. 'Four points is nothing' - O'Neill stays cool after statement win

'Elated, delighted, relieved' - O'Neill on Celtic's thrashing of Hearts

With ongoing supporter discontent, a recent tennis ball protest against the major shareholder on a golf course and a veteran manager deciding now is not the time to "wrap things up", as Martin O'Neill put it, you'd be forgiven for scratching your head when examining Celtic's current domestic situation.

They sit four points clear at the top of the Scottish Premiership. Five, really, if you factor in a goal difference at present 12 better than nearest challengers Rangers.

All this off the back of a 7-1 demolition of last season's runners-up, Hearts, who - at least until they turned up at Celtic Park - were widely viewed as viable title contenders if there's to be another three-way fight for Scottish football's main prize.

Has normal service been restored in the east end of Glasgow after the wobbles of four significant defeats in their past half-dozen? Not as far as their wily old manager is concerned.

Keen to stress that the road is yet long to the division's ultimate destination, O'Neill was full of smiles after his side's biggest win since he returned last year, but he didn't even accept that such a thrashing of the third-placed side in the division was even a 'statement' victory.

"I'm not really sure about that," O'Neill told BBC Scotland.

"We're eight or nine games into the season or whatever it is.

"It was nice to win and win in the manner we did as well. We scored some really great goals. We looked really good going forward and I thought, defensively, the back four did really well for us when we were under pressure.

"But I think they were helped by the players in front of them as well too, so overall it was very, very pleasing."

So, just how good a Celtic performance was this?

As far as former Rangers striker Kris Boyd is concerned, it was a throwback to Parkhead's favourite Australian, whose fast-flowing, attacking football delivered a domestic double followed by a treble in his two seasons in charge, prior to Brendan Rodgers' return.

"That is the closest I've seen to Ange Postecoglou's Celtic," Boyd told Sky Sports.

Former Hearts defender Ryan McGowan felt his old side simply ran into Celtic at the wrong time.

"It's a really poor performance from Hearts," McGowan said on Sky Sports.

"At the same time, you've got to give Celtic credit. It was probably their best performance of the season."

Celtic showed more cohesion and spirit than in recent performances, according to former goalkeeper Pat Bonner, who feels two youngsters shone particularly brightly in the October sunshine.

"Celtic's organisation was better," Bonner told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound.

"They worked harder as a unit. Their attitude was better, everybody doing that little bit of hard graft that you have to do and then ability takes over.

"Young Callum Osmand and Colby Donovan, they're the ones that set the tone."

Former Celtic captain Scott Brown summed up his old side's performance in one word: "Fantastic."

And he added: "The best thing about Celtic today was the pace in the forward line and how they got after Hearts. Camilo Duran through the middle is exciting me.

"Callum Osmand did more in 45 minutes out wide than Sebastian Tounekti has done probably since he signed for the club. Haissem Hassan has got a few issues defensively but going forward he's a delight to watch."

The front four of Osmand, Benjamin Nygren, Hassan and Duran caused Hearts no end of problems.

A double for the young striker, a double for the Sweden international who's now on eight for the season from midfield well before Halloween, a goal and two assists from the consistently impressive Colombian, and one of the Egypt winger's best displays since signing after the World Cup. Is this then the template going forward? Not necessarily, according to their manager.

"No, because we've got so many matches coming up in Europe and in the league," O'Neill explained.

"We're going Sunday, Thursday, Sunday, Thursday, Sunday, Thursday. So, we will have to mix it up a little bit. It's also a squad game for us at this stage. Between now and the beginning of January we are at it constantly."

As if to illustrate his point, Celtic's next fixture comes under the 'must-win' category as Celta Vigo come calling in Thursday's Europa League fixture, with both sides yet to register a point in the league phase after two defeats each.

"We'll make a couple of adjustments on Thursday evening," O'Neill said.

"We still want to try and win and I think other players coming on and getting little bits of games here and there helps immensely. It helps the whole squad and I think it helps the confidence of the team.

"It will be a tough game for us. Celta Vigo are a team in a big league in Spain, they're very, very decent, but it's a game we probably have to win.

"We have to win to give ourselves some momentum and do some catching up because we've lost two games, so we really need to win this game. We'll go all out to try and do it."

Celtic score seven in humiliation of title rivals Hearts

Hearts roll out red carpet... and Celtic walk all over it

All the latest Celtic news, views and analysis

O'Neill, fresh from the memory of two recent defeats by arch rivals Rangers, knows there is many a slip between cup and lip when it comes to the Premiership rollercoaster.

"Four points at this stage of the season is absolutely nothing," he stressed.

"I thought the team did really well. We got the goals, which seemed to match the performance, which was really nice. It's not too often you get a scoreline like that. So, we'll enjoy it this evening."

It was all summed up rather nicely by one of O'Neill's favoured sons when he was manager first time around between 2000 and 2005 - Henrik Larsson's strike partner, Chris Sutton.

"It's a strange old season for Celtic," Sutton told Sky Sports.

"Domestically, they've been flying, but in Europe it just hasn't been there. Good to see Jota back. What a contribution Callum Osmand made. Will this result lead on to more confidence in Europe?"

With Celta Vigo turning up in midweek, everyone associated with Celtic will certainly hope so.

#143. The Brighton Beckham! Premier League star scores INCREDIBLE goal from the halfway line, 30 years on from when David did the same

By OLIVER TODD, DIGITAL HEAD OF SPORT and LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER

Published: 14:33 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 15:50 BST, 18 October 2026

Brighton star Diego Gomez channelled his inner David Beckham with a remarkable goal from the halfway line against Crystal Palace.

His strike, a goal of the season contender from 51 yards, helped move Brighton up to second in the Premier League in a thumping first-half performance which saw them go 3-0 up.

Paraguay international Gomez, 23, took control of the ball inside his own half and turned, taking aim from the halfway line to beat Palace goalkeeper Walter Benitez with a right-footed shot.

Brighton had already taken the lead in the fourth minute thanks to an own goal by Jaydee Canvot, and by the 10th they were 3-0 up after Yasin Ayari got on the scoresheet.

Holding on to victory would see Brighton go second behind Manchester City, who have a flawless record but are in limbo after being found guilty of financial rule breaks.

Ironically, Gomez used to play for the Beckham-owned Inter Miami - and his effort was reminiscent of the long-range scorcher scored by the former Manchester United man against Wimbledon in 1996.

Diego Gomez channelled his inner David Beckham as his shot from the halfway line beat Walter Benitez

The Brighton star could barely believe what was happening as he ran away in celebration

"Would you look at that!"DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/qmagVbGEb4

His goal has already been making headlines in the United States, where David and his wife Victoria share a waterfront Miami property.

'Would you look at that! Diego Gomez with a goal that the Brighton fans will never forget,' purred Sky Sports commentator Bill Leslie.

'It didn't seem possible, it shouldn't have been possible. It's just become a glorious Brighton reality.

Palace custodian Benitez went pale as Brighton's team wheeled away in celebration with Gomez, who geed up the crowd and kissed the badge on his shirt.

It is the longest-range goal in the Premier League since Wayne Rooney stunned the crowd from 58 yards as Everton thrashed West Ham 4-0 in November 2017. That day, Rooney bagged a hat-trick.

Gomez has become an important player for Brighton, who he debuted for in January last year, and scored 10 goals in all competitions last season.

This is not the first time he has scored a 'worldie'. Against Barnsley in the Carabao Cup last season, he netted four times, including a half-volley from around 35 yards out.

The goal reminded fans of David Beckham's strike against Wimbledon back in August 1996

He is also a significant star for Paraguay, who he helped to the last 16 of the World Cup over the summer.

While more of a box-to-box midfielder than a flair player, perhaps it is no surprise he has a dash of magic in his locker after previously being team-mates with Lionel Messi and Luis Suarez.

Brighton are making a habit of blockbuster strikes, with Lewis Dunk having won goal of the month against for his spectacular effort against Coventry in September.

#149. Man Utd held by Leeds as winless run continues

Leeds United vs Manchester United. Premier League.

Report and free match highlights as Bryan Mbeumo's opener was cancelled out by Dominic Calvert-Lewin in a feisty draw at Elland Road; Man Utd are winless in the Premier League since August

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Manchester United delivered a more committed performance in a changed formation but were held to a 1-1 draw by Leeds as pressure on Michael Carrick continues to grow.

In a week that included defeat to Atletico Madrid and an explosive interview from Lisandro Martinez - who started at Elland Road - the noise was calmed somewhat by a display that showed character, if not enough quality to claim a second league win of the season.

United played without a recognised striker for the majority, allowing Youri Tielemans a more offensive role and he combined with Bryan Mbeumo to open the scoring in the first half.

But Carrick's side faded badly as the game went on, another fixture in which they were outrun, eventually pegged back by an instinctive Dominic Calvert-Lewin strike from a poorly defended corner.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leeds away was pitched as the worst game to end a fractious week. In reality, it forced United to scrap and that at least appeared to show appetite for the fight. "In isolation, going to Leeds and performing how they did was a decent result," reflected Jamie Carragher. They were helped by the fact that Daniel Farke's side were not at their battling best either.

Man Utd have won just one of their seven Premier League matches this season (D4 L2), their fewest number of victories at this stage of a top-flight campaign since 1986-87.

There was, however, far more intent shown than in last week's drab draw with Spurs at Old Trafford, where disgruntled fans booed the team off, albeit results will read one Premier League win from seven - and none since August.

Carrick will know that return is not good enough to dispel unwanted talk of pressure on his position.

27: CHANCE! Mbeumo connects with Tielemans' cross but heads off target unmarked.

35: GOAL! Mbeumo makes no mistake with his second chance from the boot of Tielemans, guiding a low finish past James Trafford.

45: SUB! Martinez is replaced at half-time by Noussair Mazraoui but Carrick sticks with back-three formation.

51: GOAL! Calvert-Lewin latches onto Tarik Muharemovic's knockdown from a corner and beats Senne Lammens from close range.

"We worked on it [the change of shape] this week. We wanted to match them up without the ball and go quite aggressive.

"We knew we could get a lot of joy in the middle of the pitch with them only playing two in there.

"That's probably the area of the game where we could have done more. We could have been a bit braver with the ball and taken the ball under pressure.

"But we're in a circumstance where we are not as brave as we should be, and we have to get that back because to win games for Manchester United we have to have that bravery and composure."

"There was definitely commitment. It had to be there today. I didn't doubt that. I was looking forward to the game to see that, there was definitely an edge and intensity to it.

"I spoke to the boys this morning about the history of this game, what it means to the supporters, to the football club. It definitely tests you. It wasn't a perfect performance but there was a lot in there to show determination to get a result.

"We're not getting too carried away because we didn't win the game. It felt like a bit of a fresh start today, in terms of where we're at. The boys are desperate to do well for each other and the club."

On the formation change: "There was a freshness. We had a different spine, that's a massive positive for us. A little tweak tactically, not a huge change. We had to adapt to what their strengths are."

"It says a lot about how far we've come in the last three years that we are slightly disappointed it was just a point against Manchester United. Overall, it was not necessary to be in a losing position at half-time, I thought we were the dominant side.

"We lacked a bit in our decision-making in the first half, we added clarity in the second half. We had momentum completely on our side. We threatened them with physicality, maybe it wasn't the time for our more technical players.

"We are definitely on the right path. This is a special game. I wanted to go for it, it's a sign that we're doing many things in the right way."

"We could've played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box, but just not enough numbers.

"We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game."

#152. Thomas Hitzlsperger describes his experience of coming out as gay in 2014

The former Aston Villa and Germany international came out as gay shortly after retiring in 2014

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Thomas Hitzlsperger enjoyed a distinguished career, turning out for Germany at the highest level and playing for the likes of Aston Villa, Stuttgart and West Ham.

But in January 2014, several months after hanging up his boots, his decision to publicly come out as gay had a profound impact far beyond the football pitch.

The former midfielder became one of the most high-profile former footballers to come out, speaking candidly about his sexuality in an interview with German newspaper Die Zeit, at a time when male homosexuality remained a largely taboo subject in professional football.

More than a decade has passed since then, with Hitzlsperger reflecting on the response he received and his message, and his advice for those still struggling with their identity.

"My estimation is that 95 per cent of the reactions were positive," he tells FourFourTwo. "The overall sentiment from people was that it was great that someone had spoken up. They said to me it was powerful that someone who’d played at the highest level could share his experiences.

"When I was contemplating the idea of going public, there was fear involved," he admits. "You’re thinking ‘What are people going to say? They may not like it and will criticise me’. I was dealing with my perception of what the world was like at the time, and my own fear of rejection.

"But having gone public, I realised that all my worries were unjustified and it felt like the world wasn’t such a bad place. At times, the media painted the picture of a hostile world, but then you speak up and think to yourself ‘Why is this not happening, why is the world so much better and why are there so many lovely people?’

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"That’s why I say we have to tell more positive stories and not focus on a narrative that’s so sad and tragic. We have to talk about everything, but in general my ambition is to be positive and say “Life can be pretty amazing – if you don’t think you fit in, wait until you tell people and you’ll find many who will support you.” You can’t see what’s in front of you until you tell your story and live your truth.

"I spoke about a real sense of community during my childhood from a familial sense, and now I’m part of another community – the gay one. Meeting new people has expanded my horizons. Instead of focusing on people you might lose because of rejection, rather look at all the new and wonderful people who you wouldn’t have met before, if you’d kept quiet. The best part of coming out is not having to worry any more. I now focus on my job – as a shareholder, a CEO and a TV pundit – and my personal life, and nothing else.

"Whatever I do in life I want to be successful, but if you constantly live with fear, then you can’t be your best self. I knew that not living my truth couldn’t go on and I had to make a statement for my own benefit. If it helped others, even better."

Hitzlsperger adds that his experience can help others who are struggling with their identity.

"What would I say now to those who may be struggling with their sexuality and think the world is a bad place?" he asks. "I’ve been supported by so many people and live my life now without any fears, when it comes to my personality. I was delighted to get that affirmation as well from people I worked with in the game and those that just followed my footballing journey. I was very grateful and appreciative to everyone who said something positive publicly.

"After the newspaper interview I did with Die Zeit was published in 2014, my former team-mate Lukas Podolski described my coming out as “brave” and “an important sign of our time”. My former national team boss Joachim Low said I “deserved respect from every side.”"

Football v Homophobia is a year-round initiative tackling anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination, building inclusive communities at all levels of the game around the world. For more info and support, visit footballvhomophobia.com

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#154. What awaits Everton hero Ferguson in shock Glens role?

Duncan Ferguson played 273 times for Everton and scored 72 goals

With the appointment of Duncan Ferguson at the Oval expected to be confirmed on Monday, the club's five-week search for a new manager illustrates again that there is the easy way, the hard way, and the Glentoran way.

When the east Belfast outfit parted company with Declan Devine on 14 September, the simple solution to the early-season vacancy appeared to be a reunion with former assistant Tiernan Lynch.

A two-time winner of the Irish Premiership with Larne, Lynch was freshly back on the market after leaving Derry City in August and immediately installed as favourite for the post.

Instead, the Glens made the trickier prospect of prying Jim Magilton out of his contract at Cliftonville their priority.

When the former Northern Ireland and Ipswich Town midfielder made it clear he intended to stay at Solitude, nobody would have predicted what came next.

A pivot towards Everton legend Ferguson, who also had spells with Rangers and Newcastle United, was not, as they say, on anyone's bingo card.

A to Z: Duncan Ferguson - 'The original Everton hero'

Ferguson link has caused a 'real buzz' - McCann

The appeal of bringing Ferguson's star power to the Irish Premiership is obvious, akin to the boost provided to the League of Ireland by former Chelsea winger Damian Duff's successful, if short, stint with Shelbourne in recent years.

A cult figure across two playing spells at Goodison Park thanks to both his goalscoring exploits and aggressive style - no player has ever received more than his eight Premier League red cards - the 54-year-old Scot instantly becomes the most recognisable face in the league.

Fans quickly had their own fun with the imminent appointment on Saturday, with erroneous reports of the seven-times capped Scottish striker being spotted everywhere from his prospective new side's 1-0 win over Limavady to a local chip shop on the Newtownards Road.

Glentoran are no strangers to big names in the playing ranks having had the likes of Keith Gillespie, Nacho Novo and Niall McGinn plying their trade at the Oval in recent times, but it is different when such a presence is in the dugout.

Ferguson, after all, will have been the only applicant with spells as an assistant to the likes of Carlo Ancelotti, Rafa Benitez and Ronald Koeman on his CV.

In all, the Scot worked under seven different permanent bosses at Everton, as well as two separate stints in interim charge.

After leaving Merseyside following the departure of Frank Lampard in 2022, managerial roles at Forest Green Rovers and Inverness Caledonian Thistle were hardly considered a success, admittedly both in testing circumstances.

Coupled with his unfamiliarity with the Irish League and, for all the headlines already generated, there is no doubt that the left-field appointment is a gamble.

Ferguson won the FA Cup with Everton in 1995

The Glentoran hierarchy clearly believe it is a risk worth taking. Some Oval regulars may well suggest that the club have tried just about everything else in their quest for a first league title since 2009.

Owner Ali Shams Pour arrived a decade after the late Alan McDonald delivered the most recent of the side's 23 Gibson Cups. Since then, the turbulent reign of Mick McDermott brought Irish Cup success in 2020 yet he still was the victim of supporter protests.

The calming presence of Rodney McAree delivered immediate results, but the now Dungannon boss lasted just under five months before departing for personal reasons to be replaced by Warren Feeney.

Unpopular from the off owing to his previous association with bitter rivals Linfield, the 46-times capped Northern Ireland international was unable to win over the fanbase during another short reign.

That brought about Devine's appointment with the County Antrim Shield triumph of January 2025 a high the club could not build upon. Consecutive losses in BetMcLean Cup finals created a sense of stalled momentum.

It already feels likely to be forgotten just how close Devine came to delivering that long-sought title. A win in the penultimate league game of last season against Larne and the Glens would have gone into the final day top of the table.

Instead, the disappointment of a 0-0 draw from a game in which they were the better side lingered into the subsequent performance against Coleraine and they were beaten 6-2 at the Showgrounds to ultimately finish third.

It will not have escaped Ferguson's attention that one half of the league's so-called 'Big Two' have still not finished in the league's top two for 17 years.

Alan McDonald was the last manager to guide Glentoran to an Irish Premiership title

In replacing Devine, Ferguson will inherit a squad built by and for the former Derry City and Bohemians boss.

And just as Devine's appointment brought about a sweeping clear-out in the summer of 2024, it is again a playing group that for all the expenditure over the past five transfer windows again feels imbalanced.

An over-reliance on Jordan Stewart for a creative spark led to the September return of Conor McMenamin just two months after he had signed for Coleraine - that transfer now somehow the second most surprising story of Glentoran's season.

That in turn, however, saw Joe Thomson move the other way, robbing the side of midfield drive only months after one of last season's star performers, Cammy Palmer, returned home to Scotland.

Similarly, the absence of 2025-26 top scorer Pat Hoban during the early months of this season highlighted the lack of like-for-like cover given the talented Jordan Jenkins plays in an entirely different way.

Four wins and a draw from their past five league games under interim boss Paddy McCourt, however, offers the reminder that most in the Irish Premiership would still happily swap their squads for the one Ferguson will now hope to rebuild into title challengers once again.

Those managers will not, however, be dealing with the same expectations. Nor the same attention.

#155. The untold story of Jason Wilcox at Man United: A 'no bulls*** approach, what agents and executives REALLY think about 'interfering' director - and how he is hamstrung by Sir Jim Ratcliffe at Old Trafford

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 02:00 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 18 October 2026

There is a picture of Sir Jim Ratcliffe with his Manchester United executives that offers a fascinating glimpse into the dynamic of the Old Trafford boardroom.

A furious-looking Ratcliffe is pointing his forefinger at director of football Jason Wilcox, who raises a bent finger of his own in cautious defence, while chief executive Omar Berrada shields between the two men.

It was taken during the half-time interval at Molineux last December after United conceded an equaliser against Wolves before going on to secure their last away win under Ruben Amorim.

A month later, Amorim self-destructed at Leeds in a post-match rant aimed at Wilcox and club bosses, two days after an angry bust-up between the two men at Carrington, and was sacked.

United return to Elland Road on Sunday with former Leeds winger Wilcox once again in the crosshairs following Lisandro Martinez’s criticism of him in a television interview after Tuesday’s defeat by Atletico Madrid, in which the Argentine said he ‘expected more from our technical director’ in the summer transfer market.

Martinez accepted a fine and apologised for the timing of his comments in a statement referencing Wilcox when he said ‘everyone at the club is doing everything they can to make the team successful’, but has not said sorry to Wilcox himself.

Jason Wilcox (right) has felt the wrath of a number of those associated with Manchester United - including Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left)

Wilcox still has Ratcliffe's backing but has come under criticism again this week - this time from Lisandro Martinez

Ratcliffe has quoted Manchester City’s former director of football Txiki Begiristain as saying Wilcox has the ‘best set of eyes’ in the game, but the 55-year-old knows that counts for little.

The photo at Molineux was taken almost a year to the day after Ratcliffe sacked his predecessor Dan Ashworth on the spot after a game at Old Trafford and then promoted Wilcox from technical director.

It’s understood that he still has the backing of the Ineos billionaire but there has to be a degree of sympathy for any executive working on a limited budget, which made signing top targets like Elliot Anderson in the summer impossible, with Ratcliffe looking over their shoulder.

As one agent explained to Daily Mail Sport: ‘Jason is in an incredibly difficult position. Everybody would think he’s the decision-maker at the club, but he absolutely isn’t. Manchester United is run by the owners, Sir Jim and the Glazers. If you sack Wilcox, nothing will change. It’s a mess.’

Another adds: ‘We had a deal agreed with Jason and then Jim got involved and tried to change it. He ended up killing it.’

A year after United were praised for signing Senne Lammens, Benjamin Sesko, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha, Wilcox has been criticised for focusing on a midfield recruitment drive that brought in Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans.

United faced Atletico in the Metropolitano in midweek without a recognised striker or left-back due to wholly foreseeable injuries to Sesko and Luke Shaw.

It’s understandable that Wilcox is facing questions about his suitability for such a big job after six years as City’s academy head and nine months as Southampton’s director of football. If United cannot turn their season around, should he be held just as accountable as head coach Michael Carrick?

One agent said the situation at United is 'a mess' - with Ratcliffe making a lot of decisions

Erik ten Hag was never a fan and Wilcox’s relationship soured with Amorim who hinted that he was too sensitive to criticism from TV pundits like Gary Neville.

Others have a different view. ‘Straight to the point, no bulls***,’ said a source. ‘An absolute gentleman and man of his word,’ added another.

One Premier League executive who didn’t wish to be named said: ‘Wilcox is ultra-professional, or at least he has been in my experience. Is he as hard-faced as some of them out there? Maybe not and maybe that may put him on the back foot on occasion.

‘He works for Man United, though, and I think there needs to be a certain standard of behaviour that comes with that. I feel Wilcox understands it. He has a pretty good reputation in the league.’

Wilcox chatted briefly with reporters before United played Paris-Saint Germain in Gothenburg in the summer, but has maintained a relatively low profile since succeeding Ashworth who – like John Murtough before him – was more open with the media.

Wilcox spoke with United’s in-house station MUTV in October last year, coincidentally after a run of three straight wins, a month after he appeared on stage at a gala dinner for the Association of Manchester United Players when he admitted that his coaching background means ‘I always want to interfere with what the managers are doing’.

That might not be what Carrick wants to hear but the two men are said to have a good working relationship, and the United boss said he has no problem with Wilcox keeping his head below the parapet when he spoke before the Leeds game on Friday.

‘I don't think that's for me to say whether he should or not,’ said Carrick. ‘I've got absolutely no problem sitting here and talking to you guys and leading the football club from this position.’

Michael Carrick (left) is under pressure - and Wilcox is keen to involve himself in his area

When Blackburn Rovers’ squad of 1995 gathered together last year to celebrate the 30th anniversary of beating United to the Premier League title, Wilcox took some stick from his old teammates.

‘He took it really well,’ said one. ‘He’s very self-effacing. There’s no airs and graces. He was always a conscientious lad with a great sense of humour who worked really hard – although you wouldn’t necessarily have had him down as the future director of football at Manchester United.’

Raised in Bolton, the boyhood Liverpool fan represented England at judo after achieving his black belt at the age of 14.

Wilcox joined Blackburn two years later after he was rejected by City and his father sent off 30 letters to clubs in the north-west asking them to give him a chance.

He built a reputation as a dressing-room joker as Kenny Dalglish forged a title-winning team under millionaire owner Jack Walker, and his better impersonations were said to include Bruce Forsyth and Norman Wisdom.

When Rovers edged out United by one point on the final day of the season, Wilcox was on crutches at Anfield following knee surgery – just as he had missed out on the club’s promotion to the Premier League via the Play-off Final at Wembley in 1992 because of injury, his misery complete when a bird defecated on his club suit before the game.

Wilcox did make three appearances at Wembley for England – against Hungary, France and Argentina – in a career that included spells at Leeds, Leicester and Blackpool.

In retirement, he continued to follow Blackburn as part of the commentary team on BBC Radio Lancashire, and he also wrote a regular column for the Lancashire Telegraph.

A former Blackburn title winner, it's now Wilcox's turn to feel the pressure with Ratcliffe breathing down his neck

He always felt destined to go down the coaching path, though, and joined City where he led the Under-18s to two FA Youth Cup finals before making his name as the club’s academy head.

Wilcox oversaw the progression of a number of young stars to the first-team including Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, Rico Lewis and Liam Delap – notably sticking by Palmer when others considered letting him go at 16.

He also helped City make a big profit from selling their surplus academy talent, something United are now trying to emulate.

‘Jason was always very fair at City,’ says one agent. ‘If he said your player would get a new contract if he played well, he was usually true to his word. He is very black and white. He doesn’t pussyfoot around on decisions like some.’

It was no surprise that Berrada took Wilcox from Southampton as part of the influx of ex-City staff into Old Trafford, even if the overlap with Ashworth never looked like working out for long.

Now it’s his turn to feel the heat with Ratcliffe breathing down his neck.

#156. ‘Like a fresh start’: Michael Carrick relieved by Manchester United’s draw at Leeds

Head coach insists ‘we can still have a really good season’

‘We were the dominant side,’ says Leeds manager Farke

After a week in which Michael Carrick had “the headphones on” to quieten the noise, the Manchester United head coach claimed his side’s 1-1 draw at Leeds on Sunday “felt like a fresh start” and insisted that the season can still be a good one.

Carrick’s team have seven points from seven Premier League games and have won only once in the competition, against Ipswich in August. Sunday’s draw followed the previous weekend’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham.

Yet after a week in which United lost 2-0 at Atlético Madrid, after which Lisandro Martínez criticised the recruitment of the director of football, Jason Wilcox, Carrick was relieved at the point secured against Daniel Farke’s team.

“[It’s been] quite quiet inside [the club] – the headphones have been on this week,” Carrick said. “It felt like a bit of a fresh start today – where we’re at and accepting it and doing something about it. That didn’t surprise me today. We’re not getting too carried away because we haven’t won the game, but if you keep doing the right things for the right reasons then you get what you deserve in the end.

“It definitely shows that the boys are desperate to do well for each other as much as anything else and how much they appreciate playing for this club, because there was a real purpose to the group over the last couple of days and they took it on the pitch. There was an edge to the game, an intensity. I spoke to the boys this morning about the history and what it means to the supporters, the club, to us coming over here into the territory.”

Carrick admitted United’s league position is disappointing but he believes the club’s campaign can still be rescued. “If we keep doing the right things, we can still have a really good season. We’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that. But sometimes you do struggle.

“We’ve got to find a way through it. We have to be stable enough to keep doing the right things and we’re more than capable of winning matches. I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I have no doubts that we can go on a good run. I’m encouraged by a lot of things.”

#160. Northampton become first Prem side to win in this season’s Champions Cup

Northampton secured a 28-12 win over Cardiff after seven failed attempts from other English sides to win in the Champions Cup this season; Leicester were also well beaten by Pau as they were defeated 41-17; Harlequins won in the Challenge Cup handing Vannes a 57-19 loss

Northampton became the first Gallagher Prem team to win in the Investec Champions Cup this season as they earned a hard-fought 28-12 victory over Cardiff.

After seven failed attempts from their fellow English sides, the Prem champions were pushed hard by their Welsh visitors, who at one time threatened a comeback at DPD Stadium at Franklin's Gardens.

It took a vital try from man of the match George Hendy to regain control for Saints as they restored some pride on what has been a bruising weekend for teams from their league.

Cardiff made a late change at scrum-half, with South African Johan Mulder coming in for the experienced Aled Davies.

Saints opened the scoring with a superb breakaway try after 12 minutes, with Hendy making the initial charge before passing to Alex Mitchell on the outside.

The England scrum-half's pass back infield reached James Pater and the 19-year-old full-back did well to finish, with Anthony Belleau adding the conversion.

The hosts had some daylight after having a free-kick awarded at a five-metre scrum, with Mitchell quickly finding Rory Hutchinson, whose pass inside sent Toby Thame through.

Saints led 14-0 at half-time, but Cardiff scored a try seven minutes after the restart when Harri Millard crashed in from Mulder's pass, following a tapped penalty, with Jarrod Evans adding the extras.

After Belleau was sin-binned for hands in the ruck near his own line, the visitors moved to within two points when Evans' long pass gave Grady a walk-in for an unconverted try.

Despite being down to 14 men, Northampton extended their lead when Hendy juggled Fraser Dingwall's off-load and just about held on in diving over for a crucial score.

Cardiff were not going quietly and looked certain to haul themselves within reach again when Josh Adams tore away down the left, but Hendy turned from try-scorer to try-saver with a brilliant last-ditch tackle.

Saints finally made sure of victory with a minute to go when the ball was recycled for Dingwall, who glided his way through to cap his fine showing off the bench.

Ollie Chessum made a try-scoring return from injury but Leicester fell short in their opening Champions Cup clash with Pau in the south of France.

Archie van der Flier gave the Tigers a flicker of hope when his 54th-minute try put his side within touching distance but the hosts ultimately pulled away for a 41-17 bonus-point win.

The returning Chessum powered over in his first appearance of the season. But tries from Rodrigo Marta and Jon Zabala gave Pau a half-time lead and when they stretched their advantage through Marta's second early in the second half, it looked all over for the visitors.

Van der Flier had other ideas when he went over, Billy Searle's kick taking them back within seven points, but a careless penalty and subsequent try from Aaron Grandidier Nkanang all but sealed it for the French side.

Pau sealed their bonus point in the dying stages when Searle's attempted pass was intercepted and Fabien Brau-Boirie blazed home to secure an emphatic win.

Marcus Smith shrugged off a first half sin bin to help Harlequins to a 57-19 bonus point win over Vannes in Pool Three of the European Challenge Cup.

England back Smith totalled 22 points from two tries and six conversions, despite enduring a spell on the sidelines for a deliberate knock-on.

It was a much-needed, dominant display from the home side, who managed to shrug off their winless start to the new Gallagher Prem campaign.

Quins were 26-14 up at the interval with Cadan Murley scoring twice and Smith and Will Hobson also crossing the line while the visitors responded through Wayan De Benedittis and winger Enzo Benmegal.

Further tries from Sam Riley and Smith again had Harlequins home and dry by the hour mark.

With the pressure off, Quins stepped up their pursuit of a bonus point, scoring three more tries in the final 15 minutes. Will Evans grabbed his second and third tries of the match, either side of a score from Jimmy Staples.

#165. Haaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat Ipswich

There have been few winners in Manchester City’s guilty verdict, except highly paid lawyers and the inflatable fruit industry. The fans have suffered, being forced to question everything they have been told, while being labelled “cheats”, but they were able to forget the cacophony of noise around the club as Enzo Maresca became the first Premier League manager to win his first seven games.

Ipswich were the latest victims, but they put up a fight in City’s first home Premier League game since being found to have breached financial rules. Defiance has fortified most of the City fanbase, who were able to see local boy Phil Foden instigate the triumph with a kiss of the badge, before an emblem of their wealth, Erling Haaland, secured the points to move six clear, albeit with a few scares between, courtesy of Daizen Maeda and Zian Flemming.

“I didn’t expect to win seven out of seven, but we are working well,” Maresca said. “This is the most important thing.”

Victory came at a cost as Haaland and Antoine Semenyo limped off at full-time, in addition to Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O’Reilly suffering injuries, although Maresca was left unsure of the severity as City prepare to host AEK Athens on Tuesday.

If City have felt like it has been their backs against the wall for the past few weeks, it was Ipswich’s turn. Gary O’Neil put 11 men behind the ball whenever the hosts ventured over the halfway line as City enjoyed 90% possession in the opening quarter-hour, but without truly threatening as they struggled to find space in the lowest of blocks, expertly organised and fully disciplined.

Maresca had made six changes to refresh the side and it took time to understand one another’s rhythm, with Ayyoub Bouaddi creating it from defensive midfield in another mature performance from the teenager making his first Premier League start.

It was inevitable what was coming as there was irrefutable evidence that City were dominant. As at Anfield, Jérémy Doku was a key instigator, showing mesmeric skill on the left of the area before finding Foden to sweep home for his first goal since mid-December.

“I know him from years ago, for me he’s one of the best Premier League players,” Maresca said. “Since day one, it’s my duty to help him to be again one of the best players. I’m very happy for his goal and hopefully it can be just the beginning of many goals and many good performances.”

There was an element of pantomime around the ground from the booing of the Premier League anthem, the singalongs and inflatables. It was fitting Marc Guéhi did not know Maeda was behind him, allowing the Ipswich man to latch on to a sublime curved through ball from Abdoul Ouattara and equalise two minutes after the opener.

• With Manchester City maintaining their 100% record, Enzo Maresca is the first manager to win his first seven Premier League games in charge of a team.

• Manchester City are the third team to win their opening seven games of a Premier League season, after Liverpool in 2019-20 (first 8) and Chelsea in 2005-06 (first 9).

• Erling Haaland (pictured) has now scored 100 non-penalty goals in the Premier League, reaching this milestone in fewer appearances than any other player (139). The previous fewest was 150 appearances, by Alan Shearer in 1996. Opta

After a missed chance, Haaland showed it is possible to get a better result second time around, making the most of Kovacic becoming an auxiliary winger. The header lacked power, but Christian Walton could not keep it out, palming the ball from one hand to the other and into the net before Haaland was serenaded with the clap of bananas.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

City found themselves stuck in a lull, unable to prise open Ipswich, instead having to bide their time. It was a test of patience and a sweeping move upfield concluded with a precision pass from Iliman Ndiaye and an aggressive finish from Haaland, who was later denied a hat-trick by the video assistant referee.

Farai Hallam reviewed footage of Guéhi taking out Abdul Fatawu in the area and Flemming did the rest in the 90th minute, as reward for an impressive team performance, leaving O’Neil upset Ipswich departed with nothing.

“They’re an incredible group,” he said. “Players giving everything. It’s a privilege to stand there and represent them because they’re an incredible group.”

City were left to complain about a Premier League official’s decision when 12 minutes was added on, with few knowing why, but this result will not be questioned.

Maresca called on his team to make their own noise while a cacophony swirls around them, but on-pitch success will not speak louder while what is happening off it is unresolved. The fans sang about relegation and trips to Stockport, embracing a dark situation with humour to match.

#167. How Chelsea turned nasty and ditched 'soft' mentality in Everton victory: The nuisance who led the charge and Xabi Alonso's key role as Blues finally show mean streak, writes KIERAN GILL

Published: 02:00 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 18 October 2026

The game was goalless when Thierno Barry was on the ground injured and Levi Colwill had the ball by the halfway line. Chelsea’s defender kicked it out of play so Everton’s striker could pick himself up.

Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro did not like that one bit. They both yelled at Colwill for his generosity, taking turns telling their team-mate it would have been better to try to take advantage.

Colwill was too nice in that moment. But this was a game won in the second half by Chelsea by dominating in duels, by battling for balls, and by being a little nasty.

Xabi Alonso made a point of praising his players for that edge they carried afterwards, saying: ‘Sometimes it is not about playing nice. It is about playing well. We needed a result like this. We needed to show that we can win in this way.’

Chelsea have been accused of being soft before. That has contributed to their poor record when playing up north, usually allowing themselves to be bullied at places like the Hill Dickinson Stadium. They had lost 19 of their last 41 matches north of Luton. That included being beaten 3-0 here during Liam Rosenior's five-match winless and goalless run which got him sacked.

This was Chelsea’s first game outside of London this season, and Palmer led that nastiness which so pleased Alonso. The playmaker talked himself into a caution from Paul Tierney and yet continued to be a nuisance.

Cole Palmer was a nuisance throughout as he demonstrated Chelsea's new nasty approach

Xabi Alonso praised his side's edge as his Chelsea team won 2-0 at Everton on Saturday

Even as the clock ticked over into 100 minutes after Emiliano Martinez’s injury, he pulled back Tyrique George and slid in on Jarrad Branthwaite. Palmer escaped the second yellow which would have seen him suspended for the visit of Tottenham Hotspur next weekend.

The same went for Morgan Rogers. He squared up to James Tarkowski. He crunched into James Garner. He added to the 15 fouls committed by Chelsea in this match. He too avoided a second yellow despite being constantly combative.

Even as Chelsea were preparing to take the free-kick from which they scored their second, Joao Pedro was there, winding up Jordan Pickford while Everton’s goalkeeper was trying to organise his wall.

As they told Colwill, they were not here to make friends, but to win.

Palmer did not score. Rogers did not score. Joao Pedro did not score. But Chelsea’s front three contributed in their own ways as Pedro Neto got the two goals which won them this match.

It felt like a new side to Chelsea. There was a resilient feel to the visitors, who have benefitted from the addition of Jordan Henderson to their line-up as he fights their corner with the referees. Chelsea have added players who do not want to be considered pushovers.

After full-time, the celebrations in front of the away end were more energetic than that of a regular win. Palmer pushed Alonso in front of the supporters, and Joao Pedro did the same with Neto.

There was extra appreciation from the travelling contingent for what they had seen, and Chelsea are likely to need to show more of this side to them when Tottenham visit next weekend.

#172. Wirtz delivers but remains Liverpool's conundrum

Liverpool come from behind to beat nine-man Brentford

Florian Wirtz was instrumental as Liverpool returned to winning ways in the Premier League at Brentford on Saturday, but does the German playmaker remain boss Andoni Iraola's greatest conundrum?

Wirtz has come in for criticism amid his struggles to replicate the form which persuaded the Reds to pay Bayer Leverkusen what was a club record Â£116m in June 2025.

Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard even said this week that the 23-year-old could benefit from being taken out of the team altogether, to overcome what the club's former captain perceives as a lack of confidence.

The key dilemma facing Iraola was again evident in west London on Saturday.

Liverpool bounced back from their first league defeat of the season against Manchester City last weekend by scoring twice in the second half against a Brentford side reduced to 10 men before half-time.

The visitors produced plenty of chances, particularly with their man advantage in the second half when they registered 14 of their total 21 attempts.

Wirtz was at the heart of things in the final third.

The Germany international created more chances from open play (nine) than any other player has managed in a Premier League game over the past six seasons.

The last player to create as many chances in a single game in the competition was Sadio Mane, for Liverpool against Burnley, in January 2021 (also nine).

In an away game, he is the first player to reach that tally in more than 15 years, since Samir Nasri registered 10 for Manchester City against Tottenham in August 2011.

Florian Wirtz completed 53 of the 65 passes he attempted (81.5%) - including a match-leading 38 inside the final third

Despite answering his critics with those standout statistics, the impact of his playing style on the dynamic of the team continues to come under scrutiny.

BBC Sport pundit and former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy believes a midfield which features Wirtz as the number 10 remains a problem as it makes Iraola's side too easy to play against.

"They got the job done. First and foremost, that's another win on the road, which is always positive," Murphy said of Liverpool's performance.

"But I thought they looked too easy to play against.â©The spaces are too big.

"They're playing with two wingers and Wirtz at 10, so they're relying heavily on the two midfield players to try and cover so much space.

"It was too easy for Brentford to play out and to get in behind. That would be the biggest concern today for me."

Liverpool stage comeback to win at nine-man Brentford

Haaland scores twice as Man City beat Ipswich

Injured Martinez taken to hospital as Chelsea beat Everton

Following his latest performance, no player has created more chances in the Premier League this season. He is level with Brighton's Pascal Gross on 18.

He played in Munoz to begin Liverpool's fightback, meaning Wirtz has assisted in back-to-back games for Liverpool across all competitions for the first time - although this was only his second goal involvement in seven league games this term.

He was at the heart of Liverpool's attack, with a match-leading 12 final-third entries and 37 passes in the final third.

However, only Milos Kerkez (20) lost possession on more occasions than Wirtz (19) among Liverpool players, and he won just one of his nine duels.

"They don't look solid and don't look together in terms of shape," Murphy said.

"Instead of a number 10, where Wirtz is struggling to impact games, put three midfielders in.

"Always, the priority is foundation, defence, stability, being hard to beat. The other stuff can follow from there.

"At the moment, it just looks a little bit open. Against better teams, you're going to get hurt."

Liverpool players in 'delicate' situation over 'demanding' schedule - Iraola

Victory took Liverpool up to fifth in the table, with three wins from their first seven league games under Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer.

The Spaniard oversaw the Reds' first away league win after conceding first since December 2023, ending a run of 19 winless away games when going 1-0 behind.

But, while striker Alexander Isak returned from injury, Iraola was dealt fresh blows as Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong suffered injuries on Saturday.

Iraola told BBC Sport: "When you come here, you see the results of Brentford at home and you have to be ready for this kind of battle.

"We had a lot of chances. Even at the end, we had some counters where we were three against one and need to finish. When we go 2-1, every throw-in and every free-kick can be a problem.

"We are in a delicate situation with some of the players. We were talking about this run of four games in 10 days, it's very, very demanding.

"We have to rest again because we have another big, big game against Villarreal [in the Champions League on Tuesday]."
