#174. Championship roundup: West Ham go second; Norwich beaten again

Mukasa’s first-half goal enough to beat leaders Swansea

Canaries suffer sixth straight loss; Watford beat Charlton

Nuno Espírito Santo was delighted West Ham finished a “demanding week” by toppling Championship leaders Swansea.

Divine Mukasa’s first-half strike in front of a record Swansea.com Stadium crowd of 20,973 gave the Hammers a 1-0 win and took them into second place and within a point of the league leaders. It was their second success in four days after a 6-0 romp at Lincoln, and ended a week that began with a 1-1 home draw against QPR following Jarrod Bowen’s last-gasp penalty miss.

“We wanted not only to keep the momentum, but to build on it,” said Nuno. “It was a very demanding week in terms of the opponents we had to face, but it finished really well due to the hard work of the boys. The commitment, the unity and the way they played was really good against a very good Swansea side. It was a very intense.”

Kim Hellberg defended his decision to rest Will Lankshear against Cardiff after the division’s top scorer came off the bench to rescue a point for Middlesbrough. Lankshear, who took his tally to 10 for the season in all competitions midweek, was rested him for the visit of the Bluebirds. That selection backfired as Cardiff stunned Boro with two first-half goals from Jack Moylan and Ollie Tanner. Lankshear was then introduced at half-time and inspired a fightback, levelling for Boro with his 11th goal of the campaign after Tommy Conway had halved the deficit.

“You need to manage your players in this league and look into numbers,” said Hellberg. “We have a lot of players that have no pre-season. Will is one of those who came late and has been doing a lot of good things. He’s been absolutely brilliant and sometimes you need to also protect him.”

Liam Millar scored twice as Birmingham beat QPR 3-0 at St Andrew’s. Millar swung the game Birmingham’s way in the 27th minute and then doubled their advantage just after the break. On both occasions he was assisted by Tomoki Iwata while Demarai Gray added the gloss in the first minute of stoppage time by hammering a pull-back by fellow substitute Luis Vázquez into the top corner.

Bradford moved top of League One with their first home win under Michael Duff, as Plymouth slipped up against Huddersfield. The Bantams, who appointed Duff as manager earlier this month following the departure of Graham Alexander, claimed a 2-0 home win over Stevenage thanks to goals inside the last 11 minutes from Antoni Sarcevic and substitute Will Swan. That proved enough to put them a point clear at the top, with previous front-runners Plymouth going down 2-0 at home to Huddersfield and dropping to fourth in the process. The Terriers climbed above their opponents into third after strikes from Derensili Sanches Fernandez and Bojan Radulovic.

Stockport climbed to second, edging out Bromley 1-0 with Kyle Wootton on target, while Robbie Savage’s first home league game in charge of Peterborough ended in a 2-2 draw with Burton. It looked as if Gbemi Arubi’s 89th-minute wonderstrike had earned Albion their first win in three, but Matt Garbett responded with a 96th minute leveller to snatch his side a point. Savage started his time at London Road with a 3-1 win at Leicester last Saturday.

Aaron Collins scored the winner as MK Dons beat Luton 2-1 to claim a first league victory of the season. Alex Gilbey fired the Dons ahead with a fine strike before Jordan Clark equalised for the visitors. But Collins’s penalty won the match to condemn Luton to a third defeat in their past four games.

Under-pressure Leicester manager Russell Martin celebrated a badly needed win, seeing off visiting Doncaster 2-1 – with Warren O’Hara’s 84th-minute own-goal causing some late tension. Cambridge kept pace with the promotion hopefuls after Shayne Lavery grabbed the winner in added time to leave Barnsley with a 2-1 win, while Sheffield Wednesday eased to a 5-0 win over AFC Wimbledon – Davis Keillor-Dunn with a double.

Bottom club Wigan registered a first league win since 2 September, Scott Hogan with the only goal against Reading. Notts County lost 2-0 at Wycombe and Leyton Orient beat Blackpool 2-0. Press Association

Luke Graham scored his first goal for Stoke as they won 1-0 at Pride Park to pile more pressure on struggling Derby. The Scotland defender headed in a free-kick early in the second half and that was enough to settle a scrappy contest. Derby, who are missing a number of key players, battled away and nearly snatched a point when David Ozoh’s shot was superbly saved by goalkeeper Viktor Johansson.

West Brom completed a stunning comeback after conceding two early goals as they beat Blackburn 3-2. Andri Gudjohnsen had Rovers two up before the break, before Barney Stewart pulled a goal back for Albion. Isaac Price’s penalty levelled it up before the substitute Felix Horn Myhre netted a dramatic winner for the home side a minute from time.

James Bree, Lewis Dobbin and Léo Scienza all squandered chances as Southampton dropped points at home for the first time this season with a 0-0 draw against Bolton. The trio all wasted tap-ins, while Saints were also left bereft by a penalty not being given for a Rúben Rodrigues handball.

Watford lifted the pressure on Alessio Dionisi and quelled their supporters’ rebellion against the owner, Gino Pozzo, with a deserved 2-0 win against a sluggish Charlton. After shipping nine goals in defeats by Burnley and Cardiff, Watford had slumped into the bottom three and the fans had turned their anger on Pozzo. But goals from Luca Kjerrumgaard and the substitute Jordan Zemura extended Charlton’s worrying run to eight games without a win as they were booed off at Vicarage Road.

Dionisi said later his team was “not yet strong enough for the Championship but it’s possible to improve. I’ve been a coach for 14 years and I know when my team stays near my idea. This result is important and tonight I will drink a glass of red wine.”

Portsmouth piled on the misery for struggling Norwich as they made it back-to-back Championships victories with a 1-0 win at Carrow Road. Pompey followed up their midweek victory against Sheffield United with a hard-fought success in East Anglia, with a 51st-minute penalty from striker Marezi settling the issue.

It was a sixth successive league defeat for the hosts and there were calls for the sporting director Ben Knapper to go from frustrated supporters at the final whistle.

Norwich’s head coach, Philippe Clement, had no complaints with his side’s effort – but felt they sometimes failed to see the bigger picture on the pitch.

“I am very disappointed, very frustrated,” he said. “I saw a lot of passion out there, a lot of effort, but not enough overview. It’s about getting the balance right between their hearts and their brains. I understand the frustration of our fans and all I can say is that I will work even harder than I did last season to turn it around.”

Jake Cooper’s scrambled equaliser rescued a point for Millwall as they came from two goals down to draw 2-2 with Lincoln. The visitors looked on course to put Wednesday’s 6-0 home thrashing against West Ham behind them in style when goals from Andrei Coubiș and Rob Street put them in a strong position after 33 minutes at the Den. But Millwall were able to prevent back-to-back home defeats with a much-improved second-half performance, and the visitors were hanging on for a share of the spoils after having Deji Elerewe sent off soon after Cooper’s leveller. Kyrell Lisbie had scored Millwall’s first.

League Two pacesetters Salford made it five wins in a row in the fourth tier as Macaulay Langstaff scored twice in a 2-1 success over bottom side Crawley. Barnet and Crewe remain close by just a point further back.

Barnet came from behind to beat Tranmere 2-1, Kabongo Tshimanga scoring both, and Crewe defeated Rochdale 3-2. York were held to a 1-1 draw at Newport after going down to 10 men but Shrewsbury held on 1-0 against Bristol Rovers despite two red cards in the last 10 minutes.

Ian Holloway’s Swindon are now eight games without a win in all competitions after a 1-1 draw with Walsall, Oldham eased to a 4-1 result against Cheltenham and Port Vale edged Chesterfield 1-0.

Ten-man Grimsby went down 2-0 to Northampton, Accrington took a 3-1 win over Gillingham, strugglers Rotherham lost 2-0 at Fleetwood and there was a goalless draw between Colchester and Exeter. Press Association

Oliver Arblaster’s early strike and a strong defensive display saw Sheffield United take all three points from a 1-0 victory over Bristol City at Ashton Gate. The visitors took a fifth-minute lead when a headed clearance fell to Arblaster, who connected with a sweet right-footed volley from just outside the box which gave the City goalkeeper Sam Tickle no chance. It proved enough to settle a contest high on endeavour but low on entertainment from which the Blades emerged worthy winners.

Wrexham eased the pressure on Phil Parkinson with a 4-1 win over rock-bottom Preston. Joe Worrall scored his first goal in more than two years and, after Alfie Devine briefly brought Preston level, the former Lilywhites midfielder Ben Whiteman struck next to score his first goal in Wrexham colours. Sam Smith gave the hosts breathing space just before the hour and Kieffer Moore killed it off moments later.

In a week that had seen former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard linked with the manager’s job, Wrexham’s third league win of the season was a vital one as they moved up to 14th. But Preston remain stuck on four points from 11 games, with Graham Alexander having lost his first three games in charge.

#178. Keep training fresh, find a hobby... and know when to let top players leave: what Mikel Arteta can learn from greats such as Sir Alex Ferguson, Bob Paisley and Graham Taylor as he bids to join the 10-year brigade and build an Arsenal dynasty

By IAN HERBERT, DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026

A conversation between Sir Alex Ferguson and Rio Ferdinand nearly 20 years ago encapsulates why the former Manchester United’s manager’s longevity and success surpass those of anyone who has lasted a decade or more at the helm of a British football club.

Ferguson had just spent an evening away in Europe, scouting a player, and returned the following day having left morning training to his assistant Carlos Queiroz. Ferdinand sought him out at Carrington to ask where he’d been. ‘It’s not the same when you’re not here,’ he told him.

The manager took these words to heart, ensuring that from then on United always chartered him a plane for such trips, so he would be at the training ground, even if it meant getting to bed at 2am.

The significance resides both in Ferguson’s acceptance that a manager’s physical presence was important – ‘leaders are usually unaware, or underestimate, the motivating power of their presence. No one sees themselves as other sees them,’ he observed years later – and his willingness to weigh a player’s complaint.

Mikel Arteta may not feel he needs to take lessons on keeping things fresh and intense from an arch foe like United, though the small band of managers who’ve lasted a decade in post provide pointers as to how Arsenal’s manager might see his new contract to its end point and join that ten-year brigade.

Bill Shankly, at Liverpool’s bridgehead for 15 years, and Brian Clough, 18 years at Forest, were also the all-seeing eye – present at, though not controlling, training. For Shankly, there was a beauty in training sessions being unchanging, says Gordon Milne, who played in the mid-1960s Liverpool team and later enjoyed a very successful seven years as Coventry City manager.

‘Today, coaches are often lauded for the variety of their sessions,’ Milne writes in his excellent memoir Shankly, My Dad and Me.

Sir Alex Ferguson was willingness to adapt after hearing from his player Rio Ferdinand

Mikel Arteta's new deal at Arsenal will take him to a decade in charge

‘That wasn’t us. Success and stability thrived on repetition and although this may have appeared basic, we took these principles on board.

'And because Shanks was a great believer in principles (rather than rules, which he knew would be broken), it was nigh-on impossible not to be swept along.’

It was away from the training ground that managers who’ve lasted changed things up. Graham Taylor, who passed away in 2017, was constantly looking to freshen the environment during his ten years at Watford’s helm, occasionally cancelling training and inviting those players who had a dog to turn up with it at the appointed time. They would be embarking on a walk.

’On a similar occasion, the players were asked to turn up with an overnight bag and to bring their passports,’ journalist and author Lionel Birnie, who worked on Taylor’s own excellent posthumous memoir, In His Own Words, tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘It turned out they were heading by ferry to the Isle of Wight. That was Graham. He kept the momentum going all those years by the depth of his engagement and his imagination.’

Common to some of those managers who have lasted and flourished is a resolve to refresh the backroom staff, so that the voices the players heard were changing.

David Pleat, who was at the Luton Town helm for eight years, always felt this was a secret of Ferguson’s success. Over time, the United manager employed Brian Kidd, Jim Ryan, Steve McClaren, Carlos Queiroz and Mike Phelan as his No 2s.

‘This constant change meant new ideas, a fresh voice in the dressing room and changing philosophies,’ Pleat wrote in his biography, Just One More Goal, published in 2024.

Pleat contrasts managers like Mark Hughes who always took the same backroom team everywhere with him.

Graham Taylor kept changing things up at Watford to keep his players engaged

‘Did they change their views and ideas as time progressed?’ he writes. ‘Did they adapt to the players? Did they keep their freshness as the training grounds changed? I wonder.’

Mauricio Pochettino was another who displayed such reluctance to employ new assistants, as a critical voice.

For David Moyes, whose first period at Everton spanned 11 years from 2002, longevity was built on learning and evolving as he went along and not presupposing that some of his earlier responses to situations were right.

As a 38-year-old in his early months at Everton, he let Wayne Rooney and Thomas Gravesen get away with letting off rockets in the gym. A mistake, he felt in retrospect.

But when one senior member of the squad he inherited repeatedly feigned injury before miraculously declaring himself fit for an attractive final game of the season against a former rival, Moyes flatly told him he would not be playing.

Moyes, who has received several calls from Arteta, including one last season, seems to view management as a constant form of self-improvement.

‘I’m really looking closely at the moment at what I could do to try to manage the players a bit better,’ he says in a TNT Sports interview this weekend. ‘I feel myself that I’ve had to be adaptable and try and change. I think about it a lot. I stress about it a lot.’

Bill Shankly - with his team of Liverpool coaches Bob Paisley, Ronnie Moran, Joe Fagan and Reuben Bennett - had a set of principles underpinning his 15-year spell at Anfield

John Coleman, whose two spells managing Accrington Stanley spanned 13 years and ten years respectively, puts longevity down to embedding a clearly defined culture.

‘It’s like a mother yeast,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Once it’s going, you don’t have to alter or interfere with it, but you do have to evolve. You have to adapt to the times, or you get left behind. I’ve tried to meet people and exchange ideas and listen.’

Coleman, now assistant manager at Reading, thinks it helped that he was never a professional footballer himself. ‘I had to take it my own way and prove myself that way,’ he says. Coleman, like Ferguson, Shankly and Taylor, found delegation to be an article of faith.

Shankly’s innovative obsession with his players ‘living right, sleeping right, eating right, training right’, as Milne puts it, feels immensely modern, now, and his pursuit of new ways was never-ending. One of his 1960s projects was the purchase of a German electrical muscle stimulation device, first tested on midfielder Jimmy Melia.

Melia, lying prostrate on a treatment table with his left leg wired up to the machine’s electrodes, declared he could not feel anything, even when the dials were turned to ‘maximum.’

David Moyes admitted to mistakes in his early years at Everton, before replacing Ferguson at United in 2013

Someone in the room pointed out to Shankly that the plug had not been flicked – so someone immediately rectified this, without anyone thinking of turning down the dials.

The story of Melia’s leg shooting up from the table is one Shankly’s old players discuss to this day. He engendered a sense of adventure and fun through infectious enthusiasm and so his players loved him. ‘Players have to see how much it means to you,’ Coleman says. ‘You’ve got to be obsessed with the game.’

The brutally difficult, sometimes impossible, task is releasing players who had delivered so much. Shankly struggled with this in a way that Ferguson didn’t and endured six trophyless years from 1966 because of it.

‘The hardest thing is to let go of a player who has been a great guy – but all the evidence is on the field,’ Ferguson reflected from retirement. ‘I believe that the cycle of a successful team lasts maybe four years.’

Arsene Wenger laboured under a different kind of sentimentality, which wrecked the legacy he built in the glorious first eight of his 22 years at Arsenal. The money Arsenal spent building a new stadium gave opponents bigger spending power, but his obstinate insistence on attempting to replicate Barcelona’s aesthetic without the quality of player and in a far harder league was flawed.

That obstinacy was still evident on the occasion of his 1,000th game at Arsenal’s helm, in 2014. ‘Maybe I have an idea of making the players perfect, having the ideal game, the perfect game,’ he said that day. ‘I run after that happiness week after week.’

Perhaps the greatest challenge for Arteta, if he is to make it through a decade at Arsenal, is simply surviving the contemporary maelstrom.

Arteta has already shown he is willing to vary his methods to keep his players fresh

Shankly was desolate when stepping down in 1974 and Jurgen Klopp worn out by eight Anfield years in 2024. Clough was the most sadly diminished when he walked away in 1993. He never got over his split with Peter Taylor. He stopped laughing. 'Peter made me laugh,' Clough said in an interview, heartbreaking in retrospect.

There are already ample signs that Arteta is looking for his own idiosyncratic ways of ensuring that his Arsenal environment is kept fresh, five years into his tenure. The introduction of ‘Win’, the club’s chocolate labrador, to foster a family-orientated atmosphere. Having ‘pickpockets’ at club dinners to heighten players’ sensory awareness. Bringing a 150-year-old olive tree, symbolic of history and growth, into training.

But it is to the example of Ferguson he would be wise to turn, in search of how to maintain some sanity. And Ferguson would tell the Spaniard to find himself a hinterland, however small and insignificant.

‘I find horse racing is a release but I'm also learning to play the piano,’ he related, during his last stretch as manager. ‘I'm quite determined, you know. It’s a necessary release from the pressure.’

#181. Villa's Manzambi shows Newcastle what they missed out on

Manzambi goal gifts Aston Villa win against Newcastle

Johan Manzambi saw first hand how good Aston Villa were last season and is now playing a crucial part in Unai Emery's rebuild in this campaign.

Switzerland midfielder Manzambi, who turned 21 on Wednesday, scored his third goal in Villa colours with the winner in a 1-0 victory over Newcastle - the club he turned down before moving to Villa Park in the summer.

Manzambi played a crucial role in helping Freiburg reach the Europa League final, before the Germans were comprehensively beaten by a Villa side that scored three times in the opening hour on their way to a 3-0 success.

Asked why he had joined Villa, Manzambi said: "The team was very good and I played against them in the final. It's a very good team with a big coach and that was perfect for me."

For Newcastle fans it was one that had got away, as Manzambi had looked set for a move to St James' Park before opting to join Villa in a club record deal of just over Â£50m.

Manzambi headed in the winner in the north east on Saturday, unmarked eight yards out when found by Joao Gomes' excellent cross.

It comes after he also found the back of the net in the 3-2 win at Tottenham and in the 6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce in the Champions League.

"He has made a very good impact with his qualities," said a delighted Emery. "Skills and intelligence, both he has, and his physicality is very important as well to help us defensively and to help us try to keep the duels offensively.

"So happy he has scored another goal, fantastic for him."

Among players in the Bundesliga in his position last season, Manzambi ranked first for progressive carries of 10 metres or more (116), shot-ending carries (13) and fouls won (78).

He then impressed in the World Cup, scoring twice in the 4-1 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina, getting a goal and an assist in the 2-1 victory over co-hosts Canada and also registering an assist in the 2-0 success over Algeria.

Unfortunately for Manzambi and Switzerland, a knee injury ruled him out of the last-16 penalty shootout win over Colombia and their quarter-final loss to Argentina.

So impressive were his performances last season, that Manzambi finds himself on a 10-man list for the Kopa Trophy, awarded to the world's best player aged under 21.

Also on the shortlist are Spain World Cup winners Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsi, along with Yan Diomande - whose performances earned him a move to Real Madrid, with the winner named on 26 October.

Since his first start for Aston Villa on 19 September against Spurs, only Manchester City's Erling Haaland - with six - has been involved in more goals among Premier League players in all competitions than Manzambi's five (three goals, two assists).

Team-mate Nicolas Jackson, another to join Villa in the transfer window in a deal worth up to Â£65m from Chelsea, was quick to praise the youngster.

"He's an amazing player," said Jackson. "He's still growing. Hopefully he can be better and better every game, score goals and assist me as well. Hopefully we work together and achieve many things together.

"He will go a long way and hopefully gets no injuries."

Aston Villa manager Emery reacts to victory over Newcastle

While playing a crucial role in Villa's present and future, the team he has joined is a lot different to the one he played against in the Europa League final.

From the Villa side that won in Istanbul, six of them - goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, defenders Lucas Digne and Ezri Konsa, midfielders Youri Tielemans and Morgan Rogers and striker Ollie Watkins - all left in high-profile moves, while substitutes Harvey Elliott, Jadon Sancho and Leon Bailey are also no longer at the club.

It proved a challenging start to the season for Villa as they only picked up one point from their opening four league games, but this win over Newcastle has extended their unbeaten run in all competitions to five matches.

As well as moving up to 12th in the Premier League, Villa have six points from two ties in the Champions League after thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 on Wednesday and are in the last 16 of the Carabao Cup, where they play at Bournemouth.

How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents

Sven Botman was one of six Newcastle players to be cautioned against Aston Villa

Jackson has scored five times for Villa since his move and said he was lucky to avoid a serious injury when he was caught in the first half by Newcastle's Sven Botman, who was only shown a yellow card despite an over-the-ball challenge.

"I know the referee said yellow card but it was so high and hopefully maybe next time a red card, but it was a yellow," said Jackson. "I nearly broke my leg but anyway it's part of football. The most important thing is we win and we won, so I'm OK."

Villa entertain Norwegian side Viking in their third Champions League match of the season on Wednesday before hosting a Manchester City side that have won all seven of their Premier League matches this season.

"It was very important after our poor start [to the season] that we needed to try to come back feeling confident, feeling comfortable in how we are building our structure," added Emery.

"The players themselves tried to be demanding to change the situation where we are.

"Through the [Premier] league we are going to achieve our priority this year, so the league is the competition where we must try to be very consistent."

With seven points from their past three league matches, Villa are a side on the rise again.

#185. Manzambi maintains Aston Villa progress with win to seal dismal week for Newcastle

There is a reason why Aston Villa were so desperate to hijack Johan Manzambi’s proposed summer move from Freiburg to Newcastle. The tall, quick, tricky, clever and perfectly balanced 21-year-old Switzerland attacking midfielder looked worth every penny of the record £50m plus fee Villa ended up paying and he duly delighted in showing Tynesiders what they missed.

For Newcastle and their disconsolate manager, Matthias Jaissle, there was a cruel irony that Manzambi ended up heading the winner on a day when the Premier League’s CEO, Richard Masters, was in the directors’ box to watch arguably the two teams most affected by the spending rules imposed during his tenure.

Those regulations have turned Unai Emery into a master of reinvention at Aston Villa but, in the league at least, the Spaniard’s latest rebuild has been slow to click cleanly into place. On the evidence of their fourth win in five games in all competitions, that just might be changing.

While Villa kicked off having won only once in the league this season, Newcastle sought redemption after last Monday night’s chastening 4-1 defeat at Coventry.

Emery, who changed his mind about taking charge of Newcastle before Eddie Howe took the job, said: “It was a tough match but it was very important to win after our poor start. But we set a high standard.”

Jaissle, whose team are level on points with Villa but faces an appreciably tougher reconstruction project, was left to reflect on his “frustration” and blamed his young team’s decision making. But Newcastle’s manager was also sanguine. “Big names left the club in the summer so for sure, we knew it would be challenging,” he said. “That’s not an excuse, we have to learn fast.”

There has always been a certain edge between these teams and Jarred Gillett issued two first-half yellow cards in quick succession. First Joelinton lunged in, two-footed, on Manzambi and then Sven Botman was guilty of another reckless challenge, two-footed and over the ball, on the dangerous Nicolas Jackson.

A video assistant referee check ensued but, after lengthy deliberation, it was decided the original decision was correct and Botman’s yellow did not require upgrading to a red. The Newcastle centre-half was probably a little fortunate. “It was so high it nearly broke my leg,” said Jackson. “But I’m OK; it’s part of football.”

Joelinton, meanwhile, has now been booked in each of the two games he has been involved in since returning from injury as a substitute at Coventry. Plus ça change.

The elegantly impressive Manzambi, seemingly electrically powered, exerted the best sort of revenge on the Brazilian when he gave Emery’s side the lead. That goal arrived in the 36th minute and involved an unmarked Manzambi – a creator brilliant at drifting into space – ghosting away from Malick Thiaw before meeting João Gomes’s splendid cross with a tremendous header.

Newcastle suddenly looked extremely vulnerable but they were reprieved when Emiliano Buendía’s shot rebounded off the inside of a post and deflected off Lukas Hornicek’s back before eventually being cleared by Lewis Hall. Once again, Hall was Jaissle’s best player.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It was all too easy to see why Newcastle have now gone 13 Premier League home games without a clean sheet, equalling an unwanted record set in 1998-99.

Jaissle’s frustration surfaced itself as he exchanged words with Emery after an altercation involving Alysson and Hornicek and subsequently looked suitably downcast as his side were booed off at half-time.

Those home fans were not relishing the sight of Villa’s forward repeatedly accelerating behind the sometimes dangerously high home backline.

• Newcastle United are now without a home clean sheet in each of their last 16 games in all competitions; it's the longest run in their history.

• Yoane Wissa’s seven shots on goal with none on target is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Newcastle teammate Harvey Barnes against Brentford in April 2025 (also 7).

• Unai Emery (pictured) has earned his 100th Premier League win as a manager, doing so in his 197th game in the competition (D44 L53), only eight managers have done so in fewer games in the competition’s history. Opta

Zion Suzuki had been rather underemployed but a goalkeeper briefly courted by Newcastle in the summer opened the second half by making a superlative flying save to keep Botman’s high velocity strike out. It was Newcastle’s sole shot on target.

The Villa substitute Ross Barkley almost showed Jaissle’s players how to do it when he would have scored with his first touch had Hornicek not dived smartly to turn his blistering shot around a post.

Although Newcastle’s manager sent Dan Burn on for the closing minutes – as a striker – nothing was going to come between Emery and his 100th Premier League win.

#186. Hits & Misses: Mbeumo is Man Utd's only reliable goalscorer as Eze struggles

Sky Sports' football writers analyse Sunday's Premier League action; Bryan Mbeumo continues to offer glimmer of hope for Man Utd; Eberechi Eze needs to show his worth to Arsenal with others in wait; Nottingham Forest's lack of goals continue to concern

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Michael Carrick called Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Leeds a "fresh start" on Sunday. No doubt that encapsulated the sense of relief the manager felt after watching his side battle and duel better than they had all season, showing the commitment that had been missing from most performances so far.

He will be pleased Bryan Mbeumo's form is a continuation of what went before, though - about the only player who has shown a shade of consistency during this difficult start. Three of Mbeumo's four Premier League goals have put United 1-0 ahead this term.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

His strike against Leeds marked an important momentum shift in a game that could have otherwise got away from them. Fortunately for Carrick, Mbeumo has been a reliant source since his switch from Brentford, his 15 goals more than any other United player since his debut - including Bruno Fernandes.

Just two victories from 10 games in all competitions means Carrick is not off the hook. But while Mbeumo keeps scoring, he's got something positive to hook performances on. Especially while Fernandes continues to look off-colour.Laura Hunter

Eberechi Eze has spent a year at Arsenal since leaving Crystal Palace, but questions remain over whether he is ready to become one of the club's leading figures as their ambitions continue to grow.

His talent is undeniable. The real concern is whether he can influence games consistently, and the trip to Nottingham Forest presented another opportunity to silence his doubters.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

With Arsenal struggling to break down Forest, Eze had the chance to make a difference. Instead, he was substituted at half-time, watching from the sidelines as Noni Madueke replaced him and went on to score the 80th-minute winner.

Roy Keane's assessment on Sky Sports was telling, suggesting his concerns extended beyond a single performance.

"We're still waiting for him, the talent is there," Keane said. "We just want him to be at Arsenal and be able to take responsibility and try to be the main man at a big club."

That is the challenge facing Eze. At Crystal Palace, he was the focal point, the player expected to create chances and turn games in his team's favour. At Arsenal, however, talent alone will not earn him that status. He must deliver consistently, particularly in tight contests when his team need inspiration.

Ian Wright offered some important context, describing Eze as a "moments player" who benefits from having players around him and can become isolated on the left.

There is merit to that argument. Eze offers a different threat to Madueke, whose pace, directness and willingness to take on defenders gave Arsenal a fresh dimension in the second half.

Yet that only underlines the challenge facing the former Palace man. While Madueke seized his opportunity and made an immediate impact, Eze failed to leave his mark on the contest.

Competition for places is healthy at a club with Arsenal's ambitions. For Eze, though, the task is no longer simply to showcase his ability in flashes. He must demonstrate that he can influence games regularly, take responsibility when his team need him and establish himself as a first-choice player.

The talent is there. Now, Eze must prove he can turn that potential into consistent performances and become one of Arsenal's main men.William Bitibiri

There was only so long Nottingham Forest could rely on defensive resilience before their lack of goals caught up with them. Now they are in the relegation zone.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Oliver Glasner's side have failed to score in every Premier League home game this season, and their defeat to Arsenal highlighted why they are in trouble.

Forest competed and created opportunities but lacked the quality in the final third to make their efforts count.

Liam Delap struggled to make an impact against Arsenal's defence, summing up a frustrating afternoon. Forest needed someone to take responsibility but their attacking play lacked conviction.

That is the worry for Glasner. Defensive organisation can only take a team so far; they still need goals to win matches.

Forest are now in the relegation zone with just five points. Their performances offer some encouragement, but until they find a reliable source of goals at the City Ground, it is difficult to see their situation improving.William Bitibiri

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

There was a time when Hurzeler could barely win over his own supporters. Now he has Brighton dreaming again.

Back in February, Hurzeler was booed off at the Amex after a 1-0 home defeat to Crystal Palace. The frustration was palpable. Questions were being asked, patience was wearing thin.

Fast forward to this 5-0 demolition of their fiercest rivals and the transformation is remarkable.

This is what happens when a club refuses to panic. Brighton could have pulled the trigger when the noise around Hurzeler was at its loudest. Instead, they trusted their process and back their man.

Brighton have always prided themselves on smart decision-making, from recruitment to managerial appointments.

Hurzeler is the latest example of that philosophy working.

And what better way to underline that progress than by dismantling Palace?

The boos of February feel a long way away. Brighton are going places.Lewis Jones

Crystal Palace won three trophies in the previous two seasons. On this evidence, they look a million miles away from those glories.

This was Pierre Sage's worst day as Palace boss by some distance. There have been defeats this season where you could at least point to some decent football, a positive spell or an individual performance worth celebrating. At the Amex, there was nothing. No resistance, no response.

Brighton ripped them apart in a 5-0 humiliation that exposed just how far Palace have fallen. The defensive holes were glaring. Replacing Marc Guehi and Maxence Lacroix was never going to be straightforward but the scale of the problem is becoming impossible to ignore. Palace look vulnerable every time opponents turn up the pressure.

Last weekend, Nottingham Forest missed seven big chances in their defeat to Palace. That was a warning sign, perhaps one that was easy to dismiss with three points in the bag. Brighton offered no such charity. They punished Palace's mistakes ruthlessly.

Sage must find answers quickly. If Palace continue to concede chances at this rate, the pressure on their manager will grow with every passing week. Their recent trophy haul feels a long way away.Lewis Jones

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose must have grown tired of constantly explaining how well his side had played in defeat this season, a recurring theme for the Cherries as they looked for a first Premier League win of the season under their new head coach, but no more after Sunday's much-needed, but hugely deserved victory over fellow strugglers Sunderland.

Sure, the hosts were helped on their way to the the three points by some calamitous defending from the Black Cats, but it was more that they forced their opponents into those mistakes, including for both their goals, as well as Kevin Danso's 17th-minute red card.

In fact, such was Bournemouth's dominance from start to finish at the Vitality that their final xG of 4.46 was their highest on record in the Premier League, with the German even joking after the game that he might now treat himself to a non-alcoholic beer.

It may have taken Bournemouth seven league matches to get off the mark but anyone who has watched them this season knows that first victory was just around the corner. They must now build on it, especially at home, where they have lost one of their last 15 top-flight contests.

Maintaining the Vitality as a fortress will go a long way to ensuring another fine campaign.Rich Morgan

#190. Fans punching players, darts in foreheads and stars in the stands rushed to safety - these are the ten most toxic games I've been to, and where Liverpool v Man City ranks: OLIVER HOLT

Published: 17:00 BST, 12 October 2026 | Updated: 10:49 BST, 13 October 2026

Manchester City's first game as Public Enemy No1 brought them to the home of the team arguably most impacted by their cheating – Liverpool.

The febrile atmosphere began on the streets of the city before a furious Kop End led chants of 'you cheating b******s, you know what you are' throughout the match and unfurled a string of mocking banners, before greeting every City touch with a loud exhale of 'CHEATS' towards the end.

The hostility was intense, but not quite the hottest we've seen on these shores, perhaps quelled by City's rampant second half after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off, with Enzo Maresca's side running out 3-0 winners.

Here, Chief Sports Writer OLIVER HOLT picks the 10 most toxic atmospheres he's experienced in all his years going to matches around the world.

Liverpool fans were armed with a sea of banners to greet Manchester City after they were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules

The hostile atmosphere began outside the ground and continued into a fractious Anfield

1. Liverpool 1 Chelsea 0 - May 3, 2005, Anfield

Champions League semi-final second leg. Liverpool win 1-0 on aggregate. Attendance: 42,529.

The loudest, most relentless atmosphere I’ve ever encountered in an English ground.

A night that assailed the senses, pitting two teams against each other who stood for very different things in the English game and an agent provocateur without equal, Jose Mourinho, winding things up.

So loud and intense it unsettled even Chelsea’s players.

Luis Garcia's 'ghost goal' in the fifth minute was enough to send Liverpool through to the Champions League final in Istanbul

2. Cardiff City 2 Leeds United 1 – January 6, 2002, Ninian Park

A throwback game and not in a good way. This felt like a return to the hooliganism of the 1980s as two sets of old-school fans lit into each other.

Alan Smith, the Leeds forward, was sent off, Sam Hammam, the Cardiff owner, wound up a crowd that didn’t need winding up and there was a pitch invasion.

Sam Hammam, the Cardiff owner (centre), wound up a crowd that didn’t need winding up

Cardiff fans invade the pitch at full time to taunt the visiting Leeds supporters

3. Manchester United 2 Liverpool 1 – April 17, 1985, Maine Road

FA Cup semi-final replay. Attendance: 45,775.

The first match, at Goodison Park, was remembered partly for the violence that erupted all around the stadium before the game. The replay matched it.

I was in the United half of the Kippax that day and there were stories of United fans walking around with darts in their foreheads. It was a febrile atmosphere and a fierce contest.

4. Kidderminster Harriers 4 Stockport County 0 – April 20, 2013, Aggborough Stadium

These were dark days for Stockport and this defeat relegated them to the National League North.

The atmosphere in the away end was toxic, there was a pitch invasion, a Kidderminster player was punched by a County fan, police reinforcements were summoned.

I took my 10-year-old daughter to the match. She didn’t come to football again for a while.

Lee Vaughan of Kidderminster Harriers (left) is punched by a Stockport County fan on the day that the visitors were relegated to the National League North

The atmosphere in the away end was toxic and there was a pitch invasion

5. Andorra 0 England 3 – March 28, 2007, Olympic Stadium, Barcelona

The most poisonous atmosphere I’ve ever witnessed at a football match.

Vitriol and abuse dripped from the stands as England fans voiced their opposition to then manager Steve McClaren, particularly at half-time with the Three Lions goalless against the world's 163rd-ranked nation.

It was so bad that England’s non-playing squad members had to be moved from the stands for their own safety.

Vitriol and abuse dripped from the stands as England fans voiced their opposition to manager Steve McClaren, particularly at half-time with the Three Lions goalless against Andorra

6. Spain 1 England 0 – November 17, 2004, Estadio Santiago Bernabeu

International friendly. Attendance: 48,000.

The worst racial abuse I’ve ever seen at a game.

It was not just a few isolated voices making monkey noises at Ashley Cole and Shaun Wright-Phillips. It was most of the stadium. It was revolting.

Ashley Cole was among the England players who suffered vile racist abuse from Spain fans in the Bernabeu in 2004

7. Millwall 5 Stockport County 0 – March 27, 2010, The Den

I could have put a couple of Millwall matches in this list but this was the one that made the biggest impression on me because it was the first time I stood in the away end.

Stockport posed very little threat but I was still taken aback by the level and intensity of abuse coming from the Millwall supporters.

8. Everton 2 Liverpool 2 – February 12, 2025, Goodison Park

The last Merseyside derby at Everton’s old home did not disappoint.

It ended with four red cards and a late, late James Tarkowski volleyed equaliser that nearly took the roof off the place.

The last Merseyside derby at Everton’s old home did not disappoint, ending with four red cards including for Curtis Jones (second right) and Abdoulaye Doucoure (right)

James Tarkowski's 98th-minute volleyed equaliser nearly took the roof off Goodison Park

9. Newcastle 1 Sunderland 2 – August 25, 1999, St James' Park

The Tyne-Wear derby is lively on a bad day but this felt apocalyptic.

Played in torrential rain, Newcastle manager Ruud Gullit dropped Alan Shearer and paid for it with his job when Sunderland won.

Newcastle manager Ruud Gullit dropped Alan Shearer for a Tyne-Wear Derby and paid for it with his job when Sunderland won

10. Liverpool 0 Manchester City 3 – October 11, 2026, Anfield

Not quite as cacophonous as it might have been 10 years ago.

But this was still loud and angry in the face of City’s first match since they were found guilty of serial cheating.

#194. Toby Alderweireld on his Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Adriano baptism of fire

The Belgian international was thrown in at the deep end at the start of his senior career

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During his 18-year career, Toby Alderweireld would clock up more than 600 appearances, winning league titles in three countries and racking up 127 appearances for the Belgium national side.

But everyone has to start somewhere, and for Alderweireld it was something of a baptism of fire when he was handed a brutal introduction to the professional game.

The centre-back had come through Ajax's famed academy and was used to mixing with the best players in his age group, but that did little to prepare him for the test of going up against two of his generation's best and most physical strikers in his first senior match.

The future Spurs man's first taste of the men's game came in a pre-season match against Inter Milan, who featured Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Adriano in attack, with both strikers at the peak of their powers.

Alderweireld learned a valuable lesson that day - even if his first reaction was to wonder whether he would be able to mix it at the highest level.

“My first game for Ajax, in the pre-season Amsterdam Tournament," the Belgian tells FourFourTwo.

"There were two games in two days – our first team played against Arsenal, then our second team played against Inter," with the teenage defender being given the opportunity to impress against the Italian side.

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

"I was young and played at centre-back against big guys, Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Adriano."

At that time, Ibrahimovic was in his pomp, combining physicality and a 6ft 5in frame with technical brilliance, while Adriano was renowned for his explosive power and fearsome left foot. It soon became clear that a test like this was nothing his time in the Ajax academy could prepare him for.

Alderweireld initially attempted to take this levelling up in his stride, but was soon handed a reality check.

"I thought ‘OK, this is professional football, this is a different level’," he continues. "After 20 minutes, I was like ‘This is not for me’, but sometimes you need to have your head against the wall to become better.

"It gave me a lot of insight – I thought ‘I need to get stronger’. I played a good game and it wasn’t like we lost 5-0, but physically against those two in their prime, it was a good reality check.”

And while the young Alderweireld endured a testing afternoon, those first 20 minutes would prove to be vital in helping him become the defender he wanted to be.

Alderweireld was speaking in association with BOYLE Sports 2 Goals Ahead

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#195. Isak completes Liverpool’s comeback win as Brentford finish with nine

If Liverpool’s spluttering forwards end up remembering this as the day when their luck turned then they will owe a big debt of gratitude to Yehor Yarmolyuk. This was a game with a very clear before and after.

Andoni Iraola will hope surviving one of the toughest tests the Premier League has to offer is a sign his methods are starting to work, but Liverpool’s manager will not forget it was a very different contest after Yarmolyuk’s red card for a butt on Jérémy Jacquet left Brentford trying to defend a 1-0 lead with 10 men for the entire second half.

Brentford, who later lost Vitaly Janelt to a second yellow card, could not hold out. They raged at John Brooks’s officiating after their unbeaten start ended, but they had only themselves to blame after tumbling out of the top four. Brentford pressed the self-destruct button when they had Liverpool on the ropes. Yarmolyuk was never going to get away it in the video assistant referee era and Liverpool made the midfielder pay.

Iraola was delighted with how an attack worth close to £400m made the numerical advantage count after half-time. Most important was a telling contribution from Florian Wirtz. The £100m signing has struggled with the responsibility of playing as Liverpool’s No 10 since joining from Bayer Leverkusen, but this time he was decisive. The clever pass to release Victor Muñoz for a sharp equaliser was his second assist of the season and was followed by Bradley Barcola creating a goal for the first time since his move for an initial £106m from Paris Saint-Germain, the French winger’s header teeing up Alexander Isak to complete the turnaround in the 70th minute and lift Liverpool into fifth place.

The challenge is to push on. Isak’s Liverpool career has been stop-start since his £125m move from Newcastle, injuries holding the forward back. The Spaniard was critical of some sloppy finishing from Barcola, but was readier to dish out the praise for Wirtz’s intelligence in tight spaces in the second half. It feels significant that both of Wirtz’s assists have come for Muñoz.

“A good battle today,” Iraola said before switching focus to Barcola and Wirtz. “Both had a lot of influence. Bradley and Flo, they are players that against 10 men are lovely to have.”

There was not much between the sides before Yarmolyuk’s rush of blood to the head. Isak returned after missing last week’s defeat to Manchester City and Liverpool shaded the early openings. Barcola almost punished an error from Janelt, only to miss a chance to build on his midweek hat-trick against LASK. Isak nodded over from a good position.

Brentford responded with a series of fast breaks and Liverpool had to be strong. They looked readier for the threat posed by Brentford than when they folded in this fixture under Arne Slot 12 months ago. Jacquet, quietly impressive in central defence, made a crucial tackle to deny Igor Thiago. The initial problem for Liverpool was more their expensive attack was yet to gel.

Michael Kayode was keeping Barcola in check and Keane Lewis-Potter was edging his battle with Muñoz. Wirtz was timid and Liverpool’s worries grew when they lost Dominik Szoboszlai to injury.

With Ryan Gravenberch suspended, Liverpool were light on midfield options. Trey Nyoni replaced Szoboszali and the 19-year-old’s introduction was followed by a whirlwind spell. Iraola was unhappy when Liverpool had a penalty overturned as replays showed Dango Outtara got a clear touch on the ball before colliding with Alexis Mac Allister.

Brentford were pumped up after the VAR intervention and soon made Liverpool rue a failure to clear their lines. The ball came back too easily, Mac Allister backed off Thiago, who crossed for Lewis-Potter to run in from left-back and head into the top corner.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“We were edging it,” Keith Andrews said. Brentford’s manager wants his team “to play on the edge”, but felt too many decisions went Liverpool’s way. However, he had no complaints about the first red. He said Liverpool were “cute and clever” during the incident, but promised that Yarmolyuk would learn from his mistake.

They were into six added minutes at the end of the first half when the midfielder clashed with Jacquet before a Liverpool corner. It was more of a jut than a proper blow, but it was enough to justify the sending off. Brooks checked the pitchside monitor and his decision was not a surprise.

Liverpool took a while to adjust in the second half. They encountered further complications when injury forced Jeremie Frimpong off seven minutes after replacing Ronald Araújo at right-back. Mac Allister let fly from distance, but Caoimhín Kelleher saved and Rio Ngumoha, on for Frimpong, crossed for Virgil van Dijk to volley wide.

• Florian Wirtz is the first player to create nine or more chances from open play in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané against Burnley in January 2021 (9), also for Liverpool, and first in an away match since Samir Nasri for Manchester City v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Victor Muñoz (pictured centre, with Wirtz and Trey Nyoni) scored from one of them.

• Liverpool’s Alexander Isak has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford (5 goals); only Erling Haaland v Crystal Palace (6) has a better 100% rate in the competition.

• Brentford received two red cards in the same league game for the first time since April 2013 against Sheffield United in League One. Opta

Brentford began to wobble and they were caught on the counterattack in the 62nd minute. Wirtz dropped back and played a clever pass inside Lewis-Potter. Muñoz raced clear, cut back and drilled a low shot into the far corner with his left foot.

The change in mood was dramatic. Barcola sliced a volley just wide, but the winner was coming. Mac Allister took a pass from Wirtz and crossed. Barcola headed down and Isak finished from close range.

Iraola was not happy with Liverpool’s play once they led. Brentford threatened an equaliser through Thiago and Liverpool were too rushed. There are flaws to iron out, but this was a positive week for Iraola.

#196. South Africa stutter on rain-hit day one against Australia

Scott Boland dismisses Aiden Markram and David Bedingham from successive deliveries as South Africa close on 20-2 from 12.2 overs possible around the rain in Gqeberha; Australia - who left out premier spinner Nathan Lyon - lead three-Test series 1-0 after 214-run win in Durban

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

South Africa stuttered to 20-2 in the 12.2 overs possible on a rain-hit day one of the second Test against Australia as Scott Boland struck twice in as many balls.

Boland, selected in Gqeberha as Australia omitted off-spinner Nathan Lyon and went in with a four-pronged pace attack, bowled Aiden Markam (11) off an inside edge in the ninth over before then nicking off David Bedingham (0) with his next delivery.

South Africa, 1-0 down in the three-match series after a 214-run defeat in the opening game at Durban, were 12-2 at that stage having been put into bat but reached the premature stumps without any further casualties as debutant Marques Ackerman (5no off 32 balls) and captain Temba Bavuma (4no off 13) battled.

South Africa 20-2 after 12.2 overs in first innings: Aiden Markram (11), Marques Ackerman (5no off 32); Scott Boland (2-5 from 3.2 overs)

Rain meant play started around two hours later than scheduled and it returned to bring about an early lunch after just 5.3 overs before another downpour led to the day being abandoned at 4.15pm local time at St George's Park.

Boland for Lyon was Australia's only change from the first match, with the Baggy Greens leaving their premier spinner out of a red-ball Test in which he was fit to play for the first time since 2013.

South Africa made three alterations with left-arm spinner Keshav Maharaj, wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne and batter Tristan Stubbs axed for batters Ackerman and Matthew Breetzke and fit-again paceman Kagiso Rabada.

Ryan Rickelton took the wicketkeeping gloves in Verreynne's absence and dropped down from his opening position to No 6, with Ackerman coming in to partner Markam at the top of the order.

Ackerman, 30, was opening in a first-class match for the first time and dug in on a seam-friendly wicket.

#204. Agha returns to lead Pakistan to tri-series win over Sri Lanka

Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by 37 runs to win the opening match of the ODI tri-series; Pakistan captain Salman Ali Agha returned to score a century; Watch England's first game against Pakistan in Rawalpindi on Tuesday, live on Sky Sports from 9am

Salman Ali Agha made a triumphant return to the Pakistan team with his fourth ODI century in a 37-run victory over Sri Lanka in the cricket tri-series opener on Sunday.

Agha top-scored with 107 off 90 balls as Pakistan were bowled out for 305 in 49.5 overs after Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis won his fourth successive toss and elected to field.

The batsman was among seven Pakistan cricketers summoned home at the end of August during a turbulent tour of England, having captained the side in the first Test.

Pakistan pace bowlers overcame heavy dew and threatening half centuries from Pavan Rathnayake (79) and Janith Liyanage (60) to dismiss Sri Lanka for 268 in 48.1 overs.

Captain Shaheen Afridi picked up three for 55 while Naseem Shah pinned down Sri Lanka's top-order with impressive swing bowling to finish on two for 43. Haris Rauf ran through the tail with two for 48 while seam all-rounder Faheem Ashraf grabbed two for 49, including the key wicket of Rathnayake.

Avishka Fernando, making a comeback to ODIs, top-edged Shah while Kusal Mendis struggled for 34 balls to score only 18 before he fell to Ashraf.

Kamindu Mendis (44 in 50) survived two dropped catches before Afridi struck twice in his return spell as Sri Lanka limped to 91-4 in the 20th over of its chase.

Rathnayake and Liyanage then revived Sri Lankan hopes with a 119-run stand with Pakistan pacers unable to reverse swing the wet ball due to heavy dew at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium.

But the dismissal of Rathnayake in the 38th over provided Pakistan an opening despite Dasun Shanaka, playing his first ODI since the start of 2024, scoring 28 off 18 balls.

After being summoned home, Agha was stripped of the Pakistan T20 captaincy and dropped from the side that beat Sri Lanka 2-1 in their recent three-match series. However, a prolific run of domestic form, including a triple century, earned him a recall to the ODI team.

Agha helped Pakistan recover from 118-4 in the 22nd over, building crucial partnerships with Hasan Nawaz (37) and Arafat Minhas (18), before Sri Lanka struck back in the death overs.

Eshan Malinga (4-46) and Asitha Fernando (3-59) struck repeatedly in the final five overs to deny Pakistan a strong finish. From 279-5, Pakistan lost its last five wickets for just 26 runs. Malinga claimed two wickets in a maiden over before No. 11 Haris Rauf denied him a hat-trick.

Dilshan Madushanka (2-67) removed openers Fakhar Zaman (16) and Saim Ayub (7) in his opening spell.

Babar Azam and 19-year-old debutant Saad Baig rebuilt with a 74-run third-wicket stand before Malinga removed both batters in successive overs.

Babar, who has scored just one ODI century in more than two years, fell for 45 off 57 balls, pulling a short delivery from Malinga straight to mid-wicket. Baig struck two sixes and three fours before falling to the same bowler, mistiming a pull to deep fine leg.

Agha wrested back the momentum with a 97-run partnership with Nawaz. Sri Lanka's only specialist leg-spinner, Sachindu Colombage (0-61), struggled to contain them as Agha reached his half-century off 48 balls and Nawaz also attacked.

Fernando returned to break the stand, with Rathnayake taking an excellent catch above his head at mid-wicket to dismiss Nawaz.

Agha continued to attack in a 64-run partnership with Minhas before bringing up his century with an edged boundary.

Pakistan will play England in Rawalpindi on Tuesday in the second match of the tri-series. Watch live on Sky Sports from 9am.

#206. After nearly seven years of being Man United's main man is the time drawing near when Bruno Fernandes will have to pass on that mantle? His display vs Leeds was a microcosm of his season, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Published: 02:00 BST, 19 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 19 October 2026

Even by the usual level of animosity directed towards Bruno Fernandes at away grounds around the country, this was brutal in the extreme.

‘Bruno is a ****,’ echoed the chant around Elland Road as the Leeds fans spewed their bile towards the Manchester United captain, enraged by an ugly lunging tackle on Tarik Muharemovic that earned Fernandes an early yellow card and had the natives baying for red.

It is to his credit that he led from the front for the remaining 73 minutes without giving them any more opportunities to implore referee Darren England to send him off in a full-blooded fixture that doesn’t allow players to hold anything back.

Fernandes is used to it by now. He rarely takes the bait from rival supporters, preferring to answer his critics by hitting their team where it hurts.

You would have bet on the Bruno of old having the final word at Elland Road. But he didn’t, just as he has failed to have a meaningful impact in most of United’s 10 games so far this season.

His four goals and one assist have come in his team’s only two wins, against Ipswich Town and Sabah at Old Trafford, two of the easier fixtures it has to be said.

Bruno Fernandes' superpowers have largely deserted him - his days of being Manchester United's main man look numbered

In past seasons he may have had the final word in this sort of match at Elland Road - not now

Otherwise the superpowers that earned the Portugal star the PFA and FWA Player of the Year awards with nine goals and a Premier League record 21 assists have largely deserted him.

It was a familiar story on Sunday as Fernandes reached into his box of tricks and came up empty-handed yet again.

He is not good at hiding his emotions at the best of times, and we were treated to the full repertoire of arm-throwing and grumbling (mainly at Diogo Dalot) as he searched in vain for inspiration.

Afterwards, it was put to Michael Carrick that Fernandes’ body language wasn’t the best. ‘No, he was absolutely fine today, don't worry,’ smiled United’s head coach, accustomed by now to answering questions specifically about his captain in most press conferences.

Fernandes might be fine, but the fact that Carrick has felt the need to move him out of the No.10 position he has made his own tells its own story.

Against Atletico Madrid in midweek, he played wide on the right, allowing Youri Tielemans to push forward from midfield and play No.10. The Belgian performed well enough to stay there against Leeds, and set up the opening goal for Bryan Mbeumo while Fernandes started side left and inter-changed with Mbeumo at centre-forward.

‘Today, he pretty much played where he has been playing for the most part, through the middle of the pitch, so there wasn't really too much change,’ added Carrick.

‘He played a slightly different position in midweek, but apart from that it's pretty much as usual, you know. And he's an important part of our team, Bruno. He has been for us for some time, and that's not changing.’

Youri Tielemans deserves to start against Como in the Champions League on Wednesday

Michael Carrick has been asked if Fernandes is undroppable - he may soon feel pressured to bench him

Maybe not but, on this evidence, Tielemans deserves to continue against Como in the Champions League on Wednesday. Matheus Cunha is another who can play at No.10 but has had to work around Fernandes.

Until now, that has been beyond question. His stats spoke for themselves. But Carrick was asked in Madrid if Fernandes is undroppable and the noise around him is only going to grow louder.

After nearly seven years of being United’s main man is the time drawing near when he will have to pass on that mantle?

The Old Trafford hierarchy were certainly open to that idea when Al-Hilal came calling last year with the offer of a £100million transfer fee and untold riches for Fernandes himself.

The player decided to stay despite admitting that he was ‘hurt’ by the club’s willingness to let him go, and it paid off with an incredible season leading into last summer’s World Cup.

This year, Galatasaray tried their luck and were prepared to double Fernandes’ wages. Again, he stayed, showing admirable loyalty to a club who are no nearer winning the Premier League than when he walked through the door from Sporing Lisbon in January 2020.

It would be a shame if Fernandes’ time at Old Trafford yielded only a FA Cup and Carabao Cup, but that might well be as good as it gets.

The 32-year-old will be out of contract at the end of June, although United have the option to extend it by another 12 months. Talks over a new deal have started, but there is no sign of a breakthrough anytime soon. On current form, would United want to renew?

In a summer that saw United offload Casemiro but fail to find a buyer for Marcus Rashford, would it have been better to have moved their other big earner off the books, particularly with Tielemans coming in?

Time will tell. Fernandes’ track record tells you that the loss of form is only temporary and it won’t be long before he proves the doubters wrong. That Tielemans’ ownership of the No.10 spot is shortlived and Fernandes will soon be back pulling the strings like he always does.

The longer this goes on, though, the louder the questions will grow – and the more people will wonder if one of the few great United careers in the post-Ferguson era is drawing to a close.

Career highs include working at the FA Cup final, as well as scoring at Old Trafford in front of the Stretford End. A long-term sufferer of his beloved Scunthorpe United, he is often seen on the padel court, as well as occasionally as a six-a-side call-up.

#216. Boyd criticises Hearts’ ‘lack of respect’ as Celtic deliver ‘wake-up call’

Celtic beat Hearts 7-1 to move four points clear at the top of the Scottish Premiership; Hearts have not won outside Edinburgh since January; Martin O'Neill's side are away to Hibernian in their next league game on October 25, live on Sky Sports; Hearts face Motherwell on same day

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hearts returned to Celtic Park looking for revenge but were taught a lesson by the side who snatched the Scottish Premiership title from their grasp.

After last season's final-day showdown, the Hoops reminded Wouter Vrancken's team what it takes to win the league trophy with a "devastating" performance.

It is a result that moves Martin O'Neill's men four points clear at the top of the table with Hearts left in third, a further four points behind Rangers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Encouraged by their second-half showing in Thursday's 3-1 Europa League defeat to Benfica, the manager started with the front three that finished that game in Lisbon.

And all three - Benjamin Nygren, Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran - scored in the 7-1 demolition of their title rivals.

Celtic were outstanding at times but Hearts played a part in their own humiliation.

"That first half was devastating. Hearts, I cannot for the life of me work out what they were trying to do there," said Kris Boyd.

"To come here and show the lack of respect to Celtic that Hearts have done today would be a wake-up call for me.

"You look at last year, Derek McInnes [then Hearts boss] got criticised for it from a lot of people in terms of just grinding out results. It may be an ugly watch but they were still there.

"I don't see any of that Hearts team that's going in the Celtic team. I don't see any of it, so what would make you think you're better than them?"

"That there was an annihilation. I mean, I have never seen anything like it in my life."

Hearts had only conceded eight goals in the Premiership this season, before shipping seven in 90 minutes at Celtic Park.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I couldn't work out if Hearts were really poor or Celtic were really good. It's probably a combination of the two of them," said former Hearts defender Ryan McGowan.

"The amount of times that Hearts gave the ball away in really dangerous areas for Celtic, and there would only be two passes and it was a goal, and they continually did it throughout the whole game.

"There is levels to football. Hearts obviously last season went close and this season they want to challenge it and be up there. But you also have to understand the game.

"They're 5-1 down at half-time and then whatever the manager said to them went completely out of their ears because then they conceded another goal four minutes into the second half.

"It was a really poor performance from Hearts, which you haven't said that often in the last 12 months. At the same time, you've got to give Celtic a lot of credit."

It was all too easy for Celtic on Sunday but that did not mean Martin O'Neill was ruling Hearts out of this season's title race after just nine games.

"It's easy to be magnanimous after the game but they're still big challengers," the 74-year-old told Sky Sports.

"Everything clicked for us today. We might have had two more chances but everything that we hit went into the net.

"It was nice to win today because I was concerned after Thursday night, wondering how we feel, can we get ourselves together for it?

"You ask any manager or any team, any player, they would say the same thing. Once you've put a couple of goals in front, then confidence just is so strong.

"The team played with a lot of confidence but you have to gain that confidence in the first place. And that's what we did today."

While Celtic welcome Benfica in the Europa League on Thursday night, Hearts are away to Trabzonspor in the Conference League.

"When you're not on top level in the top games, then it's really difficult to get a result," Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken told Sky Sports.

"It's good to analyse it, also the good things. Knowing where we come from and not losing the grip and confidence in what you're doing. We just have to do things better than today.

"It was not good enough because of the individual mistakes and the two set plays which killed us at the beginning of the game.

"We made mistakes that we wouldn't normally make. That's it. I'm sorry."
