#218. Eric Cantona, Frank Worthington, Faustino Apsrilla and the rest of the footballing mavericks who rocked the beautiful game

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Fantastic football content straight to your inbox! From the latest transfer news, quizzes, videos, features and interviews with the biggest names in the game, plus lots more.

Sign up to our FREE live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest games available to watch on the device of your choice. Never miss a kick-off!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Some former footballers were just quintessentially rock’n’roll, whether they were music buffs, style icons or hellraisers – or all three…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Football has always had its mavericks, but some players couldn't help but take things to another level.

From wild nights out and outrageous antics to long hair, leather jackets and a love of loud guitars, these were the footballers who brought a genuine rock ’n’ roll spirit to the beautiful game.

FourFourTwo runs down some of the players who proved that football and rock ’n’ roll were a match made in heaven...

At Baileys nightclub in Leicester in 1975, Frank Worthington dressed up as Elvis Presley and belted out the hits of the King of Rock’n’Roll.

The iconic forward worshipped Elvis and did his best to emulate that rock’n’roll lifestyle throughout a career in which he netted more than 250 goals and was idolised pretty much everywhere he went.

Hailing from Halifax, Worthington defied the stereotype of the no-nonsense northerner, displaying sublime skills on the field for Huddersfield Town, and living a flamboyant life off it, turning up for an England under 23s match in cowboy boots.

A 1972 move to Liverpool collapsed after he was found to have high blood pressure, with Bill Shankly initially sending him off to Majorca for a week to sort himself out. How did he use the time? He consorted with five different women, including a former Miss Great Britain, before returning to Merseyside with even higher blood pressure, and failing the medical again.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

A notorious womaniser, he later named his autobiography [i]One Hump Or Two?[/i] “I was living a bit too much in the fast lane,” he admitted. Not always heading in the right direction, either: once, he had four court appearances in a year because of his driving – one was for doing a U-turn on the motorway in his Ford Mustang.

Defenders had no more of a clue which way he was going – after starring for Leicester, he scored a memorable goal for Bolton against Ipswich when he picked up the ball with his back to goal outside the area, juggled it, flicked it over both his own head and the head of a bamboozled Terry Butcher, then volleyed it into the net, all in one motion. Trotters boss Ian Greaves labelled him ‘the working man’s George Best’.

Greaves had also been his manager at Huddersfield – once growing tired of Worthington playing Elvis tapes on the team bus, ejecting the cassette and throwing it out of the window. It didn’t curtail the forward’s love of the King – when he moved to Sunderland, he’d turn up at training dressed as Elvis.

Despite his talent, Worthington earned only eight England caps – the cowboy boots at the under 23 game didn’t endear him to Alf Ramsey, and he irritated future Three Lions boss Don Revie with some showboating against Leeds, amid a perception that he wasn’t committed enough. “I admit that I used to get about a bit, but I’m quieter these days,” he insisted in 1978. “Instead of going out seven nights a week, I keep it to six."

Liam Gallagher claimed that Cantona “ruined my life in the ’90s”, so brilliant was he for Manchester United, the big rivals of Gallagher’s Manchester City.

Yet the singer’s respect for him was so great that he later invited King Eric to star in the video for his 2020 single Once, dressed in full regal attire.

Cantona always created magic on the pitch, but he was banned for a kung-fu tackle on an opponent during his time at Auxerre, then infamously repeated it on a fan at Selhurst Park. This led to the

Frenchman’s lengthy ban and enigmatic musings about seagulls and trawlers.

In true rock-star style, he abruptly quit in his prime, at the age of 30. “Cantona was the last rock ’n’ roll footballer,” declared Gallagher, still going at 52.

The left-back may not have been a flair player like Worthington, but he became something of an indie icon during 15 years in the Premier League.

Baines became known for taking a guitar with him on England away trips and even penned a regular music blog for Everton’s official website, hailing the likes of Tame Impala, The xx, Can, Lana Del Rey and The Black Keys, some before they became bonafide superstars.

Like former Evertonian Pat Nevin before him, Baines had his finger on the pulse, and also adopted the sideburns of a mod for some of his career. “He’s a quiet lad, but as I got to know him, it became clear he was a massive music fan,” explained singer Miles Kane, having become pals with the defender. “We started talking music, listening and swapping tracks. He put me on to Tame Impala before they hit it off.”

Now assistant manager at Everton, the full-back even inspired Irish band The Baines to name themselves after him. There can be no greater rock’n’roll credential.

In an era when most German footballers were still listening to banal schlager music, Netzer was paying closer attention to The Rolling Stones and Bob Dylan.

A rebel from the start, Netzer’s long flowing locks were unheard of in the Bundesliga in the late 1960s – no-one could match his passing ability either, as the playmaker spearheaded Borussia Monchengladbach’s rise from the second tier to two German titles, earning the nickname Karajan, after a famous Austrian conductor. Netzer was also the star as West Germany took England apart at Wembley during qualifying for Euro 1972, before helping his country win the tournament that summer.

An aversion to authority meant he didn’t always see eye to eye with club boss Hennes Weisweiler: keen to conserve his energy for the key moments during games, rather than worrying about things like running around or tackling, he’d also worried his manager by opening a nightclub. “This is the end,” Weisweiler groaned, concerned about the distractions it would lead to. Previously, Netzer had nearly killed himself after crashing his yellow Ferrari, ruling himself out of the 1970 World Cup.

When the midfielder agreed to join Real Madrid in 1973, an irked Weisweiler dropped him for the DFB Pokal final – Netzer refused to come on as a half-time sub, then told the exhausted Christian Kulik to go off ahead of extra-time. “Now I’m playing,” he told Weisweiler, having subbed himself on, before scoring the winner.

Unwilling to cut his hair when he moved to Madrid, he twice won La Liga during three years in Spain but once took advantage of a two-week injury lay-off to covertly fly to Las Vegas without permission, after being invited to the wedding of Frank Sinatra’s daughter Tina. Obtaining a second passport and sneaking through Madrid airport in disguise, he was sat alongside Sammy Davis Jr and Neil Diamond at a Sinatra concert on the night before the wedding, while his team-mates were playing a game against Real Murcia that weekend.

Back in Madrid days later, oblivious team-mate Ignacio Zoco asked Netzer if he’d watched any TV that weekend. The German said no. “Sinatra’s comeback show was on TV,” said Zoco, who was engaged to singer Maria Ostiz. “Maria swears there was a guy in the audience who looked just like you – you must have a doppelganger.” It would be decades before Zoco found out the truth.

The legendary goalkeeper didn’t just use his hands to keep out some of the world’s best strikers – he also developed a talent for drumming.

The Czech Republic star launched his own YouTube channel, featuring videos of himself drumming along to System Of A Down, Coldplay, Thirty Seconds To Mars, Rammstein and others. Asked by FFT which band he’d join if he had the chance, past or present, he said: “Nirvana or Foo Fighters – I was always a fan of Dave Grohl.”

Cech did join folk rock band Wills & The Willing for their song Iceberg, and even released a charity single with Queen’s Roger Taylor. He’s got rhythm.

After eschewing an umbrella at Wembley to defeat The Wally With The Brolly and guide Croatia to Euro 2008, Bilic promptly recorded his own song for the tournament, too.

The former centre-back was a guitarist in the rock band Rawbau, having fallen in love with the genre as a child. “I couldn’t imagine my life without music,” he once told FFT. “For my birthday when I was 10 or 11, my father took me to a shop and bought me my first record: Highway to Hell by AC/DC. For me it was Iron Maiden, AC/DC, Judas Priest, Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath, then Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth and Guns N’ Roses.

“My brother is three years older, and you get everything from your brother. The guitar was in the corner of our room, and I’d pretend to play it like I was Angus Young of AC/DC.”

In 1996, by then a Croatia international defender, Bilic joined West Ham from German side Karlsruher. “I knew every word of every Iron Maiden song, and they’re big West Ham fans,” he explained. “After I signed, I went to the players lounge one day and thought ‘My god, is that Steve Harris?’ Ian Bishop had invited him because they were friends. We spoke and I was almost shaking.

“The first time I saw them live was in Manchester, and they invited me backstage after the gig. I thought ‘Oh, it’s going to be like what you read about in those autobiographies, with the parties and everything’. But when I opened the door, one of the band members was blow-drying his daughter’s hair! We’re still friends and text each other.”

Music helped him cope with life after playing, too. “When I had to retire early, I wasn’t in a good place,” he said. “I was into the guitar, though, and wrote some songs, lyrics, riffs – then I felt good again. I had some friends in music and we started jamming, then recorded some songs. Then Hajduk Split asked me to take over and the rest is history.”

Seven years later, Bilic had guided Croatia to the Euros when his band released the song Vatreno Ludilo (Fiery Madness). The title summed up their tournament: they thought they’d scored a 119th-minute winner in the quarters against Turkey, only to dramatically concede in the 122nd minute, then lose a penalty shoot-out.

Bilic has since had spells as manager of West Ham, West Bromwich Albion and Watford – sacked by the trigger-happy Hornets after less than six months. Fire-y madness, in that instance.

Burgos wasn’t content to be a guitarist – the former Atletico Madrid goalkeeper wanted to sing.

A huge bloke with long unkempt hair, who sometimes took to the stage topless, it’s perhaps no surprise that his vocals were a little rough and ready at times. He wasn’t about to challenge Adele for any awards, but the shot-stopper looked the part on stage, releasing five singles with his bands The Garb and the Burgos Simpatia (‘Burgos Sympathy’), drawing on influences from AC/DC to Guns N’ Roses.

Nicknamed Mono (‘Monkey’), he even performed songs on TV shows during a playing career that saw him represent Argentina 35 times, before becoming Diego Simeone’s long-serving assistant manager at Atleti. Bad cop and even badder cop – scary stuff.

When FourFourTwo asked Pete Doherty which former QPR player he’d bring back to play for the Loftus Road club’s current team, he didn’t have to think for long.

“Stan Bowles,” explained the Libertines wild child. “I always wonder how someone like him would fit in today’s game. I’d love to see him drifting around scratching his leg on the halfway line, give him the ball and see what the 24-year-old Stan Bowles could do. They thought it was funny back then when he’d take a programme off a fan and read it halfway through the game, but now he’d probably get fined and banned for two matches.”

Bowles left QPR in the year that Doherty was born, but his legend lived on – he was later voted the club’s greatest ever player.

Born in the north west, he started his career at Manchester City before a nightclub row with boss Malcolm Allison, then a spell at Bury, where manager Ernie Tagg remarked that “if he could pass a bookies as well as he passes a football, he’d be a very rich man”. The gambling addict was said to sometimes pause during games and ask fans with transistor radios whether they knew the latest horse racing results.

He possessed supreme ability, though – as a Carlisle player, he remarkably helped them beat Roma in the Anglo-Italian Cup at the Stadio Olimpico, angering the home crowd by doing keepy-uppies mid-match. The replacement for Rodney Marsh at QPR, he won five England caps and claimed to have deliberately sent the FA Cup trophy flying during a match at Sunderland. Days after the Wearsiders had won the cup, it had been placed pitchside by the halfway line for a Second Division fixture.

“There were a couple of us who had a bet on who could knock it off the table with the ball,” he said. “With the ball at my feet, I tore off straight across the park. The whole ground knew I’d done it on purpose.”

A spell at Brian Clough’s Nottingham Forest wasn’t successful – he walked out on the 1980 European Cup final after the manager left him out of John Robertson’s testimonial match, but his rock’n’roll lifestyle resulted in a song that reached number 36 in the charts.

"It was about Stan and my mate Peter Doherty,” explained Dominic Masters of The Others, after releasing the song [i]Stan Bowles[/i] in 2004. “Pete Doherty is the Stan Bowles of the music world, and Stan Bowles was the Pete Doherty of the football world.”

The Spaniard met FFT in central London in 2019 – immediately grabbing a guitar, leaping into the air and demanding that we took his photo.

OK, that might not be quite how it happened – we’d actually hired the Gibson LP Gold Top from a nearby guitar store for the photoshoot, after hearing he was a huge rock fan. He’d even played guitar on stage alongside band Los Planetas at the Benicassim Festival in his homeland.

“I like Wolf Alice at the moment,” he explained, after spending a good minute just admiring the guitar we’d brought along. “British music is so rich. When I played in Spain, no one had the same taste in music as me. They’d put on rap in the dressing room and I’d think ‘OK, come on, that’s enough now!’”

Long before Osvaldo quit football to take up music, he was displaying true rock’n’roll credentials – just by generally acting like a nutter.

The Argentina-born Italy international was suspended by Roma in 2011 for punching team-mate Erik Lamela in the face during an argument – well, he did have one of those faces – then was sold after rowing with caretaker boss Aurelio Andreazzoli and refusing to attend an awards ceremony.

It led to a £12.8m move to Southampton, where he turned Vincent Kompany inside out then chipped the goalkeeper against Manchester City, but was soon banned for three matches for a touchline fracas, then headbutted team-mate Jose Fonte during a training ground incident and never played for the club again.

At Inter, he fell out with Mauro Icardi (not exactly a stranger to falling out with team-mates himself), and was suspended for not turning up for training. At Boca Juniors, he had a contretemps with the manager for smoking in the dressing room, and was fired.

His response? To quit football at 30 and focus on music. “People look at me like ‘You're crazy, you played in some of the best teams in the world and you decided just to quit to do this?’” he admitted. “They don’t understand – it’s my passion.”

Months later, Jorge Sampaoli tried to persuade him to change his mind and sign for Sevilla, but was unsuccessful. “He told me ‘Dani, I’m not asking anything of you, you can do what you want on the pitch and off it, but I need a striker’,” Osvaldo explained. “I said ‘But boss, there’s the Cosquin Rock festival!’”

The Rolling Stones fan played gigs in Barcelona as the frontman of his own band, Barrio Viejo – with a beard, tattoos and often a look of Johnny Depp, he also later appeared on Italy’s version of Dancing With The Stars. "There are so many rules in football, and I’m not good with the rules, I like to be free,” he added. “I was going crazy and decided to live the musician’s life instead.”

Osvaldo did return to football to join Banfield on a one-year contract in 2020, but lasted only six months. At least he got out of there without headbutting anyone…

The ginger-haired goatee king was the stand-out character of the USA team that played the 1994 World Cup on home soil, and has also released not one but eight solo albums over the past three decades.

An avid fan of glam metal band Ratt, Lalas shot to fame thanks to his unusual look and his goal in the USA’s shock win over Graham Taylor’s hapless England in 1993 – everything about the centre-back absolutely screamed ‘early Premier League years transfer to Coventry City’, but sadly a move to Highfield Road fell through after the World Cup, and they had to settle for Cobi Jones instead.

Lalas meanwhile concentrated on opening for Hootie & The Blowfish during their 1998 European tour, with his band The Gypsies, and releasing a never-ending list of albums – Far from Close, Ginger, So It Goes, Infinity Spaces, Shots, Sunshine, Look at You and Melt Away

Few managers celebrate promotion by posing for photos at the training ground, using a corner flag as a microphone. But Ainsworth has always been a little bit different.

When the long-haired former Preston, Lincoln and Wimbledon winger moved into management with Wycombe, he wasn’t about to don a tracksuit on the touchline – instead, he favoured an open-necked shirt and even red cowboy boots during the Chairboys’ successful League One play-off campaign in 2020. “I don’t want to copy anyone else,” he insisted, of his managerial style. “If I did, it would probably be Jim Morrison or Michael Hutchence.”

Ainsworth has always been a rocker at heart, continuing as the lead singer of a band while managing in the EFL. “We’re keeping the Cold Blooded Hearts going and recording our own stuff,” he told FFT in 2020. “It’s been difficult because football takes over – it was much easier when I was playing and in the band Dog Chewed The Handle. Monday night is rehearsal night these days – although if we get a Monday night game on Sky, I may have to change that.”

He’s now manager of Gillingham, via a spell at Shrewsbury and a stint at QPR, where he went left-field in a different way, bringing in a Maori performer to do a performance for the squad at the training ground, in full traditional costume. Many of them were baffled.

Later asked by FFT for his opinion on the greatest rock album of all time, Ainsworth thought carefully. “I have an all-time favourite band, which needs mentioning before we get to the album – I’m such a massive fan of The Doors,” he explained. “I was a teenager when the 1991 documentary about the Doors came out and I was blown away, so anything by them is basically my idea of heaven.

“But if I’m just picking a single album, and I’m in a real rock‘n’roll mood, I’d actually have to pick a different band. In 1987, I went down to my local record shop in Blackburn and I picked up a vinyl copy of Guns N’ Roses’ Appetite for Destruction. I couldn’t believe what I was hearing and it’s still one I reach for to get the blood pumping. I have to put that down as my number one all-time album.”

Did the album title inspire his use of 16-stone human wrecking ball Adebayo Akinfenwa at Wycombe? We may never know.

Colombia’s early 90s side was one of the most rock’n’roll teams in history – take your pick from afro-meister Carlos Valderrama, rampaging goalkeeper Rene Higuita or Asprilla, who was 50 per cent genius, 50 per cent madman.

Having earned himself a move to Serie A with Parma, Asprilla then conspired to miss out on playing in a single minute of the 1993 European Cup Winners’ Cup final, after injuring himself kicking a bus door during a trip back to Colombia. “A bus driver smashed into my car – when I got out to get onto the bus, he shut the door on me, so I kicked it,” he later told FFT.

“I was furious. If I’d got into the bus, I would have hit him, but he escaped. I’m a bit calmer nowadays.”

Mere months after that 2008 interview, the former Newcastle striker displayed his new zen state, by being arrested for allegedly firing a machine gun at security forces near his farm. He’s been involved in rather less controversy in recent times, instead focusing his time on teaching his horse how to play football, by riding it while wearing a Tyrannosaurus Rex costume – there’s video footage and everything. Never change, Tino.

Chris joined FourFourTwo in 2015 and has reported from more than 20 countries, in places as varied as Ivory Coast and the Arctic Circle. He's interviewed Pele, Zlatan and Santa Claus (it's a long story), as well as covering the World Cup, AFCON and the Clasico. He previously spent 10 years as a newspaper journalist, and completed the 92 in 2017.

#219. Journey to Wembley: Halifax reach first round in a beloved stadium they may soon lose - as ambitious South Shields' FA Cup dreams fizzle out for another year

By IAN HERBERT, DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 02:00 BST, 19 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 19 October 2026

FA Cup Fourth Qualifying Round: FC Halifax 3-2 South Shields

There is not even a sign carrying the club’s name on the exterior walls of FC Halifax’s famous old stadium, which the council wants to sell, but memories of knocking a star-studded Manchester City side out of the FA Cup in 1980 are providing sustenance in tough times, an hour before kick-off on Saturday afternoon.

One of the Halifax Town directors back then, Andrew Hodgson, is remembering being part of the small group, including City manager Malcolm Allison, who gathered with the referee for an inspection of the half-frozen, half-boggy pitch on which the then-Fourth Division side triumphed 1-0.

‘The game should never have been played,’ Hodgson relates, over his beer in the supporters’ bar. ‘But Mal Allison wanted it to be played. Insisted it should be played. City were that cocky. So convinced that they didn’t even need a good pitch to beat us on. We thought all our birthdays had come at once. Great days.’

We are here in Halifax, west Yorkshire, with South Shields, on the sixth instalment of our journey to Wembley told through all 13 rounds, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final. And though the team from the Tyneside coast are 20 places and one league lower than their hosts, they are the ones with all the ambition now.

With their directors as they draw up here is American investment banker Gordon McBean, who is helping Shields access US capital markets. ‘There is a huge appetite in the US for the Cinderella stories of clubs from working class places,’ McBean says. ‘But it takes money and capital to grow.’

Shields have just spent another week in the maelstrom of activity that is accompanying the arrival of their new Chinese/American ownership consortium.

Halifax knocked South Shields out in a 3-2 thriller to reach the FA Cup first round - a boon amid fears that the council will sell off their stadium

Supporters raise funds for the club to buy equipment by selling merchandise

When we drop into the club, a few days out from this fourth qualifying round FA Cup tie, a Chinese executive currently providing commercial expertise is hot desking with other staff in a small meeting room overlooking the pitch. A lunchtime in the company of Shields manager Mike Williamson takes place against the din of builders creating a new reception area at the training ground.

The discussion with Williamson centres on Shields’ ambitions to develop players who have not made it at nearby Newcastle United, Sunderland and Middlesbrough’s academies, and the former Magpies defender certainly brings nuance to how that might happen. ‘Some lads are so full of fear that it stops them working hard. It looks like they don’t care when they do — but that’s just a self-protection mechanism,’ he says.

‘They’re so scared of failing that if they invest their whole life and fail, they feel far more vulnerable. They don’t realise that if you don’t give your everything you will always have an excuse. That’s the toughest part — the lads who never really fulfil it. It’s not always a question of lads not being good enough.’

He speaks from the perspective of a football career which saw him play at every level from Shields’ current tier to the Premier League and face rejection and criticism along the way.

This all feels a million miles away from the reality of FC Halifax, the club formed in 2008 just a month after Halifax Town were wound up. There was an acceleration up through the non-leagues, but the Shay looks a careworn place now, and it is the fans who are keeping the spirit alive.

This is the first stadium on our journey which has lacked its own official club shop but the Supporters’ Club have been providing a ‘pop up’ one for the past few years, selling everything from darts shirts, school satchels and ‘Spirit of the Shay’ gin, produced by a local distillery, from a storage space beneath the main stand. The proceeds go towards buying equipment for the team, from winter coats to training ground covers.

‘We ask the coaching staff what they need and settle the invoice,’ says Phil Merrifield, Supporters’ Club vice-chairman whose wife, Lesley, is among a group of five people helping him out. ‘It’s good to have this space,’ he adds. ‘For a long time, we had to load it in and out of our car. We live out in Doncaster so it’s a long way to bring it.’

The evidence of how much this means to the playing staff is self-evident. Manager John McGrath, kit man Mark Bett and goalkeeping coach Jon Stewart all call in to express their gratitude as they arrive for this game. McGrath’s players wave as they walk past.

Halifax fans are proud of their club, who are regulars in the National League play-offs

South Shields have big ambitions under an arriving Chinese/American ownership consortium, but their FA Cup journey has come to an end

Managers Mike Williamson (left, South Shields) and John McGrath (right, Halifax) shake hands

In the club bar, there are groans as it emerges that a match programme will not be published for the game, though the far greater concern is the jeopardy surrounding the club’s future at this iconic old ground, where Paul Hendrie’s 78th-minute goal in the mud sank City.

Calderdale Council wanted to sell it to the owner of the Huddersfield Giants rugby league team and though campaigners staved that off, there are now two other private bidders. The club’s owner, Leeds-based businessman David Bosomworth, whose investment on the playing side has kept the club competitive in the fifth tier, is not among them.

A tantalising reminder of how precious a big Cup run looks like was dangled in front of South Shields just a week ago when they arrived for their league match at Macclesfield. Home supporters were still wearing their half-and-half scarves from last winter’s third-round giant-killing against Crystal Palace. But Shields surrendered a 3-1 lead to lose 4-3 that afternoon and were outmuscled.

They carry their town’s motto — ‘Always Ready’ — wherever they go, but their technical game, prioritising passing through the lines above physicality, is by no means flawless. Aerially, they are vulnerable.

For all that strategic direction and focus, it is little less than a thumping for the first 45 minutes against Halifax. Conor Carty, the 24-year-old Irish striker signed this summer, heads the home side ahead from Connor Douglas’ cross. That Shields aerial weakness again.

Max Bardell poaches a second from close range and barely 20 minutes in, Carty has contributed a third. It might have been five at the interval, by which time Ben Tollitt has crashed a shot against a post.

Shields’ former Leicester City academy player Toby Onanaye adds such spirit when arriving from the bench that you wonder why he did not start. He scores spectacularly, after team-mate Cedwyn Scott’s goal has brought Shields back into it.

But it is an emphatic win for a side whose player budget has been in the bottom quartile of the National League these past few years. So much lies up ahead for South Shields, who we leave behind after a month on this journey.

A good FA Cup run can boost the finances of a lower-league club for seasons to come

Non-league players often balance the demands of football with other jobs, though the fifth tier is mostly professionalised

Home supporters enjoying a chat during the half-time break as Halifax beat South Shields 3-2

The ribbon was cut only last week on a cafe, called The Coal Face, which their charitable community foundation has opened at the Harton and Westoe Miners Welfare building, site of an old colliery pithead, which co-owner Geoff Thompson has saved from redevelopment.

The miners’ sanctuary is alive and thriving once more and the foundation has generated £45million in revenue for the community in the past five years.

A promotional film about the club has been developed to stimulate creative interest as the Shields’ owners look to put its story before audiences in China or the US.

Tyneside musician Jade Thirlwall, the former Little Mix singer and successful solo artist, wants to help and will look to do so as she arrives home to the North East for the 2026 Mercury Prize event in Newcastle this week. She and her family are confirmed Shields fans. This club’s journey will be fascinating to follow.

Halifax are the ones who feel in greater need of the FA Cup’s restorative powers, though, and they will head into the first round proper — a holy grail for lower-league sides — with the folk memory of clobbering that ultra-confident Manchester City side.

Back then, Halifax manager George Kirby recruited the help of a hypnotherapist who claimed he had previously placed a curse on Allison for an unpaid debt — though people generally feel the state of the pitch made most difference.

Nearly 50 years on, Halifax need all the help they can get.

#222. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#229. It's a game of four halves for Armadale Thistle as West Lothian club are forced to play TWICE in one day

Published: 16:10 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 21:35 BST, 18 October 2026

It is high noon in Armadale. The kick-off for Thistle’s first match of the day is in a couple of hours. A second, scheduled for 7.45pm, seems a long way off.

But what is the how and why for two games in one day?

The Schleswig-Holstein question inevitably springs to mind. This was the diplomatic rammy in the 19th century over the jurisdiction of two duchies separating Denmark and Germany.

Lord Palmerston, unaccountably not a regular presence on these pages, once remarked that the question was only fully understood by three people: the prince consort, who had died, a German professor, who had gone mad from trying to figure it out, and Lord Palmerston himself. And he had completely forgotten it.

The Two Games Question is similar. The simple answer to why Armadale had to play two matches at their Volunteer Park home on Saturday is that an East of Scotland League policy prohibits the rescheduling of league games to accommodate the Scottish Communities Cup, otherwise known as the Scottish Junior Cup to the fitba’ world at large.

There are nuances, background politics and cultural attitudes, however. There are also six leagues with varying stances on and affection for this specific cup.

Armadale players applaud their supporters after a marathon day of football at Volunteer Park

The shake-up in Scottish football with teams switching leagues and some semi-professional clubs deserting the Communities Cup therefore means that the simple answer is not the full answer.

But there is diplomacy in Armadale. Committee member Scott Watson, four hours into a shift extending from 8am to midnight, said: ‘The crux of it all is that regions want a league programme that is fixed. To try to move the game was difficult.’

He had no gripe with the league. ‘The East of Scotland League took us in when the pyramid started so we are not going to argue the toss with them. The East of Scotland League has seemed to get the hard end of the stick but it is not entirely their fault,’ he said.

The decision was made to go for the double-header. It put a strain obviously on the players. But there was a burden for the eight committee members who had to arrange two matches on one day with feeding players, arranging hospitality, cleaning dressing rooms and the ground – and then doing it all again.

It was summed up when Watson had to field a catering question while conducting interviews with the press. Asked by a volunteer if a certain tray of sandwiches was for hospitality, he replied: ‘I don’t know but tell them to go ahead. I have bought hunners of stuff.’

Armadale made light work of Dundonald Bluebell with a 4-0 East of Scotland League triumph

It is 2.30pm and game one kicks off. There is a glut of groundhoppers in attendance amid the 300 or more punters. Roy Little, 65, has only travelled from Falkirk but would match anyone for football adventures.

He confided: ‘I have seven tickets for games in the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January but I suspect it will be a no-go.’ The Houthis may stymie these plans but he consoles himself with the memory of attending the final of the Africa Cup of Nations this year. And his presence, of course, in Armadale.

Tugging on his Vasco da Gama bunnet – Brazil is one of his football haunts – to fend off the sunshine, he remarked: ‘There is a little bit of history here today. I believe this is the second time that a team in Scotland has played two games in one day.’

He was referring to Saturday, April 15, 1916, when Celtic beat Raith Rovers 6-0 (3.15pm kick off at Celtic Park) and then moved on to Fir Park to defeat Motherwell 3-1 (6pm kick-off) en route to the Scottish League Championship. The games had to be played consecutively because of fixture congestion and an unwillingness to extend the season to accommodate this.

Supporters of Orkney FC will point to their side playing two games in one day in 2020 but those games were played at the exact same time, 165 miles apart home and away, so involved two separate sets of players, unlike Armadale and Celtic.

History repeating itself further down the scale appealed to Little, whose presence in Armadale was predictable though not as exotic as his many travels

Football fanatic Roy Little has been attending matches across the globe for more than 40 years

‘I love going to games,’ he said. ‘I am a Falkirk fan but never had many opportunities to watch my team in Europe.’ This is said with a smile but he adds: ‘I suppose the whole travelling thing started in 1985 when I went to Nuremberg to watch a game.’ He has travelled extensively since.

‘When I first went abroad to games, it was before the whole groundhopping culture,’ he says. ‘Yes, there were a couple of random oddballs who travelled the world to games and I suppose I was one of them but it was not called groundhopping back then.’

Little, now retired, worked in the engineering industry. ‘I always had the wanderlust,’ he said.

His best trips? ‘South America is always brilliant,’ he said. ‘We think we are passionate in Scotland but it is on another level over there. I also have a particular affection for Dutch semi-professional football. I suppose it is about the same level as here today but the crowds can be big — more than 4,000 — at derbies.’

Armadale fans make the most of a double dose of hospitality on what proved an historic day

It is 4.18pm. The first game is won and Colin Strickland, Thistle manager, strides from the park after a successful afternoon.

‘We gave a really professional performance,’ he says. ‘It could not have gone any better. We managed to win the game and get the players off early. The lead gave us opportunities to replace some guys. Five of the players that started there will start in the evening game, but one will be a goalie. The other four were substituted.’

He adds: ‘We have known about this situation for a couple of weeks so we have been able to prepare for it and the club has been brilliant. They have provided ice baths, food, all the arrangements. We are young and fit so we are ready to go again.’

It is 6.27pm. The Scottish Junior Cup is in the house. It has been brought to the park by Kennie Young, Scottish Community FA secretary. It is closely followed by the arrival of the Stonehaven team bus.

Sarah Rollo, secretary of the Aberdeenshire club, is bullish as dusk falls: ‘It doesn’t matter what time of day we have to travel. The two-game situation does not bother us. We stay in our own lane. We think about ourselves, focus on ourselves.’

Stonehaven proved a bridge too far for Armadale as they claimed a cup triumph in the evening

The message is similar from Cameron Christie, coach. He says: ‘We will focus on what we do. It is very odd to be coming down the road at this time of day but we will take it the same as any other game.’

The step into the unknown starts at 7.45pm. With minutes to go of the cup tie, there is a goalkeeper slip and a Stonehaven shot finds the net, silencing the majority of the 600 or so fans.

It is enough to secure victory. ‘You win some and you lose some,’ says an Armadale fan. This, though, normally applies to a season rather than a day.

It is 9.30pm. There are fireworks in the distance but inside the stadium the fans drift sombrely to the exits. The longest day has ended not with a bang but a whimper.

#230. Savaged by Simon Jordan – and thanks to the algorithm I want to be savaged again | Barney Ronay

The former Palace chair seeming very angry indeed about others’ opinions is just par for the course as football’s age of rage ramps up another level

Yet again the mainstream wokealorium is preachifying from its pulpitrex. It’s egregious. It’s sanctiforial. It’s a wangitude of complete retardifaction.

This has not been an easy column to write. It has been difficult, gruelling in parts, but also warm, exhilarating and at times deeply erotic. Yes. I was SAVAGED by Simon Jordan. And I’ve never felt so alive.

You know who Simon Jordan is. Used to own Crystal Palace. Now a very good and listenable pundit on TalkSport, where he does the grown-up topics. Simon Jordan has strong opinions. This is his thing. His worldview says: the world is bad. The world is in need of correction. And he’s right about that, as he often is about things.

That’s what makes this all a bit surprising because I like Simon Jordan! I listen to his morning show with Jim White and it’s often really good. I respect the fact he has industry knowledge because he ran a football club. And yes that involved lots of dealings with Steve Bruce, Iain Dowie or similar, but it’s still basically the same thing.

I like the way he pops up in clips looking like an exquisitely powdered 17th-century Umbrian count, some gorgeous little angry blond glove-puppet I want to sit on my knee and pet and cosset and whisper in his ear about granditudinous hypocralism, in a way that’s just warm and fond and not, for me, in any way sexual, but which definitely is for him.

I like the way he talks. It reminds me of Jackie Chiles, the lawyer in Seinfeld, saying it’s outrageous, egregious, preposterous. Sometimes this can have a Mrs Malaprop edge. But that’s also fun and even then you get his point, which is usually good, even if you didn’t expect to agree, or can only agree secretly. When you’re right you’re right. When you’re veritudinously superfactual you’re veritudinously superfactual.

By now you’re probably wondering what happened. Well, I was definitely savaged. No one can take that away from me. And yes this was a week ago, but other stuff happened in between and I forgot about it for a while. I also haven’t fully listened to the savaging. It’s two minutes long and life is short.

In fact I only know about it because my friend and colleague Barry Glendenning is very reliable in this respect. If you’re ever cancelled, owned, or significantly beasted on the internet then Barry will let you know, as an act of love and kindness, and not, repeat not, because he enjoys it and is killing time in the pub on his phone. It’s like having a faithful and attentive online Lassie. What’s that? Slow down boy. Wait, you’re saying Michaela Strachan has called me a nonce? On LinkedIn? Good boy. Easy. There you go. Here’s a lovely bowl of vape oil and Guinness.

I have to admit I am also amplifying this, promoting myself as genuinely savage-worthy. In reality I was savaged in a minor, offhand way that I still don’t really get. I was at Croatia versus England in Rijeka. The game was meant to be played without fans as punishment for some Croatia-related disorder in Paris last year, which included accusations of people making Nazi salutes.

In the event the Croatian FA filled the ground with children, which is allowed under a loophole in the rules. It felt a bit weird in the moment. At the very least it didn’t seem to fit the spirit of the offence. Nazism, yes, bad. But also: a lovely day out for Year 8.

I still don’t really get why anyone would strongly disagree with this. It seems obvious enough. Yeah, everyone likes happy jolly children. Personally I believe the children are our future. I’ve always said that. But they’re not some kind of smart bomb that disintegrates the capacity for logic.

The counter-argument seems to be that this is joyless liberal Guardian stuff. It’s the woke mind-virus. It’s being too interested in not promoting nazism, when you should simply enjoy the laughter of little boys.

And yes Simon Jordan is right. It is annoying to be preached at. But we’re not talking libtard snowflake stuff here. We’re talking actual Nazis, people who just like and enjoy swastikas, who talk fondly about the Ustase, arguably the most vicious sect of the Third Reich war machine. I don’t know, man. The more I hear about the Nazis, the less I like the sound of them.

Plus we now have the sight of Hajduk Split fans this week walking behind an actual coffin and chanting “Auschwitz”. Does this seem like the message is being hammered home? At the very least we’re going to need more children. How many is this one going to take? Ten thousand? Maybe if we can get children to carry a coffin through Amsterdam then it’s fine and just a heartwarming event that shows lessons are being learned.

This is how it goes you see. You are supposed to LASH BACK in these situations. But it’s all a bit weird. Suddenly Simon Jordan is attacking me with children. He’s barging me out of the way in Starbucks with his mega-buggy, one hand clutched to his pearl-draped throat, saying, what about the children, the children, the children?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

You see? I’m being sucked in. Because this is what the internet will do to you. I wasn’t even the main savaging that day. I was a side-beef, an afterthought. By now the algorithm is already filling my feed with fresh SJ face-offs, the latest a “heated exchange” with Dale Vince about Robbie Savage, in itself a mouthwatering trio, perpetual savaging motion in action.

In the end this is the only real point of interest here. This stuff is utterly addictive. And with good reason: it’s designed to be. Vast amounts of expertise and resources have been poured into this irresistible machinery. David Squires did a brilliant cartoon this week about the rise of the celebrity football chat-cast, the industrial-scale, seed-funded waffle that must now justify its space by shouting above the noise, and which will always tend towards beef-culture and a narrative of opposition.

I’ve tried really hard to stay out of this. I don’t do radio or TV stuff, because, well, what’s the point, but more because nobody’s clean, nobody escapes, suddenly you’re having a charity boxing grudge-match with Stephen Warnock.

But it is worth logging for the record that we are at fever pitch. The level of rage around football right now is genuinely astonishing. The story of the Manchester City verdict is, in part, a regulatory ruling over a breach of financial rules. But really it’s the astonishing post-truth online response, the urge to assail and objectify and dehumanise over a tribunal’s interpretation of accountancy practices.

Just going to report on a game at the Etihad this week involved BRAVELY DEFYING assorted threats of violence in response to articles written in these pages. And yes, these are clearly the work of a 77-year-old hunchback in Jakarta, or a drunk and bored corporate lawyer taking a break from surfing porn on the family computer.

But it is all part of the design too. This is meant to happen. A new book called Our Minds Under Siege by Bruno Giussani, a former global curator of TED, describes the way algorithm life is actively changing human behaviour. This is not a secret. Marketing has wanted to do this since the early 20th century.

Walter Dill Scott’s Theory of Suggestion. The Drive Theory of Motivation. The deliberate creation of want and anxiety into the way we sell things. And now we have a new and commercially irresistible language. Dopamine craving. Variable social validation. The feedback loop.

The way even random scrolling is controlled and metered, designed to create a craving that’s always there inside your head, and controlled by tech platforms that openly define humans as eyeballs, want, need, hunger.

In the end, this is why Simon Jordan seems to care so violently about someone else’s opinions on the children-washing of Uefa sanctions. It’s why I’m just incredibly excited by this as an outcome, why I want more not less. Savage me again. Make me feel something. Let me exist inside the machine with you, egregious, preposterous, vibramoniously alive.

#237. Houthi conflict casts shadow as Saudi Arabia scales back sporting pipe dreams

A match delayed by missile attack warnings is not what Cristiano Ronaldo and co signed up for but it’s the new reality; the Saudi sporting juggernaut is stalling

Cristiano Ronaldo grabbed the scarf in the colours of the Saudi Arabian flag and waved it at the sparse but enthusiastic crowd, who responded with rapturous cheers. It was a gesture of defiance rather than a victory salute, encapsulating the Saudi equivalent of “Keep calm and carry on”.

Monday night’s Asian Champions League Elite game between Al-Nassr and the Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana had ended with a 3-1 win for the Saudi club coached by Ange Postecoglou, with Ronaldo, supported by Sadio Mané, scoring, the smattering of star names indicative of the lure of the Saudi Pro League. Yet this isn’t quite how Ronaldo and co would have anticipated life in Riyadh. The meagre attendance aside, Monday’s game was delayed by a threat of missile attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. A safety warning issued 15 minutes before kick-off came two days after 13 people died and more than 300 were wounded by Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport.

Saudi Arabia’s hosting of football’s Asian Cup in January and February is being questioned – it insists preparations are on track – and a combination of rapidly changing geopolitics and a reality check being applied to the more quixotic projects means the kingdom’s position in the sporting landscape looks hugely different from a year ago. Golf’s Asian Tour has postponed next month’s Saudi International indefinitely, next month’s cycling urban world championship in Riyadh has been cancelled, the Fifa esports World Cup – which had been due to start on Friday – has been postponed and the Six Kings Slam tennis event, due to be held next week, has been pushed back until late December.

Alongside the humiliating collapse of LIV Golf, the planned 2029 Saudi Winter Asian Games has been relocated to Kazakhstan, which has actual mountains with snow. In the football sphere, it has been reported that five proposed new stadiums for the 2034 World Cup may not be built. One of them is the Neom stadium, which was planned with an elevation of 350 metres, after huge cuts to the fantastical city development project known as the Line.

In September last year there were signs all might not be what it seemed. At a Washington DC investment thinktank the Newcastle chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan, dressed in suit and tie, very much in sync with the patrician vibe of the event, addressed hedge fund chiefs and entrepreneurs along with the private equity billionaire David Rubenstein.

Unsurprisingly, Newcastle’s Carabao Cup triumph was barely mentioned. Al-Rumayyan was principally there as the chair of Aramco, the Saudi oil company, and as the governor of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), the country’s largest sovereign wealth fund. PIF is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler of the kingdom and the man accused by US intelligence of approving the murder of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi.

Al-Rumayyan took time, in between banter about how the result of his golf match with Donald Trump was a “state secret”, to lecture the audience on history and why the need for Saudi to divest from oil was existential

“Portugal was one of the richest countries in the world with all the gold that they had,” he said. “And that’s like a disease. That’s what the crown prince always talks about … ‘We have the oil disease.’ We cannot rely only on oil because this will make you more dormant, less active. We have growth in population and we need to find new jobs for new people coming. Seventy-five per cent of Saudis are under the age of 35. We need to give them the quality of life they deserve and find them jobs. We cannot just rely on one commodity. We don’t want to do the same mistakes that [other] great nations have made.”

The unspoken threat alluded to by al-Rumayyan is that a nation of “dormant” young men in the birthplace of Osama bin Laden could turn to radical Islam, as the 15 Saudi nationals among the 9/11 bombers did. And now there is the prospect that the Houthi missiles and the US war with Iran may jeopardise the best-laid Saudi state plans.

“If the war affects the ability of the regime economically – by which I mean [creating] jobs – then potential for unrest grows,” says Christopher Davidson, author of From Sheikhs to Sultanism: Statecraft and Authority in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. “If rulers fail to deliver on jobs for a massive youth bulge, the seductive message of online forums becomes even more compelling for young men.”

LIV was part of that shift to leisure investments and was al-Rumayyan’s brainchild, if that’s the correct word for a project that made a reported $6bn (£4.5bn) loss for PIF. Given the country club ambience among his Washington audience, golf was addressed and al-Rumayyan was still talking about wanting to “bring the game of golf back together” and “increasing the share of [revenue] pie”, this being six months before Saudi Arabia pulled the plug on the LIV project, which filed for bankruptcy protection in September.

Yet even in Washington al-Rumayyan was strongly hinting that entrepreneurs shouldn’t come asking for money for pet projects unless they could give something back to his country beyond financial returns, explaining that from 2021 PIF had shifted investment back towards Saudi Arabia. “The trigger for us, if we want to deploy capital with asset managers, [is that] we would like to get some of the deployment back to the country [Saudi Arabia] because we need to increase and grow our local content,” al-Rumayyan said. “One of the best ways to do so is direct foreign investment.”

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

The reassuring news for Newcastle is that a trophy investment in the Premier League will survive the overseas investment cull. “They are reducing their spending but I think football is probably ringfenced, given they’re hosting the 2034 World Cup,” says Davidson. “I would imagine the PIF funding [for Newcastle] is secure going forward.” That said, the supporters’ dreams of huge spending will never happen, as most have accepted. In the Saudi Pro League, PIF this year sold a controlling stake in Al-Hilal but it continues to own three others: Al-Nassr, Al-Ittihad and Al-Ahli.

“There is pressure from the very top in Saudi Arabia for PIF to cut some corners,” Davidson says, “and that is accelerating because of the war and more focus on their efforts at domestic economy building.”

Boxing too – assuming Saudi is safe for events – will survive the cut and esports, a $38bn slice of PIF and a proven way to divert young men from extremism, could thrive. “They require very little budget but hit an enormous audience,” Davidson says.

But a World Cup stadium in the sky, skiing in the desert and futuristic cities are out, as are any more expensive overseas money pits such as LIV. “[Trump’s] Republicans struggling in the midterm election in the USA will factor into what type of sports all the Gulf states will be thinking of investing in,” Davidson says. “LIV was seen as a project closely aligned with Trump’s passions. And that may be reduced if they see the direction [of politics] swinging.”

The Saudi Pro League and World Cup 2034, though, are very much still on the agenda, even with fewer stadiums. However, that will be reliant on the cessation of the US-Iran war and the subjugation of Houthi rebels, neither of which is likely to have featured prominently in Ronaldo’s transfer negotiations when he opted to join Al-Nassr for his career sunset in Saudi but suddenly seem very pertinent.

#239. Boos and bananas on day of defiance at Man City

Haaland nets double as Man City go six points clear at the top

It started with Manchester City supporters booing the Premier League anthem and ended with Phil Foden taking an inflatable banana into his Match of the Day interview after helping see off Ipswich to pull six points clear at the top of the table.

On a day of defiance in east Manchester, City's fans made their feelings crystal clear in their first top-flight home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.

Tens of thousands inside Etihad Stadium booed and jeered when the Premier League anthem was played over the speakers shortly before kick-off, then they started chanting 'City, City, City'.

There was a chant about playing Stockport away and the gallows humour continued when City fans sang 'You're going down with the City' to Ipswich's travelling support.

City boss Enzo Maresca, who is the first manager in Premier League history to win his first seven games in charge, said afterwards he felt the air of defiance from the stands even before kick-off.

"The environment was very good," said the Italian after a game watched by 60,817, a new record crowd at Etihad Stadium.

"The fans, the club and the players are all together on this journey."

City's best start since 1897 - but injuries a concern

Manchester Cityâs inflatable banana craze

Manchester City manager Maresca reacts to win against Ipswich Town

City fans arrived at the ground to find hundreds of inflatable bananas had been placed on seats in the home sections for fans to wave throughout the game.

They were visible in the away end at Liverpool last week but this was on a different scale and the Etihad was turned into a sea of yellow.

The inflatables are a flashback to the late '80s when what began as a light-hearted joke soon turned into one of the most memorable fan crazes in English football.

They are enjoying a revival at a time when City have appealed after being found guilty of charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating 'sham contracts' to inflate sponsorship deals by Â£830m.

There were surreal scenes at one point on Saturday as fans jeered during the Premier League anthem while waving the inflatables in the air.

"You can tell they are behind us and they're pushing us," Phil Foden said when asked about the fans after scoring on his return to the side following suspension after being sent off against Manchester United on 13 September.

Foden's 19th-minute opener was his first goal of 2026.

"It's nice to play at home and you can hear how loud they are," he added. "They're giving us that extra boost that we need."

Man City's players and fans 'fueled' by boos and bananas

Manchester Cityâs inflatable banana craze

Taking over from Pep Guardiola - 20 trophies during 10 seasons in charge - was always going to be a big challenge for Maresca.

Seven matches in, City's Premier League record remains flawless.

No points dropped, seven wins out of seven despite falling behind against Bournemouth and playing for more than an hour with 10 men at Manchester United.

"For sure I didn't expect to win seven out of seven," said Maresca. "We are working well and working good.

"I'm very happy especially with the situation in general.

"Today we controlled the game for 95 minutes. We created chances, we scored.

"We finished with a little bit of suffering together but overall, it is good."

On Foden's impressive return to action, Maresca added: "I said since day one that I love Phil. I know him from years ago and I know how good he is.

"It's a matter of helping him to again be one of the best players in the Premier League."

Despite the off-field turmoil, this is City's best start to a league season in 129 years.

Only Chelsea in 2005-06 (first nine) and Liverpool in 2019-20 (first eight) have ever won the first seven matches of a Premier League campaign.

"First of all, I am very happy because it's a matter of winning games in this business," said Maresca after the game.

"We were able to win seven in a row and what made me very happy was day by day with the players, the way they are working and how I can see them improving.

"Today I thought we controlled the game, created chances and [were] good off the ball. We are doing well and I think that's the most important thing."

On his players dealing with the events surrounding the club off the field, Maresca said: "They are not worried about people who judge from outside because they know people are trying to judge them.

"Inside, I promise the players are happy. They're getting credit and I give credit to them."

#240. Celtic's rampant, ruthless display against a so-called title rival is just what Martin O'Neill needed

Published: 20:51 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 21:16 BST, 18 October 2026

If Martin O’Neill had any lingering doubts as to whether he should have stayed on as Celtic manager, this will surely have eliminated them.

The veteran boss took a few days to weigh up his future during the international break, presumably wondering whether he had the appetite for all this at the age of 74.

But he decided to remain, and a devastating 7-1 win against Hearts, still one of Celtic’s closest challengers, will have convinced him that he was right.

Let’s not pretend that everything is suddenly rosy at a club who are coming up woefully short in Europe and contriving to infuriate supporters with their incompetence off the pitch.

But a brutal demolition of the team who pushed them so close last season was exactly the kind of statement win O’Neill needed to invigorate his squad and maintain a semblance of unity in and around Parkhead.

One thing’s for sure: nobody will be complaining if there is more of this in the weeks ahead. Celtic were ruthless, but they were also hungry and relentless all over the pitch.

Benjamin Nygren celebrates after scoring Celtic's second goal in the 7-1 thrashing of Hearts

Kieran Tierney netted an early opener before having an outstanding game at Celtic Park

Callum Osmand celebrates with fellow striker Camilo Duran after scoring Celtic's third goal

Some suggested later that it was reminiscent of the side under Ange Postecoglou, which will be music to the ears of Dermot Desmond as he seeks respite from the critics.

O’Neill, of course, is just as popular as the big Australian, but he has been searching for something this season, unsure as to the quality of his new signings and the best way to disguise his team’s faults.

Might he have stumbled on a winning formula? Prompted by successful substitutions made in the midweek defeat by Benfica, O’Neill made changes that worked a treat, most notably a first start for Callum Osmand.

Quick and direct, the young striker inspired Celtic’s breathless attack. Wide on the left is not his favoured position, but he was full of energy and ambition, certainly more than Sebastian Tounekti has offered in the same role.

Osmand, of course, was the player who completed the scoring on that momentous final day of last season when two late goals in a 3-1 win over Hearts earned Celtic a thrilling title triumph.

Here, his two goals in the space of two minutes underpinned a rampant first-half performance by Celtic. His first was a cool finish after calmly opening his body, his second a close-range header.

On the other side, Haissem Hassan was also given his chance. The Egyptian winger adds another dimension to Celtic’s attack, as he showed with one delightful spin away from his marker that resulted in a run and shot off the post.

Young Colby Donovan played his heart out at right-back, Kieran Tierney returned to his best and Camilo Duran showed his class when he peeled off Stephen Kingsley and curled in Celtic’s sixth. With the Colombia striker thriving at centre-forward, record signing Kasper Hogh can have no complaints about watching all this from the bench.

As ever, though, a degree of perspective is in order. If Celtic’s recent struggles in Europe are any guide, it will be a different story on Thursday night when Celta Vigo come calling. Dane Murray will be given a proper test at centre-half, Hassan will have to do some of the defending that he patently doesn’t fancy and the team as a whole will have to find a way of shoring up centre midfield.

What’s more, it would be a mistake to get carried away with this comprehensive dismantling of hopeless opponents. If Hearts’ intention was to go to Celtic Park and prove that they can challenge once again for the title, they failed in the most humiliating fashion. Rarely has a team purporting to be potential champions made such a feeble case.

It wasn’t so much that they were outclassed in every department (statistics, rather bizarrely, show that they had more possession and more attempts on goal than Celtic). It was that they lacked character. That they were physically and mentally weak. That they were hopelessly naive – as players in their individual duels and as a team.

Wouter Vrancken has been hailed for his work as head coach this season, but boy does he have some thinking to do – about his personnel, his tactics and how best to combine the two. This looked for all the world like a Hearts team who are not nearly as good as either they or their manager thought they were. A team and leader who had forgotten about the fundamentals.

In the first half of a ridiculously open game, it beggared belief how often Hearts’ players were left exposed at the back, victims of their casual team-mates and an over-optimistic game plan. They were half-hearted in the tackle, loose with the ball and, most worrying of all, unable to see the error of their ways. Not until they were 6-1 down did Vrancken pull off wingers Josh McPake and Calvin Miller. Never again will Celtic have it so easy against a so-called title rival.

Still, they are to be commended for taking full advantage with a barnstorming display that will boost everyone at Celtic Park. With Rangers only able to draw with Dundee on Saturday, O’Neill’s side are now four points clear of their city rivals.

They are also eight ahead of third-placed Hearts, although you wonder about the relevance of that statistic now. It may well be that this season’s title race extends into the final 11 minutes of the final game, but if it does, don’t expect the Edinburgh side to be involved.

#244. Mutiny at Watford: Why the Hornets are destined for League One

Championship side Watford are in free-fall, so much so, even legendary singer Elton John has chimed in with his dismay at the current state of affairs

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just last Friday, Watford chairman and CEO Scott Duxbury claimed on the club’s official podcast that not many Championship clubs could compete with the Hornets’ quality if their starting eleven was fully fit.

Duxbury has a long list of sensational claims that have come back to bite him and one week on, his confidence looks completely misguided.

Watford are a club with no plan, no strategy and no hope, with heavy defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City leaving the Hornets staring down the barrel of relegation to League One.

Those on the outside may think this is nothing unusual, given Watford have lurched from one crisis to another, sacked countless head coaches and never finished in the Championship’s top 10 since relegation from the Premier League in 2022.

But Watford are a club with a mutiny on their hands. In a rare move, Elton John voiced concerns over the club’s direction on social media last Saturday and since then, former players including Troy Deeney, Tom Ince and Paul Robinson have all criticised how Watford is run by Gino Pozzo.

Fans have had enough, too, after years of false promises from Pozzo and Duxbury, with supporters rallying together to call for ‘Pozzo Out’ online. Roy Moore from the leading supporters group the 1881 Movement has since been invited for a meeting with Pozzo, in a bid to quell fan pressure.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

So, how did we get here? In truth, it’s been a long time coming.

Alessio Dionisi is the latest in a series of Watford head coaches who have failed to be backed in the transfer market. The Italian has sounded exasperated at the club’s squad depth since pre-season.

Who can blame him when going into the opening game of the season against Southampton, he was left with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders?

A late scramble in the transfer market saw Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic arrive on loan, while Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio also arrived on free transfers. But by that point, transfer business had already come too late and the Italian has been left with a squad unfit and low on quality.

The Hornets never replaced Imran Louza in midfield - meaning Dionisi has only one natural defensive midfielder in the squad in Hector Kyprianou - and didn’t reinvest a single penny after Nestory Irankunda was sold to Sporting Clube de Portugal.

Injuries also quickly decimated the limited options Dionisi had at his disposal, with the Italian struggling to fill the matchday squad throughout August and September.

However, he’s not the first Watford manager to have been hung out to dry. Javi Gracia quit in January and decided it wasn’t worth leaving his family behind in Spain, having grown frustrated at player’s attitudes and the ownership’s failure to land key targets.

Tom Cleverley, Slaven Bilic, Valerien Ismael and Rob Edwards – who Duxbury famously said Watford would back come hell or high water – also struggled after the squad wasn’t strengthened in key areas.

That continued reluctance to support the head coach and a failure to commit to any sort of plan or strategy has created a toxic environment around Vicarage Road.

The club have tried so many different head coaches, with so many different playing styles that players know that they can down tools after a couple of defeats and it won’t take long for Pozzo to pull the trigger.

Recruitment has been an issue for some time and can be traced back to the summer of 2019, where Watford blew most of their budget on Ismaila Sarr rather than addressing issues in defence or up front.

Duxbury promised this May that the Hornets would look to sign experienced Championship players ahead of the new season; hardly any walked through the door.

The Hornets have prioritised signing young players from abroad in recent years - given they have higher resale value - or players that have lost their way in their careers, but that has left a squad with a number of questionable attitudes and without leaders or character.

The days where Watford would have a solid core of senior pros like Deeney, Heurelho Gomes, Etienne Capoue and Ben Watson to run the dressing room are long gone, meaning they have consistently rolled over against teams when the going has got tough.

Speaking of Deeney, the club have also never found a proven goalscorer since his departure in 2021, with most strikers they’ve signed looking unsuited to Championship football.

The constant churn of head coaches and players has left the club with little in the way of identity, strategy or leadership, both on and off the pitch.

Pozzo and Duxbury rarely make public appearances, but are prone to saying one thing and doing the complete opposite. No one can really work out what Watford are trying to achieve. The owners have also tightened the purse strings, with not much explanation.

Watford didn’t spend a single penny on transfers in the summer, sold off the women’s team and shut down the club’s under-21 side, while the academy was downgraded to Category Three.

Watford’s academy was a source of real pride for fans, with the Hornets having a rich history of bringing through young players. Not anymore.

There now needs to be change at Vicarage Road. The Hornets need fresh ideas at senior management level, fresh impetus, a clear strategy and identity. But most importantly, fans need some hope again. Without serious change, things will only get far worse.
