#247. Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson

The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically

The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free.

Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.”

This was everything Sunderland fans could have wished for from their first European away game in 53 years and more. They had seen other fans experience these things, and now they could tick off the checklist: complicated travel to a pretty foreign town they would otherwise never visit, a fussy Albanian referee and a great sense of togetherness and community. There was even an injury-time winner from, miracle of miracles, Noah Sadiki.

Ask any of the 5,000 or so Wearsiders who made the trip to Portugal if the Europa League was worth it and the answer would be unanimous. Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Brighton fans would surely say something similar: European football, especially for clubs who are unfamiliar with it, is a joy and an adventure. It generates experiences that will be remembered for ever, and if the cost is that the risk of relegation goes up, that’s a price worth paying. Others at those clubs may see things differently.

The four Premier League clubs involved in the lesser two European competitions play each other on Sunday. Brighton are thriving; the other three are not. Palace were 12th before the weekend fixtures but not playing well. Bournemouth against Sunderland is a battle of third- and fourth-bottom. Whether the Europa League football can yet be blamed is debatable. Brighton surely can’t be bucking the trend just because of the lesser demands of the Conference League. Thursday’s was only the second round of Europa League league games, and the clubs involved bypassed a round of the Carabao Cup; fatigue may come but it shouldn’t be an issue yet.

There are other factors at play. Sunderland have already played Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford, the top four going into this weekend. They could easily have been a couple of goals up by half-time at Brentford. They missed a penalty to go ahead against Arsenal. They registered an xG of 2.72 in losing 5-3 at Manchester City. Only in the defeat to Brighton last weekend have they really disappointed. In the equivalent six games last season (substituting Ipswich for Burnley), Sunderland took only one point; in that sense, they are actually three points better off this campaign.

But that can’t alter the fact that four points from six games leaves them beginning to fret. There is pressure on this next run of fixtures: after Bournemouth, they are home to Leeds, then away to Coventry. Sunderland’s transfer business left a major question on the right of the forward line that has yet to be resolved. A lack of depth in certain areas has been exposed by injuries to Brian Brobbey and Habib Diarra, although both players were on the bench on Thursday.

Bournemouth have also lost key players to injury. Eli Junior Kroupi, who scored 13 league goals last season, has not played this campaign. Neither has Amine Adli, although he came off the bench on Thursday, as did Justin Kluivert, who had been out for a month. Most damagingly of all, perhaps, after impressing for England against Croatia, Alex Scott has been ruled out with a thigh injury.

The transition away from Andoni Iraola was always likely to be disruptive and, while Saturday’s 5-1 defeat at Chelsea was a jolt, their other losses this season were to Manchester City and Liverpool. There has been a sense of margins going against them, of draws that might have been wins. The concern, as with Sunderland, comes if that affects morale, and decent displays that have yielded disappointing results curdle into disappointing performances.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Palace are in a slightly different position. Other than City, their fixture list has been relatively kind. Seven points from six games would constitute comfortable survival if extrapolated over the season as a whole, but Opta’s expected points table, which has Bournemouth ninth and Sunderland 10th, has them 18th. A new manager is settling in, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Múñoz were sold over the summer, while Jean-Philippe Mateta hasn’t played since the opening weekend.

For none of those three sides can unsettled starts be blamed entirely or even primarily on Europe. That said, the evidence is clear: over the past five years, teams who did not play in Europe the previous season see their league position fall when they do play in Europe: Palace dropped from 12th to 15th, Nottingham Forest from seventh to 16th, Newcastle from fifth to 12th, Brighton from sixth to 11th, West Ham from sixth to seventh. Of those examples, only Forest even came vaguely close to relegation, but the fear nags away.

Although winning the Europa League would bring the vast rewards of Champions League football, losing in the final would probably bring in not much more than £20m for a Premier League club, plus gate receipts and whatever intangible benefits there might be from increased exposure. To put that in context, that’s roughly the difference between finishing ninth and 14th in the Premier League.

Which is to say that while fans revel in trips to Milan, Prague or Lyon, for club executives a few nice mini-breaks do not balance out the potential financial headaches.

#250. West Ham unstoppable, Norwich in trouble - Aaron McLean's EFL takeaways

Former Peterborough United and Hull City striker - and Final Score pundit - Aaron McLean gives his five takeaways following Saturday's action in the Championship, League One and League Two.

Divine Mukasa (second left) celebrates scoring West Ham's winner against Swansea with his team-mates

West Ham won their fixture with Swansea City in the Championship, thanks to Divine Mukasa's goal, and have moved to within a point of the Welsh club at the top of the table. They've scored a remarkable 30 goals in their 11 league games.

McLean: "I think it was a huge win for West Ham. Take nothing away from Swansea and I think the start they've had has been incredible, but today was always going to be a real test for them.

"After the demolition of Lincoln in midweek, it was important West Ham backed that up with three points to close the gap to just one point behind Swansea and they did that.

"I think once West Ham go back top of the league, they probably won't come off it again.

"I think the fact that Middlesbrough drew today made it even more of a reason why they needed the three points.

"Jarrod Bowen has got eight goals and keeping him was probably the best thing that could have happened for West Ham.

"There were a lot of questions asked about him and if he had gone to the World Cup, and he was a regular in the England squad, I think maybe it might have been different.

"I think the fact he wasn't selected was a huge reason why he was like, 'No, I'm captain of this football club and and I want to help get them back to the Premier League'."

Marezi has scored three goals for Portsmouth so far this season

Portsmouth's Marezi converted a penalty to send Norwich City crashing to a sixth straight loss, leaving them just one point above the relegation zone when their fans had expected them to mount a promotion bid.

McLean: "I've got egg on my face because they were my wild promotion pick so I'm as surprised as anyone that they're doing so badly.

"I thought the job Philippe Clement did when he came in last year was incredible and I really fancied them to kick on this season and not only challenge for the play-offs, but challenge for automatic promotion and be right up there.

"They've just been so disappointing and they look void of any confidence at the moment. I don't know where they go from here.

"With each game they lose, you can see the confidence streaming out of the squad. As soon as they concede a goal, you think 'here we go again'. It's like groundhog day.

"The goalkeeper [Daniel Grimshaw] is under a lot of pressure as well, he's not having the best of seasons. The goals they're conceding, some of those are easily avoidable.

"So, yeah, I think over the next couple of weeks, there are going to be huge questions asked, not only of the goalkeeper, but of Clement.

"It's not so much that they're losing games, I think it's that they're consistently losing. Good teams show they can recover, but at the moment, Norwich don't look like they've got an ounce of recovery in them."

Watford ended a miserable run of four straight losses, which looked like it would cost Alessio Dionisi his job, by winning 2-0 against Charlton and they are now three points above the relegation zone.

Watford goalkeeper Federico Ravaglia was jubilant after their win against Charlton

McLean: "That was a huge win for Watford against Charlton and they needed that, but I wouldn't say they've turned a corner just yet.

"The timing of the Charlton game was perfect for Watford and it was the right game at the right time.

"Charlton came into that game having not won in seven games. They were understandably low on confidence.

"I think it was just two out-of-form teams up against each other, and fortunately for Watford, they came out on the right side of it.

"That's especially true for the manager, Alessio Dionisi, and he desperately needed that result. I would have feared for him past this weekend if they had lost again, especially given how poorly they played against Cardiff in midweek, when they conceded five.

"I think it is a stepping stone, but I still think that the ownership are going to need a lot of convincing.

"They've shown in the past they're not scared to make changes and Dionisi is going to need a run of results if he's going to remain in his position."

MK Dons boss Paul Warne has overseen one League One win, six draws and two defeats this season

After drawing six of their opening eight League One games, MK Dons finally beat Luton Town 2-1 to get their first league win under manager Paul Warne.

McLean: "It was a brilliant result first and foremost. You know Luton are a team that are expected to be up there challenging.

"Jack Wilshere will be feeling the pressure that they're expected to be challenging for promotion.

"But I think what MK Dons have got on their side is that Paul Warne is a vastly experienced manager at League One level.

"So he knows how to get results. At the moment they're probably not getting the wins he would like, but I think that will change now.

"He took them up from League Two last season and I think he will get them going again. It will take them a little bit of time to get going and to really gel, but I think they'll be fine.

"I think as the season progresses, they'll get stronger. The team will have a lot more cohesion and I expect them to be comfortable at least in mid-table."

Rotherham United have won just two League Two games under Alex Bruce this season

Alex Bruce is enduring a tough first job in management and his Rotherham United side have slipped into the bottom two in League Two after losing 2-0 at Fleetwood.

McLean: "I think when you look at Rotherham and Crawley, the other team at the bottom of League Two, they've both got managers who are in charge for the first time.

"That lack of experience in these types of moments is showing. That's not to say that given time they won't be able to come through, but the problem they've got is the average lifespan of a manager in the EFL isn't very long, it's about nine months.

"So I do think they'll both be worried and I don't think either team has the strongest of squads.

"I'd say Rotherham out of the two will be the ones who really need to put a run of form together and move up with the players they've got.

"They were in League One last season and they're underachieving.

"In Alex Bruce's defence, he hasn't been given the money to be able to go and improve the squad, so it's very hard.

"He needs to galvanise the squad, and they need to just grind out a few results. They need to try and get themselves above that line. Today was a bad day, but it's nothing a few good results can't change."

Aaron McLean was speaking to BBC Sport England's David Anderson.

#253. Celtic boss Martin O'Neill says seven-goal slaughter of Hearts is major boost ahead of Europa League tie

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 20:23 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 20:23 BST, 18 October 2026

Martin O’Neill believes today's ruthless thrashing of Hearts could breathe new life into Celtic’s season.

Celtic delivered their best performance of the campaign thus far as they ripped Hearts to shreds at Parkhead and stretched their lead at the top of the table to four points over Rangers.

O’Neill’s side were 5-1 up by half-time and eventually ran out 7-1 winners against a Hearts team who had been touted as potential title challengers once again.

It was an excellent response from Celtic on the back of the 4-1 Europa League defeat to Benfica last Thursday as they finally stepped up in a big match this season.

O’Neill believes it should serve as a major confidence boost – and has challenged his players to step it up once again when Celta Vigo arrive in Glasgow for a pivotal European clash later this week.

With no points from their opening two matches, O’Neill admitted that Celtic have no margin for error against the Spaniards on Thursday night.

Callum Osmand celebrates with Camilo Duran after scoring Celtic's third goal against Hearts

Martin O'Neill shakes hands with Hearts boss Wouter Vrancken after Celtic's 7-1 triumph

Celtic striker Callum Osmand scored twice before being taken off at half-time as a precaution

But, sensing this dismantling of Hearts could be the start of a revival, the 74-year-old said: ‘Once we got a couple of early goals, the players got a lot of confidence from that and we carried it on throughout the 90 minutes.

‘I thought the performance was great. It certainly gives us confidence going into Thursday evening — and maybe trying to continue that on.

‘It was a tough evening against Benfica against a very good side, but I thought the second-half performance over there in Lisbon actually did give us that sort of confidence to go into the game today.

‘Did I think we were going to score seven goals? No. But it was a really terrific victory for us as we scored some excellent goals.

‘It is a big match for us now against Celta Vigo. A really big game for us because we really need to get some points on the board.

‘This will give us confidence. We still might make a couple of changes in the side because it’s pretty hectic. But sometimes just maybe playing the games is better than having the the whole week free.

‘We need to win the game because it’s a home game. We lost ground, not so much against the Benfica game, but we lost ground in the Ferencvaros game, so we have got to win.

‘And, if we could, that would definitely give us a big lift. If we don’t, that’d be three games gone. That’s a long way back from there.’

Callum Osmand scored twice for Celtic in the first half before being taken off at half-time, something which O’Neill said was purely precautionary.

All being well, he should be available to face Celta Vigo, with Cameron Carter-Vickers more likely to be back for the game against Hibs next Sunday.

Asked about the fact Celtic have now opened up a four-point gap at the top of the table, O’Neill added: ‘I think it’s very early. We were four points behind with about seven games to go last season, so it can be eroded very, very quickly. But it’s nice to win today, and winning the manner in which we did.

‘From Hearts’ viewpoint, probably just a bad day at the office. But they’ll still be challengers, they’ve got some really decent players who can play a bit.

‘If we lose on Thursday, it’ll be crisis again, so you know, I’ve been here before. You just have to try and win.’

It was a day of humiliation for Hearts as they suffered their heaviest ever defeat in a competitive fixture at Celtic Park.

Wouter Vrancken’s side capitulated during a shambolic first half that saw them ship five goals, with another two following in the second half.

The Hearts boss claimed that individual errors were largely responsible rather than his own tactical setup despite Hearts being so open at times.

‘Yeah, really disappointing and also the way it happened,’ said Vrancken. ‘We made a few individual mistakes. Two set-plays killed our game at the start of the game. Basically all of the goals were individual errors.

‘Against individual mistakes, you can’t do too much. The only thing that cannot happen is that everybody starts doubting now in their own qualities. When you are one of the guys that made a mistake, just learn from it.

‘After tomorrow, it has to be gone because there’s another game to come. We have to step up again and push and keep pushing.’

Pressed on what responsibility he took as head coach, Vrancken added: ‘It’s always about everybody taking responsibility together.

‘That’s what I said to the players in the dressing room. When we win games, it’s also a collective effort.’

Merlin Röhl's 'Life With Everton' shares an insight into the club through the German's passion for photography: now, Henry Winter learns about life through a lens with Röhl

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Merlin Röhl, Everton’s super-bright midfielder and occasional full-back, talks so passionately and intelligently about the importance of footballers training the eye to improve their game that it was no complete surprise to discover his mother is a doctor specialising in the eye. It is also no complete surprise that Röhl’s finely-tuned eye helps him develop as a photographer with a newly-published book of his work.

Röhl was walking back into the dressing-room at Finch Farm on Thursday morning when he noted two of David Moyes’ assistant managers, Leighton Baines and Billy McKinlay, chatting with a couple of players. The tableau immediately appealed to Röhl on two levels: the obvious camaraderie amongst Moyes’ squad and also the image attracted his photographer’s eye. So he got his Leica M6 out and snapped away. Staff and players are used to this now, not least because Baines himself is a talented photographer.

“We were coming in from training,” Röhl recalls, “and just sitting in front of the dressing room, a few lads, and Leighton and Billy were telling a story. They were laughing the whole time, pointing at each other. This situation meant so much to me. The connections between people. I took 20, 30 photos.”

Finch Farm has a family feel and Baines is almost a mentor to Röhl, who joined Everton on loan from Freiburg last year, impressed, and has now signed permanently. “When we talk about the mental side, and I was saying, ‘my mind works a lot’, it's sometimes the same for Leighton. We can be quite similar in certain thoughts, we share them, and then we help each other to find a balance in our life.Röhl has a very active brain. “I would say so. There are certain days where I come home from training and think about so many things, my past and the lives of other people. Something needs to help me to live a life where I can help my brain to calm down a little bit – so I pick up a camera, do some photos.“Leighton was talking the other day about ‘something has a significance, and sometimes the same thing has an insignificance’. When you’re injured, of course, the significance of your injury is so high, but also it's maybe just a small adductor injury and compared to some real health problems is nothing. That helps to put something into perspective, to just enjoy life. That helps me a lot.”

Baines and Seamus Coleman encouraged Röhl’s lens work. While providing opportunity for photography, injury has impeded some of his impact but Röhl is clearly a well-regarded team-mate. It’s why the players have accommodated his picture-taking. Rohl certainly gets close-ups. In his new photo-book, “Life with Everton”, one picture of Michael Keane and Vitaliy Mikolenko playing chess in the dressing-room captures the defenders utterly absorbed in their game and utterly unaware of the camera. It’s in black and white, which Rohl loves, also reflecting his admiration for a photographer famed for his black-and-white work. “The most famous one is Henri Cartier-Bresson! Legend! In the beginning, I looked at his photos and was like, ‘nice photos’. As soon as you know more about photography, you know more how brilliant he was. When I look at his photographs, step by step, I find something I was never thinking about, see how much detail you can put into a photo from composition, and how perfect his photos are. Röhl mentions one in particular. “There’s a picture where it was really about the background - a really small reflection of a bicycle.” Taken by Cartier-Bresson in 1932, the photo is titled “Hyeres, France” but also known as “The Cyclist”. “He was completely aware of how to put those little things in. That’s what fascinated me about his pictures.”Should it be so strange? Footballer as photographer? Eric Dier has a passion for photography as does Baines. Alfie Whiteman, the former Tottenham Hotspur keeper, has already had an exhibition of his photos. Players often talk about having “pictures” in their head, snap-shots of where team-mates are on the pitch.

Röhl nods when I mention he’s used to framing images on the field, scanning where everyone is, especially when he plays in midfield. “As a footballer, you need to do that framing. I'm a player who is visualising a lot, thinking, dreaming, about certain patterns, images and situations. And if there's another connection to being a photographer, you also need to have imagination.”Which is why Röhl’s favourite player is a Brazilian legend. “Kaka is the most famous player that I really loved to watch. He had a joy of playing, the speed and technical ability. That's something I'm still dreaming about getting on the pitch.” Starting out, Röhl played as a 10 at times in Germany. “A lot of players have a technical ability. But when your physical output is so high, when you're running so much, you're pressing, then it's so hard to be very good technically in those very important moments. It was there that Kaka was one of the best.”Of the current generation, Röhl name-checks a player he encountered in the DFB-Pokal. “When I was in Germany, I played against Jude Bellingham,” Röhl recalls of when his first club, Ingolstadt, visited Borussia Dortmund in 2021. “Oh, wow, I really enjoyed that.” Rohl played more of a no.10 role in that game and saw Bellingham close up. “The ability to keep the ball in difficult situations is something where he's incredible. He's rarely losing the ball. That puts him, really, as a stand-out player from a lot of the players at the top. He can play every position, is just so versatile, just keeps the ball - and then he scores.”

As a footballer, you need to do that framing. I'm a player who is visualising a lot, thinking, dreaming, about certain patterns, images and situations.

Röhl was only 19, playing for the Bundesliga.2 side before moving to Freiburg the following year. He’s always wanted to be a footballer. Röhl grew up in a home in Potsdam where his parents encouraged him to explore all his potential, academic and sporting, and self-development. “Both my parents are doctors. The situation at home was they created something where I can do whatever I want. A lot of people normally have ‘you need this job or that job, you need to earn the money’. My parents gave me love, freedom and all the opportunities to pursue a little bit of an artistic way of living my life.“Just having people giving you trust and love for the whole life, and putting you in a position where I have the courage to do certain things, to share my thoughts, and to express myself be on the pitch. That’s something that my parents gave me, and that's something I really, really love.” His parents were keen on their son doing his Abitur, the German equivalent of A-levels despite the demands of football. “At Ingolstadt, where I was becoming professional, it was quite difficult at that time. The manager wanted me in the first-team squad, and played me, but my school was not completely matched with the training schedule. The manager was just saying, ‘Merlin, I cannot move the training. You need to be out of school. Because you will be a professional football player, and you don't need the school’.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That didn’t go down well at home. “My parents were like, ‘No, it's the most important thing in life: go to school, get your Abitur’.’ I didn't play for a few games. I got my Abitur. Afterwards, I was playing. It worked out. I had the dream in my head. I was 16, 17, I want to be a midfielder. I want to play in the Premier League.” To develop, he analysed those in his position. “I watched players that had some similar attributes or I wanted some attributes in my game. I watched (Ryan) Gravenberch in the beginning. He takes on the ball a lot, has great turns in the middle, and also very tall.” Röhl himself is 6ft 3in. “Football opened up a new life for me, where I'm financially so stable, where I have something that I have such a big passion for. If I wouldn't have football, it would be really hard for me to find something where I would have that passion. Also the pressure of earning money would be there.” What might he have done? “Maybe medicine would be interesting. Neuro-science would be something I'm really interested in to understand our brain and how we see the world.”He’s only 24 but has already thought about his post-playing career, including studying and teaching how even elite footballers can find an extra edge. “Eye exercises,” Röhl says. “I played in the middle a lot, and both eyes need to turn a lot, even the head needs to turn about. In the beginning, when I switched the first few games to right-back, I had a weird sensation in my neck, because my neck was always being in one position, but never doing this (swivelling). Not a lot of people are aware of that: if the football changes, your eye needs to change.” He’s done different vision exercises, training the muscle, since his early days at Ingolstadt and Freiburg. “It's something I really believe in. It’s massive. Quite a few clubs have a trainer who teaches you.” They taught him certain routines. “A lot, yes. I have a stick with numbers on it.” He focuses on each number in turn to strengthen his field of vision. “Your eye needs to go from far to very near. I also do a lot of eye switches. I have a metronome. It goes 100 beats per minute, and then your eyes switch like this (Rohl moves his eyes quickly left to right, right to left). It's training a muscle. If you have fast eyes, you can track the ball faster and then switch faster to the player where you want to play the ball.”

An option for Moyes in midfield and full-back, Röhl is loving being in this Everton squad. “We got now a little bit smaller group than last year, but very strong characters, very good players. It's something that shows in training and in the games, we have people that step up in big moments, and that's very special.” Everton are currently fifth, heading into a challenging game on Saturday against Chelsea at a noisy Hill Dickinson Stadium. “Everton fans always support us. They demand a lot from us, and that's something that creates a lot of energy between the team and the supporters, and a lot of intensity on the pitch. We fight to get (deliver) the expectations of the fans. It's something that's very special. “I always have the feeling we need to win every game so we meet expectations. I like the feeling of work as hard as possible and then you get the best outcome. I find that much, much better than just to say, ‘maybe we just try to be in the middle of the table and see what comes when we play’. I really like the pressure. I really like the expectations.”And Röhl really likes Hill Dickinson Stadium. “It's big. It's loud. It's a stadium where we had last season a great moment when we drew Manchester City (3-3 in May, Röhl came on). It was very special for me that day. When we, as the players, perform it’s like the stadium explodes.

Everton fans always support us. They demand a lot from us, and that's something that creates a lot of energy between the team and the supporters.

“I'm starting to realise how big this club is. I'm sometimes trying to explain it to German people. I even tried to explain it to a German journalist last week, because I felt that he was not aware of how big Everton is. He was like, ‘yeah, you have this big club in your city. How does it feel to have Liverpool in your city?’ And I was trying to explain to him how big Everton is in this country, and how famous this club is, the history, the expectation. Some people just need a little bit of a reminder, so I'm happy to express that.”Röhl seen quickly that Everton are more than a club. They are embedded in the community, doing vital outreach work in some of the poorer parts of the country. “Step by step, I will have a deeper connection to the community work here, and try to be connected more to the club, and what they do all around the city, and to understand the city more, and the people that live here. You mentioned poor areas. This club means so much to the people and can help people to get away from certain things (in life) that are really, really hard.” Röhl donates a large chunk of the proceeds from his book to Everton Multi-Academy Trust, because of his passion for education.Blessed with a huge curiosity for other people, Röhl thinks about the mental challenges facing others. “A normal person with a normal job, there goes so much on in the brain like trying to work out the bills, thinking about the kids, and then there's so much anger inside of so many people, because everything is so hard. That's where the brain is sorting everything out.”Röhl is conscious, almost very self-conscious, of his privilege in being a professional footballer. “Football opened up a new life for me, where I'm financially so stable, where I have something that I have such a big passion for. If I wouldn't have football, it would be really hard for me to find something where I would have that passion. Also the pressure of earning money would be there.” What might he have done? “Maybe medicine would be interesting. Neuro-science would be something I'm really interested in to understand our brain and how we see the world.” Through strong eyes.

Merlin Röhl, “Life with Everton” (Buxton Press) is out now.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

#257. ‘It’s really not a drama’: Carrick sticks to the script after Martínez storm

Manchester United head coach produced a masterclass in dialling down emotion before a tricky trip to Leeds

Michael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United’s manager.

His team are bombing in the league after the club’s poorest start since 1986 and out of the Carabao Cup, and after Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid Lisandro Martínez showed up ruptures at United by calling out the director of football, Jason Wilcox.

All of this two months into a first full campaign piloting United after last term ended so rosily for the former United midfielder.

On the final day of last season, United won 3-0 at Brighton and Carrick secured an impressive third-place finish, 48 hours after agreeing a two-year deal to continue as head coach.

By last Saturday, United had six points from the first six games after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham at Old Trafford, placing Carrick’s job in jeopardy as the walls closed in on him a fortnight before the clocks go back.

A game at Leeds in January proved to be Ruben Amorim’s last in charge at Manchester United after he greeted the 1-1 draw by demanding his colleagues in the recruitment department “do their job”. With an uncanny circularity Carrick heads to Elland Road on Sunday after Martínez made similar comments. Amorim’s team were sixth going into that game; Carrick’s start the weekend 13th.

On Friday, though, came a masterclass from Carrick in dialling down emotion as Martínez’s explosive comments about Wilcox – “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director” – were addressed and he repeatedly referred to the “really good feeling” at the club.

“It’s really not a drama for us as a group,” he said. “The boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad … so we’ve moved on pretty quickly.”

If this seems less than credible, and almost certainly a stance coached by United’s PR mandarins, what else would Carrick be expected to say? More obvious was how the zen-like performance required from the club’s leader was being delivered. Even when he broke from the script to interrupt an inquisitor this strengthened the sense of Carrick being in control – hardly easy given the heightened glare on United since Tuesday evening.

When the positive vibes trope was challenged by a questioner saying: “We’ll have to take you at face value”, Carrick’s interjection came with a smile. “I’m telling you the truth when I say that,” he said. “Do you not believe me, no? The players totally believe me. I’m telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while, actually, and that’s it, plain and simple, you know? We’re emotional, we’re passionate, we care a lot.”

When signing on to be the permanent United manager, Carrick had overseen only 21 games at elite level – in two caretaker spells at the club. United had 17 league games to play when he replaced Amorim, and Carrick has shown signs of faltering this season when having to compete on four fronts.

Elimination by Brighton at the earliest stage of the Carabao Cup was not a great calling card regarding an ability to juggle competitions, and there was a surprising reaction from him after the 2-0 opening-day loss at Hull. He bridled at the suggestion United had lacked “passion” during a first-half horror show. “Oh come,” Carrick said. “That’s ridiculous.”

A faulty United rearguard is hampering an attack that is functioning far better and has the most shots (125) and most touches in the opposition box (205) in the Premier League. Nine goals from six matches is not paltry but greater ruthlessness would transform a promising front six into a potent one. Carrick has to find the right blend from Benjamin Sesko, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Baleba has sparkled in his first two appearances – against Spurs and Atlético – and might have provided the shield from the No 6 berth to ensure a less leaky defence had he not arrived injured.

This has to be the hope for Carrick. Playing Tielemans at No 10 at Atlético suggests the manager may doubt the 29-year-old’s legs, and questions have been raised about whether United are putting in enough of the hard yards. Their 671.4km distance covered in the league is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2km is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

The trip to an always febrile Elland Road that saves a particular welcome for their cross-Pennines rivals presents a stern challenge. Leeds are ninth and have lost once.

“It’s a great rivalry,” Carrick said, who was full of praise for his Leeds counterpart, Daniel Farke. “There’s big history between the clubs, the areas. That’s what makes these types of games special. You’ve got to embrace the history, what it means.

“I’m sure it will be a fantastic atmosphere on Sunday. It brings an intensity and it’ll be a little bit extra again, on Sunday against us … Of course, we have to be ready, and the boys will be.”

Carrick requires a positive result, though in denying this, he again sounded the right note. “I don’t need results, we all need results,” he said. “It’s not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me, bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this club. It’s not about me, so please …

“I don’t go into every day at work, in this situation, this game, thinking about me. It’s about what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to, and that’s what drives us. So whatever’s best for the club and for the team on Sunday is the most important thing.”

#263. Rangers 'pop balloon' as Neil gift wastes chance to go top

Dan Neil's mishit backpass gifted Dundee an equaliser in Rangers' 2-2 draw at Dens Park

As far as optimism goes, Rangers were blown full of positive energy as they made the Saturday-night trip to Dundee on the back of seven straight wins.

However, a Dan Neil error felt "like a balloon popping", said manager Derek McInnes, resulting in the Ibrox side fluffing their chance to move back to the Scottish Premiership summit after a gripping 2-2 draw at Dens Park.

McInnes' men were punished for a disjointed first half when the impressive hosts went ahead through Bradley Fink, but Badredine Bouanani fired in a leveller just before the break.

Rangers lifted their intensity and level of dominance after the interval and were heading for an eighth consecutive victory when Nicolas Raskin slammed in a long-range stunner.

But a mishit Neil backpass to goalkeeper Ivor Pandur was pounced on by Callum Jones to earn Dundee a deserved point, opening the door for Celtic to extend their lead at the top to four points when they welcome Hearts on Sunday (15:00 BST).

"We've made a mistake for Dundee's equaliser and it was like a balloon popping," McInnes told BBC Scotland. "We then had to dig deep and go again, and we never quite managed to get to the same levels.

"It does feel like a missed opportunity, but in fairness to Dundee they were good value in the first half - it shows you why they are where they are in the league.

"But we can't come away from home and have to score three goals to win a game."

Dundee & Rangers fight out captivating draw

Can Hearts prove credentials at scene of title heartbreak?

Visit our Rangers page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

McInnes was critical of his side's first half but praised the 25 minutes that came after the break, saying the dominant period "shows what the team are capable of".

"When we play in that manner, we're a very good team," he added.

The problem is 25-minute performances don't win leagues, said Rangers title winner Derek Ferguson post-match.

"If Rangers want to win games in this league, then they can't just play for 20 or 25 minutes," the former midfielder said on BBC Sportsound.

"When you look back at it, they were sensational for that amount of time, but that has to be for 70 minutes or so if they are going to win league titles."

While McInnes was keen to point out that his team should not be required to score three goals to win matches, he did touch on a theme of wastefulness.

'Like a balloon popping' - McInnes on Dundee draw

Rangers' expected goals (xG) rating of almost two reflects the goals they scored at Dens Park, but over the course of the season they are underperforming.

The Ibrox side have scored 13 league goals from a total accumulated xG of just under 20 - an underperformance of almost seven goals.

Having worked so hard to reel Celtic back to within touching distance after a shaky start to the campaign, McInnes cannot afford a pattern of profligacy to plague his team with a challenging run of fixtures on the horizon.

"We had so many better chances than [Raskin's goal] to take the game away from Dundee," McInnes said on Sky Sports. "It's something we need to be far better at.

"It's the same kind of theme for me a lot of the time. We've had dominant performances but not really had the goals to show for it."

#265. Losing Ollie Watkins could have broken Aston Villa but Nicolas Jackson has made them better

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Fantastic football content straight to your inbox! From the latest transfer news, quizzes, videos, features and interviews with the biggest names in the game, plus lots more.

Sign up to our FREE live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest games available to watch on the device of your choice. Never miss a kick-off!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Nicolas Jackson departed Stamford Bridge for Villa Park earlier this year

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Aston Villa essentially signed a brand new starting XI over the summer - they almost had to.

It was a period of substantial change for the Villans, who lost Amadou Onana to an ACL injury during the World Cup, Youri Tielemans to Manchester United, Ezri Konsa to Arsenal, Ollie Watkins to Al-Hilal, and Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martinez to Chelsea. The spine of the squad was ripped out.

With a raft of outgoings and incomings, there was always going to be a period of transition. A time where the new players need to get up to speed with new teammates and the demands that come with working under a new manager. This, of course, is reflected in Villa’s league position.

After the opening six games, Villa sit 16th with just five points to their name. In truth, it mirrors their start to the 2025/26 campaign, where they earned six points across the same period. That said, this is new ground for Emery and Villa. Such squad upheaval was always going to present teething issues.

And while Taylor Harwood-Bellis isn’t of the same standard of Konsa, and Joao Gomes is a different profile to Tielemans, there’s an argument to be made that Villa upgraded in the final third.

Nicolas Jackson moved to Chelsea in 2023. The Senegal international had enjoyed a fruitful second season in Spain with Villarreal, where he scored 12 and provided four assists despite starting just 16 league matches. A direct goal involvement every 100 or so minutes was a solid return.

It’s fair to say that Jackson’s Stamford Bridge spell didn’t go quite according to plan. Granted, across two Premier League seasons, he bagged 24 goals and provided 10 assists. However, ill-discipline marred his time in west London. A loan stint with Bayern Munich hardly did the 25-year-old many favours. Well, when you’re playing second fiddle to Harry Kane, that’s to be expected.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Even so, eight goals and one assist across 1004 minutes of Bundesliga action is not to be scoffed at. However, Jackson never really looked quite at home in Bavaria. He needed a club where he’d be first choice to rediscover his best form, and while it’s early days yet; the Senegalese hitman looks right at home on the Villa frontline.

Filling Watkins’ boots was always going to be easier said than done. The England star scored at least 15 league goals in each of his last four seasons at Villa Park. The 30-year-old endured a tough start to the 2025/26 campaign, scoring just three league goals before Christmas, but recovered for the second half of the season, ultimately netting 16 times in his final year at the club.

Even so, Jackson has scored more goals after six league outings this season (2) than Watkins managed after his opening 13 Premier League appearances last term (1). He’s scored three times across two Champions League games for good measure, too.

The summer signing is also offering more in the final third than Watkins did in the previous campaign. That’s not to say Watkins underwhelmed last season. On the contrary, his goals and assists were vital as Villa secured a top-four finish and claimed Europa League glory at the expense of Bundesliga side Freiburg.

The difference is that Jackson offers a little more on the ball than Watkins in a key area. Whereas the latter operates as a low-touch finisher, waiting for chances in the opposition box, the former is happy to drift across the frontline, drag markers out of position and, in the process, open up space for teammates to exploit.

This is particularly effective given the signing of Johan Manzambi, the Swiss a dynamic, box crashing midfielder who has scored one and provided two assists in the league.

As such, it’s hardly a surprise that Jackson is averaging more touches per 90 this season (33.7) than Watkins was last (28). Even then, the former is only averaging marginally fewer touches inside the opposition box per 90 (5.4) than the latter in the 2025/26 campaign (5.6). Jackson may pull away to the flanks, but he’s just as active in the penalty area as his predecessor.

He’s also prepared to pull the trigger more frequently than the former Villa man, with Jackson’s shots per 90 higher (2.8) than Watkins (2.2). With more successful dribbles per 90 (2.6 to 0.8), chances created per 90 (0.9 to 0.7), passes per 90 (16.1 to 15) and a better pass success rate (80.9% to 72.7%), Emery has a more rounded forward to call upon in his favoured 4-2-3-1 setup.

Watkins’ departure was a tough one to swallow for Villa fans. He’d become a mainstay for the Midlands side following his 2020 arrival from Brentford, and a nigh-on ever-present given his impressive injury record.

Yet the departures of Tielemans, Rogers and Watkins required a tactical rethink. Emery needed a forward who’d offer the directness of Rogers and the goalscoring capability of Watkins. In Jackson, he has the best of both, affording Emery the relevant attacking flexibility that’ll amplify Villa’s offensive unpredictability, whereas with Watkins, it was a little more one-dimensional.

For that reason alone, Jackson can be viewed as an upgrade on Watkins. Time will tell if the club-record signing truly exceeds the standards set by Villa’s recent leading marksman.

#268. The Florian Wirtz mystery: why has he not found Leverkusen form at Liverpool?

Two of our writers pick over the German’s contribution to Liverpool and what the £116m forward could yet produce

Some criticism has been OTT and a fee rising to £116m heightens demands but, yes, compared with his performances in Germany and for Germany Wirtz has underwhelmed at Liverpool. The past week has encapsulated his Liverpool career so far. In the Champions League rout of Lask he was everywhere, exploiting gaps between and behind the Austrian club’s defence and knitting together a dominant display against limited opposition. In the previous game against Manchester City, however, when Andoni Iraola needed big players to step up in the absence of Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai, Wirtz was ineffective, wasteful and withdrawn when his team were chasing the game at 0-1. It also did not help his cause that Rayan Cherki, a cheaper alternative whom Liverpool considered and passed on, completed City’s victory with a sublime goal. AH

The physicality and intensity of the Premier League appear to be Wirtz’s biggest issues. He can be swamped, knocked aside, leaving Liverpool’s central midfield exposed. Iraola this week rejected the notion that the playmaker is struggling with English football, although his answer almost veered in support of the argument. “It’s not about whether they are foreign teams or English teams,” the head coach said. “It’s about different kinds of games. Some games are more comfortable, with more time to think, sometimes less. It’s not about the competition.” But, as Brentford are likely to demonstrate on Saturday, there is less time to think and little opportunity to get comfortable in the Premier League. Wirtz produced three assists in 11 Champions League games last season, the same amount as he did in 33 Premier League matches. His passing accuracy this season – from an admittedly small sample – is 80% in the Premier League and 91.5% in the Champions League. AH

That is a question that can be levelled at many of Liverpool’s signings since the 2025 title win. The shift towards acquiring expensive “finished products” has left many pining for the hunger and spirit of emerging talent that characterised the club’s re-emergence under Jürgen Klopp. Wirtz does not have an ego to match his price tag. He is a conscientious, dedicated professional who Iraola, like Arne Slot before him, has found to be a good listener willing to put team instructions first. He is also, it seems easy to forget, only 23. Wirtz may not be a demonstrative force but he shows personality on the ball, always looking to receive it and take responsibility. His talent is clear but has not been seen consistently enough in a Liverpool shirt. AH

Wirtz was sold on Slot’s vision for him as the central, creative force of a new-look Liverpool attack that would turn the slender wins of the title-winning season into dominant, emphatic victories. It never happened, and Slot was sacked without finding a position that best suited Wirtz. Iraola immediately confirmed Wirtz would be his No 10 and got to work on him building a close rapport with Isak. There were some promising signs before Isak got injured again. Wirtz can justifiably argue that forces beyond his control have conspired against him at Liverpool and that, as his relationship with Bradley Barcola and Isak improves, so will his end product. He would also be helped by the addition of an out-and-out defensive midfielder who could offer Wirtz licence to roam and greater protection to the Liverpool defence. Monaco’s Lamine Camara, whose proposed move to Chelsea collapsed on deadline day, is of interest. AH

Unbelievably so. In his final two seasons in the Bundesliga you could make the case that he was the best player in it. He racked up goals and assists in European competition too (he was excellent in the Champions League in 2024-25 before injury halted him in the knockouts) but you can’t just describe it in terms of numbers. He dominated the big matches and acted as the conductor of Leverkusen’s orchestra. Teams who tried to kick him out of games almost universally failed, making the idea he can’t hack the Premier League physically a flawed explanation for his difficulties. AB

Partly it was, but on a technical and tactical level his success was also partly down to the freedom Xabi Alonso allowed him. As Alonso said in November 2023 (during Leverkusen’s unbeaten double-winning season) every player had responsibility to patrol an allotted zone “but Flo is different” – he was given licence to prod opposing defences as he saw fit. Alonso’s rotation of him made sure he remained fresh and impactful, his hat-trick in the 5-0 win over Werder Bremen that clinched the title in 2024 coming after he was brought on as a half-time substitute. AB

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

I don’t think we can say that isn’t a factor – but this is something Wirtz himself predicted. Many in his entourage thought he would be better served by joining Bayern Munich instead of Liverpool and he acknowledged he was taking the tougher option. He knew it was a risk but was determined to challenge himself. Another point is how different the Bundesliga is tactically; it has a similarly high tempo but is far more chaotic, which is perfect for a player with his sang froid to exploit. AB

He has been given greater freedom (and a little less responsibility off the ball), more akin to his Leverkusen role, but what has been important is having Klopp cheerlead for him. The manager has not missed an opportunity to say how great Wirtz is or how his good international form is “good for Liverpool”. Klopp also gave him the captaincy for the last game (and a half), showing Wirtz and the world that he believes not only in his talent and influence but in him as a leader. It feels like the more contact he has with Klopp, the better for him and his club. AB

Wirtz can be a class act, a lovely footballer to watch, and it would be premature to write off a gifted talent who – as the previous answer about Isak and a defensive midfielder suggests – has not had the platform to fully express himself at Liverpool. But the question of whether the Premier League suits him and whether he suits this Liverpool team continues to gnaw away. Wirtz needed a strong start to the season after the difficulties of his debut campaign at Anfield and, with one assist and no goals in six Premier League appearances, that has not materialised. There was encouragement in his overall performance and in his understanding with Barcola against Lask, as there has been on several Champions League nights, but Iraola needs his playmaker to produce a repeat in games such as Brentford away. Wirtz will remain categorised as a luxury player if another difficult Premier League assignment passes him by. AH

Maybe. The deck has been largely stacked against him since he arrived: there were too many changes to a champion team in the summer he arrived, plus he was expected to pull the strings in a side that still had Mohamed Salah. He has overcome big setbacks before, such as the 2022 anterior cruciate ligament injury that took a long while to get over, so he has the character to go with his class. Wirtz has the ability to succeed at Anfield but unless the conditions around him change I think it will be very hard to do so (I can imagine him being great for Bayern in a couple of years, post-Michael Olise). AB

#275. My old teammate Miroslav Klose is bucking a trend in German coaching | Philipp Lahm

‘Miro’, now in charge at Nürnberg, knows the value of consistency and identity in an era of tinkering coaches who did not play professionally

You learn the most from the best. The Champions League winners are Paris Saint-Germain, and they could achieve a historic hat-trick this season. Since the tournament’s rebrand in 1992, they would be only the second club to accomplish this feat, after Real Madrid’s run from 2016 to 2018.

I see clear parallels between the two. For Madrid, nine players started in all three of their final victories. Similarly, PSG won their two finals with virtually identical lineups. The only change came during their title defence in Budapest, where Gianluigi Donnarumma no longer featured in goal, Luis Enrique having parted ways with the Italian European champion.

At its core, football has not changed. For two giants of the tournament’s predecessor, the European Cup – Ajax (1971 to 1973) and Bayern Munich (1974 to 1976) – seven players started all three finals. Had injuries not interfered, that number would have been higher. There is a similar pattern in Madrid’s five consecutive wins from 1956, with nine players appearing in at least three of those finals and three featuring in all five. Continuity plus selection: that is the eternal recipe for success.

Today’s elite managers have internalised this, as the numbers prove. We see remarkably similar patterns at PSG, Arsenal and Barcelona. In each case, a core of six to eight players establishes the team’s identity and anchors the XI in crucial matches. The next tier consists of the remaining three to five regular starters, who are pushed by four to six squad players. Thus, the backbone of a squad comprises about 16 players, with the rest providing depth.

Total playing time (roughly 5,000 minutes per season) is distributed as follows:

remaining regular starters: 50 to 60% each

fringe squad places: sharing the remaining maximum of 20%

Benchmarking also reveals there is no alternative to the standard operating system: ball-oriented defending. Managers also rigidly adhere to their formations, typically a 4-3-3 or 4-2-3-1. Substitutions are made like-for-like to preserve structural integrity.

Another encouraging trend is that all three clubs reserve a portion of their fringe squad places for at least three young talents, often products of their academies. To test their potential at the highest level, they are given consistent minutes. At Arsenal, 20-year-old Myles Lewis-Skelly seems to be establishing himself permanently.

These principles are enforced over years and across all development levels by the current champions of France, England and Spain. This approach can also be observed at smaller clubs and, in a similar fashion, with national teams such as Morocco. It represents a universal blueprint for footballing success – one heavily influenced by the Spanish coaching philosophy, spearheaded by Pep Guardiola, Mikel Arteta and Luis Enrique.

The most significant deviations from this blueprint can be found in Germany. I see three pieces of evidence pointing to a unique German path. First, man-marking is experiencing a strange revival. Second, many Bundesliga clubs grant fewer opportunities to homegrown talent, despite paradoxically maintaining expensive academies. Third, a vast number of managers have no professional playing background.

These coaches frequently alter systems and formations, before and during matches. At times, they deploy players out of position. The most prominent example was Julian Nagelsmann, who as national coach hindered his side’s development through constant, fundamental changes.

Yet there are exceptions. One is Miroslav Klose. We shared the pitch in more than 80 international matches. He was a magnificent teammate, a true team player who understood his precise value to the group. He is a World Cup winner and was the tournament’s record goalscorer from 2014 until last summer. Naturally, someone with that background possesses a deep understanding of hierarchy, discipline and the tactical awareness of what makes a collective function.

Miro, now in his third season at Nürnberg and sitting in a promotion spot in the 2. Bundesliga, carries the DNA of a great manager. I recognise the methods that lead to success in his work. What sets him apart from many others is that he does not overcomplicate things. He does not tinker with his core system or formation. He identifies who meets the club’s demands and who does not, rarely altering his starting XI.

Through these repetition effects, Miro has identified a core that provides stability. The winger Mohamed Zoma, who made his Italy debut last month, and the attacking midfielder Julian Justvan get about 90% of the playing time, while the central midfielder Finn Ole Becker secured about 80% before a recent injury. The defensive midfielder Adam Markhiev, a Finland international, is practically ever-present when fit. Miro had to rebuild his defence after summer transfers but seems to have quickly settled on his back four.

He also gives youth a chance, sticking by the academy graduates Tim Janisch and Eric Porstner even after mistakes. Since the turn of the year, the young striker Piet Scobel has featured every single week. Miro’s grasp of the club’s identity is also evident in his decision to appoint a local Franconian, the goalkeeper Jan Reichert, as the captain.

The manager’s position at Nürnberg is finally occupied in a way that allows something substantial to grow. Thanks to Miro, the club, stuck in the second tier since 2014 bar a single season, is again capitalising on the potential of their location. FCN have a grand history: only Bayern Munich have won more German league titles. The club legend Max Morlock scored Germany’s first goal in a World Cup final, in 1954.

The club also have immense potential. They benefit from a massive catchment area with virtually no local competition. The huge metropolitan region around Nuremberg, a city with 550,000 inhabitants, is economically robust, and the club boasts a 50,000-capacity stadium that is due for modernisation.

Above all, the club are deeply rooted in their community, supported by a vast and fiercely loyal fanbase. They remain a traditional, member-owned club. To the people here, “Der Club”, as they call it, truly means everything.

Philipp Lahm’s column was produced in partnership with Oliver Fritsch at the German online magazine Die Zeit.

Diego Demme credits Ralf Rangnick for revolutionising his diet and making him the ultimate pro

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

He may have ruffled feathers along the way, not least at Old Trafford, but Ralf Rangnick has also helped countless players spread their wings throughout his forty-plus years in management.

After winning the 2. Bundesliga with Hannover 96, Rangnick masterminded back-to-back promotions with Hoffenheim before leading Schalke 04 to the DFB-Pokal and UEFA Champions League semi-finals.

Rangnick's magnum opus came as Director of Football for RB Leipzig and Red Bull Salzburg, where he was tasked with constructing the modern Red Bull football architecture, designing scouting networks, and overseeing global club strategy. He then became Leipzig's manager in 2015.

Widely known as the 'Godfather of Gegenpressing', Rangnick helped influence a wide range of German coaches like Thomas Tuchel, Julian Nagelsmann, Ralph Hasenhuttl, Marco Rose, and Roger Schmidt. He hasn't just been a role model for coaches, but also for footballers like Demme.

"I think the most I learned is from Rangnick in terms of how to be professional. It was 10 years ago, but he was professional with everything; he gave us the best treatment, the best food, the best massages," stated Demme in an exclusive FourFourTwo interview.

Diego Demme has announced his retirement from professional football 💐 Thank you for everything, Diego! Wishing you all the best for the future ❤️ https://t.co/SspHcpi6oISeptember 24, 2026

Across a 16-year career that saw him represent the German national team and spearhead Leipzig from the 3. Liga to the Champions League, Demme worked with a range of elite coaches like Nagelsmann, Schmidt, Joachim Low, and Luciano Spalletti. However, nobody taught him more than Rangnick.

"He always wanted the best, and I liked the meals that he gave us to eat after the games so much that sometimes, I'd end up cooking those same meals after my gym sessions. Nagelsmann was very tactical, but I think I learned the most from Rangnick because we worked for many years together."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It was Rangnick who convinced Demme to join Leipzig in January 2014 after a 30-minute conversation at the airport, just as Paderborn were closing in on their first-ever promotion to the Bundesliga. In Demme's case, it ended up being one step backwards and two steps forward, as he helped the Red Bulls to two promotions in three years.

With Demme running the show in midfield, Leipzig consolidated themselves as one of the best teams in the Bundesliga, eventually reaching the 2018/19 DFB-Pokal Final in Rangnick's final match in charge before becoming Red Bull's Head of Sport and Development.

Demme lasted just a few months under Rangnick's replacement, Nagelsmann, before leaving for Napoli in 2020. His leap of faith paid off as he won the 2019/20 Coppa Italia (Napoli's first trophy in six years) as well as the 2022/23 Scudetto (Napoli's first league title in 33 years).

Let's get to know our new midfielder, Diego Demme! 🇩🇪 💙 #ForzaNapoliSempre https://t.co/X1YsCdiIkRJanuary 16, 2020

Whilst Demme has since hung up his boots after a swansong at Hertha Berlin, Rangnick is still going strong in the coaching game at 68 years-old. After an unconvincing spell at Manchester United, he's building a new legacy with Austria, leading them to a Round of 16 finish in Euro 2024 as well as their first World Cup appearance in 28 years.

Rangnick has rubbed quite a few players like Cristiano Ronaldo, Jesse Lingard, and Anthony Martial the wrong way with his uncompromising approach to discipline and willingness to confront established stars. Perhaps it's why Rangnick has never quite succeeded at a major club.

His methods may have left a bitter taste in some players' mouths, but for others, they were food for thought and fuel for success. For Demme, Rangnick concocted the perfect recipe for maximising his footballing potential, and the lessons he served up proved to be every bit as valuable as the meals.

#278. Celtic 7-1 Hearts: Another Tynecastle title dream dies a death at Celtic Park as Benjamin Nygren and Callum Osmand both score twice to ruthlessly rip apart Wouter Vrancken's men

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 18:24 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 19:00 BST, 18 October 2026

Earlier this week, Tony Bloom reaffirmed his vision for Hearts and spoke of his belief that they will be crowned champions of Scotland within the next ten years.

It made for some nice soundbites, as was the case when Bloom laid out the same blueprint after his involvement as a Hearts investor started just over a year ago.

Yet, in each of Bloom’s first two seasons at the club, it has been here at Celtic Park where Hearts have seen their title ambitions crushed.

The circumstances may have been different. What happened towards the end of last season was a travesty, given some of the refereeing calls that went against them. The final-day debacle against Celtic and subsequent pitch invasion will forever be a stain on Scottish football.

But the two outcomes have ultimately been the same; Hearts’ title dream died here in the east end of Glasgow last May, and it died here once again yesterday.

There will be some who view that as a premature assessment in mid-October. Wouter Vrancken’s side are eight points behind Celtic and four behind Rangers with almost 30 games still to play.

Callum Osmand knows Celtic's third past beleaguered Hearts goalkeeper Beau Reus

But the damage inflicted here felt too significant, the flaws exposed in this team too glaring, and the prospect of this team being title contenders felt too fanciful for even the most ardent of Hearts fans.

By quite a distance, this was the worst performance Hearts have delivered during Bloom’s involvement with the club.

They were absolutely annihilated by a Celtic side who themselves came into this with fragile confidence after being dismantled by Benfica in the Europa League on Thursday night.

After conceding twice from set-plays in the opening ten minutes, Hearts completely and utterly capitulated. It was a horror show. On the touchline, Vrancken did nothing to change the flow of the match.

There was a naivety to how his team set up here. It was as if Hearts arrived at Parkhead and believed they were better than they actually are.

Like they expected to turn up and roll Celtic over on account of how good they have been in attack at times this season under Vrancken.

But, defensively, they were appalling. Teams of genuine substance do not capitulate like this. Hearts were 5-1 down by half-time – and they were lucky it wasn’t seven or eight.

Wouter Vrancken set his Hearts side out ambitiously and was negligent in reining them in

Any notion of this team winning the title this season is for the birds. So open, so weak, so naïve; this defeat was entirely on Vrancken.

As a man who made part of his fortune as a professional poker player, Bloom will already recognise that this season is a busted flush.

Indeed, the same could have been said of Martin O’Neill and Celtic had they lost this match. Yet, credit where it’s due, O’Neill rallied his players and delivered a statement result.

For the first time this season, Celtic actually turned up and delivered a big performance in a match of genuine consequence.

The pressure on O’Neill will lift for now. He dropped Kasper Hogh yesterday and the decision was vindicated entirely by Celtic turning in their most stylish performance of the season.

The challenge now will be to sustain this in the Europa League clash here with Celta Vigo on Thursday night as Celtic look to breathe some life into their European season.

On the back of the 4-1 hammering against Benfica in Lisbon on Thursday night, O’Neill opted to freshen things up by making four changes to his Celtic team. The most eye-catching saw Hogh dropped to the bench, with Camilo Duran operating as the central striker and Callum Osmand and Haissem Hassan on the wings.

O’Neill had spoken on Thursday night about Hogh’s form and the fact that the £11million club-record signing has failed to score in over two months.

Kieran Tierney nods home the opener to kickstart a day Celtic fans will long remember

Insisting he still has faith that Hogh will eventually come good and score over 20 goals this season, the Celtic boss explained that the Danish international striker ‘had to earn the right’ to be in the team.

The other changes saw Liam Scales and Benjamin Nygren come into the team, with Auston Trusty and Oliver Sorensen dropping to the bench.

Hearts drew 1-1 against Nordsjaelland on Thursday night and boss Wouter Vrancken made three changes for this trip to Parkhead. Defenders Stephen Kingsley and Jordi Altena started along with midfielder Sabri Guendouz, with Harry Milne, James Wilson and Christian Borchgrevink dropping out.

Hearts actually started the match reasonably well and looked like they were on the front foot in the opening five minutes or so. But the whole thing fell apart in double-quick time. The concession of two goals from set-plays saw them go 2-0 down after only ten minutes.

First, a Mika Baur corner was flicked on by Scales and Kieran Tierney had the simple task of heading in from point-blank range.

The lead was doubled when Nygren wriggled free and converted from another Baur corner. From Hearts’ point of view, the defending was criminal.

To score twice from corners was certainly a feather in the cap of Celtic’s new set-piece coach Ross Grant, who joined the club from Hearts back in the summer.

Jamie McCart contrives to knock the ball over for Celtic's fifth goal before half time

Yet, so deplorable was the defending from Hearts, it hardly required the most creative set-piece routines in Grant’s playbook. Rather, it was all painfully simple.

For all that they have won plaudits for an exciting style of football going forward, defensive frailties are now rapidly becoming a theme of Hearts’ season under Vrancken.

As was the case when they were ripped to shreds by Benfica in Lisbon a couple of months ago, this was another example of a team who don’t know how to stop the bleeding once it starts.

Back in the side after an injury lay-off, Osmand scored twice in little more than 60 seconds to put Celtic 4-0 up after 38 minutes, one of which was a really classy finish with his right foot.

It was Osmand who scored deep into stoppage-time here to clinch the title when the teams met here on the final day of last season, a goal which sparked a mass pitch invasion.

Hearts pulled a goal back when Laurent Mendy fired low into the bottom corner from the edge of the box, but any notion of a comeback was swiftly extinguished.

Baur danced through a couple of feeble efforts at tackles from Hearts players and dinked the ball over Reus, before Kingsley’s attempted clearance cannoned off Jamie McCart and rolled back into the net.

This was utter humiliation for Hearts fans, many of whom had seen enough. With their team 5-1 down at half-time, some of them headed for the exits.

Truthfully, they were lucky it was only five. It could easily have been seven or eight in the first half alone. Celtic were utterly rampant.

Benjamin Nygren fires home Celtic's second goal as Hearts afternoon quickly turns sour

It took a last-ditch block from McCart to deny Nygren after a smart interception from Tierney sparked a rapid Celtic counter-attack.

A jinking run from Hassan saw the Egyptian winger hit the post, with Nygren also forcing a good save from Reus.

On days like this, you wonder what neutral observers must make of Scottish football. Celtic have been a laughing stock in Europe this season, yet this is what they do to their domestic rivals.

Duran made it 6-1 early in the second half when he swept a clinical left-foot finish low past Reus. There was still effectively a full half of football to play but Hearts were desperate for the final whistle.

Celtic made it 7-1 when Nygren netted his second goal of the game with just under ten minutes remaining.

A day of complete and utter humiliation for Hearts and Vrancken. The scars from this defeat may take quite some time to heal.

Celtic (4-3-3): Sinisalo 7; Donovan 7.5, Murray 7, Scales 7, Tierney 7.5 (Emenalo 60); McGregor 7 (Oxlade-Chamberlain 60), Baur 8, Nygren 8; Hassan 8.5 (Forrest 70), Osmand 8 (Jota 46), DURAN 8.5 (Hogh 60). Booked: Jota, Baur, Donovan. Manager: Martin O’Neill 8.

Former Fulham striker Louis Saha believes the luck will turn for his former club and they should not sack the manager

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fulham should not push the panic button yet and sack head coach Alvaro Arbeloa, according to former striker Louis Saha.

Arbeloa has come under increasing pressure with Fulham winless in their opening six Premier League games and are rooted to the bottom of the table.

Last weekend’s capitulation at Portman Road when Ipswich came from 1-0 down to win 2-1 in stoppage time heaped the pressure on the Spaniard.

But Saha - who spent three and a half years at Craven Cottage - says his former side should not look to make a change in the dugout so early in the season.

Saha said: “Thomas Frank is being linked to the Fulham job but I’m not a fan of that, I don’t think they should be ready to press the panic button this early in the season.

“We have seen close results and tight games that could’ve gone either way, it won’t help Alvaro Arbeloa or Fulham if they are linked with other managers.

“Thomas Frank is a good manager and I can only wish him to find the right club. But I'm not going to push for any club that I love to change managers, when it’s not the right time.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Fulham have Hull City next and although Hull have really impressed this season, I think Fulham will go and get their first win of the season and go from there.”

Arbeloa replaced the popular Marco Silva in the summer and has struggled to get the team to adapt to his style of play. Arbeloa only previous managerial experience came when he was interim manager at Real Madrid last season but Saha says he needs more time to make his mark at Craven Cottage.

Fulham face Hull at home on Saturday before trips to Coventry and Aston Villa and then Newcastle at home before the next international break.

Speaking to FourFourTwo via BettingLounge, Saha added: “It's normal to have a transition period when you change leagues and come to a club who had a good foundation for four or five years with one manager.

“Fulham are a very difficult team to play against. I think that's still the case, but they are getting punished under Alvaro Arbeloa.

“If you want to stay in midtable and push towards Europe, you have to be able to hold onto leads and get over the line in games, that hasn’t been happening.

“Fulham are facing strong criticism, in some ways fair, because the Premier League is so brutal. One thing I’m not worried about is the style of play.

“I've seen them play a few times and I still feel that they've been unlucky. But football is not about luck, it's about getting the results, and that's what Arbeloa is going to be judged on.

"He has to turn things around very quickly. It's a tough moment, but I have hope that they can turn it around.”
