#286. Kirby 'stressed' by abrupt Vidosic exit from Brighton

Fran Kirby has scored 10 goals and supplied six assists in the Women's Super League for Brighton since joining six days before Dario Vidosic was appointed in July 2024

Former England striker Fran Kirby says the departure of Brighton head coach Dario Vidosic on the eve of the season left her feeling "stressed" and "disappointed".

Vidosic guided Brighton to the club's first FA Cup final this year and finished a club-record fifth and seventh in the Women's Super League before leaving abruptly on 28 August, nine days before their opener against Arsenal.

He was replaced by Real Sociedad manager Arturo Ruiz on the same day.

"It wasn't easy when I heard," Kirby told the Women's Football Weekly podcast. "I was a bit disappointed.

"I had a really good relationship with Dario and think he's a fantastic coach that can go on and achieve amazing things with top clubs.

"But we had Arsenal coming up and hadn't had a coaching session with the new manager.

Ruiz named Brighton boss after shock Vidosic exit

Brighton lost their season curtain-raiser to the Gunners, the only game Arsenal have won so far in the WSL, and went winless through their first four league matches under Ruiz.

The 29-year-old did secure his first victory in the English top-flight before the international break, thrashing promoted Charlton 5-1.

However, this Sunday, Brighton travel to champions Manchester City, who have won all five WSL matches this season, for a game live on BBC Two (Sunday, 14:30 BST).

It is the first time the two sides have met since City won 4-0 in the FA Cup final in May.

A seven-time winner of the WSL with Chelsea, Kirby conceded 2026-27 has not been easy.

"We're under no illusions â it's been a tough start," said Kirby. "Getting the manager in so late and trying to adapt to his style of play. It's difficult when it comes so close to the start of the season.

"People say, 'Who have you got after the international break?' and it's Man City. We're trying not to think too much about it."

Watch full coverage and follow live text updates on BBC One, BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website

Under Vidosic, Brighton became a team seeking to dominate the ball, and during his first season in charge, they were very successful with only Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City averaging more possession per game.

They were physical too, committing the most fouls and accruing the most yellow cards in both 2024-25 and 2025-26.

"They could soak up pressure, and then build from the back," women's football journalist Annabel Bassett from The Brighton Base said. "They would overload in midfield and then possessed a real goal threat. It all came together."

That culminated in that inaugural FA Cup final in May, where they initially played well before being overrun.

Vidosic's departure damaged hopes for further progression, although Ruiz's success in leading unfancied Real Sociedad to Champions League qualification through finishing third in Liga F last year offers encouragement.

At 29, Arturo Ruiz is the youngest manager in the Women's Super League

It has been a slow start. Following that opening defeat by Arsenal, Brighton dropped points against struggling Birmingham City and Aston Villa, despite strong performances.

Two League Cup wins helped, and the nature of that commanding victory over Charlton suggests Ruiz's style is starting to take root.

"We still want to play," said Kirby, "[but] now it's more about how we harm the opposition quicker. There was an element previously where we overplayed when we could have gone forward.

"It's hard to change the mindset quickly, but we've got a great group of people.

"I'm very black and white. Tell me what you want and I'll do my best for you."

Bassett has noticed the desire for possession has become even more pronounced.

"[Ruiz] talks a lot about nullifying opponents," she said. "He likes to win the ball high and their key threats are on the flanks to open up space in the middle.

"He seems really willing to try things and the message from the club is that behind the scenes, everything is working."

For his part, Ruiz is also confident his methods are getting through.

"I'm really happy with the performances and the work we have been doing," he told BBC Sport. "We could have done better to get more points but the beginning is very difficult without previous time to build identity and clarity.

"I hope that from this Sunday we can be more solid and have more consistency and clarity with and without the ball."

Beating Charlton was important for Brighton before the pause in action, especially given hosts City are on a club-record run of 15 straight home wins.

"They're a quality side," Kirby said. "You can nullify one player but then they've got another two or three.

"But we've got quality that can harm teams. Hopefully, we can put on a good performance."

#292. All that was missing from Rangers' slapstick defending was a banana skin and someone throwing a bucket of water over themselves

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 18:13 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 18:35 BST, 18 October 2026

As every budding football coach will tell you, winning matches is all about getting the small details right.

Things like not lapsing into a trance when a long ball is knocked towards you down the channel. Not being completely unaware that there’s an opponent breathing down your neck when you take a square ball on the edge of your own box.

Goodness me. At times, all that was missing from Rangers’ slapstick defending routine at Dens Park was a treacherous banana skin and someone throwing a bucket of water over themselves.

All good things come to an end. The seven-game winning run which Derek McInnes’ side had put together between beating Aberdeen away on August 30 and Kilmarnock at home a week back was never going to go on forever.

But what a poor way to drop the ball. Rangers were not outdone by a moment of magic or simply being outplayed by a team hitting their straps. They slipped up by pointing the blunderbuss straight at their foot and pulling the trigger.

Last Friday, there was talk from Manny Fernandez of the team claiming the highest number of clean sheets in the league.

Embarrrassment for Rangers after Dan Neil blunder allowed Callum Jones to make it 2-2

Dan Neil looks crestfallen after the gaffe that proved so costly to the Ibrox side

It was hardly a fanciful notion, either. The consolation goal which Rangers conceded to Killie the previous weekend was the first one they’d let in after four matches in which Ivor Pandur’s goal hadn’t been breached.

Derek McInnes’ side had lost three goals in their first two league matches, but just one in their next five — or six including the League Cup rout over Celtic.

A more settled back four who’d steadily got to know how each other operated seemed to be on the same page as the deep-lying midfielders. After a difficult start, it looked like Rangers had the fundamentals out of possession right. All of that went out of the window on Tayside.

Dujon Sterling has been praised to the hilt of late and rightly so. The day before, his manager said he’d back him against anyone in a one v one.

What the full-back was thinking of when Dundee sent a long ball into his area shortly before half-time, only he could say.

Slow to react as Ashley Hay gathered, Sterling’s belated action was to meekly knock the ball into the path of Bradley Fink. The Swiss made short work of rounding the keeper and deservedly edging Dundee ahead.

The visiting fans hadn’t seen the last of the comedic defending, though. After Rangers had turned the game on its head thanks to spectacular goals from Badredine Bouanani and Nico Raskin either side of the interval, Dan Neil had an aberration of his own.

Demanding the ball from Raskin without first checking if it was on was his first mistake. His second was failing to simply pass the ball back to his keeper once Callum Jones came into the picture.

Bradley Fink has already put Dundee in front after a mistake by Dujon Sterling

Dujon Sterling trudges off at full time after his defensive gaffe saw Rangers stumble

Ransacked on the edge of his own penalty area, the midfielder — who’s also been terrific of late — could only watch on in horror as Jones scored his first goal in Dark Blue to claim a point for Steven Pressley’s side.

But here’s the thing. While sleep won’t have come easy for Sterling or Neil after their high-profile blunders, it would be wrong to lump the entire blame for the loss of two points at their doors.

These days, the dogs in the street know what Dundee are about. Bravely setting up with two strikers and two wingers, they take the game to you. They mix it up and they look to ask questions. They aren’t a surprise package. Yet their approach seemed to spook McInnes’ side for long enough.

Dundee were much the better team in the period leading up to Fink’s opener. Hay thumped the bar with a header. They fashioned a number of half-chances and looked far more assured of themselves than the visitors.

Rangers struggled to exert any semblance of control on the game. They were lax at the back, second best in midfield. There was too big a gap between Kim Min-su and Ryan Naderi up top. It briefly felt like things had reverted to the early weeks of the campaign.

Sterling was the fall guy, for sure, but the collective display was miles off it.

The one shining light for McInnes was the display of Bouanani, a surprise starter who displaced Kevin Kelsy. On loan from Stuttgart, the winger had made just one start in his four appearances to date.

Lively and imaginative, he fully justified his selection. His goal to equalise was a peach. Having seen his initial shot blocked by Imari Samuels, he found the top corner with the rebound. Simply unstoppable.

Bluntly, Rangers were fortunate to go in level at the break. There was a marked improvement when they re-emerged. That is, until Neil’s error floored them.

Where was that sense of urgency in the opening 45 minutes? McInnes’ men took fewer touches, made better runs and demanded more of each other.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes was let down by his team's slapstick defending

With the midfield connected to Kim and Ryan Naderi, Dundee were penned in for a spell.

Raskin’s goal was a thing of beauty. Kim found Neil who fed the Belgian. His strike from 25 yards dipped and crashed in off the underside of the bar.

It should then only have been a case of how many goals Rangers would win by. Neil’s costly error came with 21 minutes remaining, plenty time to repair the damage.

It just all became a little bit panicked and messy. One goalmouth scramble aside, Rangers really didn’t look like scoring.

They played some good stuff from a goal down, but the purple patch didn’t last long enough to put the game to bed. The conspicuous individual errors were only part of a collective display which wasn’t good enough for long enough.

At what point is it safe to say that Pressley was an inspired appointment by Dundee?

If the figure in the home dug-out at Dens Park hasn’t won over the doubters by now, then he never will.

An eighth-place finish last season was commendable and came on the back of Pressley himself acknowledging that he faced a major battle to win hearts and minds.

Nico Raskin had scored a super goal for Rangers to put the Ibrox side 2-1 in front at Dens Park

The performance of scorer Badredine Bouanani was a rare bright spot for Rangers

Not only are Dundee presently sitting proudly in fourth place, their results to this point have been achieved despite a brutal injury list which counts Simon Murray and Fin Robertson among the long-term casualties.

Pressley is evidently not only a fine man-manager and a shrewd tactician. He’s a problem solver.

While a first win over the Ibrox men since November 2017 was beyond his depleted side, a deserved share of the spoils against an in-form opponent will add to the growing sense of momentum.

With St Mirren, Kilmarnock and St Johnstone coming up, Dundee have an opportunity to ballast their lofty position.

Wild horses aren’t going to drag their manager down the road of speaking about a top-six finish, let alone a return to Europe for the first time since 2003-04. But the fact that supporters are even contemplating such achievements is a measure of the job he’s done.

Romesh Ranganathan is possibly the busiest man in all of showbusiness – balancing his very many television commitments with his love of Arsenal.

Ranganathan is currently on the BBC's The Traitors, where he's picked as a Faithful (we won't give you any more spoilers than that) and has to navigate the pitfalls of the castle alongside friend Rob Beckett.

The comedian spoke to FourFourTwo about his life following the Gunners in 2021…

I’m Crawley born and bred, and people are forever having a go at me for not being a Crawley Town fan. It’s my dad’s fault. When he first came over from Sri Lanka, he stayed in north London and soon became a really militant Gooner. He ended up opening what was just an Arsenal-themed pub in East Grinstead. Punters would come to watch my dad lose his s**t over Arsenal – he’d shout, scream and go mental. This was when we were good, so imagine what he was like when we became rubbish! I went to Crawley when Arsenal played them in the FA Youth Cup [in 2003]. It was the first time I ever saw Cesc Fabregas. The Arsenal kids were all unbelievable, but a 16-year-old Cesc was on another level – he scored from the halfway line... just insane. They won 9-0.

Who was your childhood hero, and did you ever meet them?

I’ve always loved Ian Wright – both as a player and a personality. But I quickly learned you can make an absolute dick of yourself in front of your heroes. I was once with Kevin Bridges in a hotel bar, the morning after a big night’s drinking. We noticed Wrighty in there, but I felt so hungover and didn’t want to meet him. I desperately wanted him to like me, but didn’t feel equipped to be interesting or amusing. We got up to leave, but then he suddenly walked over and introduced himself.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

All I could do was garble some gushing nonsense. Even Kevin told me, “Jesus, that was f**king awful banter you were inflicting on the poor guy.” I ended up having to ask a mutual acquaintance to apologise for my s**t chat. So I’ve decided, in the same way I prepare for a show, I’m going to work up material for the next time I see Ian. I’ll try it out in the car until I feel ready.

Hector Bellerin – I’ve met him and he genuinely loves Arsenal. I think it’s unfair that people expect players to have personalities, too. The physical prowess they show is so amazing that to ask them to be eloquent speakers as well is a bit much. We don’t have a go at great speakers because they can’t kick a ball, do we? But Bellerin is intelligent and a very funny bloke.

What was your finest moment when you played?

I honestly don’t have one, because I’m horrendous. When I was a teacher, they roped me into the annual sixth-formers vs staff game. I came on as a reluctant substitute at the end, then shinned an absolute sitter over the bar.

Let me tell you, I’ve never received so much abuse – not even at any of the gigs I’ve done since. It got so bad that I couldn’t enter the staff room or walk around school for a week. I self-isolated for my own good.

I think it’s unfair that people expect players to have personalities – but Hector Bellerin is intelligent and a very funny bloke.

Which footballer do you admire that never played for your club?

I remember one game against Chelsea at Highbury, and I couldn’t believe – this is a compliment – how much of a prick Dennis Wise was. You’d never see it on TV, but he was constantly in our players’ ears, giving them all sorts of s**t on the wind-up. Wise was one of those hateful players you’d love to have in your team.

Do you have any matchday routines or superstitions?

My dad’s superstition was to make us go for fried chicken before every game. He swore it helped Arsenal win, but I should also tell you: he died of a heart attack... My only routine is to get to the stadium early, but the problem is it looks like I’m desperate for attention. ‘Look, Romesh has turned up early for some selfies, the absolute narcissist’. But it’s just my superstition. Honestly.

Which player would you pick as your room-mate?

Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang. I’d give him the best night of his life and lay on so much entertainment, to convince him to stay. “You see mate, it wouldn’t be like this if you joined Real Madrid…”

What’s the strangest thing you’ve seen or heard at a match?

I was at Highbury, and an Arsenal fan got angry as I wasn’t singing enough. This was before I did any stand-up, so it wasn’t because he’d recognised me. But every time a new song started, he’d look around at me as if to say, ‘Well, are you going to f**king sing or not?’ It became very uncomfortable and I felt obliged to join in. I was singing like a hostage. You could see the quiet terror in my eyes as he growled, “Sing up you tart.”

Where’s the strangest place you’ve met a manager or player?

I was in Portugal with my wife and kids a few years ago, on holiday. We were all in the hotel restaurant, when suddenly Calum Chambers turned up and tapped me on the shoulder. I’d recorded a show with him in the past, so he knew me, but it was really weird seeing him there. He was with three of his mates and asked me if I knew anywhere decent to go out. I said, “You’re talking to a fat dad on his family holiday, so unless you’re keen on a kids’ quiz night or going on the flume rides, you’ve got this all wrong.” Mental.

Who’s the worst player you’ve seen at your club?

I’m not one for slagging off players, but Igors Stepanovs was truly awful. There was a 10-minute spell during his Arsenal career when I was definitely as good as him – that’s how awful he was.

Who would you play alongside in your fantasy five-a-side team?

I’d have Gianluigi Buffon in goal, simply because he looks so rock ‘n’ roll. Thierry Henry is up top, obviously. Ronaldinho is in there, because he’s the best YouTube compilation player of all time and seems like he’d be a laugh. I’m hardly a natural finisher, as my old school will testify, so I’ll stay at the back, shoring things up – or at least trying to – with Martin Keown.

He’s such a defensive monster that I’d either have absolutely nothing to do, or he’d be continually screaming at me. It could prove to be one of the most torrid afternoons of my life, but it would take some of the edge off that staff game at Hazelwick School.

#295. Swansea must use West Ham defeat as fuel - Matos

Swansea lost for only the fourth in 21 home Championship games under Vitor Matos

Vitor Matos has told Swansea City to use the frustration of defeat by West Ham United as fuel in their bid to keep pace in the Championship promotion race.

Swansea's four-game winning streak came to an end as they lost in the league for only the second time this season thanks to Divine Mukasa's first-half goal.

The Swans, who remain top of the table despite defeat, had their chances against the second-tier title favourites, with Ben Cabango going closest when he hit the woodwork.

And Matos says the manner of the West Ham loss means it should not halt Swansea's early-season momentum.

"I think it's important that when the game finished we all felt that we could have taken something out of the game," said the Swansea head coach.

West Ham and Southampton are the only teams who have beaten Swansea in 11 league games this season

"I think that's the most important thing today, that we played against a really good opposition, a team that of course is one of the main contenders to go to the Premier League, and we felt that we can compete and we can beat them as well.

"That frustration, that's something that should stay, but that's something that more than anything should give us the fuel to push ourselves in training, push our standards and keep improving."

West Ham climbed to second in the table having become the first visiting side since Southampton in April to win a league game at Swansea.

The game was tight until Mukasa struck, but opened up from that point as Swansea went in search of an equaliser.

The hosts' two best chances fell to Cabango at set-pieces, with the centre-back rattling one shot against the bar and then dragging another wide of the target when he appeared to destined to equalise.

West Ham win top-of-the-table meeting at Swansea

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

West Ham had further opportunities, with Lawrence Vigouroux making second-half saves from Jarrod Bowen â twice â and Pablo.

Matos felt Swansea proved their credentials despite losing a league game on their own ground for the first time since April.

"What I saw today, I think we can compete against every team and that's what we need to do," Matos added.

"We need to keep pushing ourselves to beat the best teams of the league. West Ham is one of the best teams.

"We tried [against them]. Unfortunately, we could not get something out of the game and that's the story."

#302. Honeymoon is over for Hibs boss Reedijk as hapless Leith men make it SIX months without a league win at Easter Road

Published: 17:38 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 18:06 BST, 18 October 2026

Speaking ahead of Saturday’s clash with Falkirk, new Hibs boss Marink Reedijk couldn’t possibly have been any more enthusiastic about the prospect of making his Easter Road bow.

The Dutchman spoke of being ‘buzzing’. Of hearing ‘fantastic stories’ about the stadium he hopes will be his home for a good few years, at least.

Clearly nobody gave the guy a heads-up about just how miserable Easter Road has become lately.

This is one of Scottish football’s finest arenas which, on its day, can produce an atmosphere unmatched by anything else in the country. No question, it can be a special place to play.

But it doesn’t feel like that these days. In fact, it’s verging on toxic.

You have to go back to April 4 for the last time these supporters celebrated a home Premiership win. That’s over six months. It is completely unacceptable.

Marink Reedijk has been left in no doubt as to the size of the task facing him at Easter Road

Since that pre-split victory over Kilmarnock, Hibs have taken just one point from the 24 on offer in Leith. Is it any wonder these fans are absolutely scunnered? Fair play to them for continually turning up.

The best part of 18,000 of them were in attendance on Saturday, hoping to see something different from a team which has disappointed for so long. Instead, they got more of the same.

Every loose ball – and there were too many to keep track of – was met with a groan, as was the response to watching bad decision after bad decision both on and off the ball.

Reedijk has been in charge at the club for four halves of football, and each one of them has concluded amid a chorus of boos. He must be wondering what he’s signed up for.

Now, let’s get one thing clear. The new manager can’t carry the can for what’s gone before. Nor should he take the blame for the way in which Saturday’s defeat played out.

That should rest firmly with the players, who once again found a way to throw away three very gettable points against a team who, let’s not forget, hadn’t won here since 2014.

The fans are never going to need any help getting themselves up for big European nights or Edinburgh derbies but, most weeks, they rely on those on the pitch to give them something to get behind. And it just ain’t happening at the moment.

Jacob Murrell scores the first of his outstanding double to put Falkirk on course for victory

Hibs set the tone for another wretched afternoon within 13 minutes when Azeem Abdulai – making his first start for the club since joining in the summer – failed to control a routine ball into his feet as the hosts launched a promising counter-attack.

Five seconds later, they were trailing thanks to Jacob Murrell’s rocket of a finish after being played in by a fine Ryan Strain pass.

Falkirk’s second was even worse from a Hibs perspective. Thibault Klidje’s ridiculous attempt to backheel his way out of trouble down at his own corner flag was punished in emphatic fashion by Murrell once again as the American registered his fourth league goal of the season.

Owen Elding bundled home – with the aid of his right arm by the looks of things – before the break to give Reedijk’s men a lifeline, but that was to be the highlight of the afternoon.

Afterwards, the manager was eager to point out their dominance throughout the second half, and it was hard to argue with that assessment.

Falkirk barely crossed the halfway line as Hibs penned them in. The stats show that the hosts enjoyed more than 70 per cent of the ball too. But that doesn’t count for a whole lot when you aren’t good enough to do anything with it.

This wasn’t an onslaught by any stretch, with Scott Bain in the Falkirk goal only properly tested once by a Jamie McGrath effort from 18 yards with a little over ten minutes to play. That was pretty much it.

The supporters are desperate to give Reedijk a chance, and you suspect they’ll be willing to suffer for a little while longer while he puts the building blocks in place.

American forward Murrell has now scored four goals and looks a great acquisition by Falkirk

Yet it’s going to be nigh-on impossible for the former Beveren boss to implement his much-heralded attacking style if individuals can’t do the simple stuff.

Hibs welcome Celtic to Easter Road next time out, before making a midweek trip to St Mirren. Then there’s the small matter of a Premier Sports Cup semi-final against Hearts to round off that week.

A Hibs side playing at their peak would likely come unstuck in at least one of those. God knows how this version will fare. Indeed, it could get a lot worse for the league’s bottom side before they start heading in the right direction.

Falkirk, meanwhile, will hope this win can kickstart their season.

John McGlynn’s side had shipped stoppage-time goals in three of their last four going into the weekend. Five points went out the window during that run.

But they never really looked like letting it happen again here. Of course, Murrell will get the headlines for an excellent double but this triumph was down to hard graft more than anything else.

Lewis Neilson and Liam Henderson were outstanding at the back, while Brad Spencer and Harry Barbrook in front of them didn’t allow the likes of Josh Mulligan time to breathe.

This was arguably as ugly a win – and they’ve had plenty – as the Bairns have had since returning to the top flight last year, but McGlynn won’t care about that.

His side have style and some substance to boot. Hibs are still searching for both.

#303. The Traitors star Rob Beckett opens up about life as an Arsenal fan to FourFourTwo

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Rob Beckett of The Traitors fame talks Wrighty, 'fat' Ronaldo and going on a bender with an England keeper

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rob Beckett admits he should have been a Crystal Palace fan – but a love of Ian Wright rather skewed things.

Most recently, the comedian has been a star of The Traitors alongside friend Romesh Ranganathan as a member of the faithful.

But back in 2021, Beckett spoke to FourFourTwo exclusively about his life following the Gunners…

What was the first game you ever attended?

Tottenham vs Arsenal in the early ’90s – it was 0-0 and there were loads of fights. We were south London – I should be a Palace fan, really. But I just loved Ian Wright, so I started watching Arsenal. I’m an Ian Wright fan first and an Arsenal fan second. I feel quite guilty – I mean, I did have a season ticket for a few years, but I feel semi-ashamed because I should be Palace or Millwall. I don’t get too upset about it like other fans either – give me 10 minutes after a defeat and I don’t care. You can’t get in trouble for switching to a worse team, can you?

Is Wrighty your favourite footballer ever, then?

Always! He was from near me in south London – he looked like he enjoyed it whenever he played; he was a bit dirty and would have a fight. He’d kick Peter Schmeichel and I loved all that – like when Martin Keown smacked Ruud van Nistelrooy on the head. I reckon I should have watched boxing instead really, because I hate it when people say that having a scrap in football is disrespectful and it’s such a shame – no, it’s f**king brilliant. I’d love for football to be a bit more like ice hockey: imagine how good it would be if Roy Keane and Patrick Vieira could just have a two-minute scrap and have it out properly.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Have you got to meet many of your footballing heroes?

Well, I got to meet Wrighty when I did a radio show, and I was crap because I was so nervous. Then I saw him in the street. He just shouted, “Oi, what’s happening?” and gave me a cuddle. I was like, ‘Oh my god, he knows who I am!’ Then I started working with him on Absolute Radio and it’s so weird: they say don’t meet your heroes, but it should be ‘don’t meet your heroes unless your hero is Ian Wright’. Definitely meet him – he’s more than you can ever imagine.

It was quite funny, because I’d start to get annoyed with him whenever he turned up late. I’d be sat there thinking, ‘For f**k’s sake, mate’. A few years ago, I’d have been desperate to meet him, and now I’m getting the hump because he’s turning up to work late. But he’s a lovely bloke. I was at a hotel with my wife once for our anniversary, and Wrighty was there with his wife. He sent us over a bottle of champagne when my wife didn’t actually get me anything that year. I got an anniversary present from Ian Wright instead of my wife...

Nah, I had to give up my season ticket. Between having kids and touring, I very rarely go. I see those guys who sing “over land and sea” and think, ‘What the f**k’s happening in your home life?’ You know that lot?

It’s a waste of a life, I’ve got to be honest. I think you can be too committed as a fan – you really need a balance in your life.

I had to give up my season ticket… I think you can be too committed as a fan

What’s the greatest goal you’ve ever seen live?

I saw Aki Riihilahti score from about 35 yards for Palace, and was directly behind it. I must have been young, but I saw it bend – it wasn’t the best goal ever, but position-wise I couldn’t have been any better. It probably wasn’t even that good, but in my head it was unbelievable. It was the first proper long-range goal I’d seen!

What’s the funniest thing you’ve ever seen or heard at a game?

Lloyd Griffith [fellow comedian, once of these pages] dropping his phone into a toilet at half-time during the Euros final at Wembley. You know when something happens and you just explode?

Who’s the one footballer you’d love to take on a night out?

I bumped into Paul Robinson while on a massive bender in Edinburgh, when he played for Blackburn. He came out on the piss – I’m not sure if he’s calmed down, though. He just came to see my show up there. He once got smuggled into Arsenal for a meeting with Arsene Wenger apparently, but Wenger didn’t want him and signed Richard Wright instead. Great decision.

There’s Jimmy Bullard, too – he’s brilliant but he can be too much. So it just depends on how big this night out is going to be. But someone I’ve not been out with is Jack Grealish. I’d love to have a drink with him, because everyone loves Jack Grealish now, don’t they? Phil Foden is great too, and I love Emile Smith Rowe and Bukayo Saka, but they’re only kids. You need someone who’s had a bit of a life – you know, some headcase from the Championship. But no, I’d do laughing gas with Grealish.

Which player would you choose as your room-mate?

Someone really little, I’d imagine. Andrey Arshavin – really small, really quiet. Would probably rather be in Russia. The smallest player who’s ever played football, I’d say.

I bumped into Paul Robinson while on a massive bender in Edinburgh: he came out on the piss

Which player do you like even though they never played for your club?

That’s two-fold. We could have had someone like [Didier] Drogba upfront with Thierry Henry. But do I want to weaken another team or just make Arsenal great? I’m overthinking this now! I think either Ronaldinho or fat Ronaldo. It’s awful that he’s just become ‘fat Ronaldo’ now, isn’t it?

Who from your club’s past would you bring back for the current side?

At their peak? In this team it has to be a centre-back or defensive midfielder, so if I could have a young Tony Adams coming through at 20 now, and you know you’re getting 15-20 years of him at the back, that would be great. I’d say either Adams or Patrick Vieira. We’re all right with our attackers at the moment, but we need a leader to help us out a bit.

I really like Smith Rowe. I think he’s brilliant – especially after the North London Derby [where he scored one, assisted one and won the man of the match award].

If you could drop yourself into your all-time five-a-side team, who would you be playing alongside?

I’ve got to go with David Seaman in goal. There may be better goalkeepers, but he’s so lovely – you’ve got to think about morale. I’d have Patrick Vieira in the middle. Thierry Henry upfront, of course. And then… f**k it, I’ll go Dennis Bergkamp as well. Just because then I’ll really enjoy it – I’ll just be playing with a load of club legends.

But then I’ve not got Ian Wright, have I? Right, get rid of Henry and stick Wrighty in there for the banter. I’ll just stay at the back with Dave…

Mark White has been at on FourFourTwo since joining in January 2020, first as a staff writer before becoming content editor in 2023. An encyclopedia of football shirts and boots knowledge – both past and present – Mark has also represented FFT at both FA Cup and League Cup finals (though didn't receive a winners' medal on either occasion) and has written pieces for the mag ranging on subjects from Bobby Robson's season at Barcelona to Robinho's career. He has written cover features for the mag on Mikel Arteta and Martin Odegaard, and is assisted by his cat, Rosie, who has interned for the brand since lockdown.

#310. Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared

The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

Key ins: Bruno Guimarães (Newcastle, £75m), Ezri Konsa (Aston Villa, £51m), Piero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m)

Key outs: Leandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m), Gabriel Jesus (Barcelona, £8.6m), Fábio Vieira (Hamburg, £7.7m), Christian Nørgaard (Everton, £7m), Ethan Nwaneri (Borussia Dortmund, loan)

It is all change at Villa and, although a little trepidation is inevitable, a refresh was probably overdue. At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. Last summer there was concern Villa had gone stale and 12 months ago they ended up fretting on deadline day – Harvey Elliott and Jadon Sancho joined on loan – but there was no such chaos this time. Ben Fisher

Key ins: Johan Manzambi (Freiburg, £51m), Nicolas Jackson (Chelsea, £47.5m), Ibrahim Mbaye (PSG, £47m), João Gomes (Wolves, £34m), Zion Suzuki (Parma, £30m), Taylor Harwood-Bellis (Southampton, £25m), Matteo Ruggeri (Atlético Madrid, £21.4m), Leon Goretzka (Bayern Munich, free), Aaron Wan-Bissaka (West Ham, loan), Alejandro Garnacho (Chelsea, loan)

Key outs: Morgan Rogers (Chelsea, £117m), Ollie Watkins (Al-Hilal, £51m), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal, £51m), Youri Tielemans (Manchester United, £35m), Donyell Malen (Roma, £21.6m), Lewis Dobbin (Southampton, £9m), Lucas Digne (PSG, £8.5m), Emiliano Martínez (Chelsea, £7.5m), Evann Guessand (Crystal Palace, loan)

The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?

Perhaps Bournemouth’s best business was keeping hold of their coveted key players, chiefly Eli Junior Kroupi, Rayan, Alex Scott and Tyler Adams. Bournemouth rejected bids from Chelsea for Scott and stayed true to their plan of resisting offers to give Marco Rose the best chance of succeeding, with the club attempting to juggle European competition and the league for the first time. The arrival of the Portugal centre-back António Silva, 22, from Benfica looks a typically smart replacement for Marcos Senesi, 29. Kroupi’s freak foot injury, which will probably keep him out until November, may have proved a blessing in disguise in terms of retaining the 20-year-old. BF

Key ins: António Silva (Benfica, £21.4m), Álvaro Rodríguez (Elche, £21.3m), Juanlu Sánchez (Sevilla, £11.1m), Michele Di Gregorio (Juventus, loan)

Key outs: Luis Sinisterra (Cruzeiro, £5.2m), Enes Unal (Getafe, free), Álex Jiménez (Fiorentina, loan), Marcos Senesi (Tottenham, free)

Avoiding a repeat of last year’s upheaval was a major boost. Keith Andrews held on to his best players and made smart additions to a solid squad. Mamadou Sangaré has added quality in midfield since joining from Lens and looks the bargain of the summer. Callum Wilson has brought experience up front after signing on a free and Jaidon Anthony provides cover on the flanks after his £15m move from Burnley. El Hadji-Malick Diouf, signed from West Ham, offers potential at left-back. Jacob Steinberg

Key ins: Mamadou Sangaré (Lens, £39m), El Hadji Malick Diouf (West Ham, £35m), Jaidon Anthony (Burnley, £15m), Jannik Schuster (Red Bull Salzburg, £14m), Callum Wilson (West Ham, free)

Key outs: Ethan Pinnock (Coventry, £6m), Jordan Henderson (Chelsea, free)

Deadline day deals to bring in the exciting Nigeria forward Femi Azeez from Millwall and the Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés from Stuttgart made it 12 signings in another summer of transition, Azeez’s arrival being announced almost 12 hours after the window shut. The departures of Jan Paul van Hecke, Carlos Baleba and Carl Rushworth brought in more than £140m as the Brighton model continues to deliver big profits, although losing last season’s top scorer, Danny Welbeck, to Chelsea for a mere £5m may be the biggest loss if the new striker Promise David cannot bring the goals. EA

Key ins: Luka Vuskovic (Tottenham, £46m), Zadok Yohanna (AIK, £21.5m), Chema Andrés (Stuttgart, £18.9m), Pascal Struijk (Leeds, £18m), Femi Azeez (Millwall, £15m), Jaouen Hadjam (Young Boys, £11.1m), Costinha (Olympiakos, £11m), Michael Svoboda (Venezia, £4.3m), Promise David (Union St-Gilloise, loan)

Key outs: Carlos Baleba (Manchester United, £70m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham, £52m), Carl Rushworth (Coventry, £22.5m), Diego Coppola (Paris FC, £15.3m), Danny Welbeck (Chelsea, £5m), Joël Veltman (West Ham, free), James Milner (retired), Solly March (released)

Xabi Alonso’s appointment as manager was the biggest signing of the summer. Chelsea have been sensible since turning to the Spaniard. Morgan Rogers has started well after joining for £117m. Maxence Lacroix adds power in defence, Marco Palestra versatility on the flanks. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson can raise standards in the dressing room. But there was the usual revolving door. Money was made on a host of outgoings. Marc Cucurella, one of the world’s best left-backs and sold to Real Madrid, looks a bigger loss than Enzo Fernández. However a worry is that Chelsea did not replace Fernández after selling him to Manchester City for £125m, their late £47m move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara collapsing at the last. JS

Key ins: Morgan Rogers (Aston Villa, £117m), Maxence Lacroix (Crystal Palace, £52m), Marco Palestra (Atalanta, £47m), Geovany Quenda (Sporting, £40m), Valentín Barco (Strasbourg, £34m), Emmanuel Emegha (Strasbourg, £21.6m), Pep Chavarría (Rayo Vallecano, £16.3m), Emiliano Martínez (Aston Villa, £7.5m), Danny Welbeck (Brighton, £5m), Jordan Henderson (Brentford, free)

Key outs: Enzo Fernández (Manchester City, £125m), Marc Cucurella (Real Madrid, £52m), Andrey Santos (Manchester United, £50m), Nicolas Jackson (Aston Villa, £47.5m), Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest, £45m), Trevoh Chalobah (Como 1907, £25.7m), Tyrique George (Everton, £18m), Marc Guiu (RB Leipzig, £14.5m), Tosin Adarabioyo (Tottenham, £7m), Axel Disasi (Crystal Palace, loan), Alejandro Garnacho (Aston Villa, loan), Benoît Badiashile (Napoli, loan), Robert Sánchez (Como, loan), Mykhailo Mudryk (Tottenham, loan)

It remains to be seen whether Coventry have struck the right balance in the market. Frank Lampard wanted to maintain momentum but add power and physicality. Coventry also sought to address their lack of Premier League experience with Taiwo Awoniyi and Ethan Pinnock. Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers last season but the step up means the pressure is on Awoniyi, never prolific for Nottingham Forest, Sidiki Cherif, a promising 19-year-old, and Ellis Simms to deliver before Haji Wright returns from injury. Stephen Mfuni, a teenage loanee from Manchester City and their 11th and final summer signing, increases their left-back options. BF

Key ins: Caleb Yirenkyi (Nordsjælland, £23m), Carl Rushworth (Brighton, £22.5m), Sidiki Cherif (Fenerbahce, £20.5m), Loum Tchaouna (Burnley, £20m), Aurèle Amenda (Eintracht Frankfurt, £15.4m), Taiwo Awoniyi (Nottingham Forest, £9m), Ethan Pinnock (Brentford, £6m), Gustavo Hamer (Sheffield United, £6m), Stephen Mfuni (Manchester City, loan), Frank Onyeka (Brentford, undisclosed), Dan Bentley (Wolves, undisclosed)

The lost tug of war with Sunderland over Malick Fofana summed up another chaotic deadline day for Palace, who were still scrambling for signings in the final minutes and confirmed the arrivals of Ben Chilwell, Quinten Timber and Darío Osorio after the window shut. The new manager, Pierre Sage, will at least be pleased to have secured more defensive reinforcements after losing Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea, with the loanees Honest Ahanor and Axel Disasi adding much-needed depth. Palace also kept hold of Ismaïla Sarr – presuming he doesn’t join a club in Saudi Arabia before the Sunday deadline there – after rejecting an approach from Liverpool for the Senegal forward. EA

Key ins: Anan Khalaili (Union St-Gilloise, £21m), Quinten Timber (Marseille, £15m), Zavier Gozo (Real Salt Lake, £11m), Axel Disasi (Chelsea, loan), Evann Guessand (Aston Villa, loan), Honest Ahanor (Atalanta, loan), Darío Osorio (Midtjylland, loan), Dwight McNeil (Everton, swap), Takehiro Tomiyasu (Ajax, free), Óscar Mingueza (Celta Vigo, free), Ben Chilwell (Strasbourg, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Maxence Lacroix (Chelsea, £52m), Daniel Muñoz (Nottingham Forest, £22m), Brennan Johnson (Everton, swap), Borna Sosa (Cologne, loan)

It was a window that revealed the extent of The Friedkin Group’s ambitions, the strength of the club’s finances after the move to a new stadium, the state of the relationship between the manager and chief executive and the expertise of the senior leadership team; and none of it was positive. The owners deserve some credit for listening to fans and halting the self-defeating sale of Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest but otherwise it was a modest window that descended into a shambles. The club’s best player was sold for a below-market fee, a move for Folarin Balogun collapsed and although the equally desperate search for a right-back ended with Ainsley Maitland-Niles signing, David Moyes was left with one striker and a smaller squad than he started the day with, despite repeatedly urging his employers to strengthen. AH

Key ins: Tyrique George (Chelsea, £18m), Merlin Röhl (Freiburg, £17.3m), Hayden Hackney (Middlesbrough, £16.5m), Christian Nørgaard (Arsenal, £7m), Ainsley Maitland-Niles (Lyon, £4.3m), Brennan Johnson (Crystal Palace, swap), Jack Grealish (Manchester City, loan)

Key outs: Iliman Ndiaye (Manchester City, £60m), Beto (Fiorentina, £15.4m), Tim Iroegbunam (Hull, £13m), Dwight McNeil (Crystal Palace, swap), Idrissa Gueye (Al-Diriyah, free), Nathan Patterson (Torino, free), Séamus Coleman (released)

It was a summer of change at Craven Cottage. Marco Silva departed after five successful years in charge and was replaced by the inexperienced Álvaro Arbeloa, who has focused on adding youth. Gonzalo García, César Palacios and Manuel Ángel followed Arbeloa from Real Madrid and Shea Charles is an exciting signing from Southampton. Some stalwarts have left. Raúl Jiménez joined Wolves and Harry Wilson went to Leeds. Fulham looked to strengthen. They secured the midfielder Hugo Larsson and centre-back David Affengruber on deadline day but missed out on another target, the right-back Andrei Ratiu. JS

Key ins: Gonzalo García (Real Madrid, £34.3m), Shea Charles (Southampton, £30m), David Affengruber (Elche, £10.3m), César Palacios (Real Madrid, £8.6m), Jonah Kusi-Asare (Bayern Munich, £5.2m), Manuel Ángel (Real Madrid, £3.4m), Hugo Larsson (Eintracht Frankfurt, loan)

Key outs: Sasa Lukic (Ipswich, £9m), Issa Diop (Ipswich, £8.5m), Harry Wilson (Leeds, free), Raúl Jiménez (Wolves, free)

“Think of us like a volcano,” said Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, in early July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Two months on the Ilicali has presided over 18 signings, investing more than £150m and his manager, Sergej Jakirovic, has choreographed two Premier League wins. The horizon looks infinitely brighter than in June, when the playoff winners sold two players for a combined £8.5m to avoid breaching English Football League spending rules and a near-certain six-point deduction. Hull, remember, spent last season under a two-window EFL transfer embargo. They have compensated for that this summer and, although time will tell whether all those new faces are compatible, reasons for optimism remain real. Not least because last season’s cult hero loanee forward Joe Gelhardt has signed permanently from Leeds. Louise Taylor

Key ins: Nobel Mendy (Rayo Vallecano, £20m), Konstantinos Tzolakis (Olympiakos, £20m), Lucas Herrington (Colorado Rapids, £17.1m), Ilyas Ansah (Union Berlin, £14.5m), Mohamed-Ali Cho (Nice, £13m), Brooke Norton-Cuffy (Genoa, £12m), Jens Hjerto-Dahl (Tromsø, £10m), Tim Iroegbunam (Everton, £13m), Christos Mouzakitis (Olympiakos, £12.9m), Sorba Thomas (Stoke, £7.5m), Joe Gelhardt (Leeds, £6.5m), Jack Butland (Rangers, £3.5m), Lucas Gourna-Douath (Red Bull Salzburg, £3.4m), Elliot Stroud (Mjällby, £3m), Robinio Vaz (Roma, loan), Hidemasa Morita (Sporting, free), Matt Targett (Newcastle, free), Óscar Zambrano (Maribor, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Ivor Pandur (Rangers, £6m), Cody Drameh (Genoa, £3.9m), Abu Kamara (Portsmouth, £2.5m), Kyle Joseph (Middlesbrough, undisclosed fee)

The late addition of Burnley’s striker Zian Flemming brought Ipswich’s summer spend close to £200m. That appears to be the cost of giving yourselves a genuine shot at survival. Arrivals such as Exequiel Palacios and Julio Enciso should have no business in the lower reaches, and the former Fulham pair Sasa Lukic and Issa Diop add crucial experience. Gary O’Neil can call upon enviable depth in midfield and speed on the flanks, where Abdul Fatawu and Daizen Maeda look sharp. But time will tell whether Ipswich strengthened their defence sufficiently for regular tests of the kind they failed at Old Trafford on Sunday. Nick Ames

Key ins: Julio Enciso (Strasbourg, £26m), Emersonn (Toulouse, £24m), Exequiel Palacios (Bayer Leverkusen, £23.5m), Zian Flemming (Burnley, £20m), Abdul Fatawu (Leicester, £20m), Abdoul Ouattara (Strasbourg, £17m), Florentino Luís (Burnley, £16m), Daizen Maeda (Celtic, £10m), Sasa Lukic (Fulham, £9m), Kjell Scherpen (Union St-Gilloise, £8.6m), Issa Diop (Fulham, £8.5m), Chuba Akpom (Ajax, £7m), Kayne van Oevelen (Volendam, £3.4m), Cédric Kipré (Reims, £1.7m)

Key outs: George Hirst (Stoke, £6m), Arijanet Muric (Sassuolo, £6m), Harry Clarke (Preston, £3.5m)

In an ideal world Daniel Farke might have wished for one more high-calibre attacking recruit but that should not detract from a very decent window, featuring seven extremely sensible signings. The importance of the acquisition of the England goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City should not be underestimated. Trafford will almost certainly provide Leeds with a few more extra points – not to mention enhance their play courtesy of his stellar footwork. Just in front of him Tarik Muharemovic looks an outstanding defensive buy. Harry Wilson raises creativity levels and the attacking tone. LT

Key ins: James Trafford (Manchester City, £40.5m), Tarik Muharemovic (Sassuolo, £34.1m), Nico Elvedi (Borussia Mönchengladbach, £6.8m), Michael Zetterer (Eintracht Frankfurt, £4.3m), Jean-Mattéo Bahoya (Eintracht Frankfurt, loan), Melvin Bard (Nice, loan), Harry Wilson (Fulham, free)

Key outs: Pascal Struijk (Brighton, £18m), Joe Gelhardt (Hull, £6.5m), Lucas Perri (Torino, loan), Sebastiaan Bornauw (Hamburg, loan), Joël Piroe (West Ham, loan), Illan Meslier (Arsenal, free)

The final window of Richard Hughes’s spell as sporting director raised more questions over Liverpool’s direction under Fenway Sports Group, owners soon to be enriched by a £2bn investment from 1892 Holdings. The shift towards paying big money for big names continued with Bradley Barcola’s arrival from Paris Saint-Germain while Jérémy Jacquet and Victor Muñoz followed the older policy of developing young potential. Yet weaknesses remain at right back, defensive midfield and on the right wing, where Mohamed Salah’s exit was foreseen from December. Squad depth is lacking and a lot rests on the return to full fitness of Hugo Ekitiké, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni. AH

Key ins: Bradley Barcola (PSG, £123m), Jérémy Jacquet (Rennes, £55m), Víctor Muñoz (Osasuna, £34.5m), Ronald Araújo (Barcelona, loan)

Key outs: Curtis Jones (Inter, £25.7m), Harvey Elliott (Valencia, loan), Mohamed Salah (Trabzonspor, free), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid, free), Andy Robertson (Tottenham, free)

With Enzo Fernández’s deadline day signing for a British record-equalling £125m, Enzo Maresca can have zero complaints about a first window as Manchester City’s head coach. The No 8 follows two No 6s, in Elliot Anderson (£116m) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (£85m), and the wide players Allan Elias (£34m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£60m plus £5m) as major signings, the total spend on incomings about £457.5m. Factor in how City have generated about £281.8m in outgoings for a net spend of £175.7m, the divisions third-biggest of the window, and this sizable investment has to work - particularly the acquisition of Fernández. Jamie Jackson

Key ins: Enzo Fernández (Chelsea, £125m), Elliot Anderson (Nottingham Forest, £116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (Lille, £85.7m), Iliman Ndiaye (Everton, £60m), Allan (Palmeiras, £32m), Mathys Detourbet (Troyes, £21.6m), Gerónimo Rulli (Marseille, £1.7m)

Key outs: Sávio (Tottenham, £75m), Nico González (Newcastle, £52m), Tijjani Reijnders (Al-Qadsiah, £52m), Rodri (Barcelona, £51.3m), James Trafford (Leeds, £40.5m), Nathan Aké (Fenerbahce, £7m) Omar Marmoush (Tottenham, loan), Jack Grealish (Everton, loan), John Stones (Inter, free). Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free)

This was the window of the midfielder for Manchester United, with three recruited: Youri Tielemans (a No 8), Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba (No 6s). Yet missing was a left-back despite the targeting of Lewis Hall, and others, plus reinforcements for the rest of a creaking rearguard. The reason? A lack of money or, maybe, a reluctance to spend unless the finance was generated by transfers. Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury (preventing his sale) and Joshua Zirkzee’s reluctance to move were factors. Will the specialist Luke Shaw, plus the stand-in options of Parick Dorgu (a wing-back/left forward), Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui (right-backs), Lizandro Martínez (centre-back) and Baleba prove adequate? JJ

Key ins: Carlos Baleba (Brighton, £70m), Andrey Santos (Chelsea, £50m), Youri Tielemans (Aston Villa, £35m)

Key outs: Rasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m), Casemiro (Inter Miami, free)

Newcastle describe their transfer window as “transformative” and, with reinvention the name of the game on Tyneside, it is easy to see why. After selling Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães for a grand total not too far off £250m, they have signed eight – mainly young – players. Along the way the spine of a team now managed by Matthias Jaissle rather than Eddie Howe has been renewed and new cult heroes including the former Benfica right-back Amar Dedic and the former Manchester City midfielder Nico González are emerging. The deadline day arrival of the exciting 21-year-old Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille is regarded as quite a coup. Have Newcastle choreographed a triumph from a window that, at one point, looked potentially disastrous? LT

Key ins: Nico González (Manchester City, £52m), Matias Fernandez-Pardo (Lille, £51m), Bazoumana Touré (Hoffenheim, £43m), Aladji Bamba (Monaco, £30m), Amar Dedic (Benfica, £29.5m), Lukas Hornicek (Braga, £25.7m), Ewen Jaouen (Reims, £21.6m), Sean Steur (Ajax, £20m)

Key outs: Sandro Tonali (Tottenham, £92.5m), Bruno Guimarães (Arsenal, £75m), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona, £69.3m), Nick Woltemade (Juventus, loan), Kieran Trippier (Wolves, free)

Receiving £116m for Elliot Anderson was proof that among the chaos in recent years, Forest have carried out some smart recruitment. After appointing Oliver Glasner, the club worked to provide for his needs, splashing out on Ousmane Diomande, while Xaver Schalger was a sensible acquisition for free, as was Daniel Muñoz at £22m. A No 9 was the priority and it required a club record £45m to acquire the long-term target Liam Delap, who fits the bill perfectly. Whether not sourcing a direct replacement for Anderson will hurt them remains to be seen but at least they did not panic, making it a measured window where they were able to trim the squad. Will Unwin

Key ins: Liam Delap (Chelsea, £45m), Ousmane Diomande (Sporting, £34.2m), Daniel Muñoz (Crystal Palace, £22m), Steven Benda (Fulham, free), Xaver Schlager (RB Leipzig, free)

Key outs: Elliot Anderson (Manchester City, £116m), Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry City, £9m), Omari Hutchinson (Milan, loan), Stefan Ortega (Olympiakos, free), Jota Silva (Olympiakos, loan), Morato (West Ham, loan)

After last summer’s 14 new faces this had been a bit of a conservative, almost slightly underwhelming, window. Or at least it was until Crystal Palace tried to hijack Sunderland’s agreement to sign the Lyon winger Malick Fofana and the two Premier League clubs engaged in an astonishing deadline day tug of war involving private jets from both sitting on the tarmac at Lyon airport and Fofana undergoing a medical in France unsure as to his destination until finally choosing Wearside. Arguably Sunderland’s biggest achievement was keeping last season’s star players. If persuading Granit Xhaka to stay rather than defect to Chelsea was vital, Régis Le Bris will be similarly delighted to have retained widely admired individuals of the calibre of Enzo Le Fée, Robin Roefs and Noah Sadiki. LT

Key ins: Malick Fofana (Lyon, £31m), Dayann Méthalie (Toulouse, £24m), Kevin Danso (Tottenham, loan), Thomas Meunier (Lille, free)

Key outs: Eliezer Mayenda (Rennes, £17.1m)

A comprehensive reboot, from back to front, featuring a club record outlay for a window and one of the most lavish by any club ever. In the first summer window since the departure of the longstanding chair Daniel Levy, the hierarchy have backed Roberto De Zerbi in an attempt to put the trauma of last season behind them. All the new signings have Premier League experience and – apart from Mateus Fernandes and Sávio – are aged 25 or over. In other words, they ought to be ready to hit the ground running. The opening two matches did not go to plan. It will get better. Won’t it? David Hytner

Key ins: Sandro Tonali (Newcastle, £92.5m), Mateus Fernandes (West Ham, £85m), Sávio (Manchester City, £75m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Brighton, £52m), Tosin Adarabioyo (Chelsea, £7m), Omar Marmoush (Manchester City, loan), Martin Dubravka (Burnley, loan), Mykhailo Mudryk (Chelsea, loan), Marcos Senesi (Bournemouth, free), Andy Robertson (Liverpool, free)

#311. The whole Rangers team shares blame for Dan Neil's and Dujon Sterling's costly blunders, claims goalkeeper Ivor Pandur

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:43 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 17:49 BST, 18 October 2026

Ivor Pandur is adamant that Rangers will take collective responsibility for their weekend failings at Dens Park.

The Ibrox men’s hopes of extending their seven-game winning streak were dashed on Tayside as Dundee capitalised on two major errors.

Dujon Sterling’s indecision in the first half allowed Bradley Fink to nip in and put the home side ahead.

Rangers turned the game on its head with spectacular goals arriving from Badredine Bouanani and Nico Raskin either side of the break.

Just as the three points looked secure, though, a stumble by Dan Neil on the edge of his own box allowed Callum Jones to square the contest.

Refusing to let Neil shoulder the full responsibility for the concession of two precious points, goalkeeper Pandur says the blame must be shared throughout the squad.

Dan Neil, above left, is crestfallen after his gaffe allowed Dundee to make it 2-2

Dundee's Callum Jones celebrates with team-mates after taking advantage of Neil mistake

Rangers keeper Ivor Pandur says team takes collective responsibility for mistakes

‘Mistakes will happen in football,’ said the Croatian. ‘It’s a game of beautiful moments and of mistakes.

‘One day it’s one, another day it’s the other. But we’re not a team who points fingers. As a whole, we created a lot and should have scored more.

‘It’s not about individuals here. We need to understand how important these games are. If we want to be a title-winning team, we need to act and behave in that certain way.

‘I think we’re on the right path, but it was a frustrating game for us.’

After an uncertain start at Ibrox to his time in Glasgow, Neil proved his worth as Rangers went from strength to strength in September. And Pandur is convinced that the former Sunderland midfielder will pick up where he left off after a difficult night at Dens Park.

‘You cannot take anything for granted in football,’ he added. ‘The reality is Dan is a great guy, an unbelievable player and really important for our team.

‘If he makes a mistake or scores a goal, that doesn’t change. He’ll continue to be important for us. It can happen to everybody and it does.

‘For us, it’s about not getting into that position where one mistake really costs us the game. We could have been more in front and had an easier ending.’

Pandur expressed his dismay that Rangers didn’t put the game to bed after giving themselves a shake at half-time.

‘It was really frustrating,’ he said. ‘We really felt that and it’s not a nice feeling, especially coming from a winning run.

‘We know it’s two points dropped and we’re not happy about it. But we’re in this together and we’ll have these moments in the season.

‘It’s a moment where we need to show what we want to achieve.’

Rangers also drew along the road at Dundee United on the opening night of the Premiership season — a result which signalled a tough start to the campaign.

Dan Neil wants the ground to swallow him up after his costly gaffe at Dens Park

Asked if he believed the team was now in a better place to bounce back, Pandur replied: ‘Yes — we have togetherness and a good feeling between each other. We all support each other and we can get through this moment easily.

‘We just need to get our heads down, see what was wrong and what can be done better to control the game a little bit more. That’s why we have a week to train and improve.

‘We won a lot of games in a row. When we were not the better side, we still managed to get a win in some of those. We hoped Saturday would have been the same.

‘It’s hard to point your finger at exactly what was wrong but we’ll look back at it and improve.’

The plus points for Rangers were two spectacular goals, with Raskin’s dipping strike arguably even better than Bouanani’s earlier curling effort.

‘I haven’t seen a better goal than Nico’s for a long time,’ Pandur reflected. ‘That was supposed to be the moment.

‘That hurts me even more. That should have been the moment people talk about after the game. He scored an unbelievable goal and, like Dan, he’s really important for us.

‘He’s also a great guy and that will have taken a bit out of him. But Nico will have more of those moments, and winning ones as well.’

Alex Scott believes recently retired Millie Bright has learnt from the best in Emma Hayes

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alex Scott has backed Millie Bright to become a football coach, believing the former England defender has learned from one of the best in the game.

Bright retired from international football in October 2025 before announcing her retirement from all football in April 2026.

The former Lionesses team-mates shared the pitch for England, including at Euro 2017, with Scott backing Bright as a coach of the future.

Alex Scott believes Millie Bright has the qualities to become a successful football coach following her retirement from playing.

Bright, who earned 88 caps for England, called time on her international career in October 2025 after missing Euro 2025, before announcing her retirement from all football in April 2026.

The former Chelsea defender was a key figure for club and country, helping the Lionesses win Euro 2022 and captaining England in Leah Williamson’s injury absense to the reach the final of the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Scott, who won 140 England caps during her own playing career, believes Bright has gained valuable experience from working under Emma Hayes at Chelsea.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"Do I think Millie would make a great coach? Absolutely," Scott said.

"She has been in a Chelsea environment and learnt under Emma Hayes, who is an incredible coach, with everything she's won at Chelsea and is now coaching the USA national team.

"So no doubt Emma has passed on a lot to Millie, so Millie would make a great coach."

Scott and Bright's England careers overlapped, with the pair both part of the national team's Euro 2017 tournament.

Scott was speaking after returning to her former secondary school, Langdon Park School in Tower Hamlets, where she surprised pupils and reflected on the people who helped shape her own journey in football.

The former England international joined a football training session with the students and highlighted the influence that teachers, coaches and positive role models can have on young people.

The visit also marked Scott's introduction as an ambassador for the Chase football coaching programme, which aims to shine a light on the positive impact coaches can have in communities across the UK.

Ayisha Gulati is the women's football writer at FourFourTwo. She has interviewed names including Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmati and enjoys telling stories that capture the excitement on and off the pitch.

#320. Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

FourFourTwo's dedicated FPL columnist, and one of the top players in the world, BigManBakar selects his best differentials for GW7

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Six Gameweeks in and the data is telling a very clear story.

The managers who are pulling away from their FPL mini leagues are not just owning the template, they are finding the players nobody else has thought about yet.

A differential here means anyone owned by 15% or fewer managers, and right now there are some genuinely compelling options sitting well under that threshold. Here are six worth targeting this week.

Dominic Solanke (£5.8m, 1.2% owned) vs Coventry (h)

Under 2% ownership for a player who scored against Manchester United last week and is expected to lead the line as the central striker. Solanke could be a very smart Yoane Wissa replacement for those looking to freshen up their forward options, and with penalty duties likely to come his way and a good run of home fixtures starting against Coventry City this week, the timing feels right to get ahead of the curve on him.

Savio (£6.5m, 0.8% owned) vs Coventry (h)

This picks represents a player under 1% ownership operating on the wing and has played 90 minutes in each of his last three Premier League fixtures. The options in midfield below £7.0m are genuinely thin this season, and Savio is one of the most appealing differentials available in that price bracket right now. Coventry at home is a kind opening fixture and the home run that follows only strengthens the case further.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Gonzalo Garcia (£6.1m, 7.2% owned) vs Hull (h)

Fulham striker Garcia is getting regular minutes, on penalties and facing Hull City at home this week before Coventry follows shortly after. The Spaniard also enables managers to put serious budget to work elsewhere in the squad at his price, which makes him an attractive option if you're looking to free up funds for upgrades in other positions.

Two very winnable fixtures in quick succession is exactly the kind of run you want your forward sitting on.

Nico O’Reilly (£6.3m, 9.4% owned) vs Ipswich at home

With Manchester City coming off an exhausting midweek game in which O’Reilly didn’t feature, he is likely to start at left-back and that role carries genuine upside against Ipswich Town.

We've seen Josko Gvardiol cause all sorts of problems from that position in recent weeks, and there is every reason to expect O’Reilly to operate in a similarly advanced role. City also carry the best clean sheet odds of any side this week, which means he has a realistic shot at points at both ends of the pitch.

Jan Paul van Hecke (£4.9m, 6.4% owned) vs Coventry (h)

Of all the defensive options to consider this week, van Hecke is probably the pick of the bunch. Nailed on to play, solid for defensive contributions and carrying aerial threat from set pieces, meanwhile, Coventry are ranked 19th for Expected Goals (xG) this season which makes the clean sheet potential very real.

The upcoming home fixture run also makes Van Hecke an appealing longer term hold, and at under £5.0m he offers outstanding value for everything he brings.

Luka Vuskovic (£5.1m, 4.7% owned) vs Crystal Palace (h)

Brighton have kept four clean sheets in six games this season, more than any other side in the Premier League, and Vuskovic has been quietly accumulating points throughout without attracting much attention. De Cuyper has taken most of the spotlight from the Brighton backline, but Vuskovic is nailed for starts, decent for defensive contributions and brings aerial threat from dead ball situations. Arguably the most sensible long term defensive pick from the Brighton setup, and Crystal Palace at home this week is a very manageable fixture to begin with.
