#330. Champions League review: PSG’s benchmark, Viking uprising and an Italian-German dilemma

The competition returned after the international break as the reigning champions put on a devastating display and Italy looked for its next saviour

Famous faces in the crowd for English teams’ home matches on Wednesday. While Prince William delighted in his beloved Aston Villa’s 6-0 romp over Fenerbahce, Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City homecoming was spoiled by Paris Saint-Germain showing they still represent the benchmark in European club football this season.

The center-circle inquest led by Erling Haaland after Vitinha put PSG 3-0 up was a jarring contrast to the triumphalism shown when City were winning at Liverpool last weekend. The Parisians put on a devastating display in the first half and, although the defiance City exhibited at Anfield on Sunday was on display again in the second half, PSG held on for a 4-2 win. “We could’ve lost this match if they scored the chances they created,” said a magnanimous Luis Enrique.

City may soon be absent from the competition, after they were found guilty of more than 100 charges of breaking the Premier League’s financial regulations. If City wish to sign off with a valedictory trophy lift they now know the standard they must meet – and beat. PSG have had their own issues with financial regulations in the era of petrodollar state ownership but, with the club president Nasser Al-Khelaifi a major powerbroker in European football, they have become an establishment club. While City are now pariahs, PSG have become near untouchables, not least on the field of play.

“He who brings glory to Rome, Rome honors for ever,” read a banner in the Stadio Olimpico. “Your hands are blessed and the people will give you eternal glory!” José Mourinho won hearts during his time in charge of Roma. But his popularity ratings are nowhere near as high in Madrid, though the manner of Real Madrid’s 4-3 comeback win over Roma will calm the gathering storm he has faced since returning to work for Florentino Pérez. The comeback came via Madrid’s next generation: Carlos Espí, 21, pulled the scoreline back to 3-2; the unlikely aerial threat of the 5ft 8in Endrick, 20, made it 3-3; and Antonio Rüdiger scored the winner, via a second assist for Arda Güler, 21. Mourinho embracing youth is a fresh development. This week saw Mourinho block a loan move to Milan for Endrick, and he admitted in Rome: “The first half was the coach’s fault; the second half was the players’ fault.”

A record 78 goals flew in this game week; the previous record was 71. On the wrong end were the Serie A clubs. In addition to Roma’s defeat, Como lost 3-2 at Feyenoord, the decisive moment coming via an own-goal for Robert Sánchez, the keeper loaned from Chelsea. Inter also lost, 4-3 to Club Brugge, whose performances in the competition in recent years meant the result was not much of a surprise. Napoli lost 3-1 to Villarreal, the Yellow Submarines’ first Champions League win in eight matches. Neapolitan focus was on a running battle between Massimiliano Allegri, the Napoli coach, and Kevin De Bruyne. Scott McTominay’s return to the team has pushed De Bruyne deeper. The Belgian made clear his feelings on playing there with some highly demonstrative body language.

There were two hat-tricks this week. Bradley Barcola ignited his Liverpool career with a treble at Lask, whose defending during their 6-3 defeat was suboptimal to say the least. That 4-3 Brugge win was mostly thanks to Nicolò Tresoldi. The striker was born in Italy, but moved to Hanover when he was 13, and he plays for Germany’s under-21s. Italian soul-searching after missing out on the last three World Cups has cast Tresoldi as a new savior. “I always speak Italian at home; I was born in Italy too,” he said post-match. “We’ll see.”

Paolo Di Canio, on Sky Italia, was pessimistic: “He has already chosen.”

After Bodø/Glimt’s exploits over the last couple of seasons and the national team’s admirable World Cup showing, the true football hipsters have a new destination in Norway. Viking play a thousand miles south-west of Bodø, in Norway’s oil capital, Stavanger. The club has co-managers in Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim and Morten Jensen: the pair were interviewed for the top job before deciding it was best they share duties. Viking are in the Champions League for the first time since the 1992-93 season, and at one point on Tuesday the Eliteserien champions led Bayern Munich 2-0. But a seismic shock was averted via two Harry Kane goals and another from Luis Díaz that put Bayern 3-2 up. Once Herman Haugen headed home at the back post, Viking had rescued a point with a 3-3 draw. “I could have played another 90 minutes,” said the captain, Zlatko Tripić, “I’m so incredibly proud.”

“I expect more. I’m not going to close my mouth; we need more ambition, we need to talk more about winning Champions Leagues and Premier Leagues in terms of other things.” Lisandro Martínez was undeterred by Peter Schmeichel’s soft-shoe questioning on Tuesday’s CBS broadcast after Manchester United’s defeat to Atlético Madrid.

“If we don’t say the truth, nothing will change,” added Martínez, whose Manchester United contract expires in June. Martínez’s interventions exposed the cracks at United – and highlighted the dubious merits of having a football celebrity do a journalist’s job.

A quick turnaround sees the third round staged next week, with Manchester United heading to Como for another examination of Michael Carrick’s regime. That follows a difficult Sunday trip to Leeds for United.

A couple of heavyweight ties catch the eye. Barcelona’s 4-1 win at Galatasaray continued their perfect start to the season, and Tuesday sees them visit PSG, a meeting of the two favorites to claim the title. On Wednesday, Arsenal v Bayern may trigger unhappy memories among Gunners fans. Arsenal lost 5-1 to Bayern three times in succession over the 2015-16 and 2016-17 seasons, and lost in the 2023-24 quarter-finals to the Germans too. Arsenal did, though, beat Bayern in last season’s Champions League.

#335. Nottingham Forest fans accuse their own club of 'going woke' as they ban 'misogynistic' chant - and tell them they face 'education sessions' if they sing it

Published: 13:46 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 13:51 BST, 18 October 2026

Nottingham Forest are the subject of fan discontent after banning a 'misogynistic' chant and warning their supporters of consequences if they continue to sing it.

The song, which references 't**s and f***y', has been sung by the Forest faithful for a significant period.

But on Saturday afternoon, the club released a statement titled 'a message to supporters', where they insisted that this must no longer be the case.

'Nottingham Forest is proud of the inclusive environment it has worked hard to create, and remains committed to ensuring everybody feels welcome, respected, and valued,' they said.

'We recognise that a particular chant has a long history among small sections of our support. While it is only sung by a minority of supporters, the potential impact of this chant and its misogynistic nature cannot be overlooked.

'This issue has also been raised by Nottinghamshire Police and Kick It Out, and after discussing further with our Fan Advisory Board, we are committed to delivering a united message: any form of discrimination, including misogynistic chanting, will not be tolerated.'

Nottingham Forest have banned supporters from singing a famous chant and warned of consequences if they continue to sing it

Forest added that those found to be singing the song could 'face education sessions or further action, including club bans and being placed on acceptable behaviour contracts.'

They added: 'The club may also face sanctions if such chanting continues.

'We ask all fans to consider the impact of their words and help ensure Nottingham Forest remains an inclusive environment where everyone belongs.'

However, the statement left some fans confused and frustrated, with several taking to social media to express their thoughts.

One said: 'Oh Nottingham, is full of woke wet wipes,' before another added: 'Concentrate on putting the ball in the back of the net rather than this woke nonsense.'

Another wrote: 'You having a laugh? Been sung for years.'

An extra supporter said: 'Pretty sure that chant started because of the massive population of females compared to males in the 60-70s? Older fans could well correct me on that though. The majority of female fans around us sing it as well.'

Others used their own experiences to suggest the club's decision was wrong as one said: 'As a mum of boys I don’t like this chant. But I’d rather live in a world where people are free to say things I don’t like.

'I’m curious as to what these “education sessions” will be. With the police involved it sounds akin to forced “reeducation” in a totalitarian regime.'

A final fan wrote: 'Modern football eh. This song has been sung for decades. I started going in 1986 and it’s more of a twist on the myth that Nottingham had a ratio of 4 women to every man.

'And before anyone jumps on with abuse I take my two teenage girls who don’t get offended by it.'

Forest are next in action on Sunday afternoon when they host Arsenal at the City Ground.

#339. Hong Kong club hope David Silva can be their hero – but just for one day

Former Manchester City player is coming out of retirement at 40 to play one match for ambitious Supreme Sha Tin

Hong Kong, China (as is the official football name), has long tried to follow the advice of Han Solo in Return of the Jedi: keeping their distance from China while trying not to look like they are keeping their distance. It is all about maintaining an independent football association and the trappings and privilege that come with it. There was some talk a few years ago about getting a Hong Kong team in the Chinese Super League, when the spending was in full flow, and although that did not happen the local Premier League has belatedly got in on the act – kind of.

This glittering city is not known as a football hotbed but has a long history in the sport that started when it was a British colony and has continued since it became a special administrative region of China in 1997. George Best, Peter Shilton, Arie Haan, Bobby Moore, Diego Forlán, Nicky Butt, René van de Kerkhof, Tony Morley, Gordon McQueen and Craig Foster have played in the territory and soon David Silva will too.

Shortly after the trophies Silva helped Manchester City to win between 2011 and 2018 were tainted by the findings of the Premier League’s independent commission, the 40-year-old picked up the boots that thrilled the Etihad Stadium for so long and is returning to action, though there is confusion as to how long he will be in action for.

Last week it was announced that Silva had joined the Hong Kong Premier League club Supreme Sha Tin, more than three years after retiring owing to an anterior cruciate ligament injury picked up during pre-season training for Real Sociedad. There had been three seasons in San Sebastián after his decade with City, with whom he won four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and five League Cups. Add 125 caps for Spain, the 2010 World Cup triumph and the Euros on either side and it was quite the career – and it is not quite over.

Supreme Sha Tin were promoted last season and tried to sign Juan Mata but have landed a bigger name. “I am very happy to join Supreme Sha Tin for this experience,” Silva said. “I am really looking forward to going to Hong Kong to enjoy the culture, the people and the food.”

That was the video posted on the club’s Instagram account with Silva’s introduction. “Our founders struck it big with this deal!” was the reaction and there were promises made to fans of special perks of behind-the-scenes access to training.

“We are officially announcing that the legendary Spanish No 21 midfielder, David Silva, has officially joined Supreme Sha Tin!” The post then added: “David Silva will be in Hong Kong soon to settle in, link up with squad training, and build up to peak match fitness before making his pitch debut. Stay tuned!”

It sounded as if Silva would be with the club for the remainder of the season, 17 games for the team to try to climb the table after a slowish start. It made headlines around the world, much to the confusion of the player. “I am surprised because in the end it is only to play one match,” Silva said. “The news made it look like I had signed for a season and it has kept me busy all afternoon. It is a league match, but it is still just one match.”

Whether it is good for Hong Kong football to bring a 40-year-old out of retirement for only one game is not a question for Silva to answer. He is not doing it for the money either.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Silva said: “It is in Hong Kong, a city I love very much … Some have expressed concern about the financial side for me … But that is not the case here. Thanks to my father and my adviser, with whom I have been investing well for years, I have achieved great success.”

Investing well and achieving success are precisely what the ambitious Sha Tin owner, Jim Wong Chi-chuen, who also plays for the team, wants after taking over three years ago. Along the way, the club have been rebranded and before this new season he appointed the girl group Collar as club ambassadors.

A change of image was necessary because the coach who delivered promotion, Lo Kwan-yee, a former Hong Kong footballer of the year, was reportedly arrested in June in relation to match-fixing allegations. Local media reported that the allegations relate to the period before Lo joined Sha Tin but Wong said the club had been affected. “We’ve lost some sponsors and, financially, they haven’t been replaced,” he told the South China Morning Post. “The financial pressure on me is greater than I expected, but I want to push this forward and make it work. I’m trying to do something very pure.”

When scandals and sham contracts are making the headlines, the sight of Silva in full flow is as pure as it gets. If he can be a hero, even if for just one day, it could be the talk of Hong Kong for years to come.

England beat Greece 8-1 on aggregate to progress to the final qualifying round for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After finishing second to Spain in their initial qualifying group, England are navigating the play-offs to secure their place at next summer's World Cup.

The Lionesses overcame Greece 8-1 on aggregate to advance to the final round, where they face Ukraine over two legs.

When are the remaining qualifiers, and what do England need to do to reach Brazil?

While Sarina Wiegman's side would have loved to avoid the added hurdle of the play-offs, they know exactly what is at stake as they bid to secure their place at next summer's tournament.

Finishing second to world champions Spain in their initial qualifying group meant England had to navigate two rounds of play-offs to reach Brazil.

First up, they faced Greece. After securing a 3-1 victory in Crete, the Lionesses returned home to Leicester and produced a clinical 5-0 display to seal an emphatic 8-1 aggregate win.

That result booked their place in the final qualifying round, where they will face Ukraine, who progressed after beating Slovakia 4-1 on aggregate.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Lionesses will face Ukraine in Round 2 of the World Cup qualifying play-offs, with the two-legged tie taking place between 26 November and 5 December.

The first leg is planned on 26 November at a venue to be confirmed, with Ukraine unable to host matches at home amidst the ongoing conflict with Russia.

England will then face Ukraine at Wembley Stadium on Saturday 5 December (5.30pm GMT).

The two sides are already familiar with one another, having met twice during the league phase of qualification. England won 6-1 away from home in a match played in Turkiye, before a 3-0 victory at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium.

With England reaching the 2023 final, ultimately losing to Spain, they know what is riding on these final two matches to ensure they reach Brazil.

Ayisha Gulati is the women's football writer at FourFourTwo. Fresh from a summer covering the Lionesses’ triumphant Euro 2025 campaign in Switzerland, she brings a passion for all things WSL, UWCL, and international women’s football. She has interviewed names including Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmati and enjoys telling stories that capture the excitement on and off the pitch.

#348. FC Copenhagen Women have a ‘startup-like’ brand. Now they need results

A famous name and record attendances have given FCK a platform but a difficult start in Denmark’s top-flight shows success on the pitch is not guaranteed

On an August day in 2024, 5,165 fans gathered at Vanløse Idrætspark to watch FC Copenhagen (FCK) take on B73 Slagelse in their first league match. For Denmark’s most successful men’s club, with 16 league titles, it marked the realisation of their desire to establish a women’s team, through collaboration with the existing FC Damsø, and an ambitious project with aims of having a wide-reaching impact on and off the pitch.

The 26 months since have brought a whirlwind of success, the club securing back-to-back promotions to reach the A-Liga. Now they are in the top division and “playing with the big dogs”, as their head of women’s football, Romaney Pinnock, coins it, and they must adapt to stay there.

“The plan was always to get here as soon as possible,” Pinnock says, “with a bit of breathing space in case that didn’t happen … Now we have to figure out how to establish ourselves. I think the massive opportunity here is to join something so new but under the umbrella of a very established strong brand and club. It feels as if it’s startup-like but there’s a nice safety net.”

Having the infrastructure of the wider club behind them is a positive. They have drawn on their marketing and commercial expertise to build a distinct identity for their women’s team, giving them a different kit, bringing in their own sponsors and establishing a unique matchday experience. Their most recent derby against Brøndby drew 8,047 to Parken, an A-liga record.

Secure foundations, however, take time to build. Operating in a semi-professional environment, their first season at the top has come with teething pains. They parted ways with their head coach Kasper Klarskov Nielsen after three matches and sit second from bottom after 10 fixtures. Many players continue to juggle football with work or study while trying to adapt to the physical demands of the top flight.

“It’s been tough so far,” the forward Maria Hovmark says. “It’s our first year in the league and we have to get used to that. Around 80-90% of the girls have never played in the top league so it’s a challenge … It’s also a huge challenge for the club because they’ve never been through this as well. It’s a chance for all of us and we’re slowly getting there.”

FCK’s rise is being played out in the context of a league working to establish itself. The country has produced highly technical players such as Pernille Harder, and the Danish Football Association (DBU) is trying to develop a stronger domestic game through greater investment, increased exposure and the establishment of minimum standards while also featuring in European competition. The champions, HB Køge, have returned to the Champions League for the first time since 2022 and Brøndby will be involved in the Europa Cup last 16.

“I expected more of an egalitarian setup because of the politics of Denmark and what I’ve found is actually women’s football is still at the early stages of a journey,” says Pinnock, who is South African and was previously head of women’s football at Bristol City. “There are a few clubs who are really pushing the envelope but the majority need to lift their game. That is also an opportunity. It’s exciting to see how we can look to our neighbours and say: ‘How are they doing it?’”

FCK are operating on a different model to Køge, who have been able to invest immediately on the pitch. FCK’s longer-term ambition is to challenge for trophies, compete in Europe and become players in the global transfer market. They also want to develop homegrown players who regard staying in Denmark as an attractive option, while bringing experienced talent, such as Hovmark, back home.

“The league is going more professional in terms of some teams being more full-time now,” Hovmark says. “It is getting more serious and I think that attracts people. That also brings the level higher.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

The wider societal impact the club can have is key for FCK. Their “Hall of Femmes” campaign with their main partner, Andel, gives young female footballers the opportunity to be featured on banners at Parken and offers two annual scholarships for players aged 14-19. FCK are also testing an academy model in which girls and boys train together according to their age, ability and development needs rather than by gender.

For now, the priority is to ensure they remain an A-Liga side. The club, however, have an eye on on-field success and patience will not last for ever. “We’re going to get a grace period of two or three seasons,” Pinnock says. “Then we’ve really got to embrace the FCK model, which is that we’ve got to be winners and we’ve got to head for the top.”

#354. Revealed: The day Roy Keane squared up to poppy protest footballer James McClean in half-time f-word rant about his photo with an Irish boxer

Published: 10:56 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 13:15 BST, 18 October 2026

Poppy protest footballer James McClean has opened up on an explosive clash he had with Roy Keane during his international career with the Republic of Ireland.

McClean, 37, won 103 caps for his country between 2012 and 2023, and came across Keane while the former Man United hardman was assistant manager to Martin O'Neill from 2013 to 2018.

And, writing in his autobiography The Walls, as serialised in the Irish Independent, McClean reflected on what it was like to work with Keane.

Noting that there were a few 'outbursts' and 'flare-ups', the winger revealed how they had a bust-up at half-time of a post-season friendly against Mexico in New Jersey in June 2017.

It was a game that Ireland lost 3-1 after an under-strength team struggled to cope with their opponents as several players, including McClean - who was captain and at left-wing back - were playing out of position.

'Martin had just finished his bit when Roy came over, got right in my face and started f***ing me out of it,' recalled McClean.

James McClean opened up on a brutal bust-up he had with Roy Keane on international duty

Keane was incensed after McClean posed on the pitch with Irish boxer Michael Conlan

‘"Look at you, the f***ing captain, f***ing giving off, yeah? You were taking pictures before the game with f***ing Mick Conlan. Your head isn’t f***ing on it".'

McClean explained that following the pre-match warm-up he had posed for a photo on the side of the pitch with Michael Conlan, an Irish professional boxer who was a friend of his, after which he 'saw Roy staring over'.

McClean, who had given away a penalty in the first half, didn't hit back at Keane at the time, but inside he was 'spewing over it for the entire flight home' and tried to nip the issue in the bud.

Keane initially 'brushed it off' before he visited McClean in his room while he was doing a gym session.

McClean added: 'I sat on the bed as he leaned on the desk table and went off on another one. He accused me of having a big ego.

'He said he’d never been critical of me in the press or around the group, and now, the first time he’d said anything, I’d pulled him up over it. Then he started going off about the Lamborghini at Sunderland, which was f***ing six years earlier. I was thinking he must have been seething for the afternoon, gathering information.'

The Lamborghini reference was in relation to McClean's time at Sunderland when O'Neill, then managing the Black Cats, had allegedly dropped the winger after he found out about him buying a 'f***ing three-hundred-grand' supercar.

The clash came at half-time of Ireland's 3-1 defeat by Mexico in a summer friendly in June 2017

In their conversation, Keane also admitted he often went 'home and screamed into the pillow' because the 'standard was so poor' in training during his time with Ireland.

After defending his attitude in a tete-a-tete with Keane, McClean outlined his respect for the assistant boss and how much he cared about playing for his country.

McClean continued: 'He said the photos didn’t look like good preparation. I disagreed, and it went around in circles a bit until we just said we’d leave it.

'Roy was sound with me after that; I knew he couldn’t have any complaints with my performances. I scored in our next match, a friendly with Uruguay, and did a selfie celebration afterwards to make my point.'

#356. Christian Pulisic is no longer a focal point for the US or Milan – and that’s OK

The winger is 28, and younger teammates are rising into the high-pressure spots he has usually occupied

Usually, the second weekend of October sees Christian Pulisic flanked by compatriots as the Star-Spangled Banner plays. Last year, he was involved in US friendlies against Ecuador and Australia. But this year, with Fifa having folded the October window into September, Pulisic didn’t have the chance. On Sunday, his pre-match music was O Generosa, the Serie A anthem, which he observed with a soft smile.

Mark Twain’s first visit to Italy left him describing the country as “a vast museum of magnificence and misery”, and it’s a fitting summary of Pulisic’s three-plus years with Milan. The magnificence: 43 goals and 25 assists in 138 appearances. The misery: just one trophy since he arrived in July 2023, a 2025 Supercoppa Italia held in Saudi Arabia.

For years, Pulisic’s club career was a source of chronic frustration in between the reprieve of international duty. Now, after Mauricio Pochettino opened the team’s next era by selecting 13 top prospects (but not Pulisic, recently recovered from injury), his international standing is in a shakier state than ever, a decade after he debuted.

In a continuation of a frustratingly familiar theme, Pulisic’s fourth season with Milan hasn’t started smoothly. The lower-leg microfracture he suffered against Belgium at the World Cup this summer has kept him off Ruben Amorim’s teamsheet, with just two league starts. He opened Sunday’s visit to Sassuolo as the right half-space winger beneath Gonçalo Ramos.

Pulisic still commands quite a lot of attention. Mid-table Sassuolo were more willing to let the ball find Diego Moreira than Pulisic, with the American’s touches garnering additional defensive bodies. As opponents converged whenever he entered the final third, he often cycled possession to fellow US international Yunus Musah, trailing behind on the right side of midfield.

Pulisic dropped into the defensive half often in search of creating numerical advantages, part of a relatively free-roaming deployment. He led Milan players with 5.3km (3.2 miles) covered in the first half, although his industry failed to create much. He was a key part of the buildup to Milan’s only goal of the day, playing the pass before Luka Modric’s assist and offering the Croat a helpful decoy run.

By the 77th minute, Pulisic’s sole shot had been blocked and his only created chance was stifled by the goalkeeper. Pulisic has a goal contribution in just four of his last 22 appearances in Serie A.

Having turned 28 last month, Pulisic is in the next, veteran phase of his career. Teams expect an attacker nearing 30 to be prolific. A player who is steady if unspectacular at this point can fall down the depth chart if a younger, more dynamic alternative presents themself.

With a quarter-hour left against Sassuolo, Amorim opted for one: Pulisic off, Alpha Cissè in.

Since arriving from Hellas Verona this summer, Cissè has been a bright spot for Milan. The 19-year-old was lauded by Amorim early in the season, starting as Pulisic recovered from his World Cup injury. In just 242 league minutes, Cissè has scored twice; Pulisic, now up to 190 minutes under Amorim, has one goal.

“I love Cissè. I love Cissè,” crooned the coach in late August.

That’s not to say that everything is against Pulisic. This week, Gazzetta dello Sport reported he is one of three key players the club hopes to renew early in the Amorim era. He has history to fall back on, having led Milan with 17 goals in all competitions two seasons ago.

“I can only say that I am very happy at Milan right now and for the near future as well,” Pulisic said at a San Siro meet-and-greet during the window, flanked by a wall of shirts bearing his name. “So, yeah, I’m not thinking about the contract renewal but I am very happy here. I want to stay at Milan.”

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Cissè’s rising presence mirrors Pulisic’s new reality with his national team. Pochettino ushered in the next generation as Pulisic remained in Italy, giving debuts to several teenage attackers who are hungry to work into the fold. Cavan Sullivan validated the hype with an audacious account-opener against Mexico, while others – such as wingers Mathis Albert and new Crystal Palace signing Zavier Gozo – began what they hope will be long careers representing the US.

Pulisic has struggled on international duty under Pochettino. He’s scored just once since the start of 2025, in a tune-up friendly against Senegal. His mostly poor performances at the World Cup hardly reinforced his bona fides to the Argentinian, who declined to directly address Pulisic’s situation during the recent international window.

It’s far too soon to write Pulisic off. He covers considerable ground. His more decisive touches can generate threats, though too often he appears caught in two minds about his best course of action. After years of being cast by Milan and, especially, the US as an attacking focal point, he may be more dangerous as an auxiliary option with a lower touch volume.

Internationally, his rising teammates could afford Pulisic a lower-pressure role. Sullivan has relished early acclamation of being the face of the program. Folarin Balogun weathered the pressure – well, the more normal kinds – of being the team’s chief goalscorer at the World Cup, bagging three goals in 316 minutes. With Pulisic absent, Pochettino used his usual spot at left-wing to shoehorn in both of his chief playmakers, Gio Reyna and Malik Tillman; given his past form at Milan, he could still slot in at right-wing while making Sullivan a useful alternative to all three from the bench.

Pulisic’s entire career had been framed in the context of a home World Cup. Perhaps being freed from that years-long pressure can enable him to rediscover his best form, to Milan’s benefit as well as his national team’s.

But with the World Cup gone and his performances leaving something to be desired, we’re left to wait and watch to see who Pulisic is, and will be, as a player.

New York streetwear powerhouse Kith has teamed up with adidas Football once again to drop their 2025 Fall collection â a bold capsule that merges football performance with street-style flair.

The collection, released under the Kith Football Club banner, includes jerseys, matching shorts, zip-ups, and track-inspired outerwear, with designs that nod to both football history and urban fashion. Flame motifs pay homage to the 1998 World Cup, pinstripes are laced with co-branded embroidery, and jacquard colour-blocking adds a modern edge.

For the first time, denim is featured in jackets and pants, offered in blue and black washes, spliced with Adi-break panels and performance details. Accessories complete the capsule, including co-branded trucker hats and classic caps, a flame tote bag, and three fully printed soccer balls.

The footwear lineup is equally striking: the Supernova Indoor returns in suede, nubuck ponyhair, and denim, the Predator Sala â a 1994 classic â is reimagined in premium glove leather. The Koresco National also makes a comeback in new leather and suede colourways.

Fronting the campaign are Paul Pogba and Paulo Dybala. Both World Cup winners and style icons in their own right, the two perfectly embody the collectionâs dual focus on football heritage and lifestyle.

The Kith x adidas Football Fall 2025 collection is available from September 19 via Kith's online and in-person stores.

#364. Richarlison backs criticism of Roberto De Zerbi in another pointed social media post before Tottenham boss responds - as rift deepens amid star's exile

Published: 11:54 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 11:56 BST, 18 October 2026

Exiled Tottenham star Richarlison has shared a pointed social media post where he backed criticism of Roberto De Zerbi.

Richarlison, 29, was set to depart north London this summer after appearing to fall out with the Spurs boss, who claimed the forward 'said too many times he wants to leave'.

A move never materialised, however, and the Brazilian has been kept out of the first-team squad since.

His omission comes at a time where Spurs are struggling at the bottom of the Premier League after scoring just three goals in six games, and Richarlison shared a post on his Instagram story of quotes from former Everton striker Duncan Ferguson.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily about the Brazilian, Ferguson had said: 'You don’t leave a player like that out unless there’s been a real murder: he’s chinned him or there’s been a proper scrap on the training ground.'

Sharing the quotes, Richarlison added: 'Thanks Duncan Ferguson, you are right.'

Richarlison shared a pointed social media post where he backed criticism of Roberto De Zerbi

Richarlison has been exiled from Tottenham's squad after appearing to fall out with De Zerbi

Ferguson was a coach and two-time interim boss at Everton during Richarlison's four-year spell at the club, yet De Zerbi was unmoved when pressed on the 29-year-old's latest actions at his pre-match conference ahead of Monday's game against Coventry.

'It's not my problem anymore,' he said. 'You have to ask Vinai (Venkatesham, CEO) or Johan (Lange, technical director). It's not my problem.

'I know as a coach I have to support and take responsibility even when it's not my responsibility.

'I have not decided anything in this situation. If he wants to speak to me he can find me in my office until 8.30pm in the evening.

'But I don't want to speak any more because my focus is on the Coventry game.'

Richarlison's latest post comes after he also took to social media within hours of Tottenham's 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa last month to post videos of himself training in what was interpreted as a pointed move at the time.

He captioned the video of him undertaking drills: 'The focus remains'. His second post was another clip of him undergoing sprint training, accompanied by the caption: '35.4km/h - I broke my record'.

Meanwhile, Richarlison made his first appearance since his exile on Tuesday for Tottenham's Under-21 side in the EFL Trophy against Cheltenham Town.

The Brazilian scored Spurs' equaliser against the League Two outfit, and also notched in the subsequent penalty shoot-out as they lost 7-6 on spot kicks after a 2-2 draw in normal time in the group stage clash.

'Happy to do what I love most in life. I was missing it!', Richarlison shared on social media following the match.

Richarlison made his on-pitch return for Spurs' Under-21 side against Cheltenham on Tuesday

Richarlison, who will be without first-team football until January given he is not in Spurs' Premier League squad and they have also been knocked out of the Carabao Cup, was praised post-match by Cheltenham manager Steve Cotterill.

Cotterill told reporters that he felt the Brazilian's attitude was 'absolutely first class' when featuring against the League Two side.

‘I thought his attitude tonight was immaculate,' Cotterill said. 'He could have easily come down here and thought I ain’t too bothered about tonight, he could have done that.

'He’s used to playing in front of 60,000 every week, his attitude tonight was absolutely first class and it was great for our lads to play against someone of his stature.’

#366. Manchester City are suddenly box-office in age of charge-rage and mega defiance | Barney Ronay

This is by far the most interesting this club have ever been and they faced PSG, a kind of twin entity in all this as oil state glove puppets

Another day, another note of unreality; another vivid and brilliant spectacle that feels as though it has been whipped together out of meringue and burnt sugar. Time flies when the world is closing in. Two weeks on, this was Manchester City’s first home game since the verdict dropped, the irrefutable body of evidence was refuted, and English football entered its state of ongoing whiplash.

In the stadium this felt like watching someone dance while the world burns. This was a brilliant game pegged out around six goals, a collapse, a comeback, posts and bars struck, saved penalties, and a performance of state-of-the-art omni-football from this brilliantly high-grade Paris Saint-Germain team.

Pep Guardiola was even present in the stands, looking oddly haunted beneath a flat cap. Looking in fact quite a lot like Vincenzo Pentangeli in The Godfather Part II, the mute Sicilian brother who turns up in the courtroom and has a congressional hearing dismissed just by glowering wordlessly. Well, it’s the best defence anyone’s come up with yet.

City’s players gave everything against superior opponents. The crowd roused itself from a state of sullen defiance to a state of angry defiance and occasionally even jubilant defiance. At times there was even a resurgence of that euphoric state of the glory years, the collective cognitive dissonance, hard white lights blotting out the sky, nothing out there beyond the spectacle. Take me to the place where you go, where nobody knows if it’s night or day.

There has been some talk in recent days about whether City’s games should be broadcast or even played at all. Is it all just empty, dystopian, an insult to sport? On the other hand, this is by far the most interesting City have ever been. It has been a cold project at times, frictionless football, the hand of a sovereign state at your back, victory without content.

Well, not any more. In the age of charge-rage and mega-defiance City are suddenly total box office. No more denials. Just go full Nosferatu. Embrace the darkness. Smear and accuse. Say, yeah OK we did cheat but the real cheat is the rules. This is all deeply gripping main character stuff, performative villainy, like Milton’s Satan in Paradise Lost, who sees the rules, rejects them, and ends up stealing the whole show from boring old rules-obsessed God.

City had perfect opponents here in PSG, who are a kind of twin entity in all this, brothers by another mother. Oil state glove puppets. Twice punished for cheating the financial rules.

But then, nothing explains the world like football. Abu Dhabi versus Qatar in Manchester. Lawfare. Tribal populism. All of it played out against the background of an embattled British prime minister, vultures already picking away at his entrails. Andy Burnham always promised to offer something fresh and different. To be fair he could still be the first prime minister hounded from office because somebody really needed to overpay for Kalvin Phillips.

The Etihad was a febrile place before kick-off. There was smoke, fury, a crackle in the air, and a pointedly heartwarming club heritage video on the big screen, local people looking happy and real, legacy footage of skinny-legged Alfs and Herberts, men with comb-overs in brown overcoats. Then through to the stolen glory years, trophies lifted, last-day title pippings, with the final shouted caption: “The blues are in dreamland.” Yeah. That doesn’t quite sound how you think it does.

Mainly there was a chance here to boo everything and everyone. The PSG team was booed. The singing of the PSG fans was booed. The Champions League anthem was obliterated. A City Till I Die Tifo was hoisted because yes, death must come into it. The early songs were “City’s going down with a billion in the bank”, and the classic “Gary Neville is a wanker, is a wanker”. Whatever happened to not looking back in anger?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

But then, this has always been a project defined by defiance, the raised fist, the punkish V-sign, even if this involves prostrating yourself for the benefit of an inherited billionaire monarchy. The banner that read “Sheikh Mansour, Manchester thanks you for 10 great years” is still there. It was always an odd sentiment. Why were you thanking him back then when the whole thing was self-funding, a sponsorship miracle, beloved of airlines and phone companies? It makes more sense now. Of course. He’s paying for it all.

PSG were brilliant here early on, Luis Enrique was up on his feet in rumpled black tracksuit bottoms and hoodie, handsomely ravaged, like a Jedi out for a jog. And by the time Vitinha made it 3-0 on 32 minutes the score could have been anything. The midfield was suffocating in and out of possession. Désiré Doué was sublime on the left, all fast-twitch spring and balance, like a squirrel on a branch.

And for long periods City’s fans fell silent. You can’t blame them. The sense of grievance may be misdirected, but it is undeniably real. If City’s fans are angry about being overlooked, conspired against, forced to kneel before some distant overlord, well, that’s because they are. Welcome to the world, welcome to east Manchester, welcome to the lighted empty boxes of New Islington, rental engines for an overseas state.

All that love, hunger, connections has been hijacked in the most tantalising way, sold back to you in the form of stolen glory. Please don’t put your life in the hands of a petro‑state propaganda machine, who’ll throw it all away. Here at least they had a brilliant game, players that gave everything, and spectacle if not victory.

Keira Walsh and Alexia Putellas were teammates at Barcelona but are now competitive and local rivals at the top end of Women's Super League

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Born in Rochdale and a product of Blackburn Rovers' academy, Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh admits that she still doesn't know London intimately well a year after making the move from Barcelona.

But the England midfielder has a new friend and a new rival to see the sights with following Alexia Putellas' own transfer to the capital this summer.

Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Putellas is now plying her trade at London City Lionesses, who are running Manchester City and Walsh's own Chelsea close at the top of the Women's Super League.

Walsh told FourFourTwo that her former Barca teammate was in contact before her surprise move, saying: "She messaged me a little bit and then said, ‘Maybe I'll see you in London soon’ and I said, ‘I think you might do!’

"We’re actually going to meet for dinner from time to time, so it'll be nice to catch up.

"I can‘t show her the ropes of London yet as I still don’t know much about London myself!"

Chelsea and London Lionesses are set to meet on Sunday, December 13 in what already looks likely to be a top-of-the-table encounter.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But Walsh said: "I'm going to be facing her but she’s a friend, a really great team-mate and a good captain.

"First and foremost, I do want her to be successful. I want her to have a really good year here.

"She's a big name, so fans are going to be looking out for her, but she's definitely got the talent to back that up."

Walsh's own return to England last year, with Chelsea, was a boon for WSL - and she believes adding Putellas to the mix only raises the league's profile yet further.

Walsh said: "I hope she has an impact in the league. To see the likes of Alexia coming over and playing here, it shows where women's football is at in England.

"It’s really exciting to have one of the best, if not the best player in the world in our league.

#375. Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson

There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms

Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it was perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.

The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.

How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.

The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.

But no one should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anyone who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.

The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their clubs, which in part underlies the present crisis.

That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.

At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual, always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

Perhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brooke argued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear in Oliver Bullough’s Butler to the World,. In the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.

But how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of the profitability and sustainability rules, or the squad cost ratio that has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.

Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.

How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?

#376. Emiliano Martinez update: Chelsea's goalkeeper undergoes surgery and set to be out for weeks - but wife says it's 'nothing serious' after sickening collision at Everton

Published: 08:50 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 10:44 BST, 18 October 2026

Emiliano Martinez underwent successful minor surgery after his sickening collision with Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite with Chelsea's goalkeeper set for weeks on the sidelines.

Xabi Alonso's men secured their first clean sheet of the Premier League season with the help of Martinez, who was injured while bravely coming to clear a 67th-minute set-piece. He was then replaced by 21-year-old Mike Penders for the remainder of Chelsea's 2-0 victory.

The operation was believed to be for a jaw injury after Martinez had been carried away on a stretcher and taken to hospital. He was conscious as he left the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The 34-year-old Argentinian later released a statement from his hospital bed in which he wrote: 'Thanks to everyone for the messages, the operation went well. The most important thing is that we won and with a bow at 0 (goals). We'll be back in a few weeks.'

His wife, Mandinha, added it is 'nothing serious' and that he will 'soon be back to normal'.

Between now and the November international break, Chelsea have to face Tottenham Hotspur at home (Premier League), Liverpool away (Carabao Cup), Manchester United at home (Premier League), and Sunderland away (Premier League).

Chelsea star Emiliano Martinez's wife says his sickening head injury is 'nothing serious'

The Argentine goalkeeper's agent posted a positive update in a photo from hospital

Penders, the Belgian who arrived this summer after a season on loan with Strasbourg, will fill in as Chelsea's No 1 in the meantime. His potential is high, though this will see him promoted earlier than expected as Alonso had been keen for his goalkeeper to carry experience.

A Chelsea statement released on Sunday morning read: 'Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez has undergone successful surgery on a fractured jaw.

'Martinez was injured following a collision midway through the second half of our 2-0 victory over Everton at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Saturday.

'Martinez was taken to hospital for further assessment, which confirmed a fractured jaw that required surgery.

'Everyone at Chelsea wishes Emi a speedy recovery and will support him throughout.'

Penders had gone into this season hoping to become Chelsea's first-choice goalkeeper when he thought he would be competing with Robert Sanchez.

Martinez was struck in a sickening collision during Chelsea's win away at Everton

However, mistakes made in Chelsea's opening game of the season away at Fulham led to Sanchez hastily being loaned to Como, the Italian side managed by Cesc Fabregas.

Martinez was signed for £7.5million from Aston Villa as Sanchez's replacement on a three-year contract, which, in Penders' mind per sources, pushed him further away from the starting line-up.

Circumstances will now see the 6ft 7in youngster get his chance to show Alonso and everyone else how ready he is as Chelsea goalkeeping coach Ben Roberts prepares him for playing rivals Tottenham at Stamford Bridge this Saturday.

Penders did well in handling being thrown in at Everton, coming to clear one cross towards the back of his box which the away end appreciated and navigating the extra 13 minutes added on to the end of the game. Teddy Sharman-Lowe, 23, will act as Penders' back-up.

#381. Why does everyone hate Arsenal?

What does Arsenal fan hatred say about modern football culture?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gooners are by far the most disliked fanbase in the Premier League. How did they gain this unwanted status?

"Arsenal fans are insufferable": this is a sentiment that in recent years has become a kind of universal truism, a reality so deeply ingrained in the psyche of the modern English football fan that to question it is to risk outing yourself as some sort of deranged secret Gooner.

The gloating celebrations and extreme emotions, the unhinged online activity, the perceived sense of entitlement: these Arsenal-coded behaviours have created an antipathy towards the current Premier League champions' fanbase that seems to outstrip anything experienced by modern supporters of any of the other 'Big Six' clubs.

But how did Arsenal fans become so hated in the modern football world? What exactly is it that irritates people? And is the hatred of Arsenal fans primarily just an indication of how much time we're all spending online, and how fan media is rotting our brains?

Personally, I have no dog in this fight. As a Norwich City fan, I tend to find that supporters of the so-called 'Big Six' are all roughly as irritating and tunnel-visioned as each other. But it's clear that there are several things going on here. While Arsenal antipathy has certainly ramped up under the reign of Mikel Arteta — an at times obscenely pretentious LinkedIn fanatic whose tactical dark arts, touchline gesticulation, and excessive use of hair gel has understandably rubbed many neutrals the wrong way — this sentiment dates back decades.

After I attempted to gauge public opinion via my football team's WhatsApp group, North London-bred Gooner Billy Howard-Price fleshed out the history of the club's outward perception: "The 'same old Arsenal, always cheating' chants, us using the offside trap [in the '80s and '90s], 'boring boring Arsenal' from the George Graham years: there's a lot of interesting stuff at play there. Legitimate stuff that predates AFTV and perceived 'North London elite' stuff."

Fellow Gooner Shay Olupona adds that "Boring Boring Arsenal applies to last season too. 'Cornered' the league, set piece FC ole ole etc." It's true that the perceived negativity and rigid play of Arteta's title-winning side has worsened the hostility. But the hate was already there, and I'd argue that a huge amount of it stems simply from Arsenal fans being far more visible on social media than any other supporter base. And for that, we have Arsenal Fan TV to thank.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Launched by Robbie Lyle in 2012, AFTV quickly emerged as the UK's most prominent football fan channel, its emotional stadium vox pops and astoundingly irrational studio debates becoming a huge part of English football lore over the last decade. The channel has been hugely influential beyond the capital, inspiring the birth of countless other fan media platforms around the country.

Every club has countless irritating fans; but the existence of AFTV, and the wider Arsenal social media eco-system that the club's enormous London fanbase facilitates, has meant that annoying Gooners are ten a penny. Unrivalled exposure leads to unrivalled resentment.

"It becomes cyclical," says Reading supporter Nick Mandolos. "Arsenal fans whine about being hated on social media = more people get annoyed by them, it goes round and round. A lot of people feel they're looked down on by Arsenal fans, and so mock them mercilessly. AFTV was probably the killer. That and the jolly come lately, bucket hat-wearing middle class North London gooners."

What's interesting is that growing up in the 2000s, I remember the Gunners being largely admired for the attractive, free-flowing football they played under Arsene Wenger, which was perhaps even easier to enjoy because the club was no longer regularly winning titles. This suggests the hostility massively accelerated with the advent of social media, as well as the rise in more casual support prompted by both the Arteta era and the broader embrace of football culture amongst middle-class, urban indie types.

"Anecdotally, 90% of people who have only recently started following football support Arsenal, and they do harm the reputation of “real” supporters," says Liverpool fan Pete McNelis. "I associate a certain type of Arsenal fan with the loud voice at the pub who doesn’t understand passing out from the back."

It's also worth considering whether there's a more sinister element to some of the anti-Arsenal agenda. Specifically: is it a coincidence that the Premier League club with by far the most diverse matchgoing fanbase, the club far more closely associated with Black British culture than any other, is also the one that everyone finds unbearable?

Evidently, there are tons of valid concerns that have handed Arsenal the unwanted but in many ways justified status of having the most irritating fanbase. But given how deeply entrenched unconscious racial biases are in the UK (see: BBC's The Traitors), I don't think it's a massive stretch to suggest that this could factor into some people's outlook.

The idea of the insufferable Gooner has a range of legitimate foundations, and is linked to events that have played out across the stadiums, press conferences, and broadcast studios of English football over many years.

But Arsenal antipathy is also an interesting reflection of changing social dynamics, shifts in who watches football and what cultural cache is attached to the sport. Above all, it's about an ever-growing engagement with football via our unhinged, rage-baiting social media culture, a culture that discourages nuance and rewards idiocy. In this context, the insufferable Arsenal fan has risen above the parapet; but that doesn't mean we should all accept this characterisation as a universal truth.

#383. Wrexham had to block outside noise - Parkinson

Wrexham's victory over Preston was their second home win of the season

Manager Phil Parkinson says Wrexham had to "block everything out" as they responded to recent criticism with a convincing 4-1 Championship victory over Preston North End at the Racecourse.

Wrexham returned to winning ways after suffering a disappointing 2-1 home defeat by West Bromwich Albion in midweek.

Reports suggesting pressure was beginning to mount on Parkinson following a slow start to the campaign.

"I have managed over 1,000 games so I'm used to that," Parkinson told BBC Radio Wales Sport.

"When you lose at any level, criticism comes the manager's way and the players' way and you've got to accept that.

"Obviously the criticism of Wrexham is intensified because of the profile of the club."

Parkinson: We showed character, we showed mentality and it's an important win for us

First goals for the club from Joe Worrall and Ben Whiteman helped Wrexham establish a 2-1 half-time lead.

Sam Smith and Kieffer Moore's second half goals completed an emphatic victory over the Championship's bottom side.

"We couldn't wait to get back out here today," Parkinson said.

"I look at it as a challenge. Me and Steve [Parkin] were itching to get back in with the lads on Thursday and bring the group together.

"We thought long and hard about the team selection and the style of play we needed to implement.

"Sometimes you've got to block everything out and put in a performance like we did today.

"I'm very confident we've got a squad that can be really competitive this season. I really am."

Parkinson also pointed to an extensive injury list as a major factor in Wrexham's inconsistent start, with players including Max Cleworth, Nathan Broadhead and Dan Sheaf currently sidelined.

"I don't want to keep going on about the injuries, but it's been unprecedented, probably the worst spell we've had in my time here.

"We've lost a lot of quality and football ability on the pitch.

"But those players will come back and we'll have great competition for places. I really believe in this group.

"While we're waiting for those players to return, it's about galvanising the squad and finding ways to be more effective."

#385. Mikel Arteta’s new contract reflects where the power now lies at Arsenal | Ed Aarons

From transfers to stadium works and even the training-ground dog, there is no doubting the Spaniard’s influence at the club

If anyone doubts Mikel Arteta’s status as No 1 at Arsenal in the week he committed his future to the club until 2030, just ask Win the dog. The chocolate labrador who played a starring role in the celebrations when Arsenal were crowned Premier League champions in May has become part of the family at the training ground in Hertfordshire since being introduced by Arteta in May 2023.

Kai Havertz, David Raya and Mikel Merino, who issues commands in Spanish and has spoken about spending time with Win when out for three months with a foot injury, are particular favourites. But, according to sources close to Win, a therapy dog trained not to bark, there is no contest when it comes to her preferred human: Arteta.

The manager is understood to have taken Win home for Christmas last year, having been instrumental in her arrival a few days after his side had finished as runners-up to Manchester City for the first time. Cuddly replicas are available in the club shop. The real version spends most days at Arsenal’s training centre, with her primary carer a full-time member of staff based there.

“I carefully chose the dog and in my opinion it’s the perfect representative of who we are right now,” said Arteta in 2023. “Win needs accountability from us because we have to look after her as well; her emotions and what she needs.”

It is an example of Arteta’s attention to detail that has helped to transform Arsenal from also-rans into champions. Ominously for the rest, the Spaniard promised on Wednesday, when he signed a new four-year contract understood to be worth more than £20m a season, that this “is only the beginning” of what Arsenal hope could be a trophy-laden dynasty under his leadership.

The length of deal was significant given that it would take Arteta, who will mark his seventh anniversary in the job in December, past a decade at the helm – even if he still has some way to go to match Arsène Wenger’s record of almost 22 years in charge. Wenger’s first day was 30 years ago last week and he quickly assumed control at the club. The influence of Arteta, made Arsenal captain by Wenger in 2014, has grown steadily since he was appointed after a stint as Pep Guardiola’s assistant at Manchester City.

Arteta, upgraded from head coach to manager in September 2020 having won the FA Cup six months after replacing Unai Emery, has seen various executives depart as his power has increased. The 44-year-old, who became the second-youngest manager after José Mourinho to win the Premier League, has a direct line to the co-chair Josh Kroenke and is able to exert a major say over most big decisions – on and off the pitch.

Arsenal’s announcement this week that they had decided against a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium came after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would be caused by a temporary move to Wembley or elsewhere. The owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment (KSE), is also thought to have been put off proposals to increase the capacity to 70,000 owing to the cost, despite agreeing a record $4bn (£3bn) deal to buy the MLB side Los Angeles Angels last month.

That did not stop KSE from making Arteta the best-paid manager in the Premier League with a hefty salary increase from the £10m plus £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League that he agreed in 2024. Only Atlético Madrid’s Diego Simeone is thought to earn more.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Arteta is understood to have had the final say in the decision not to pursue interest in Malick Fofana after the Belgium forward was offered in the final days of the transfer window because he wanted to ensure the 16-year-old phenomenon Max Dowman would not be denied opportunities. He may regret not bringing in another forward after Christos Tzolis sustained a hamstring injury with Greece that is expected to keep him out for at least three weeks, but it is clear Arteta has been calling the shots even since the arrival of Andrea Berta as the sporting director in March 2025.

Such is the intensity Arteta brings to the job that it remains to be seen whether he can last as long as Wenger, although there are few signs that operating in such a high-pressure environment has affected him physically.

The odd grey hair aside, he barely looks different from the day he was announced in his first managerial role. With the twin motivations of making Arsenal back-to-back league title winners for the first time since the 1930s and European champions after coming so close last season when they lost to PSG in the final on penalties, Arteta appears to be here to stay.

Chelsea goalkeeper Emi Martinez has been rushed to hospital after suffering a sickening head injury during their trip to Everton.

And the Argentinian was booed as he was stretchered off the pitch at the Hill Dickinson Stadium with the visitors 1-0 up after Pedro Neto's goal.

#391. Borussia Dortmund to 'address' away kit controversy after fan revolt

Borussia Dortmundâs brand-new away kit for the 2025/26 season has sparked fury among supporters, prompting the club to acknowledge the backlash and vow to respond.

The kit, which combines a white base with black sleeves and neon yellow detailing, was worn for the first time in Saturdayâs 2-0 Bundesliga win over Heidenheim.

But instead of excitement, its debut was met with anger in the stands and online. Fans unfurled banners blasting it as âthe cruelest jersey in the leagueâ while chants of âWe want black and yellow jerseysâ rang out before kick-off, a pointed reminder of the clubâs traditional colours.

Across social media, the reaction was no kinder. Many supporters branded the design a betrayal of Dortmundâs historic identity, with critics arguing it looks more like a training top than a shirt fit for the famous Schwarzgelben.

Managing director Carsten Cramer took personal responsibility for the fallout, telling reporters: "The criticism has been received, and we are addressing it. The responsibility lies with me. We won't always be able to please everyone when selecting jerseys."

Sporting director Sebastian Kehl was more measured, reminding fans that opinions on kit design are always split.

#394. Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery

Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week

“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.

Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidents we all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.

Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time as Argentina captain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.

Despite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.

“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”

Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentina came against Benin on Tuesday – a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.

Messi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?

Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.

But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.

But the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When he quit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.

Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspirating the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.

Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.

But against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.

To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and then clad himself in the same flag that fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.

But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.

The cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.

“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.

As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.
