#398. Andoni Iraola is using his own weapons to win games and Liverpool's £400m attack is finally heading in the right direction as Alexander Isak emerges as the Reds' most important player, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 07:00 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 07:00 BST, 18 October 2026

The calculators were out at the Gtech Community Stadium.

A quick maths lesson in the media room before kick-off deduced that Liverpool’s front four cost a whopping £399.5million.

The quartet of Alexander Isak (£125m), Bradley Barcola (£123m), Florian Wirtz (£116m) and Victor Munoz (£35.5m) had started just one game together before and that, a home match against Fulham, ended in a goalless draw.

So the knives would have been out if those had blanked and the Reds had left a bitterly cold west London armed with anything but three points.

This is a tricky place to go and many big teams falter on this turf but, given they started the weekend nine points behind the league leaders, this was must-win for Andoni Iraola.

In the end, Wirtz threaded in Munoz for a splendid goal to equalise, then Barcola picked out Isak to finish for 2-1. Any narratives about Liverpool’s big-money flops were put on hold – for now at least – and, instead, the away fans could toast to their awesome foursome.

Liverpool's clash with Brentford was a must-win for Andoni Iraola - and his side delivered

The prolific and ruthless forward line does not tell the full story of this game. Far from it. For large parts, Liverpool were stodgy and, had Brentford not gone down to 10 men late in the first half, this could have easily ended up a completely different outcome.

These things even themselves out over the course of the season, we are often told, and after being left aggrieved at Ryan Gravenberch’s red card that ruined their chances last week, this time they were left thankful for Yehor Yarmolyuk’s bizarre headbutt and subsequent sending off.

Until then, the Reds were looking vulnerable and at risk of falling to the same fate they suffered on this ground last year, when Brentford bullied Arne Slot’s side and exploited many weaknesses.

Some of those issues are still clear but Iraola is now using his own weapons to help win games. Last year, Liverpool could not hurt teams and then were too flimsy at the other end.

The chief reason for this is Isak, all £125m of him.

His goal was his fifth of the season which sees him surpass last term’s tally already. Without his goals, Liverpool would be six points worse off and in the bottom half.

That might be a stretch but his brace in a 2-0 win at Ipswich, strike in a 1-0 victory at Bournemouth and now the match-winning goal in this 2-1 triumph has helped three tricky away trips turn from draws to wins.

With him fit last Sunday against Manchester City, who knows whether the Reds would have taken one of their early chances at 0-0 and made the game an alternative spectre.

Alexander Isak scored the winner at Brentford. He is not Liverpool's best player - but he is their most important

Bradley Barcola may have been wasteful at time but he dazzled again after his Champions League hat-trick

Isak is the sort of player who can drift in and out of games. But that is what the best strikers do — just think of the amount of time Sky Sports have highlighted Erling Haaland’s lack of touches only for the Norwegian to make them look silly by winning the game with his next shot.

The Swede, then, may not be Liverpool’s best player but he is certainly their most important. Three match-winners already this term, one can only wonder how different last season might have been if this instinctive poacher was fit all year.

His fitness is still questionable and it would not be a surprise to see him rested for Tuesday’s Champions League match against Villarreal for that reason.

Isak scored the winner but the supporting cast in attack also caught the eye. Munoz, the lesser-heralded of the star forwards, scored a fine goal from the right-hand side at a time when it felt Brentford were starting to settle into playing with 10 men.

Rio Ngumoha, a substitute, is also worthy of praise and he was a contender for man of the match. Against stubborn defences like this opposition, the 18-year-old’s unorthodox style is devastating and a real tool.

Barcola was wasteful but still dazzled at times. The Frenchman had clearly left his shooting boots in Austria and looked shaky in front of goal after his midweek hat-trick at LASK, but this was another notable performance, including an assist.

He was at the heart of everything, as was Wirtz. The German has been criticised this week — some of it harsh, most of it fair enough — but this was a metronomic display, creating nine chances which is more than any Liverpool player on record in a Premier League fixture.

More of this from the attackers and Iraola knows the possibilities are endless, though he would have boarded the flight home knowing his team remains a work in progress.

With a full contingent of players, Brentford would have been a good bet to get at least a point, and Iraola might worry at how many times the Bees got in behind his defence in the first half.

There are also battle scars with Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong set for ‘some time’ on the sidelines with muscular injuries. It is unclear how serious either are with the duo set for scans in the next 24 hours.

But despite the fitness worries and minor teething problems that still need solving, the Liverpool boss can raise a glass knowing his £400m attack is heading in the right direction.

With Isak et al on form and remaining fit, the Reds can prosper this year.

#405. Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson, Dan Roan, Laura Scott and Sami Mokbel assess Manchester City's position

Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport.

City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating "sham contracts" to inflate sponsorship deals by Â£830m.

The club have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and they have "irrefutable evidence" the ruling "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

In their appeal, City will argue the payments were made by the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder of the sponsors, while there are inconsistencies in the Commission's judgement.

Therefore, City say the sponsorship amounts were legitimate and not topped up by the owners.

James Severn, Member of the London Solicitor Litigation Association (LSLA) and Partner at Penningtons Manches Cooper, told BBC Sport the appeal is "not simply an opportunity to invite a new panel" to get the verdict overturned.

"City will need to identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness, which materially affected the Commission's decision," Severn said.

"The Appeal Board nevertheless has broad powers to allow or dismiss the appeal, vary the decision or make any other order it considers appropriate."

Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009

Etihad Airways, one of City's principal sponsors at the centre of the case, had previously stated that the Abu Dhabi government had not paid for its sponsorship of Manchester City.

That came in court documents as part of a US investigation in New York in 2015.

City will argue this does not have the full context of the situation and is not proof they have been inconsistent with evidence.

The club are adamant government documents fully support their case - but, Severn said, if these were already available to the Commission they may not be much use in an appeal.

"The bank statements, government records and contemporaneous payment documents could be powerful evidence if they establish a clear audit trail showing the disputed funds came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the owners," Severn added.

"However, if that evidence was already before the Commission, which nevertheless concluded that the arrangements were a sham, City will face an uphill struggle to demonstrate the finding was materially wrong."

Shortly before City's appeal was confirmed, Etihad Airways issued a statement saying it had never been "given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon".

Severn said Etihad Airways' complaint "does not, of itself, establish procedural unfairness".

"Etihad was not the respondent and is unlikely to have had an independent right to participate in the proceedings," Severn said. "It is likely to have been open to either party to obtain and present such evidence to the Commission.

"If the Appeal Board is prepared to consider new evidence from Etihad, it is likely to carry greater weight if supported by contemporaneous documents."

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester Cityâs inflatable banana craze

A key part of City's defence will be that the Independent Commission relied too heavily on the emails obtained through the Football Leaks files.

"If City can demonstrate the Commission fundamentally misunderstood the emails, failed to consider their proper context or reached conclusions inconsistent with other contemporaneous documents, that could amount to a material factual error," Severn added.

"City's difficulty is that the Commission heard extensive witness and documentary evidence but nevertheless made serious findings of sham arrangements and disguised owner funding."

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport the commission found "the documents were retrofitted to fit the crime".

"The Commission must have concluded that the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses put up by Manchester City were poor," Maguire said.

"However, from a legal point of view, this is an area they could attack if Manchester City's team can prove that the commission itself was a flawed construct in the sense that the members were Premier League picks rather than Manchester City's, and therefore the deck was stacked against the club to begin with.

Severn added that the retired senior judges and leading barristers, who sat on the Commission, have "spent their careers interpreting complicated facts, dealing with witnesses and applying relevant weight to evidence".

While adding that it would be "impossible to assess reliably" the chances of City winning their appeal, Severn added that "doing so will not be easy".

But Maguire believes that while it will be difficult for City to be successful, "there is a route".

City have brought in Mark Howard KC to advise the club in their appeal, while Etihad Airways has enlisted the services of respected law firm Quinn Emanuel.

Maguire said: "Given the lawyers that have been recruited by Manchester City, they may go down what's been described to me as a mess and noise approach.

"That means trying to discredit everything to do with the process of the Commission rather than necessarily the evidence that was presented.

"I've seen the documents that Abu Dhabi presented to the New York case. I'm not a lawyer, but from an accounting point of view, they can be seen in more than one way."

Even though Premier League regulations state an appeal must be heard within 12 weeks, or by Christmas Eve, Severn added that "given the scale and complexity of the proceedings, a final outcome may not be known for some time".

#407. Why Pep Guardiola's next job could be the one that defines him - more than Barcelona or Manchester City

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Fantastic football content straight to your inbox! From the latest transfer news, quizzes, videos, features and interviews with the biggest names in the game, plus lots more.

Sign up to our FREE live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest games available to watch on the device of your choice. Never miss a kick-off!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

What next for a manager who has just seen over a third of his managerial career seriously questioned by Premier League charges?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The seismic impact of Manchester City’s guilty verdict on 114 of their 115 charges will reach as far and wide as arguably anything in football history, including the legacy of Pep Guardiola.

The former Manchester City boss made his first return to the Etihad Stadium following his summer departure for their 4-2 loss to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Tuesday night. The timing of it was not lost on anyone.

Regardless of whether or not City somehow get off on appeal or a technicality, the Catalan will be forever tainted and surely can’t allow this to be the final act of his managerial career. Amid the infinite questions surrounding the case, sanctions and everything else, one is: what’s next for Guardiola?

First will be the continued full support of City and everyone connected to the case. In the days after the news that rocked the game, he made it crystal clear where he stood on the issue and backed up by sitting behind the embattled and shamed duo of Khaldoon Al Mubarek and Ferran Soriano on Tuesday night.

While that may seem incredibly hypocritical given he regularly said he would accept any verdict and once claimed, “If you lie to me, the day after I am not here. I will be out, and I will not be your friend any more”, it’s not difficult to see why Guardiola has taken this stance.

If he were to admit to City’s guilt on committing industrial-level financial cheating from 2009 to 2018, he would be admitting that every single one of the 20 trophies won in his 10 years at the club – including six Premier League titles and a Champions League – were tainted, tarnished and totally irrelevant.

Given he spent three more years at City than he did at Barcelona and Bayern Munich combined, it would be effectively erasing close to 60 per cent of his time on the touchline regardless of the obvious brilliance of both his coaching and his teams.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

And that’s before we even get started on what might come from the ongoing Negreira case centring on payments from Barça to the former vice president of Spain's Technical Committee of Referees. Safe to say, it’s been an autumn of discontent for Guardiola.

It’s unlikely to get any better for him in the winter months as the appeal plays out, with City’s chances of a reprieve looking slim at the absolute best. He’s already set for a year out of the game, having turned down the Italy national team job citing rest and personal reasons.

At 55, he should theoretically have plenty of years left on the touchline, and for a complete football obsessive, what else would he do in the decades to come?

Guardiola has never managed a small club or one with limited resources, which is often held against him when compared to his three greatest career rivals, Sir Alex Ferguson, Jose Mourinho and Jurgen Klopp.

All three near-built clubs from the ground up, restored them to their former glories and won the biggest prizes in the game without the biggest budgets. It’s a somewhat harsh appraisal of Guardiola given he started with Barça and quickly became the most in-demand manager on the globe. Los Cules may have won the Champions League just two years prior to his arrival but the transformation was remarkable.

There’s also the irony that any idea of Guardiola doing that now is near-impossible, more than a little bit in part due to the state ownership of City and PSG and everything that comes with that. The game is completely distorted with a European Super League of finances long in place.

Serie A’s demise has come alongside that, presenting potential landing spots for Pep. His European playing career did end in Italy – not without its own scandal – so he clearly has an affinity for the peninsula. Entertaining the Azzurri job spoke further to that.

The great task there is restoring either Juventus or Milan to the top table. Both clubs, fittingly, are full of drama, so would suit Guardiola’s ongoing arc. There’s been no Italian Champions League winner since Mourinho with Inter Milan in 2010 and Juve have lost five finals since last lifting the trophy 30 years ago. Talk about a career mode challenge.

A return to Barcelona can never be ruled out, while making Manchester United great again would be the perfect next bizarre storyline for the ever-developing Premier League soap opera.

We can rule out the Spanish job on account of their ongoing dominance and possibly his own Catalan ties. Brazil and England are the two biggest jobs and tasks, and Guardiola has been linked to both jobs. It would require either Carlo Ancelotti stepping down or Thomas Tuchel failing to win the Euros in 2028. Neither is too far-fetched.

Whatever may come for City in the coming weeks, months and years, it will always be attached to Guardiola no matter the level of his greatness. What comes for him may be the sport’s next big plotline.

Peter writes freelance for FourFourTwo and has previous experience at Evening Standard and Football365 among several others. He now works for us alongside OneFootball, the Sporting News and Stats Perform. One of the very few Irish people living in London and even fewer to support Manchester United, he spends time away from football rewatching TV shows and attempting to play tennis.

#409. Eric Cantona's transfer, Roy Keane and Alf-Inge Haaland's infamous clash, players called 'scum'... Sir Alex Ferguson was surprised by the deep hatred between Leeds and Man United, so where does it come from?

Published: 07:00 BST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 07:00 BST, 18 October 2026

There was a time not very long ago when the former Leeds United idol Alan Smith was being courted about a return to the club’s coaching staff. Smith, working in youth football in Florida, was identified as someone with the background, pedigree and personality to inspire the next generation of young Leeds prospects.

‘We couldn’t make it happen,’ a source close to the negotiations tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘I am sure there were several reasons but Alan has never forgotten how his family were abused after he moved to Manchester United back in the day. We believed that was still in his mind.’

Leeds United and Manchester United. Colourful, bitter and deep. There are few football rivalries like it.

‘When I was in the academy at Leeds you knew all about it,’ recalls former Leeds goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

‘It didn’t matter how young you were. It was there. Back then it was an option for us to be ball boys at home games. Some lads couldn’t be bothered. Sitting there in the cold and wet.

Leeds will host their rivals from across the Pennines at 2pm on Sunday. It feels like another big test for Michael Carrick and his team but inside Leeds’ fabulous old ground, it will be no more frenzied than normal simply because that is just not possible. Even hate has a ceiling.

Alan Smith played 228 times for Leeds but fans never forgave him for moving across the Pennines in 2004

What has always been less clear is why the rivalry goes so deep. The two clubs do not share a city or even a county. There is not a single seismic event or game around which such mutual enmity can be built.

Some talk about the day Eric Cantona left Leeds for Old Trafford in 1992 as a pivotal moment and indeed the moment United captain Roy Keane first clashed with Alf Inge Haaland during a game five years later.

But the truth is the loathing and suspicion goes back way further than that. Even former United manager Sir Alex Ferguson was surprised by it when he arrived from Scotland in the 1980s.

Hit on the head by a cup of Bovril after being called a ‘Manc b******’ on an early scouting mission to watch Leeds play Crystal Palace, Ferguson returned to his club wondering just where all that came from. ‘It’s from the 1960s,’ said his kitman Norman Davies.

Talking to those on both sides of the divide, there seems truth in that.

Some talk romantically about the tone set by the War of the Roses – Leeds do wear Yorkshire white and United Lancashire red – but it seems fanciful that a dislike so visceral can really be tracked back to the mid-1400s.

More significant may have been Johnny Giles’ switch from United to Leeds in 1963. Giles became synonymous with Leeds’ aggressive style of play as they twice won the English title, in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

Former United midfielder and European Cup winner Pat Crerand is blunt about all that.

Some talk about the day Eric Cantona left Leeds for Old Trafford in 1992 as a pivotal moment in the rivalry

Alf Inge Haaland and Roy Keane's mutual dislike began in this fixture

‘Don Revie’s Leeds team never got the credit they deserved, but maybe that’s because of the way that they behaved,’ Crerand has said.

‘People had grudging respect for the success we had at United under Sir Matt Busby because of the way we played.

‘But there was no respect for Leeds and that partly explains the rivalry.’

The reverence duly served to United teams that played in the Busby era and indeed under Ferguson stands in contrast to the enduring image of the ‘dirty Leeds’ of Revie’s days.

It is probably unfair but public perception and what it means was a theme touched on this week by perhaps Leeds’ most famous supporter.

Gary Edwards is an author and painter and decorator who has not missed a single Leeds game – bar the Covid era – since 1968. Amusingly, Edwards refuses to paint anything red and has been known to paint over the colour for no payment.

‘I only do one coat for free,’ Edwards says with a laugh. ‘But yeah, the rivalry is deep and from our point of view there is that feeling Man United have always felt they have a god-given right to anything.

‘They fancy themselves, don’t they? Maybe they do try and look down on us a bit. They feel that everyone in football should bend over backwards for them.

Paddy Crerard, who played for Manchester United in the 1960s, believes Leeds were never given the same level of respect as Busby-era United

‘It’s not jealousy from us, as some people say it is. When I started going to matches, we used to beat them regularly.

‘But here in Leeds we just feel we don’t lie down for anyone, especially not them.’

In Manchester, those who have crossed the divide still talk about it. Lee Sharpe – who is actually from the Midlands – left Old Trafford for Yorkshire in 1996 and still gets called ‘scum’ by his mates.

The late Gordon McQueen – a Scot – went the other way in 1978 and found himself verbally abused so incessantly at a pre-season game 30 years later that he decided to go home.

Ferguson, meanwhile, could never quite get his head round it. Sources this week revealed to Daily Mail Sport that one of the reasons the two clubs have always managed to exist cordially at boardroom level is because of the friendship between Ferguson and his fellow Scot Eddie Gray, a Leeds club ambassador.

‘Eddie and Sir Alex are part of the glue between the clubs,’ says a source from the modern Leeds era. ‘They have a really good and funny relationship going back to their days in the game.

‘They will chip away at each other but in the boardroom the sight of those two sitting at a table winding each other up keeps the mood exactly as it should be. It takes the edge off everything. They are desperate to beat us, mind.’

Ferguson is these days known to light-heartedly mock the quality of the wine served in the Elland Road boardroom but was not always so generous. His two autobiographies are regularly pillaged for anecdotes – less so a diary of the 1994-95 season that contains this startling extract after a defeat in Yorkshire.

‘You can feel the hatred, the animosity,’ writes Ferguson. ‘ I said to the players afterwards, “Now you know what it’s like to lose here”.

‘The Leeds supporters were awful. I almost want them to be relegated because of their fans. I don’t think they deserve to be in the Premier League. Such hatred really is incredible.

Ferguson's friendship with former Leeds winger and manager Eddie Gray has meant animosity in the stands and on the pitch has never spilled into the boardroom

‘A TV camera caught a woman screaming abuse at me. What chance have you got? You could understand the animosity better if it was Liverpool and United because they are just down the road from one another.

‘You can’t say the same for Leeds. You are expecting a pitch invasion at any moment.’

In Yorkshire, there is an acceptance that things have sometimes crossed the line. Even when the teams met at Elland Road during the Covid lockdown, Leeds supporters tried to gather outside to ‘greet’ the United coach.

‘It’s not just one way, though,’ adds our Leeds source. ‘I have been in the directors' box at Old Trafford and received dog’s abuse. Never in my life have I experienced anything like that.’

Sunday’s meeting should be tamer on the field than some have been. In 1965, for example, an FA Cup semi-final featured a punch-up between Jack Charlton and Denis Law. Leeds won the replay 1-0 but lost the league title on goal average to their rivals. Four years later, in January 1969, crowd trouble at Elland Road during a match between the sides left 50 in hospital.

Leeds’ modern travails mean that not often in recent years have the teams competed at the same level – they met just twice between 2004 and 2020 for example – but tensions have endured.

Jack Charlton and Denis Law faced off in a 1965 FA Cup semi-final clash

... and the confrontations have continued down the decades - with Jermaine Beckford and Wes Brown squaring up during Leeds' win in the FA Cup at Old Trafford in 2010

Former Leeds midfielder Kalvin Phillips, for example, refused to countenance a switch to United when they expressed interest in 2022. He moved to Manchester City instead.

Meanwhile, two years earlier Marcus Rashford was compelled to remove a social media post welcoming Leeds back to the Premier League following a backlash from fans of his own club.

‘If you play for either club you have no choice but to understand it,’ adds goalkeeper Robinson.

‘When Leeds were two divisions down, Man United fans were still singing about how much they hated them.

‘It’s about keeping up tradition isn’t it? Modern-day Millwall fans think they have a tradition to uphold and it’s the same at Leeds, even if the actual origins have got a bit lost.

‘It’s always Leeds’ biggest game and that filters through to the dressing room. It’s like nothing I’ve ever known.’

Guest of honour for Sunday's game will be former Leeds and United midfielder Gordon Strachan. The 69-year-old was captain of Howard Wilkinson’s Leeds team that pipped United to the title in 1992. Cantona left the following autumn and a period of Old Trafford dominance followed.

Gordon Strachan will be guest of honour at Elland Road, having moved from United to Leeds in 1989 and won the First Division title there in 1992

‘I still can’t look at Howard the same way after that,’ admits Edwards. ‘It didn’t start the rivalry, though. No, it was long before that. I went to my first game in 1968 and it was there then.

‘I actually feel a bit sorry for Man United right now and that’s a strange feeling.

‘I went to a game at Old Trafford last season and they were wearing half-and-half scarves.

‘I’d go there thinking I may get lynched. I’d rather that than wear one of those things. There will be none on sale on Sunday. That’s not what we do in Leeds.’

#412. Robbie Savage the panto villain puts scepticism aside to leave Leicester reeling

Peterborough’s new boss has long been a divisive figure but a stunning 3-1 win at struggling former club offered a glimpse of his fearless philosophy

It felt as though the stars had aligned when Robbie Savage’s first League One match in charge of Peterborough – his first EFL managerial role – happened to be at Leicester. He made his name here and forged a divisive and enduring reputation that has made him a permanent fixture in English football.

Savage has long been a joker figure – an image born in his playing days, when he hurtled around midfield with long blond hair bouncing, launching into challenges that at one point made him the most booked player in Premier League history. A pantomime villain, a prankster and an eccentric who was once fined £10,000 by the Football Association – and two weeks’ wages by Leicester – for using the referee Graham Poll’s toilet before a match. (Savage blamed an upset stomach brought on by antibiotics).

That persona followed him into the media after retirement and it hardly screams management material, yet Savage has quietly built a more serious reputation on the touchline in recent years.

At the phoenix club Macclesfield, he was handed his first chance in the dugout by his mate Rob Smethurst, the owner, and won promotion to the National League North with a mammoth 109 points – winning 35 of 42 games. Last season, he guided Forest Green to the National League playoffs, losing to Boreham Wood.

Perhaps because of his personality, scepticism has shadowed the 51-year-old throughout his fledgling managerial career. In a lengthy interview with the Peterborough board, he won them over with his passion and ideas for restoring confidence in a young, talented, but struggling squad. Darragh MacAnthony, the club’s chair, suggested Savage’s character and work rate were required from “top to bottom” at the club.

Even so, when Savage took the Posh job he immediately addressed “the doubters” before anyone had really expressed any doubt. He pointed out he was told he was not good enough when he was released by Manchester United – one of the forgotten members of the Class of ’92 FA Youth Cup winners – and that he had battled his way into the Leicester team.

At the King Power Stadium on Saturday, he was so animated on the touchline it bordered on parody. He approached the travelling Peterborough fans and pumped his fist towards them – a gesture most managers save for after a victory, but Savage performed before kick-off. He was equally lively when the game started, dressed in baggy dark grey trousers and jacket, if not crouching on the edge of his technical area then shouting instructions, clapping his hands, pointing his fingers. There was a lot of pointing on his way to an impressive 3-1 win away.

His exertions were so energetic the jacket came off within 10 minutes. “I’m exhausted,” he said. “I think I’ve done 10k in the technical area, kicking every ball for my team.”

It is no surprise he was handed a two-match ban last season for yellow cards received for overexuberant celebrations and overexuberant discussions with officials. When Lucca Mendonça crunched Bobby De Cordova-Reid, Savage leapt and punched the air with as much enthusiasm as he celebrated Owura Edwards’s opening goal.

Plymouth came from behind to beat Wimbledon 2-1 with a stoppage-time goal from substitute Xavier Amaechi which put them clear at the top of League One. Jayden Stockley had put the Dons ahead in the 16th minute, with Caleb Watts equalising ahead of the break. It looked like the points would be shared before Amaechi swept the ball home in the fifth minute of added time.

New Peterborough manager Robbie Savage had a dream start with a 3-1 win at Leicester, to pile more pressure on Foxes’ manager Russell Martin. Posh took an early lead through Owura Edwards and Harry Leonard before an own goal from Warren O’Hora made it 3-0 just before the break. Emil Riis scored a second-half consolation for the hosts.

Mark Harris and Cameron Brannagan scored as high-flying Oxford secured a 2-1 win over Notts County at Meadow Lane. Bradford were held to a goalless draw by Leyton Orient at Valley Parade, slipping two points behind Plymouth.

Huddersfield missed the chance to go second after Sheffield Wednesday fought back with two late goals to snatch a 2-2 draw at the Accu Stadium after Jamal Lowe scored a penalty deep into stoppage-time. Kyle Wootton scored twice as Stockport came from behind to beat Barnsley 3-1 at Edgeley Park to sit third.

Gassan Ahadme’s late goal gave fifth-placed Cambridge a 1-0 win over 10-man Blackpool at the Abbey Stadium, where there had been a 15 minute delay to kick-off because of issues affecting supporters entering the ground.

Reading are sixth after a 5-1 away win at strugglers MK Dons while Luton were comprehensive victors at Wycombe with a dominant 4-1 display to spoil a day of celebration for Tom Hounsell. Efforts from Kasey Palmer, Nahki Wells, Jamie Donley and Devante Cole were more than enough against a home side who announced Hounsell as permanent head coach before the game.

Leon Ayinde’s first EFL goal was enough to move Doncaster out of the bottom four with a 1-0 home win over Burton. Mansfield edged home 2-1 in their first ever game against Bromley to halt a run of four games without a victory. Wigan remain adrift at the bottom of the table after a 1-0 defeat at Stevenage.

As at Macclesfield and Forest Green, his football was fast and direct. A ball over the top allowed Bolu Shofowoke to round the Leicester goalkeeper before Harry Leonard tapped in.

The Posh fans started chanting Savage’s name just before half-time, then called for him to give them a wave. But he was so engrossed in the Peterborough attack that led to their third goal that he didn’t hear them.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

That marauding style does leave them exposed at the back, but Savage doesn’t care. “My philosophy is: the best players are at the top of the pitch,” he said. “If I can get it there as quick as we can, by limiting the passes, but on the floor, through the lines, you can push the full-backs out. At times we were 2-1-1-6. That’s how we play. We are open. But let’s be brave.”

Even then, Emil Riis’s back-post tap-in – Savage held his head in his hands as though the world was ending after conceding – took only a lick of gloss off the occasion. It was a stunning result for a side that had won once in the league all season, scored four times and gone seven weeks without a victory.

“I’m just humble to come up against somebody like Russell Martin, who’s managed in the Premier League,” Savage said. “Two and a half years ago I was up at Hebburn and Stockton, playing in front of 200-300 people. My team have come to the King Power and put in a performance like that. I’m so proud of them.”

At the final whistle, Savage hurried around the pitch, where he must have shaken the hand or slapped the back or hugged every player, coach and staff member from both teams. The Peterborough fans stood and chanted his name long before and well after he returned to pump his fist in celebration.

Savage will be entertaining this season. And he may just surprise a few people with his football, too.

#415. 'I had so many medals under the bed' - Green on Chelsea success

Paul Green (left) and Emma Hayes (right) built a formidable team at Chelsea

When Paul Green left Chelsea after 13 years, he had achieved so much success that the majority of his medals were hidden away in a box under the bed.

It was only when he had gone that he truly began to appreciate what he had done.

The former Chelsea head of women's football formed a formidable partnership with ex-manager Emma Hayes and helped lead the Blues to 19 major trophies.

He left suddenly in February amid reports of unrest in Chelsea's hierarchy.

Asked about his exit, Green told BBC Sport: "Look, football clubs move on and a lot of people have changed at that club in recent years.

"I think ultimately they chose to go in a different direction but I feel very proud of the job that I did there and I left the club in a lot better position than when I first went in there."

Under Green's leadership, Chelsea won six successive Women's Super League titles, the last coming under current manager Sonia Bompastor in 2025.

They became the most dominant force in the WSL and reached the Women's Champions League final in 2021.

"It was an incredible time. There was a lot of potential that Emma Hayes sold to me and that came to fruition," said Green.

"What the [players] went on to achieve, in my eyes, will never be beaten and it will be difficult for any team to replicate that type of dominance.

"It was some of the best times of my life. It's probably not until you're out of it that you actually appreciate what the success was.

"I had so many medals that were just chucked under the bed in a box. I've had time to get them framed. Now I've got a new chapter here at Bay FC."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Are the European Women's World Cup play-offs working?

Women's billion-dollar boom leaves players behind, says Fifpro

Green had seven months out of football before he was appointed as chief football officer of San Francisco club Bay FC in September.

He admitted the response to his Chelsea exit had been "overwhelming" and he needed time to adapt, spending time with his family in the meantime.

"It was people just in the general women's football world who really appreciated the work and success that we had there," said Green.

"Of course, that touched me and it took me forever to get back to everybody who had reached out because there was that many.

"I guess all things have to come to an end at some stage and I've gone in a different direction now.

"In the early days, having a lack of structure was difficult because I had gone from 13 years of having certain routines. That part was difficult."

It is clear that Green is excited by the future at Bay FC.

He has taken over a project that is being led by former Football Association (FA) director Kay Cossington and comes under the multi-club ownership of Bay Collective.

Green hopes to use his extensive knowledge in the transfer market to recruit some of the world's best players and to build an effective organisation.

"They sold me the vision for the club. It became too good an opportunity to turn down," said Green.

"The potential there of building something really special is what I'm looking forward to. I think it's got some similarities to the early days at Chelsea."

Bay FC are moving into new training facilities next year and Green has vowed to act in the transfer window to improve their league position.

They are currently third bottom with three matches left in the National Women's Soccer League 2026 season.

"The team hasn't done as well as everybody would like it to do. We are where we are in the league so we need to try and improve the roster immediately," said Green.

"With the connections and network that I've built up over 20 years, I'm confident that I can bring in a few players to help the good nucleus of talent we've got.

"You have to have the infrastructure right off the pitch in terms of staffing and facilities and that's something we are working on."

Aggie Beever-Jones (left) went on to win Euro 2025 with England

During Green's time at Chelsea, he oversaw the development of several English players including homegrown talents Aggie Beever-Jones and Lexi Potter.

Potter made her debut in England's 5-0 win over Greece last week, while Beever-Jones was part of the squad who won Euro 2025.

However, there is concern for the future of England's youngsters with gametime for homegrown players reducing in recent years.

"Players still need exposure and the way we tried to do it at Chelsea was by having a good loan programme," said Green.

"You need to find the right partner club to develop the player. But if you haven't got that resource, maybe young players have to go abroad to play.

"There is the proposal of a 'B team' that a lot of other European leagues have that works very successfully in Germany and Spain.

"I do think if they came in at level three of the pyramid that would help because the academy isn't what it used to be. I know that's very controversial."

The FA's director of women's football Sue Day said it was an area that needs addressing, while England manager Sarina Wiegman admitted her concern.

"Not enough of our young players are playing enough football and I think we'd all agree with that," said Day.

"I don't think you ever want to, even if you could, impose anything regulatory. We all need to work together in this system to make it work.

"The FA, the clubs and the league are all on the same side. Clubs are going to create value from investment they are putting into developing players."

Michael Carrick might be able to use his coaching ability to turn things around on the pitch at Manchester United, but is he the man to fix things off it?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Michael Carrick brought a veneer of calm to Old Trafford last season, but that has disintegrated in rapid fashion this season.

His tenure as permanent Manchester United boss is being defined by an unruly, factional dressing room coming apart at the seams.

Tuesday night’s dispiriting Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid has extended the team's winless run to five matches, and sparked a civil war.

Man United are floundering - what else can be said about a paltry return of two wins from nine matches in all competitions, an early Carabao Cup exit, six points from their opening six Premier League fixtures, and inability to capitalise against ten men in games versus Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur?

They are, for all intents and purposes, a team devoid of competitive edge. And on-pitch disjointedness is only half the problem. The deeper issue is cultural.

Argentine international Lisandro Martinez broke rank in the aftermath of Man United's defeat at the Wanda Metropolitano on Tuesday night, delivering a scathing public broadside against director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s transfer strategy.

In doing so, he extinguished any lingering hope that squad unity was something Carrick could stand behind as a success during his brief spell. The defender was reportedly confronted by a teammate during the flight back to Manchester.

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

Navigating such turmoil demands a managerial giant, and it is not Carrick's doing or fault that the club finds itself in its current mess. He is, for all his understated dignity, manifestly not that man.

The former midfielder is neither an inspiring orator capable of galvanising disparate egos with his rhetoric, nor is he a Sir Alex Ferguson-esque autocrat who can lay down the law - he hasn't been there long enough, for starters.

Carrick’s once-praised stillness now appears passive and faced with a fractured dressing room taking pot shots at the boardroom, a gentle word is insufficient. Perhaps it speaks to Carrick's authority that Martinez felt compelled to speak out in such terms in midweek.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30October 13, 2026

Carrick’s brief has completely changed, but his managerial toolkit has not. When he took the reins as caretaker in January following Ruben Amorim’s acrimonious departure, the remit was predominantly pastoral.

These were hugely talented players lacking confidence and drive, who had been tactically micro-managed to the point where many no longer cared. Carrick let them play, recalled certain players and allowed them the time and space to do what they do best.

He soothed bruised egos, simplified the instructions and put an arm around the wounded. Lo and behold, it yielded that most famous of textbook interim bounces, and he steered the club to a third-place finish. The pressure was off, the season had already been mothballed. With the benefit of hindsight, the hierarchy's message to Carrick over the summer should have been a firm handshake and 'thank you for your efforts, but we'll take it from here', before hiring a managerial heavyweight.

Now, though, he's the permanent man, albeit probably not for much longer.

The honeymoon is long over, and the pressure cooker has been turned up to eleven. Managing Manchester United through stormy weather requires ruthlessness, authority, ideological clarity, and the rare ability to inspire footballers to run through brick walls. That hasn't happened.

National reports are already detailing three-man shortlists to replace him, touting Brighton's Fabian Hurzeler alongside Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann. The writing is very much on the wall. Carrick may retain personal affections of the Old Trafford faithful, but goodwill does not heal a fractured culture. The dressing room has reached a point of no return, and Michael Carrick is not the man to glue it back together.

#421. McInnes rues conceding equaliser that burst Rangers' bubble and cost Ibrox men points in Dens Park thriller

Published: 23:27 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 23:48 BST, 17 October 2026

DEREK McINNES claimed Dundee’s equaliser felt like a balloon popping for his Rangers side as they threw away two points from a winning position at Dens Park.

Behind through Bradley Fink’s opener, the Ibrox men turned the game on its head with two wonder goals from Badredine Bouanani and Nico Raskin arriving either side of the break.

Seemingly coasting towards the seventh straight league win which would have taken them top of the table, Dan Neil’s stumble allowed Callum Jones to claim a deserved point for the Dark Blues.

Clearly frustrated that a much-improved second half display didn’t seal another three points, McInnes reflected: ‘I think it’s two parts. I think the first half, Dundee maybe shaded it. Certainly they were a handful.

‘We spoke ahead of the game with the players about we needed to defend. Defenders needed to be good defenders. We knew Dundee would mix the game up, they would come after us on full press.

‘We also knew that we had to use the ball and move the ball quicker.

McInnes can't hide his frustration as his Rangers side dropped two points in the title race

‘Their front two (Fink and Ash Hay) were a handful, they will be for any back four this season. We never quite got to grips with them in the first half.

‘But we scored a brilliant goal from Bouanani, which justifies the selection for me.

‘We defended with a lot more purpose. The performance for 20-25 minutes culminated in Nico’s goal.

‘It should be a winning goal, because it was such a high-quality goal. The disappointment is that we had the game there, we were dominant. We had the game by the scruff of the neck.

‘Dundee were struggling to get out of their own half. We were in such a good place. It was almost like a balloon popping when we made a mistake, which can happen.’

Neil’s error came after Dujon Sterling’s mistake allowed Fink to give Dundee the lead.

‘The first goal is avoidable,’ McInnes stated.

‘I just thought we were a bit sleepy and a bit not ready to deal with it.

‘And then the second goal is a mistake. Listen, I’m not going to criticise any of my players for it, but it is a mistake and it was difficult to say anything other than that because we were so good in the game.’

Jones (second from left) is hailed after he capitalised on Neil's error to equalise

Rangers lost their impetus once Dundee levelled, though, with McInnes believing his players had to respond in a more productive manner to the set-back.

‘We never really got back to that same level,’ he continued.

‘Although we did have enough balls in their box to score. We should be scoring.

‘I think what it does do, it kills your momentum, first of all, because football’s not just a physical game, but mentally.

‘It also gives Dundee something to hang on to. All of a sudden Dundee are thinking, we might just get something here. But we still worked the ball into good enough areas.

‘We still have two wide players and two strikers. We still got enough balls in the box. We still had opportunities. We still made them defend.

‘So. although we didn’t quite get to the same sort of level, I still thought we were the dominant team and we were the team that looked more likely to win it.’

Bouanani curls in a leveller just before half-time for his first Rangers goal

Dundee boss Steven Pressley felt his players were well worth the point that maintains their outstanding start to the season.

'To use an old cliche, it was a game of two halves,’ he said.

'I thought our first half performance was a really outstanding and very dominant performance.

'We restricted Rangers to very few chances and we created a number of chances and chances that we felt we could have capitalised on more.

'We were really strong in the duels and the second balls, the aspects of the game that I spoke about prior to the game.

'But the pleasing thing as well is when we got on to those second balls, we were courageous in our play and we really tried to play.

'So, I couldn’t have been prouder of the group.

'But the one thing we did expect was a reaction from Rangers.

'We had to ride our luck at times. Against the Old Firm, you have to dig in and suffer a bit.

'We did all of those things and then we still came back for more.

'Some really great things to take from it and a little bit of perspective. We’re the first club to take a point off Rangers in eight games, so our players should be really proud of their achievements tonight.'

#422. The Premier League so far: draws, underperforming xG and other data pointers

Goal averages are crumbling as players take fewer touches in the box and forwards underperform against xG

Goals are on the up in the Premier League. The average of 2.70 non-penalty goals per game in 2026-27 is higher than last season and two of the four previous campaigns. Yet we should have been even more royally entertained. Matches have averaged 2.88 non-penalty expected goals, the second most in the past six seasons. Chances have been going to waste.

If the 20 teams converted at the par rate, there would have been almost two extra goals per week. As few as that sounds, the proportion of games drawn is higher than in any past Premier League season. Some tied matches might have been settled had the finishing been up to the mark.

This is an issue across the Premier League. Fourteen clubs have scored fewer goals than expected, whether penalties are included or not, up from 10 last season. While there are eight teams that are within a goal of their underlying numbers and may see an immediate change of fortunes this weekend, the remaining 12 are split 8-4 towards the underachievers.

It is not just season-wide averages that are crumbling but week-by-week performances, too. There were 24 instances of a team scoring at least one goal fewer than their xG implied they should have across the first five match weeks, twice as many as occurred in the opening 50 games last season.

There are numerous possible explanations. Chance quality does not appear to be one of them, as the expected goals per non-penalty shot average only drops once more decimal places are applied than feels healthy.

At first glance, volume of touches in the penalty area has barely shifted either. A Premier League team is averaging 24.8 touches in the opposition box per game, down just 0.6 on last season.

The breakdown by team is more revealing. Four of last season’s top five are having fewer box touches per match, with Aston Villa and Liverpool having seen around a third disappear from their averages.

The one team from the quintet to increase is Manchester United, but they have only played one club that finished in the top 10 last season and five of their eight goals occurred against Championship runners-up Ipswich. A finely tuned attacking machine they are not. United top the Premier League for non-penalty shots, and are joint-second bottom for the average expected goal value.

They have not been helped by their top player for non-penalty xG: Bryan Mbeumo is one of 10 players who have scored at least one goal fewer than underlying numbers imply he should have. As he underachieved by 1.19 last season, this is not especially odd. The issue is how reliant United are upon the 27-year-old. This problem is not exclusive to this combination of club and player either.

The top player for expected goals at almost every Premier League club is having a bigger share of the xG pie than they enjoyed last season. This need not necessarily be a concern, as the figures will drop once playing time and chances are more equally shared within squads.

The most involved players themselves may help explain why goals are down, though. The top players from each club have collectively scored 6.8 non-penalty goals fewer than expected, almost 40% of the shortfall across the division from just 20 players.

Thierno Barry has been the player taking the chance for 49.4% of Everton’s non-penalty expected goals this season, up from 17.7% last term. It’s a massive increase in responsibility for a relatively young player – he has scored twice from chances valued at 3.5 xG.

Alexander Isak has seen a greater leap in share of team expected goals, though injuries meant he did not feature that often last season. There are seeds of growth for him at Liverpool, but he remains relatively new in terms of minutes played for the club. As with more than half of Premier League clubs, Isak is playing under a new man in the dugout.

Isak’s replacement at Newcastle, Yoanne Wissa, underperformed against xG by more than two goals last season, as did Marcus Tavernier at Bournemouth. They may not be the best players for their clubs to funnel their chances through. At least they are preferable to the situation at Tottenham, where centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is their leading player for non-penalty expected goals.

Elsewhere, the players with the most xG for Fulham (Gonzalo García) and Ipswich (Emersonn) are 22 years old and new to English football. Hull’s Oli McBurnie, meanwhile, has never scored more than six goals in a Premier League campaign. Erling Haaland remains a reliable presence in the xG-heavy frontman stakes, but the situation at Manchester City may affect his form.

Excessive reliance on players who can be forgiven for underperforming could prove to be a small-sample statistical quirk that is quickly remedied. Until it is, do not bank on the goal rate reaching the expected goal level in the Premier League.

#427. Ranking the Premier League's all-time greatest super subs

Mikel Arteta may be attempting to rebrand them "finishers" but there's only one phrase in the footballing lexicon to sum up today's focus: super subs.

Yes, we're looking for those players renowned for making a devastating impact off the bench, those guaranteed game-changers a manager turns to when in desperate need of a goal.

First, an honorary mention for some who missed out, such as one-season wonder Adam le Fondre, who holds the record for the most goals off the bench in a single Premier League campaign - five of his eight came in a three-game spell in January 2013.

Hernan Crespo boasts the best goals-per-game ratio but his six in 16 substitute appearances for Chelsea represents a small sample size, likewise ex-Norwich and Leicester forward Mark Robins with five in 14 outings as a replacement.

To make the all-time top 10 Premier League super subs, players need to have consistently delivered throughout their careers, providing goals and assists.

So here we go, I've ranked mine below - you can have your say in the comments, too.

Theo Walcott, replaced on 168 occasions, holds the record as the most subbed off player in Premier League history. Yet it's his impact coming on to the pitch we're interested in here.

Bursting on to the top-flight scene as an explosive teenager, the flying forward was often used by Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger to stretch defences with his pace and movement - a lactic acid-inducing sight for flailing full-backs.

The England international pieced together an impressive substitute CV throughout his Premier League career.

No-one has more than Walcott's 14 assists as a sub - Ryan Giggs and Marc Albrighton are level - while he also scored 10 goals as a replacement across his time with the Gunners, Everton and Southampton.

It puts him fourth on the list for overall goal contributions off the bench.

This was a toss up between Victor Anichebe and Divock Origi, with both forwards contributing exactly half of all their Premier League goals as a substitute.

Ex-Everton, West Brom and Sunderland striker Anichebe edges it having notched a couple more - a tally of 13 placing the former Nigeria international in joint-eighth on the all-time list - while he also chipped in with five assists off the bench.

Roman Pavlyuchenko was also unlucky to miss out - 45% of his 20 Premier League goals came as a substitute for Tottenham.

Anichebe scored 50% of his 26 Premier League goals as a sub - the joint-highest percentage for any player to have scored at least 20 times in the competition

There's a good case for Danny Welbeck, who as the only current player in the top three, with 19 goals, still has time to catch those above him.

Welbeck was a goalscoring sub at Manchester United and Arsenal but perfected the art on the south coast, with 12 of his tally coming during six years with Brighton.

The 35-year-old is now at Chelsea but - with apologies to Danny - there is another former Blue whose stats demand a place on this list.

Daniel Sturridge has two fewer substitute goals then Welbeck but has scored a slightly higher percentage of his overall Premier League tally as a sub - 22%.

The former England man, who played for Manchester City, Chelsea, Bolton, Liverpool and West Brom in the top flight, was good for an assist, too.

In fact, when you take his total goal contributions of 24, he provided at a more prolific rate than every substitute in Premier League history - bar Edin Dzeko and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer.

Richarlison matches Sturridge for minutes per goal contribution, but with eight fewer the Brazilian, perhaps harshly, misses out.

Sturridge scored 17 of his 76 Premier League goals as a substitute and also made seven assists off the bench

A World Cup and Champions League winner, one of the few trophies Olivier Giroud hasn't got his hands on is the Premier League title despite a knack for scoring important goals off the bench.

The Frenchman is second on the all-time substitute scoring list, accounting for 21 of his 90 top-flight goals - that's almost a quarter - with only Dzeko, Solskjaer and Javier Hernandez boasting a better minutes-per-goal record as a sub.

Giroud honed his ability to make a late impact at Arsenal and Chelsea, making 103 substitute appearances in total across 10 seasons in the Premier League.

Good feet for a big man. Tore Andre Flo was a menace for Premier League defenders not merely because of his tall, gangly frame but for the silky touches the Norwegian often showed with his giant boots.

Flo scored 34% of his 38 Premier League goals as a substitute - the eighth-highest ratio for those with 20 top-flight goals or more, while he is also joint-eighth overall for goals from a substitute.

The first of those came just three minutes into his Chelsea debut in 1997, and it was with the Blues he enjoyed his best Premier League output before a later stint at Sunderland.

Having also provided three assists as a sub, he ranks fifth for minutes-per-goal involvements, contributing to his side scoring once every 78 minutes on average when used off the bench.

Twelve of Flo's 34 Premier League goals for Chelsea came as a substitute

The Little Pea. Small in stature but a giant headache for tiring defenders.

Of all players in Premier League history to have scored at least 10 goals as a substitute, only one - Sergio Aguero, and it feels a stretch to call the competition's sixth-highest scorer a super sub - has netted at a more prolific rate than Javier 'Chicharito' Hernandez.

He has 19 in 78 sub appearances, a rate of 0.24 per game, with 36% of all his Premier League goals coming after he started on the bench - predominantly for Manchester United but also later in his career at West Ham.

He netted on average every 88 minutes when used as a replacement.

Indeed, only Jermain Defoe and Giroud have scored more goals as a substitute than the Mexican, while he sits among a leading group of seven - including Defoe - who have scored five match-winners as a sub.

Aged 40, Edin Dzeko is still scoring goals for Bundesliga outfit Schalke. His record as a substitute in the Premier League, however, remains among the greatest.

Dzeko netted 50 Premier League goals for Manchester City, with more than a quarter of those coming as a substitute.

Only Aguero and Hernandez, of players to have scored at least 10 goals as a sub, have better goals-per-game ratios than him. When you break it down to minutes per goal, Dzeko is level at the top with Solskjaer - scoring on average every 83 minutes.

He stands alone once you add assists, too - 17 goal contributions during 56 top-flight games as a replacement means Dzeko returned on average every 63 minutes.

The most important of those goals, of course, came in stoppage time against QPR on the final day of the 2012 season. Everyone remembers the Aguero moment, but it was substitute Dzeko's header two minutes earlier that levelled the game.

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer is perhaps the most iconic of super subs, largely for that Treble-clinching night in Barcelona.

The baby-faced Norwegian, having started Manchester United's FA Cup final win over Newcastle four days earlier, came on in the 81st minute of the Champions League final to toe-poke a stoppage-time winner after Teddy Sheringham had equalised against Bayern Munich moments earlier.

It capped a vintage few months for Solskjaer's super sub legend, having bagged four in the final 10 minutes of an 8-1 win at Nottingham Forest in the February.

Sticking strictly to his Premier League output, Solskjaer is joint-fifth on the all-time substitute scoring list with 17, netting 19% of his 91 top-flight goals off the bench, with a ratio of 0.2 goals-per-game as a sub.

His rate of scoring on average once every 83 minutes off the bench is a competition high that can only be matched by Dzeko. The caveat is, like Dzeko, Solskjaer was playing for one of the most dominant teams in the land.

Nwankwo Kanu's impact as a substitute was felt immediately at Arsenal.

Coming off the bench on his debut, the Nigerian forward collected a throw-in meant for a Sheffield United player - after the opposition kicked the ball out for an injury - and crossed for Marc Overmars to score. It sparked a famous FA Cup rematch.

In the Premier League, he was just as ruthless. Kanu, who joined from Inter Milan having earlier won the Champions League at Ajax, made 56 of his 119 top-flight appearances for Arsenal as a sub.

When you take in spells at West Brom and Portsmouth, too, he netted 17 goals off the bench - 31% of all his top-flight strikes - which places him joint-fifth on the all-time substitute scoring list.

But he was almost as prolific at creating them, making 12 assists as a substitute - a tally only bettered by three players in Premier League history.

Kanu made 119 Premier League appearances in six years at Arsenal

OK, goals are currency and Jermain Defoe has netted more as a substitute than any other Premier League player.

Remarkably, the 24 he scored when coming on all came in different fixtures - which, of course, means he has also scored in more games as a substitute than anyone else. And, as mentioned, a league-high five of those were match-winners.

He scored six times as a substitute in his debut Premier League season, earning West Ham a 3-2 win at Ipswich with his first top-flight goal, and netted for the final time in the competition 17 years later after coming on to rescue Bournemouth a stoppage-time point at Watford.

Simply put, throughout his career, Defoe - also England's highest-scoring substitute with seven goals - was the ruthless finisher a manager wished to see when anxiously glancing at their bench in need of a goal.

Defoe scored a Premier League record 24 goals as a substitute

Arsenal UEFA Women’s Champions League clash against Barcelona has been moved. Here is everything you need to know about why it has been rearranged

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal’s away game against Barcelona has been pushed back by 24 hours, causing outrage amongst fans who had already booked their travel and accommodation.

The Gunners were originally due to face the Spanish giants at Camp Nou on Wednesday, November 11, but the fixture will now take place on Thursday, November 12.

A planned general strike in Spain raised concerns about transport disruption and matchday arrangements, causing the fixture to be rearranged.

Arsenal Women’s Champions League fixture against Barcelona at Camp Nou has been rescheduled following concerns over a planned general strike in Spain over housing, wages and the cost of living.

Barcelona raised concerns over the potential impact of the strike action on hosting the match.

Barcelona initially wanted to bring the fixture forward, but that would have created a scheduling issue for Arsenal ahead of their WSL trip to Liverpool.

The changes have inevitably caused disruption and added cost for travelling fans who had already booked accomodation and travel.

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

Kick-off remains at 6.45pm local time, which is 5.45pm in the UK, with the venue unchanged.

This much-anticipated match is a replay of the 2025 Champions League final, in which the Gunners overcame the odds to beat the European giants in Lisbon.

Barcelona initially sought to bring the fixture forward to Tuesday, November 10, to avoid a clash with the planned strike.

However, that option would have created a scheduling problem for Arsenal, who are due to travel to face Liverpool in the Women's Super League on Sunday November 8.

Moving the Champions League match forward would therefore have left Arsenal with too tight a turnaround between two important fixtures and potentially required further changes to their domestic schedule.

The decision to move the game back by a day avoids that issue while allowing the match to remain at Camp Nou.

Arsenal will face Barcelona on Thursday, November 12, at Camp Nou.

Kick-off is scheduled for 5.45pm UK time (6.45pm local time), with no change to the venue.

#433. Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac: City saga stirs up a world of alternate histories | Max Rushden

Even New Romantics have a view but this long story will not be cut short amid endless hypotheticals and split narratives

It’s Wednesday afternoon (UK time) and I find myself interviewing Tony Hadley on TalkSport about his upcoming big band tour. We play a bit of Spandau Ballet, chat about the classics and his career – hanging out with Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. In as much as you can deduce in a 10-minute chat on Zoom, Tony seems like an absolute gent.

We do always try to bring it back to sport – Tony is an Arsenal fan, there’s a bit of Arteta, Leeds at the weekend. Tony brings up Billy Bremner and suggests that my co-host Charlie Baker and I are too young to remember him playing. We are, and how wonderful to be called young.

Right at the end I go for a slightly cumbersome question/joke about Manchester City. “And I know Manchester City are top of the league, but they’ll probably be bottom of the league by the end of the season?”

Hadley is a pro. Maybe he’s been waiting for this hardball question about the charges. “You just never know what’s going to happen – the world is a crazy place. I’ve got to add to all the big band songs we’re doing … at the end we do a Christmas catalogue which is great fun as well.” What a sidestep.

What am I doing? It’s quarter to midnight in Melbourne, I’m in my shed looking at Tony Hadley on a little box on my laptop asking what he thinks City’s punishment might be. Quick, put a call in to Boy George. What’s Midge Ure saying? Simon Le Bon has things to say, but they are embargoed until Drive Time.

Perhaps this is Enzo Maresca’s best strategy. The City manager’s only way out of answering difficult questions is to organise a 20-date big band tour of the UK so he can do the Hadley pivot and talk about how he really brings the house down with his spectacular Christmas medley.

It would certainly add to the monotony of every Premier League manager giving us their prepared “I’m a football man and all I’m interested in is football – I’ve got enough things to worry about at Coventry/Leeds/Bournemouth, etc.”

But such is the magnitude of the story that even these press conferences are interesting. For the first time since filming players walking off a bus in big headphones became part of the spectacle, I am interested in seeing players walking off a bus in big headphones on Sunday afternoon.

We couldn’t ask for a more perfect place or a perfect time for this game to take place. Liverpool away. The side City have pipped to the title by a point or two three times since the cheating began. I know two of the titles came after the cheating officially finished but don’t think I need to mention that. What if City couldn’t have afforded John Stones (height: 1.88m) and had settled for, say, Victor Lindelöf (1.87m)? How vital was that extra one centimetre of Stones in clearing that ball off the line against Liverpool at the Etihad in January 2019?

The hypotheticals never end. Sliding Doors meets Biff’s Almanac. Nicky Bandini explained on Thursday’s Football Weekly that Serie A has two histories depending on where you stand on Juventus and Calciopoli: “I think that’s the truth that English football isn’t ready for yet. Whatever happens with these decisions, whether they successfully end up appealing things or they don’t, you’re going to have one group of supporters who are absolutely certain they didn’t win these trophies legitimately, and therefore they don’t count, and you’re going to have one group of supporters who don’t care and are going to claim those trophies whether or not they get taken away from them.

“I think that’s the grim future that lies ahead for the Premier League. You’re going to have two alternate histories, the same that happens in Italy, where the number of titles that Juventus has won is constantly repeated differently by different sources because one side or another is not going to accept the judgment even after the final appeals are exhausted.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

I’m minded to side with those who favour stripping City of the titles but not assigning them to anyone else. Not just because it’s fun to see how many people say Asterix. Football just isn’t that simple. If City don’t sign those players, they sign other players. Those other players don’t sign for someone else. Games are different, results are different. Players train in different cities, different managers get hired and fired. People live in different places and move to different countries, meet different people. Different marriages, different children. It’s one thing telling Sergio Agüero that the goal isn’t real, but what about his whole life after 2011? Does he have to redo it all?

And then we get to the reason we fell in love with football: geopolitics. If the sanctions aren’t of the highest severity it’s impossible not to wonder whether anything has happened in the corridors of power, or on one of those benches in Spooks or Slow Horses when two people sit on a bench in Regent’s Park with identical briefcases and walk off in separate directions with the other one. Will the UAE really refuse to scrap investment in a tech hub between Cambridge and Oxford if Manchester City are relegated to League Two? It’s ridiculous that the two are even connected.

And while we all wait for the punishment to drop on a quiet Friday, perhaps during the next international break, City have football matches to play, whether they’ll ultimately mean anything or not. Pundits will say “galvanise” a lot. We will all talk about an “us against the world mentality”.

Who will be the first player to tell Erling Haaland to look forward to Salford away next year? My money would have been on Enzo Fernández until I remembered he’s probably frantically checking whether there’s a relegation release clause in the contract he signed in the summer.

I’d imagine it’ll be hard for Elliot Anderson to spend much time thinking about the possible sanctions while he’s trying to fend off Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz. Regardless of the result on Sunday we’ll draw conclusions about what impact this news has had – and we may be wildly wrong.

I do sympathise with most City fans. Perhaps not the guy on a radio phone-in comparing this rule-breaking to Emmeline Pankhurst’s fight for female suffrage. But that complete loss of objectivity is part of the beauty of football and sport – somewhere we all lose all rational sense.

At my most pious I like to think I’d save my ire for the owners. They’ve dragged the club into this, they should go, but even that is an almighty mess to untangle. At the same time, if I were City, would I really swap the journey they’ve given me and these highs for finishing 12th every season for the past 15 years? Am I better than that? Like all moral dilemmas, it’s easy to have a strong opinion when it doesn’t affect you and you’re in a shed talking to a New Romantic.
