#435. Dundee 2 Rangers 2: Dark Blues dig deep to bring an end to error-strewn Rangers' winning streak

Published: 22:39 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 23:25 BST, 17 October 2026

Asked on Friday if it was imperative that his side applied pressure to their rivals by winning the day before they faced off, Derek McInnes claimed that it was too early to talk about turning up the heat.

With the first lap of the track in the Premiership race still to be completed, the Rangers manager probably had a point.

Nonetheless, this will still feel like an opportunity lost for the Ibrox men as they prepare to pull up a chair and watch Celtic and Hearts go toe-to-toe at Parkhead.

Even after a wretched few days, Martin O’Neill’s side will still walk out on top of the table with scope to increase their lead. Should they do so, Rangers will only have themselves to blame.

For the Ibrox men to stand any chance of knocking their city rivals off their perch come May, they cannot let too many chances like this one slip through their hands.

With no European football to concern them this season, McInnes’ men will be up first in many a weekend card until January at least.

If those opportunities to apply pressure are not taken, it’s extremely hard to see how their challenge stays on course.

Callum Jones slots home past Ivor Pandur to level the scores again at 2-2

This was a jarring night for the Ibrox men. Since that dark evening when they lost on penalties to Jablonec, eight straight wins had been chalked up — seven of them in the Premiership.

They just didn’t do enough to add another victory to the ledger and with it assume top spot in the Premiership overnight.

You had to hand it to Dundee. Steven Pressley could fill a hospital wing with the walking wounded right now. His depleted side did extraordinarily well to dig out victories against Motherwell and Falkirk. This share of the spoils will feel like another huge step in the right direction.

It was a frustrating episode for McInnes. He witnessed two magnificent goals from Badredine Bouanani and Nico Raskin but was left to rue two errors.

The first, an uncharacteristic lapse by Dujon Sterling, allowed Bradley Fink to hand Dundee the lead.

Having done the hard part and got their noses in front, Dan Neil erred horribly on the edge of his own box to allow Callum Jones to square an engrossing encounter.

Neil is consoled by Kim after his error gifted Jones the chance to equalise

Dundee started well. Drey Wright’s smart ball over the top fashioned their first chance. Ash Hay’s touch was heavy and the chance to work Ivor Pandur was lost.

Hay’s ability to link the play was evidenced when he chested the ball into the path of Alan Forrest. Pandur was right behind the winger’s tame strike.

Dundee forced three early corners. Pressley will have been bemused that his side didn’t make more of them. Ryan Astley’s strike, straight at Pandur, was as good as it got.

Rangers were struggling to penetrate. Bouanani did well to dart to the line and drill the ball across goal. Dundee keeper Owen Goodman stretched out a leg and the danger was gone.

With a third of the game gone, the home side looked more threatening. After Astley had forced Pandur to tip his header from distance over, Hay thumped the crossbar with a header from Ethan Hamilton’s corner.

Bouanani threaded a gem of a ball between two Dundee defenders to pick out Sterling. There was nothing wrong with the cutback. There was plenty wrong with Neil’s attempt to convert when the ball fell to him just inside the box. His strike lacked conviction and accuracy.

Pandur’s latest attempt to build from the back by playing a straight ball to Kim Min-su was risky. Hamilton nipped in and fired just wide of the Croatian’s goal.

Coming on 37 minutes, Dundee’s opener was hardly ill-deserved. A long ball found the Rangers defence at sixes and sevens. Hay strived to get it under control. Just when it seemed to be getting away from him, Sterling intervened with a loose touch and inadvertently knocked it into Fink’s path.

The Swiss thought about chipping the keeper, sidestepped him and found the net via the inside of the near post.

Fink rolls the ball into an empty net after rounding Pandur to open the scoring

Rangers were immediately grateful for the pace of Olwethu Makhanya as he lengthened his stride to prevent Joe Bevan making it two.

The visitors then awoke from their slumbers, levelling two minutes from half-time.

Kim’s initial shot was blocked by Owen Bevan. When the ball was recycled to Bouanani on the right, the winger’s first attempt was charged down by Imari Samuels.

Undaunted, the Algerian curled the ball into the top left corner to ensure his side were level at the break. For all it took a slight deflection, it was a brilliant hit. Quite the moment for the winger to claim his first Rangers goal.

Disjointed and careless on the ball for 45 minutes, there was an expectation that Rangers would improve after the break. This was not misplaced.

Kim’s dancing feet opened up the target. His shot was inches wide.

The forward then cushioned the ball into Bouanani’s path with his chest. Goodman did well to tip the shot away for a corner.

Djeidi Gassama was next to work the Dundee keeper with a low shot through a packed penalty box.

When Dundee finally came up for air, Fink met Jones’ free-kick at the back post. He ought to have got more on his header.

Rangers completed the turnaround on the hour mark. It was another peach. Taking the ball from Neil 25 yards out, Raskin must have been the only man in the ground who thought that shooting was his best option. What did the rest of us know?

Lashing the ball in off the underside of the crossbar with very little back-lift, it was a stunning contribution from the Belgian.

Raskin fires home a spectacular effort to put Rangers in front in the second half

McInnes seemingly had the response he wanted. Bouanani forced Goodman into another fine stop.

Dundee needed to produce something special to level. Failing that, an error by a Rangers player would have been just as welcome. Step forward Neil.

Trying to control a routine ball on the edge of his own box, the midfielder completely fluffed his lines, a heavy touch giving Jones the chance to pounce.

Alert to the situation, the midfielder took full advantage. Having taken one touch to put himself in control of the situation, he slotted home beyond the advancing Pandur. Neil could only look to the heavens.

Rangers huffed and puffed thereafter. They could have no complaints as their winning run ended.

#437. The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager

Fabian Hurzeler has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to being one of Europe's most feted young managers

When Brighton lost at home to Crystal Palace in February, Fabian Hurzeler was booed by his own supporters and subjected to chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning".

"There are only two options," said the German after the 1-0 defeat by their fierce rivals left his team floundering 14th in the table with one win in 12 Premier League matches.

"Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."

Eight months on, Brighton are reaping the benefits of keeping faith with the man who became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in June 2024 at the age of 31.

Palace return to Amex Stadium on Sunday (14:00 BST kick-off) to face opponents who are third in the table after statement wins over defending champions Arsenal and Europa League winners Aston Villa.

Hurzeler's stock has rocketed after 11 wins in 18 top-flight games, a run that has propelled the Seagulls back into Europe and left fans - who shouted "you don't know what you're doing" at him just a few months ago - worried that he could be lured away.

Following last Saturday's win at Sunderland, there was chat on the post-match phone-ins that Hurzeler, rewarded with a new long-term contract before the end of last season and given Â£150m to spend on signings in the summer, could be a prime target for a big club looking for a manager.

"You learn more about yourself and the people around you when you are losing games," former Brighton striker Glenn Murray told BBC Sport in reference to last season's poor run.

"Hurzeler has come out the other side and the way he has got this group of players performing is exceptional."

Scott McCarthy, from the We Are Brighton fan site, said Hurzeler appeared to have lost the crowd to such a degree at one stage last season than even a few wins would not be enough to turn it around.

"He looked like a manager who was out of ideas," McCarthy told BBC Sport.

"Leaving the stadium after losing at home to Palace, the only conversation fans were having was: 'he has got to go'.

"It's totally different now. It's worked out phenomenally."

Will Brighton manage to keep hold of Hurzeler, who has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to reported interest, external from Manchester United?

Hurzeler signs to 2029 as Brighton rival elite clubs

Hurzeler's Brighton choice and Barber's favourite moment - fans' forum

Hurzeler (left) has been linked with Manchester United should they decide to replace Michael Carrick (right)

The determination Hurzeler demonstrated in the face of anger from fans following last season's defeat by Palace has been evident throughout his 10-year coaching career.

In 2016, after one injury too many following spells in the reserves at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich, the former midfielder gave up playing professionally to accept a player-manager role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23.

It was the start of a coaching journey that has led to the Premier League.

To make ends meet at village club Pipinsried, which is about 30 miles from Munich, football-obsessed Hurzeler worked for an art dealer selling paintings to wealthy Bavarians.

In an interview with the Guardian, external in 2024, he revealed he was fired from that job because he was spending too much time watching games.

"If you want to sell something to a person, you have to try to convince them by doing something," he said when comparing selling pictures to managing Premier League players.

"And you can't go there and say: 'Look at this picture, it's an amazing picture'. You have to understand the needs and the wishes from the clients.

"That's a little bit similar to being a coach.

"The most important thing is to understand the person behind the player. What are his needs? What are his values? How is he educated? How was his past? Where does he get education?"

Hurzeler's obsession to succeed runs deep.

While managing St Pauli - who he left in 2024 to join Brighton after guiding the Hamburg club back to the Bundesliga following a 13-year absence, external - he was invited to Tottenham's training ground to watch Ange Postecoglou's side train.

Hurzeler - who was born in Houston, Texas, before moving to Germany at the age of two - asked so many questions that Postecoglou had to ask another member of his coaching staff to step in and take over.

Hurzeler is covered in beer by his players after St Pauli's promotion to the Bundesliga in 2024

He also picked up tips from Roberto de Zerbi at Brighton, a few months before replacing him after Kieran McKenna,, external who had been heavily linked with the job, opted to stay at newly promoted Ipswich.

Despite respectable back-to-back eighth-placed finishes, Hurzeler's time at Brighton has not been without its difficult moments.

In addition to fans calling for his dismissal last season, the Seagulls were thrashed 7-0 at Nottingham Forest in his first season in charge, while former Arsenal and England defender Martin Keown labelled Hurzeler "wet behind the ears", external on the BBC's Final Score following Brighton's 4-2 defeat at Chelsea in September 2024.

So what is the reason for the shift in fortunes since his own fans called for his dismissal?

"It's partly because Hurzeler went back to basics," adds McCarthy.

"He relied on an experienced core in the side to get out of the hole, which is testament to him because it shows his pragmatic side. You get managers who are wedded to their philosophy and won't change.

"Hurzeler realised what he was doing was not working and that it could cost him his job, so tried something else. You can now see this is a team more in his image, because they press insanely."

Will Hurzeler leave Brighton if another club comes for him, or stay and attempt to write his name in club folklore by qualifying for the Champions League?

"I personally don't think he will go," says McCarthy.

"The money would obviously be tempting but he is a very intelligent guy. He didn't become a Premier League manager at the age of 31 without having his head screwed on.

"Does he want to go to another club where he isn't going to get time? What has happened at Brighton has shown he needs two-and-a-half-years to build a squad."

Back in Pipinsried, Hurzeler's name is still revered - and he has not forgotten where his coaching journey began.

"Yes, he does enjoy coming back every now and then - to see if everything's in order," Sepp Ankner, their chief finance officer, told The Athletic, external in 2024.

"When he does, he talks to everybody. He's really retained that connection with Pipinsried."

But his rapid ascent means gilded surroundings might not be far away for Europe's hottest managerial property.

#440. Bayern Munich unveil stunning 2025 Oktoberfest kit

Bayern Munich and adidas have unveiled the clubâs annual Oktoberfest kit â and this yearâs edition might be the most authentic nod to Bavarian tradition yet.

The release celebrates the 190th edition of the modern Oktoberfest beer festival, which began in 1810 with the royal wedding of Bavariaâs Crown Prince Ludwig (later King Ludwig I) and Princess Therese von Sachsen-Hildburghausen.

Fittingly, the 2025 kit blends football heritage with Alpine craftsmanship.

Built on a light beige base, the shirt draws inspiration from traditional Tracht garments worn during the festival, accented with deep green tones that echo the colours of Bavarian attire. Embossed Lederhosen-inspired textures and jacquard detailing elevate the design, pushing the Oktoberfest aesthetic to its fullest expression.

Finishing touches include a reimagined club crest in Bavarian-style lettering and the return of the adidas Trefoil logo, reinforcing the retro-meets-traditional feel.

The kit is completed with black shorts and socks featuring green trims, while a wider collection adds a cap, training top, button-down tracksuit jacket, and matching pants, all styled in grey with subtle green accents.

Bayern will debut the kit in their home clash against Werder Bremen on September 26.

As always, the Oktoberfest drop comes in limited supply, but this yearâs highlight is a special collectorâs edition box containing the full kit (jersey, shorts, socks). Fittingly, only 1,900 boxes are available worldwide.

#443. Football Daily | Watford, a ‘fake news’ sacking and an apology to Elton John

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

There are only two things certain in life – death and taxes Reece James knack and Watford managerial news – and Football Daily’s bingo card lit up with both on Friday. But while Chelsea’s statement on their crocked right-back having successful knee surgery was a cut-and-paste job from the last time James was injured, the quotes by Watford manager Alessio Dionisi were much more exciting, mainly because it contained an actual apology to Elton John and the remarkable news that the club’s trigger-happy owners have not already sent the Italian the same way as an apple in Michael Owen’s house.

Having already made four managerial appointments in 2026 and 28 since the Pozzo family purchased the club in the summer of 2012, the owners have shown uncharacteristic restraint despite Watford winning just three of the last 21 Championship games (even Oxford United have more victories in the division during that time despite being relegated to League One in April). Pressure on Dionisi has now increased after John – which feels like an inappropriately underwhelming way to refer to one of the most talented and flamboyant pop singers of all time – admitted he was “upset” at the club’s form in a now-deleted post on a Social Media Disgrace on Sunday.

“As a lifetime supporter of Watford FC, I am very upset and disappointed at the decline over the past few weeks – I really feel for the supporters who have to watch this,” Elton crooned after the 4-0 home defeat to Burnley. “I’ve called the chauffeur, you little chancer”, he didn’t add. Things worsened for Dionisi on Tuesday with struggling Cardiff romping to a 5-1 win to leave the Hornets in the Championship relegation zone, with some reporting – incorrectly, as it turned out – the Italian had been sacked during the game. But despite the unconfirmed reports of his demise, Dionisi remains very much in post.

“There is good news, bad news or fake news probably. In this case for the moment, it is fake news [that I have been sacked] but I don’t decide,” he told the BBC on Friday, not wholly convincingly. “For Elton John, I am sorry because I don’t know him. But football is wonderful because everyone speaks [their mind]. I have been a coach for 14 years, and it is normal. In my past there was negative and there was positive moments. At the moment it is a negative moment. Inside the training ground there is only one mentality, only one street for everyone.” Absolute goosebumps, Alessio. Cheers for that. We know not of the cryptic road you speak – Vicarage? Yellow Brick? The road to nowhere? – but we’ll have to see if Dionisi becomes the latest Watford manager to find himself out on the street, kicked to the curb through a front door marked ‘Do One’, following Saturday’s visit of Charlton Athletic.

“I think I have an angel on my shoulder. I’m actually fortunate to be alive at all. I was 20 and playing for Dortmund when three pipe bombs went off right next to our bus on the way to a Champions League match. A lot of young people probably would not even believe that it happened, or how bad it was, but it marked us all. There was a deafening noise, and then I remember the bus nearly tipping over. I looked behind me and saw blood on the floor. Smoke, screams. I remember being at the hospital later that night, waiting for Marc Bartra, who had his wrist badly cut up. The next day, someone told me that a huge piece of shrapnel was lodged in the headrest of the seat next to Marc. My usual seat. That day, the seat was empty. My legs were feeling a bit tight, and the seats in the front reclined. So I sat up there instead, and it may have saved my life” – Mikel Merino recalls how a last-minute change of seats on the Borussia Dortmund coach that was hit by explosives on its way to the home leg of their Champions League semi-final against Monaco in 2017 may have saved his life in a wider interview with the Player Tribune.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United legend has delivered both barrels to Bruno Fernandes – again – in the wake of another Red Devils defeat.

After defeat in the Champions League this week, Manchester United have won just two of their nine games since Michael Carrick was appointed as permanent manager over the summer.

With the club in crisis once more, Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy in an explosive post-match interview – and Keane has had his say on the state of the mentality at Old Trafford.

When asked about the leaders at Carrick's disposal, The Overlap regular Keane took a pop at club captain Bruno Fernandes and his predecessor, Harry Maguire, suggesting that the former isn't “a happy lad” at the club and that he struggles with criticism himself.

“Bruno, Maguire... They're probably busy doing podcasts, I can't imagine them pulling him [Martinez],” Keane began. “Bruno's body language, he doesn't seem a happy lad at the moment.

“They're pulling nobody. This reflects where Manchester United are and where this dressing room is. Maguire gets left out of the England squad: he's all upset with that. Instead of rolling his sleeves up during the summer, ‘I'm going to go to New York and do a podcast for a few weeks.’

“That's his mindset. I made a mistake with Bruno on this programme [criticising the Portuguese in a previous podcast]. Bruno goes on a podcast with [Steven Bartlett] this is the Man United captain, he goes on there, has a little dig at me, no problem, he's entitled to respond.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“"That's the mindset of a Man United player, I'm going to start doing these little gigs instead of getting Man United competing at the very top. So this idea, when I see a player have a little b**** the last few days, I'd be more annoyed at Maguire and Bruno for getting things off their chests on podcasts. You get your priorities in place as a footballer.”

Keane went on to compare the difference between the modern-day and his own playing career, noting that he was more likely to feature on a magazine cover instead – as he does on the current issue of FourFourTwo – but said that United currently lack players to hold each other to account.

“Back in our day it was more magazines than podcasts, but if a player went off and said something, even silly, he'd come in the dressing room, and lads would say: 'What are you talking about?'

“You'd put him in his place in that sense, not a big bust-up. Man United is a circus. If you can, try and do your talking on the pitch. If you have to let off a bit of steam, ok, but try and do it on the back of some victories, or when you've won a league title or something like that.

“These players have done nothing for the last few years at Man United. Two years ago we were finishing [15th] or whatever, getting knocked out by Grimsby, and they're coming up with all these comments.”

United travel to in-form Leeds United this weekend, as Premier League action returns.

#446. Getting to know Man Utd boss Olid

Olid, who managed Hearts from 2021-2026, began coaching at the age of 26 and favours a possession-based style with an emphasis on building from the goalkeeper

It's been a whirlwind 10 weeks for Eva Olid since she became manager of Manchester United.

Her surprise appointment at the start of August after Marc Skinner's departure meant she joined one of the biggest clubs in England just a month before the Women's Super League season started.

When we meet in a Manchester coffee shop - an unlikely setting for someone who doesn't drink coffee - it is her first real pause in a schedule that has left her with little chance to discover the city she now calls home.

"It's been good but really busy," Olid tells BBC Sport. "It's just been work, home, work, home."

Olid, 41, enjoyed exceptional success in her previous role at Hearts - taking them from bottom of the table to Scottish Premier League champions within five years.

Despite that, she was relatively unheard of south of the border, so top of her to-do list when she arrived at the team's training base at Carrington was to explain to her players what she was all about.

"My first day I showed them what I did in the past and who I was," she says. "I tried to be myself from second one. I showed that I'm a person before a coach.

"I didn't have time to be aware of where I was. I just went there, be myself trying to transmit to the players how I see football, to work hard, that I'm going to be there for them, that I want to make them better players. Trying to transmit the key messages that I wanted the players to take from the first moment."

Olid's introduction to life at United was far from straightforward.

She inherited a thin squad and new policy of prioritising developing academy players over making signings, while also wanting to implement a new attacking style of football.

It was a big ask. Perhaps too big. In her opening two games, United lost 2-1 at London City Lionesses before a galling 5-0 home defeat by Chelsea.

Olid believes that humbling loss to a title rival - in front of United's own fans - proved to be a turning point in her relationship with the team.

"It was a difficult week," she says. "There were honest conversations. I took responsibility for a lot of things. I think that was a good starting point for the players.

"I was confident. It's crazy to say, I was confident because I knew what the problem was. And when you know the problem, you can change that."

Olid - a defensive midfielder during her playing career, who took pride in doing the simple things well - decided to strip things back.

"I spoke, they spoke, and we knew what we had to do," she says. "That week was difficult - a lot of emotions - but going to Arsenal, we fought for each other, there was hard work. I think it was the perfect starting point for a good moment."

A 1-1 draw at the Emirates was the start of a five-game unbeaten run during which they have climbed from the bottom of the WSL to seventh.

"When you are in Manchester United, you need to find a way to win," she says. "It's a challenge - how you can win and at the same time develop players and at the same time implement a new style of play.

"You need to find the balance of all that together. And I think these last weeks, we got to that point."

Now Olid has settled into her role, she is keen to explore what Manchester has to offer, starting with finding some decent Spanish food.

"I have to say that the tapas... sorry, but some of the tapas bars are not 100% authentic," she says.

"I had this experience in Scotland and I needed time to find a good tapas bar. Because you want it to feel like home. A little taste of home."

Olid admits she has yet to embrace driving on British roads but has become a fan of public transport.

"I was not brave [enough] to drive here," she says. "In Scotland I was moving a lot by bus and here I need to find the ways to move by tram."

And there is one Manchester landmark Olid has already visited: Old Trafford.

"I came 13 years ago to a game - as a fan of football, and what I remember was amazing," she says.

"On Saturday I went for second time and they showed me the changing rooms. The day that we play there this season, I will feel the happiest person in the world, like really like a dream."

#447. Hogh hasn't scored a goal in two months ... are Celtic running out of patience with their £11m striker?

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 22:30 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 23:20 BST, 17 October 2026

There was a line from Martin O’Neill’s media conference in Lisbon the other night which hinted at a growing frustration with Kasper Hogh.

Hogh, who had missed a sitter at the back post from only two yards out, was subbed off at half-time after a woeful first half which saw Celtic go 3-0 down against Benfica.

Now on a goal drought which stretches over two months, it was another night where Hogh, a club-record signing at £11million, didn’t cut the mustard.

O’Neill was asked afterwards whether there might have been any temptation to keep the Danish striker on the pitch just purely to try and get him a goal. A scuff, a deflection, one off his backside – any goal at all.

‘No, I think you have to earn the right to be on the pitch,’ came the response from O’Neill. Ouch. It hardly required the detective skills of Poirot to understand what O’Neill was getting at.

In fairness, he qualified it slightly by insisting that he has no long-term concerns over Hogh. In the fullness of time, there is a confidence that he will come good and score goals for Celtic.

Kasper Hogh is struggling for form in a Celtic jersey following his £11m move from Bodo/Glimt

Hogh spurned a good scoring chance in Celtic's 4-1 loss to Benfica

But how long do they give it? Having spent top dollar to sign Hogh from Bodo/Glimt, how long can Celtic afford to wait on him to get his act together?

That’s one of the burning questions facing O’Neill as he prepares to lead his team into battle with Hearts once again at Parkhead this afternoon.

It was notable on Thursday night that Celtic were much-improved in Lisbon once Hogh had gone off the pitch.

O’Neill moved Camilo Duran to play through the middle as a striker, with Callum Osmand and Haissem Hassan playing on the wings.

Celtic looked far more of a threat, much more direct and quicker at the top end of the pitch. They created quite a few good chances beyond the one which Duran converted with a header.

None of this reflects overly well on Hogh, of course. He arrived with a big pricetag and big reputation, a striker who could score goals in the Champions League.

But his Celtic career has largely been a non-event so far. His only goals came in a bundle back at the start of the season in August courtesy of a first-half hat-trick against Kilmarnock at Rugby Park.

Celtic fans thought they had signed a worldie. But that game must be qualified in the sense that, at that point, Kilmarnock were all over the shop and conceding four and five every week.

That first-half display was potentially the worst 45 minutes of football any team will produce in the Premiership this season, particularly in defence. Hogh scored a series of tap-ins.

But the way he has consistently failed to deliver in big matches over these past couple of months now has to be a serious concern for Celtic.

The numbers are unforgiving. All in all, it’s three goals in 807 minutes of football. And none at all in over two months.

A big-money striker signed to score goals who is not scoring goals and not playing well. At Celtic, that is a problem that quickly grows teeth.

Unsurprisingly, those close to Hogh are quick to defend him. His team-mates still speak of a player with a big character and bucketloads of ability.

Martin O'Neill may decide to bench Hogh for Sunday's Premiership match with Hearts

‘Kasper’s a great guy,’ said Callum Osmand, who was impressive when he came off the bench against Benfica on Thursday night.

‘He knows how to act and how to hold himself and he’s a top professional. I don’t think I’ve ever seen him put a bad thing in his body, but, yeah, he knows what he’s doing.

‘Obviously his goals speak for themselves at Bodo and I’m sure it will come. He’s a top player. I see him every day in training and, yeah, he’s a really, really great guy, top player.

‘So, yeah, I’m sure it will come. He’s a really, really top player. I think he maybe just needs one to go in.

‘I think it is a lot about confidence, the attacking positions, and when your confidence is high, you play better and sometimes it’s about getting that goal, but he’s obviously a top professional.

‘He knows what he’s doing and I’m sure it will come. He’s been in the game for a long time and he’ll know better than me.’

For those who watched Hogh in the Champions League over the past couple of seasons, there is no question that he is a player of good pedigree and ability.

But the basic reality is that he is not showing it for Celtic. Patience, for all his ability and his pricetag, is not infinite.

Celtic need him to step up and start delivering in big matches, something which he has fundamentally failed to do so far.

There is a very good case to be made for O’Neill benching Hogh for Sunday afternoon’s clash with Hearts at Parkhead.

If that were to happen, it would be the clearest signal yet that patience is starting to wear thin with the Danish striker.

Would it be a shock if O’Neill started Duran through the middle and told Hogh to wait his turn on the bench?

Not really. The half-time substitution in Portugal already felt like a statement.

Hogh is 25 years old. He is not a young kid. And nor is he a project player. He was signed for the here and now.

He has the physical tools and the pedigree. But Celtic do not buy record signings to show glimpses and then go quiet.

They buy them to lead the line and put the ball in the net with the regularity that wins titles and keeps European campaigns alive. The clock is ticking louder than ever.

Another barren afternoon against Hearts and the conversation will shift again. It won’t be long until Hogh’s name has the word dud attached to it.

#453. Football Daily | Guardiola returns to Manchester as City spin into dizzy mess against PSG

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

It is quite funny that PSG felt like the good guys at the Etihad Stadium but if we briefly detach ourselves from the notion that the European champions’ own sportswashing and cashsplashing has also done immeasurable damage to the beautiful game, then their 4-2 Bigger Cup shellacking of Manchester City was pure cinema, baby!

Not just because Désiré Doué was unplayable or that Vitinha put on an absolute clinic or that Luis Enrique was more forward-thinking than Magnus Carlsen reading a horoscope in playing his right-back as a striker, but also because the camera kept cutting – deliciously – to the faces of glum City fans as they watched their expensively assembled squad spin into such a dizzy mess that £125m Enzo Fernández and £116m Elliott Anderson appeared in Manchester to be auditioning as a double act for next year’s Strictly.

Although PSG eased off in the second half as City rallied to a brave 4-2 home defeat, it was a miserable outing for all of those dressed in sky blue or trendy flatcaps sitting in the stands. Pep Guardiola was – we think – not one of the City fans that had spent the weekend chanting “we’re Man City, we’ll cheat when we want” at Anfield – but the former manager returned to Manchester for a well-timed visit on Wednesday to support City’s beleaguered owners, backing up last month’s statement that he remains “behind my club”.

While we did not hear from Pep on the night as he sloped off from his heated seat back to his sabbatical – with British TV viewers instead treated to the valuable and impartial TNT Sports pundit and literal on-the-payroll City ambassador Joleon Lescott, who “broke his silence on the guilty verdicts” in predictable fashion – we did also enjoy some relatively stain-free football on Wednesday. Aston Villa romped to a 6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce, Bradley Barcola notched his first Liverpool goals (a hatty) in the 6-3 win at Lask and Real Madrid secured a last-gasp 4-3 win at Roma. In a fast-changing world, it was heartening to feel the warm embrace of familiarity with Madrid manager José Mourinho using his post-match press conference to speak, not of his side’s remarkable comeback (three corners in the final 10 minutes, naturally) or even of his emotional return to the Italian capital after his Tin Pot triumph with Roma in 2022, but as an opportunity to deliver a monologue against Spain’s football authorities. Football is healing.

Join Michael Butler from 5.45pm for red-hot Bigger Vase updates from the early kick-offs, including Torreense 1-3 Sunderland and Lyon 2-1 Crystal Palace before Simon Burnton takes you through the 8pm starts, including Benfica 2-1 Celtic and Bournemouth 4-1 Sturm Graz.

“Couldn’t they do it tomorrow morning? Do we have to come by bus and almost arrive at the stadium when we find out Vinícius has a four-match suspension? They do things shamelessly now. The cat is out of the bag. A Spanish team that has earned three points for Spanish football, for the rankings, for the prestige of Spanish football. You want to kill a player two hours before the match? It doesn’t seem normal to me.” – José Mourinho laments the timing of the Spanish Football Federation’s announcement that Vinícius Júnior will receive a four-match ban, including ​El ​Clásico, after ​being sent off for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair against Villarreal last Saturday. The announcement came hours before ​Mourinho​’s R​eal Madrid side – featuring Vinícius – faced Roma in the ​B​ig Cup​ last night, coming from behind to earn a 4-3 win.

double quotation markI was stunned at reading the comments in support of Manchester City keeping their trophies, coming out of the mouth of their Bigger Cup rivals at PSG (yesterday’s Quote of the Day). Given the example of the organisers of the Tour de Lance … sorry, the Tour de France, this kind of ‘keep the awards you won’ stuff might get him sent to the Bastille. Or consider Formula One. They’ve got all kinds of rules about driver behaviour on the racetrack, and additional rules about what the crew can and cannot do to your car. Cars get inspected before each race, and there are also mandatory post-race inspections for every car. You might drive your car first across the line to the cheers of the crowd, but if the post-race inspection discovered that you cheated in how your team designed your vehicle, your memory of crossing the line is all you get to keep. Think about that for a minute. If the Premier League and Fifa cannot clear the bar for morals in sport set by the UCI and FIA, that says a lot. And none of it good” – Peter Rehwaldt.

double quotation markMy friend Bernard grew up in Coventry. And as a boy he thought the team was called ‘Coventry City Nil’. I would get out more, but I’m a Manchester United fan” – Brendan Hughes.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Peter Rehwaldt. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

#456. Sutton's predictions v boxer & Ipswich fan Fabio Wardley

The pressure is mounting on Manchester United boss Michael Carrick after his side's poor start, but will things improve when they face rivals Leeds on Saturday?

"I cannot remember the last time Leeds were seen as favourites going into this fixture but I don't fancy Manchester United's chances at all," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Leeds are just a much more rounded team. Their fans must be relishing this game."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week seven, he takes on former heavyweight boxing world champion Fabio Wardley, who supports Ipswich Town.

Wardley can reclaim his WBO title when he meets Daniel Dubois at London's O2 Arena on Saturday.

The fight, a rematch of their thrilling battle in May, when Dubois stopped Wardley in the 11th round to take his crown, will be shown live on DAZN and you can listen to live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live as well as following a live watchalong on BBC iPlayer.

Wardley took Sutton on at predictions before that first fight too - so will either outcome be different this time?

"I beat Fabio last time - he's from Ipswich so he doesn't stand a chance of beating me," Sutton said.

"But good luck to him on Saturday night and I hope he wins his rematch - he's got a better chance against Dubois than he has against me."

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

'Life on the line' for Dubois & Wardley in re-match

It took Ipswich 19 matches and until 30 December to rack up three wins the last time they were promoted to the Premier League, in 2024-25, but their new-look side have already matched that total in their first six games.

"Whenever you get promoted there is going to be a large amount of player turnover because, if you want to stay up, then you need to bring some players in who are going to be game-changers, and are going to offer you the different perspectives or different outlets you will need at this level," Wardley told BBC Sport.

"With a bunch of new players and a new manager in Gary O'Neil too, there was always going to be a question mark as to how well they would gel, or even how quickly, but the team are looking great.

"You only have to look at the start we've made to the season to answer the question of whether we look like we belong in the Premier League.

"Three wins from six games is a great start for any team coming up from the Championship and the boys are doing really well right now."

Wardley has seen two of those wins for himself, with both of them coming thanks to last-gasp goals.

"My training camp has been very strict and very stringent so I've been very busy with a lot of what I've got going on, but of course I've tried to make it to Portman Road as much as possible," he added.

"I went to the first game of the season against Sunderland, which ended with a nice little last-minute winner for us, with Jack Clarke sticking that one in.

"And just before I came away for the build-up to my fight, I was at Saturday's game against Fulham, which ended in a similar fashion really.

"We went 1-0 down early on but clawed it back and then scored two goals in three minutes, with the winner coming in added time.

"Winning like that proves the team have got character. The boys are showing a lot of resilience and we are going to need it this season."

Chris Sutton and Fabio Wardley were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Tractor Boy first, Heavyweight boxer second!

Everton are still unbeaten and, as well as their results, they have really impressed me with the way they have played so far.

Bournemouth had a better xG than Chelsea last weekend, but lost 5-1. That game showed again how Xabi Alonso's side are going to be enjoyable to watch this season but very difficult to predict.

You just don't know what you are going to get with Chelsea at the moment but at least you know what to expect from Everton.

They are always so well organised and should probably have beaten Hull last time out, with the number of good chances Thierno Barry had.

I can see them making things awkward for Chelsea and maintaining that unbeaten start.

Brentford are another team to have made an unbeaten start, and while I thought they were a bit lucky to get a draw at Aston Villa last week, they have plenty of momentum.

Liverpool got a big win on their travels in the Champions League against LASK on Wednesday but there are two ways to look at that result.

On one hand, they looked good going forward and it was great for Bradley Barcola to open his account with a hat-trick.

But, at the same time, they conceded three goals and they still have that vulnerability about them at the back.

If the Reds empty the midfield again in this game then they are going to be in trouble, because Brentford are quite direct and will keep looking to run in behind the Liverpool defence.

The sceptics will say Barcola needs to start delivering in the Premier League too, and Florian Wirtz has been taking a bit of a battering for his performances.

The question I asked on the Monday Night Club was 'what kind of player actually is he?'

They have paid so much money for him but is he a dribbler? No. He's not the kind of player to shoot and score from the edge of the box either.

He's got an intelligent football brain but Liverpool wanted more than that. When you spend so much on a player, you want some numbers from him.

This is a tricky game for Liverpool, and I don't think they will win it. They definitely won't keep a clean sheet, either.

This feels like a massive game for Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa, who is still waiting for his first league win.

They had it in the bag against Ipswich last week so losing that game so late on was just desperate for them.

I've watched Fulham a couple of times this season, against Liverpool and Manchester United, and they played well both times without getting over the line.

After this game, they go to Coventry next. I know the Cottagers are not a club known for going through managers but if they lose this then the pressure will really be on Arbeloa.

Hull, in contrast, will be relishing this after the start they have made.

Their identity is as a team who will have a real go at you and their approach is a bit like a bull in a china shop.

It has been working pretty well so far and I think they will fancy their chances against a Fulham side who might be lacking a bit of belief.

Despite that, I am going to go with Fulham here. I don't think their results have really reflected their performances so far, but that might change on Saturday.

Manchester City will have learned a lot from their defeat by Paris St-Germain.

I was there for Radio 5 Live and I thought City's second-half display was a magnificent response.

For those teams to meet at this early stage of the Champions League it was always going to be a good game, but it was never going to be tense because neither side were going to be knocked out.

PSG showed how good they are in the first half hour, but City will have gained a lot of confidence from their response. If they end up playing PSG again later in the competition, that second half will have done them the world of good psychologically.

There is obviously a lot of noise around City at the moment but in that game and against Liverpool last week, you could see the unity in their team.

They played with such intensity in the second half against PSG that I wonder how much that has taken out of them, but they will want to keep their foot on the throttle.

Fair play to Ipswich, for coming back to beat Fulham the way they did, but I don't see them getting anything here.

We know Gary O'Neil's side will have a go and I really like their approach this season, but City will have too much quality for them.

Fabio on the Ipswich players who have impressed him this season: A few do stand out. Julio Enciso is doing a lot in the middle of the park and then there is Leif Davis, who has been there for a long time and is part of the core of the team. Another one who doesn't always get much of a mention is our goalkeeper Christian Walton. He had to battle for his place and has been in and out of the side but he always seems to claw his way back in and he has proved why he is the main man between the sticks.

Fabio's prediction: The boys have got a tall order on Saturday. Look, playing City is no joke for anyone in the Premier League, especially a team that has just come up, but as I've been saying this week about my own situation in my fight, having an underdog mentality can be a good thing - it does free you up and kind of take the weight off your shoulders, and it allows the boys to play and just do their thing.

It's a big ask to go away to City and get a result but hopefully they can pull something off and come away with at least a point. 1-1

Newcastle's defeat at Coventry on Monday was such a wild game. The way the Magpies play, they just go for it, and load players into the front line.

They lost 4-1 in the end but the scoreline could have been anything with the number of chances Newcastle had.

Aston Villa have made a slow start to the Premier League season results-wise but I think they done all right, bearing in mind what their manager Unai Emery has had to deal with in terms of the players they lost.

Johan Manzambi is getting fitter every game and Nicolas Jackson has found some great form.

It takes time for a team to come together but I thought they were really good against Brentford last weekend, but just weren't ruthless enough. That wasn't a problem against Fenerbahce on Wednesday, though.

This is a really hard one to call and the only thing I know for certain is that there will be a few goals.

Both these teams play in Europe on Thursday but neither of them are in great form. Sunderland have lost three in a row, while Bournemouth have not won in the league so far this season.

The Cherries have been a team who have got in front but let things slip a few times this season but, against Chelsea, they went 2-0 down right from kick-off, then did it again with their third goal inside the first few seconds of the second half.

Bournemouth boss Marco Rose had probably told his players "don't do anything stupid" at the break, so he must have been absolutely livid at that.

They really need a positive result here but so do Sunderland. It's going to be close, and I can't pick a winner.

I am not quite sure how Crystal Palace beat Nottingham Forest last week, because Forest had some incredible chances.

I don't see the Eagles getting anything here, though, because Brighton are absolutely flying at the moment.

The Seagulls showed great resilience to hold on at 1-0 with 10 men in their win against Sunderland last week and ended up scoring a second goal right at the end too.

Again, both teams play in Europe on Thursday so they will have to find the right balance with their team selections - but I don't see it affecting Brighton any more than it will Palace.

I found Lisandro Martinez's outburst about Manchester United's recruitment very strange, especially after his mistake that cost his side victory over Tottenham.

You'd think Martinez would keep his head down after making a mess of the cross that let Dominic Solanke equalise - If I am United's director of football Jason Wilcox then, in January, I am buying a big left-sided centre-half who can deal with crosses to take his place.

While some Manchester United fans might agree with what Martinez said, there is a time and a place to do it and it felt like a really poor error of judgement.

It just shows what kind of state Manchester United are in at the moment, though. Don't forget that Spurs played them off the park early on in that game.

Maybe they will up their game and find a way to win this time because they are getting desperate - but I don't see it.

I think Leeds will beat them, and beat them convincingly.

So far this season I have backed Manchester United most weeks but I have had enough of that. I must have lost my head to stick with them so long - not any more.

Nottingham Forest held Arsenal 0-0 here last season but I don't think they have got a clean sheet in them this time.

Forest were actually pretty good in their defeat against Crystal Palace, but just didn't take their chances.

I can't see them causing Arsenal too many problems, however. The Gunners had a good win over Lille in the Champions League on Tuesday and this should be just as comfortable for them.

Tottenham will be fresh from their training camp in Marbella and we are about to find out if it worked.

If they don't beat Coventry and get their first win of the season, then they will probably have to go back out there next week as well.

Being serious, they do look like they are improving already and they played well against Manchester United last week.

Coventry are a dangerous counter-attacking team, and their pace in forward areas will cause problems, but this is going to be Tottenham's night.

Chris was the only predictor who saw Manchester City's win at Liverpool coming.

Including City's 3-0 victory at Anfield, he got four correct results with no exact scores from the 10 games in week six, giving him 40 points.

His guest, Starsailor frontman James Walsh, managed two correct results with no exact scores, leaving him on 20 points.

The collective efforts of the BBC readers saw them get five correct results with no exact scores, to end up on 50 points.

But it was AI who took the weekly win with a total of 80 points, thanks to four correct results plus an exact score in Aston Villa's 2-2 draw with Brentford.

There was only one game where everyone picked the right outcome, Chelsea's 5-1 victory over Bournemouth, although hardly anyone got the correct score.

From more than 35,000 predictions, the most popular scoreline was a 2-1 Blues win. Almost 9,000 of you went for that, while only four of you got it spot on.

#461. Osmand braced for bad blood when Hearts visit Celtic for first time since title denouement

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 22:30 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 23:19 BST, 17 October 2026

Celtic striker Callum Osmand is braced for a hostile affair when title rivals Hearts visit Parkhead on Sunday afternoon.

The teams will clash for the first time since Celtic’s dramatic – and highly controversial – last-gasp win on the final day of last season to clinch the title.

It was Osmand who scored the third and final goal deep into stoppage-time which then sparked a mass pitch invasion as Celtic snatched it at the death.

There have since been major recriminations and criminal prosecutions on the back of Celtic fans entering the pitch and accosting Hearts players.

There is still a lot of bad blood on the Hearts side in terms of how things played out in arguably the most dramatic final day in the history of Scottish football.

Osmand expects Hearts to be title challengers once again – and fully expects another lively clash on Sunday afternoon.

Callum Osmand celebrates after clinching the title for Celtic back in May

Osmand races towards an empty net to clinch the title for Celtic against Hearts

Osmand returned to action in Celtic's 4-1 loss to Benfica on Thursday night

‘It could be a hostile one,’ said the 20-year-old striker. ‘But, no, our fans, I think we saw that one’s already sold out, so it could be a really good game.

‘I don’t know if it gets better than that in terms of what happened last season, but it’ll be good to play against them again.

‘Yeah, I think you always have to (feel like Hearts are contenders). Obviously what they’ve done last season was amazing.

‘They lost a few key players, but they brought in some good players and they’re a really top side, so we can’t underestimate them.

‘We’re just going to need to keep ticking away and hopefully we get a good result. I think it could be a different type of challenge against them compared to last season. It will be tough.

‘We should be working hard and hopefully we come away with a good result. We’ll have to pick ourselves up from Benfica and hopefully we get three points against them.’

Osmand had been out of action for almost two months before coming off the bench to make his comeback in the second half of Thursday night’s Europa League defeat to Benfica in Lisbon.

Celtic looked much more dangerous as an attacking force with Osmand and Haissem Hassan on the wings and Camilo Duran playing through the middle as the striker.

Osmand is determined to try and knuckle down and get a run of games under his belt to prove his worth to Martin O’Neill’s side.

There is a chance that O’Neill may look to freshen up the forward line this afternoon, particularly given the misfiring Kasper Hogh continues to struggle for form.

‘It was a really good feeling to be back on the pitch,’ said Osmand. ‘It’s obviously a tough one to come into. Benfica were a really, really good side.

‘But, yeah, it felt good. When you’re out there, you don’t really think about anything but playing. But, yeah, I’m so glad to be back on the pitch and hopefully I can stay on it this time.

‘I’m comfortable playing anywhere across the front line because I’m on the pitch, to be honest. But, yeah, not that I’ve never played there, I’ve rarely played left wing before.

‘It’s something that I still need to learn the ins and outs of. But I thought I’d done alright when I came on.

‘I was just trying to be as confident as possible and just trying to forget about everything around me and just go and try and make something happen.

‘But, yeah, it was a really tough game to come into. Wherever I’m needed, I feel like I’ll just give my all to play there.

‘It’s been tough for me. It’s a frustrating one. The hamstring one was a freak one and then the ankle was a tiny little one that’s like just an annoying one.

‘No one is more frustrated than me and I just want to be on the pitch and I can understand the frustrations with everyone.

‘Like I say, I’m the one that will be the most frustrated out of everyone. But it is hopefully, fingers crossed, I just stay on the pitch now.

‘I’m going to make sure I do everything I can to stay fit and, hopefully, touch wood, nothing happens.’

#463. Winning is not enough for Manchester City to move on from this crisis | Jonathan Wilson

It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too

The language of football is a fine and highly nuanced dialect. The majority of people involved in the game speak it with a high degree of sophistication. Minor deviations from the familiar, almost imperceptible to outsiders, can set off alarm bells: what’s really going on there? Why isn’t he happy? What’s she hinting at? But it’s an argot developed to talk about football, and when applied to other subjects, it can sound extremely jarring.

Erling Haaland is one of the brighter, more engaging players. There’s an appealing quirkiness to him that suggests he has a higher-than-usual level of self-awareness. He doesn’t mind stepping outside the norms, being a bit different. But consider his assessment of Manchester City’s 3-0 win at Liverpool on Sunday.

“It was tough,” he said. “It was hard but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone. [It’s] important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about, and the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That’s the only thing we can do.”

Strip away the context and he could be talking about an injury crisis, or perhaps the resignation of a manager or a suspension to a key player. The tropes are familiar: it was hard but we stuck together and so we prevailed. “You want to win games, it’s as simple as that,” he went on. “Perform well, play good football and win games. This was a mental battle, [it’s] never easy coming back from internationals.”

But of course this wasn’t really about coming back from internationals; that’s not what made this difficult for City. This was about the verdict of the independent panel looking into the charges brought against City, the fact that the club have been found guilty of the greatest act of sustained cheating in the history of English football. Nobody knows what’s coming next.

The gravity of the situation still seems to have not dawned on many in football. City, as is their right, continue to maintain their innocence and have appealed. The propaganda battle goes on. But this is no longer about whether the financial regulations were fair. Although City voted against FFP regulations when they were first passed in 2013, their membership of the Premier League obliges them to comply. They raised no serious objections and made no concerted attempt to amend them in the years that followed.

The excuse that they only spent what others did but that they operated under stricter controls because of a lack of historic success is not merely irrelevant but entirely bogus: in the nine years under investigation, City’s net spending on transfers, before taking into account wages, was over £1.2bn ($1.6bn), around 50% more than any other Premier League side. And for all their talk of being proud disruptors, of rebels taking on the “red cartel”, that spending transformed City into the most dominant side English football has ever known, with six league titles in seven years. They are, precisely, an argument for why spending controls are necessary.

None of that, of course, is Haaland’s fault. He is a footballer offered a very competitive salary to play alongside very good players for a very good manager for a club for which his father played. This is another of football’s absurdities: it’s always the manager and players who end up becoming the faces of the institution, being quizzed about things that have very little to do with them as the executives and directors responsible lurk away from public scrutiny.

“My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear,” Enzo Maresca said. “Guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy.”

Which on the one hand is absurd: nobody knows whether the three points City claimed at Anfield will still be theirs by Christmas. Nobody knows what division they will be playing in next season. Nobody knows how bad the sanction could be. And this is not some unfortunate event that has befallen City; this is the direct consequence of the actions of their directors. But on the other, what else can players and managers do? How else can they respond to this situation other than by being professional and trying to win games, even if none of it ultimately means anything?

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

What this is emphatically not, though, is just another football crisis from which City can move on by winning football matches. This is a crisis unlike anything English football has ever known, and it is one with which football’s language is struggling to cope.

This article was amended on 13 October 2026 to state that Manchester City voted against the introduction of FFP regulations in 2013. An earlier version said that they had not.

The TNT Sports presenter on why she believes the Ballon d’Or should belong to Harry Kane

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Harry Kane has had the greatest season of his career and deserves to win the 2026 Ballon d’Or. After an exceptional year, the 33-year-old striker has every right to be honoured with the most prestigious individual award in football.

Whether it’s based on numbers, trophies, performances or standout achievements, Kane has reached new levels. He scored a staggering 73 goals for club and country in 2025-26. It’s a number some players can only dream of achieving in their whole career, let alone in a single season.

To do that in just 65 matches makes it even more incredible. The numbers almost sound unbelievable, they’re so outlandish. To put them into context, it is the most goals any player has scored in a single season in the modern era except for one occasion: when Lionel Messi hit 82 goals in 69 matches in 2011-12. The Argentine would pick up the Ballon d’Or that year.

Kane’s goalscoring feats helped Bayern Munich to the domestic treble, the first time the club have lifted three trophies in a campaign since he joined. To finish off an astonishing year, he then captained England to a bronze medal at the World Cup, which is the Three Lions’ best finish ever on foreign soil.

While other players may have won bigger team honours, when it comes to recognising an individual, there has been no player in better form than Kane. That is also outlined by him breaking a 49-year Bundesliga record this year, by reaching the 100-goal mark in just 98 matches – comfortably clear of the 129 games it took Dieter Muller to hit a century.

What Kane achieved in this last year is simply mind-blowing. Many questioned his decision to play in Germany, but it has been a pivotal move for his career. The 2023 switch has taken him to another level, as proven with the records broken and trophies won in Munich.

Kane is a natural finisher and his goalscoring is as good as we’ve ever seen. He’s a player that makes the most of every chance he gets and scores all types of goals from absolutely everywhere. He’s the type of striker that you just expect to score in every game, and the majority of the time he delivers. He’s prolific, but it’s also the quality of the goals that make him special.

Sign up for our free live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest matches, their kick-off times, channels and streams

On the biggest stage this summer, Kane scored a sensational goal against the Democratic Republic of the Congo – a lethal strike that helped save England’s World Cup. The combination of power, strength, accuracy and technique he showed in that moment are skills you see him applying in the Champions League and Bundesliga regularly. His ability to perform this consistently at the highest level is outstanding.

And it’s not just his ridiculous scoring numbers. His all-round play and ability to bring other players into the game has become even more evident recently, and why England manager Thomas Tuchel describes him as the “full package”.

Time and time again, Kane continues to write his name in the history books for both club and country, yet every single record he breaks, you never expect him to just stop there. You expect him to add to that goal tally and to reach a new height – despite that, he remains humble and driven to keep striving for more.

Kane’s journey is inspirational and embodies what hard work and determination can help you achieve. At the age of 19, he was struggling to make an impact on loan at Norwich and went on to a spell at Leicester, before a return to Spurs saw his career really begin to flourish. He is an example for any young player to aspire to, as he’s now remarkably hit his peak in his 30s.

Kane is a true global superstar of this sport who deserves every bit of praise that comes his way. He’s now adding to his trophy haul with every season, and the biggest individual award in world football should belong to him too.

Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or, 25 years ago, so it’s about time another was honoured. It’s pretty cool that the best number nine on the planet right now is English. With the ceremony being held in London, Kane’s birthplace, on October 26, he couldn’t be a more fitting winner. I believe Harry Kane deserves to win the Ballon d’Or this year – he’s earned it.

#465. Big scorelines, one-sided games - are Women's World Cup play-offs working?

England have lost just once this year but have still not qualified for the 2027 Women's World Cup

The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.

The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.

Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.

England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.

It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.

It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.

'Unplayable' Stanway a free-scoring warrior for Lionesses

One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.

The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.

Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.

Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.

So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.

"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.

"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.

"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."

The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.

Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.

It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.

England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.

They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.

England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.

Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.

In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.

There were several heavy aggregate results in European qualifying

When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .

That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.

England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.

The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.

A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.

There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.

Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.

"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.

"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."

What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.

Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.

Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.

But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

#472. Aston Villa had better players and a better plan than lumbering Newcastle - this was a harsh indication of the Magpies' current situation, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 20:17 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 22:31 BST, 17 October 2026

On the day Newcastle United revealed a slower version of their Blaydon Races anthem, the team on the pitch responded with a performance every bit as lumbering.

When the match ball burst in stoppage-time, it was a signpost for the deflating mood that would soon descend on St James’ Park. At least, that was, after the home masses had let their feelings be known with a chorus of boos.

It was just as well that this game also marked the unveiling of the club’s new pour-your-own beer pumps, for the locals needed something to numb the pain of a second defeat in a week. On this evidence, there will be plenty more.

The sight of head coach Matthias Jaissle breaking the glass on the emergency option and throwing Dan Burn up front in the closing stages told of Newcastle’s desperation, as well as the absence of a workable Plan A. Come full-time, there had been just one shot on target — and that was from a defender. The club have spent £175million trying to replace Alexander Isak, and Burn is where they have ended up.

Unai Emery’s Villa, by contrast, had a plan. They also had better players, including match-winner Johan Manzambi. Remarkably, the visitors are still below Newcastle in the table, not that they will be for too much longer. Villa are unbeaten in five in all competitions and this was Emery’s 100th win in the Premier League.

‘I hope there are 100 more,’ said the Spaniard. ‘This was very tough and for us it was very important after our poor start [to the season] that we needed to try to come back feeling confident, feeling comfortable in how we are building our structure.’

Aston Villa had better players than Newcastle, including match-winner Johan Manzambi, as they beat the Magpies 1-0

The midfielder, who nearly joined Newcastle in the summer, was the game’s star man and scorer of its only goal

Matthias Jaissle's side are heading towards the bottom three after a second defeat in a week

Much of that structure centres on the athleticism and ingenuity of Manzambi. Newcastle missing out on the signing of the Switzerland World Cup star was a sliding-doors moment in their summer, and it was among the reasons why Eddie Howe headed for the one marked ‘exit’.

Had Manzambi and Victor Munoz — the Spaniard who defected to Liverpool — signed, Howe would likely have still been in charge. Sliding doors and, now, a team sliding towards the bottom three. That is the reality of their current plight.

‘Johan has skills and intelligence,’ said Emery. ‘His physicality is also very important to help us defensively. He decided he wanted to be with us [and not Newcastle]. We have Champions League. He has had a very good impact with his qualities.’

It is easy to see why Manzambi was so desired by Newcastle, who thought he was ready to join. The midfielder, 21, was the game’s star man and scorer of its only goal. Not that he had to be so great to convert a free header from six yards — for that he had the pinpoint cross of Joao Gomes to thank and, more so, the failure of defenders Sven Botman and Lewis Miley to react to his presence in the goalmouth.

The moments that followed exposed the fragility of Newcastle’s confidence. Manzambi netted in the 36th minute and the hosts were fortunate not to enter the break at 2-0 down or worse. They lost shape, energy and ideas. It was like watching a boxer lose his legs after the first punch. Emiliano Buendia hit the post after a back-to-front offensive that was devastatingly simple in its execution — pass, pass, chance. It infuriated Jaissle, who yelled at Joe Willock for not stopping the move at source on the edge of Villa’s own area. The midfielder protested his innocence, in a manner to suggest he believed the job of closing Gomes belonged to someone else.

That is never a good sign and was reminiscent of his team-mates’ abdication of responsibility for the goal moments earlier.

Newcastle (4-2-3-1): Hornicek; Miley, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Joelinton (Burn 90), Gonzalez; Fernandez-Pardo (Toure 56), Willock (Osula 56), Barnes; Wissa

Subs not used: Pope, Schar, Dedic, A Murphy, Steur, Bamba

Booked: Thiaw, Botman, Gonzalez, Joelinton, Wissa, Osula

Aston Villa (4-2-3-1): Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Mings, Wan-Bissaka (Torres 77); Kamara, Gomes (Barkley 72); Alysson (McGinn 46), Manzambi (Mbiaye 72), Buendia (Goretzka 72); Jackson

Subs not used: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Bogarde, Madjo

Jaissle had demanded his team come out swinging in response to Monday’s 4-1 defeat at Coventry, and they did, albeit with a little too much fight. The ferocity of Botman’s tackle on Nicolas Jackson needed 60 seconds of attention from Stockley Park, who eventually deemed the on-field yellow sufficient. It was a borderline red.

Jackson later said: ‘I know the referee said yellow card but it was so high and hopefully maybe next time a red card. I nearly broke my leg. The most important thing is that we won, so I’m OK.’

Joelinton was also booked during the same passage for a typically robust challenge on Manzambi, requiring Villa’s medical team to divide their attention.

Still, here was proof of a team ready to scrap for each other, and that resolve did at least extend until the very end, when they threatened to nick what would have been a barely-deserved equaliser amid the chaos of Burn. What was missing throughout, however, was quality and control. Marquee signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo remains without a goal and was hooked on 57 minutes after another subdued outing. The others in attack repeatedly ran down blind alleys.

These two clubs have long been kindred spirits in their attempts to storm the Premier League’s elite. But whenever they have lowered the drawbridge, the following season has invariably seen them thrown back in the moat.

Newcastle, you suspect, are set to sink even deeper this season.
