#475. How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson, Dan Roan, Laura Scott and Sami Mokbel assess Manchester City's position

Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups.

If City were the winners, then there had to be losers.

Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals.

The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.

Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018.

And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket.

City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of Â£830m, plus another Â£90m in expenses.

Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition.

BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight.

When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today.

Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05.

The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United.

City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League.

Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success?

This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim.

Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League.

It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners.

It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money.

Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed.

Missed potential Champions League earnings

What Manchester's 'super-profit' deal with City owners has paid out so far

Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at Â£844m.

Â£217.8m in missed Champions League prize money

Â£88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League

We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons.

For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place.

For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment.

For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money.

But City also earned prize money themselves during this period.

Across the competitions, City were paid Â£1.17bn:

Â£812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues

Â£300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories

'Period of deception' - Pochettino on Man City verdict

"We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month.

"No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done."

You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition.

BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money.

Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned Â£148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking Â£29.9m from the Europa League.

The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received Â£71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid Â£17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of Â£53.5m.

Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth Â£6.6m.

The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup.

Spurs gained Â£5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success.

Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of Â£119.9m.

The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football.

Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United.

Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe.

Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison.

Manchester United won the Europa League in 2016-17, receiving prize money of Â£37.8m. As part of that amount, the Red Devils' market pool payment, which is based upon the value of the television rights, was Â£26.6m.

While we cannot say for certain that Liverpool would have won the Europa League, they were a club of similar stature to Manchester United, which provides a comparison.

The market pool share may also have been slightly lower with both Liverpool and Manchester United involved.

Together with Premier League place money of Â£10.6m - Liverpool finished below City in all nine relevant seasons - the total financial impact on the Merseyside club was Â£52.3m.

As for the FA Cup, City won it just once in the period they were scrutinised over, beating Stoke in 2010-11. The difference in prize money was Â£900,000, with the runners-up going into the Europa League.

Everton missed out on the Champions League once, in 2013-14, and on four other occasions they finished one place below the final Europa League spot.

The Champions League place is calculated to be worth Â£32.6m - the Â£39m earned by Manchester City minus the Toffees' Â£6.4m winnings from the Europa League they competed in instead.

The combined impact on missing out on the Europa League four times is Â£23.2m.

Add on the Â£10.6m from Premier League prize money, and the total financial effect is Â£66.4m - making Everton the third-most impacted club.

While parachute payments provide something of a cushion, relegation from the Premier League is still a considerable financial hit.

Could the teams who finished in 18th place, one spot from safety, argue that they might have stayed up but for City?

There are a couple of ways of looking at this.

Firstly, the results against City who took at least four points off every 18th-placed team other than Birmingham.

Secondly, the mere fact that City were able to assemble a squad far better than their finances should have allowed. Could they otherwise have been involved in relegation battles?

Again, this is not to say City would have been relegated. It is about chance.

BBC Sport has taken the total prize money earned by the team finishing in 20th in the following season. That suggests a minimum return for having stayed in the top flight.

Deducted from that is the first season of parachute payments to give a net amount.

Hull were relegated twice in the period, costing the Tigers Â£93.78m.

The Tigers finished below City in the table four times, adding Â£5.2m in place money to the sum.

It leaves the East Yorkshire club as the second-most impacted on Â£99m.

Swansea are fourth in the table with Â£63.1m. Of that total, Â£54m is from relegation and Â£9.1m in place money from the seven seasons the Swans were in the top flight.

Newcastle suffered relegation by finishing 18th in 2015-16, costing them a projected Â£60.4m, of which Â£7.9m was place money.

Norwich (Â£43.8m), Wigan (Â£39.6m), Burnley (Â£31.1m), Bolton (Â£26.4m) and Birmingham (Â£25.1m) also suffered relegations in 18th place.

Alongside Tottenham, four other teams missed out on Champions League football by one place across the eight seasons when City qualified.

The biggest impact was on Chelsea, who finished fifth in 2017-18.

City earned Â£79.2m from reaching the quarter-finals of the Champions League, with Chelsea getting Â£39.4m from winning the Europa League. That left Chelsea with a deficit of Â£39.8m.

Also just missing out on the Champions League were Everton (5th in 2013-14, Â£32.6m deficit), and Arsenal (5th in 2016-17, Â£22.1m deficit).

The only team not to experience much of a financial impact were Manchester United, who were fifth in 2015-16.

City got no further than the round of 16 in the Champions League, earning Â£42.6m, while United won the Europa League that season, receiving Â£37.8m. It left the Red Devils with a deficit of Â£4.8m.

In the Premier League there is no specific prize pot for being crowned champions.

Broadcast revenue is allocated on a merit basis by final league position.

It is a 1+1 system, so the club in 20th get the base payment. Then the team in 19th get the base payment two times. For 18th, it is that base amount three times, and so on.

It means that the only financial difference, in prize money at least, for the team finishing runners-up in one of Manchester City's three title-winning seasons is one base payment.

Could any team claim they might have finished one place higher?

The value of a Premier League place rose sharply in line with the broadcast deals over the period of City's offences.

In 2010-11 it was Â£755,881 per place, and by 2016-17 it was up to Â£1.94m.

If any compensation were to be considered, Everton, Liverpool and Stoke City would have the biggest claim of Â£10.7m, having finished below City in all nine seasons.

West Brom and West Ham's total is Â£9.9m, with Swansea on Â£9.1m.

At the other end of the scale are the seven clubs who spent one season in the Premier League, including Blackpool (Â£756,756), Portsmouth (Â£800,424) and Huddersfield (Â£1.93m).

#483. “Andy Robertson? I think he should retire, and I’ve told him that!” Scotland and Liverpool legend Sir Kenny Dalglish gives FourFourTwo a message for the man who’s about to break his international appearance record

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

In an exclusive interview, Dalglish discussed his record-breaking Scotland career – and an honour that he could be weeks away from losing

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sir Kenny Dalglish has held Scotland’s appearance record for 48 years – next month though, he could finally lose the honour.

Dalglish finished his international career with 30 goals, equalling Denis Law for a record that still stands today, but surpassed Law’s previous national record of 56 caps in 1978.

The Celtic and Liverpool great eventually ended his international career eight years later with a total of 102 caps, but Spurs defender Andy Robertson reached 101 earlier this month, and could move to 103 when Scotland take on North Macedonia and Switzerland in the Nations League in November.

For the new issue of FourFourTwo magazine, out this week, Dalglish sat down with us for a wide-ranging interview on his life and career. As part of it, he spoke about his days playing for the Scotland national team.

“To get one cap for your country was fantastic, and to score my first goal as well,” he said. “Denis Law was someone I looked up to as a boy, so to get to the number of goals he scored, I don’t mind sharing that record.”

Asked to pick out his favourite games from his international career, Dalglish said: “The first one would be the most memorable one, but maybe also Spain at Hampden, we beat them 3-1, and any time we played against England and beat them…”

Dalglish won his 100th cap against Romania at Hampden Park in 1986, and was presented with it before kick-off by the legendary Franz Beckenbauer. “I don’t know why, I never had any affiliation with Beckenbauer!” he joked. “He was a great player – I don’t know how it came about that he presented it, but he was very magnanimous and said some kind words.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

As for his thoughts on his appearance record being broken in the coming weeks, Dalglish had a cheeky message for Robertson, who he got to know well during the full-back’s days as a Liverpool player.

“He’s a good guy, and it’s not a problem if he does it,” Dalglish said. “But I think he should retire, and I’ve told him that!”

During the hour-long interview for FourFourTwo, Dalglish also picked out five of the most significant years of his life, as part of Gordon & MacPhail’s Vintage Moments series.

In partnership with the legend, the whisky specialists have created 15 box sets of five ultra-rare single malt Scotch whiskies, distilled in years that correspond to Dalglish’s key life milestones – the year of his birth (1951), the year he joined Celtic and the club won the European Cup (1967), the year he married his wife Marina (1974), the year he joined Liverpool (1977) and the year he managed Blackburn to the Premier League title (1995).

“I got a phone call and was asked if there was any interest,” explains Dalglish, who had a personal tasting session earlier this year. “I thought, ‘Well, it’s always nice to be remembered, isn’t it?’ For me, the important thing was what it was all about – dates that are synonymous with the life that you’ve led. They weren’t looking for any scandal, just your thoughts on what has happened. What did you enjoy?”

Dalglish won a staggering 29 major trophies during his time in football, and lifted at least one in 19 different years, so narrowing the most significant years of his life to just five was challenging.

“It was difficult to leave some of them out,” he admitted. “There are a lot of things you don’t realise until you start talking about it, then you go, ‘Hold on a minute, what about this year? What about that one?’”

Gordon & MacPhail are curators of the oldest, rarest single malt Scotch whiskies, and the only company in the world to possess single malts of every vintage from 1948 to the present day.

The limited edition box sets of Sir Kenny Dalglish’s Vintage Moments by Gordon & MacPhail are available for £100,000, which includes the opportunity to meet Dalglish in November. For more info, see gordonandmacphail.com or email vintagemoments@gordonandmacphail.com.

You can read the full wide-ranging interview with Dalglish about his life and career in football in the new issue of FourFourTwo magazine, out this week.

Chris joined FourFourTwo in 2015 and has reported from more than 20 countries, in places as varied as Ivory Coast and the Arctic Circle. He's interviewed Pele, Zlatan and Santa Claus (it's a long story), as well as covering the World Cup, AFCON and the Clasico. He previously spent 10 years as a newspaper journalist, and completed the 92 in 2017.

#485. Revealed: Marcus Rashford has been undergoing regular treatment all season in bid to beat injury that has affected performances for Man United

Published: 22:30 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 22:30 BST, 17 October 2026

Marcus Rashford is having running repairs to be available for Manchester United this season as the England star continues to struggle with the hip injury that has dogged him since the World Cup.

Rashford has started six of United's nine games this season having returned to Old Trafford in the summer following loan spells at Barcelona and Aston Villa.

The 28-year-old has yet to score or make an assist, and failed to convert a volley in front of goal during Tuesday's Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid.

However, sources say that Rashford has been undergoing regular treatment all season to be available for head coach Michael Carrick, and it is inevitable that the problem has impacted his performances.

It remains to be seen if Rashford – who withdrew from England's recent Nations League games – starts against Leeds at Elland Road on Sunday with Matheus Cunha able to revert to the left flank after Amad Diallo's return from injury on the right freed up Bryan Mbeumo to play through the middle.

'Marcus has done a lot of good things,' said Carrick. 'He obviously had a slight injury where he pulled out with England, and he's had to manage that a little bit.

Marcus Rashford has started six of Man United's nine games so far this season despite a hip injury

'He's not quite getting that little bit of a break, putting himself in good positions and having some opportunities. He had one the other night maybe that he felt he probably could have done better with, but he's in there to make a difference.

'He keeps doing the right things, and you get the rewards in the end. So as long as he keeps doing that, he'll be okay.'

Bruno Fernandes has also been carrying an injury that forced him to sit out one of Portugal's games during the international break and appears to have affected his recent performances for United, although Carrick said that was not the reason his captain came off in the 80th minute in Madrid.

'He's been carrying some sort of issue, but he's pretty much over that now, to be honest, and he'll be back to his best,' added the United boss.

'A lot of players do carry them and it goes under the radar. People just think everyone's 100 per cent fully fit and it's probably not very often the case.

'We've got to share the load in all sorts of different ways: that's working, quality-wise, performing, being available.

'It's not an individual thing. When it's all good, it's not always just Bruno. Certainly if it's not so good, it's not all Bruno. He's a fantastic footballer, and he has a big impact on our group.

'Just because he may not be hitting the headlines or the highlights like he did last year doesn't mean that he can't, and that he won't, and I'm sure he'll do that pretty quickly.'

#489. Have any footballers ended their career with more own goals than goals? | The Knowledge

Plus: the earliest trophyless seasons, scoring off one’s backside (part II) and the origins of ‘shithousery’

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“How many professional players have ended their senior careers with more own goals than goals for their own team?” wonders Peter Clark.

In the past we’ve looked at the players with the most own goals, but we haven’t looked at those who ended their professional career in debit. “Southampton cult hero Francis Benali scored only one ‘positive’ goal in his career and was legendary for banging in goal-of-the-month contenders at his own end, most notably a bullet header against Oldham in the 1993-94 season,” writes Daz Pearce. We could only find a couple of OGs for Benali, the other being against Manchester United in 1999-2000. But we were unable to find a comprehensive Southampton database, so there’s a chance we’ve missed some beauties.

Another unsentimental defender, Riccardo Ferri, the formidable stopper in Internazionale’s title-winning side of 1988-89, scored six goals and eight own goals in Serie A. He may be in credit overall – he scored three more goals in cup competitions, but we only have his OG data for Serie A. “Jamie Carragher finished his career with four goals and seven own goals,” writes Dean Whearty. “He even managed to score two in one match against Manchester United in 1999!”

And another in the FA Cup final of 2006, though that had a happier ending for Liverpool. Some sources credit Carragher with five goals at the right end, including an equaliser against Middlesbrough in August 2008. But the official Premier League site puts that down as an Emmanuel Pogatetz own goal.

“Sven van Beek is the all-time leading own-goal scorer for the Eredivisie, with eight in a career at Feyenoord, Willem II and Heerenveen, over the course of 12 seasons and 193 matches,” writes Rob de Hair. “He only managed to score five goals for his own team in those matches. ESPN provided a ‘highlight’ reel here.” Van Beek is still playing in Qatar, and appears to have netted five goals at the right end for Al-Shahania.

Another player on minus three is Luigi Zannier, a defender who played for several Italian clubs, including Milan, in the 1950s and 1960s. In Serie A matches, he scored three and put in six at the wrong end.

Zannier and co have nothing on Everton’s Billy Balmer, however. “At the turn of the 20th century he netted eight goals during open play; all, unfortunately, at the wrong end of the pitch,” writes Gavin Buckland. “In more than 300 appearances for the Toffees his only goal at the right end was a single penalty in 1899.”

“What is the earliest point in a season a team in the top flight has been confirmed as having a trophyless season?” asks Matt Walker.

The concept of a trophy has changed in the last 15 years, particularly since Arsène Wenger referred to fourth place – and Champions League qualification – as a trophy. But this is The Knowledge, not La Vibe, so we are only referring to actual shiny things you can lift above your head in triumph.

In England, the flicker of a trophy is often extinguished at the start of January, when Premier League teams play in the third round of the FA Cup. Tom Reed cites the example of Bournemouth last season. “They were knocked out of both domestic cup competitions by 10 January. Despite having a good season, they had no realistic expectation of winning the Premier League, and weren’t in Europe either.”

But, as Tom points out, Bournemouth were not mathematically out of the title race at that time. Tom has calculated that Derby County, who finished the 2007-08 season with only 11 points, are the earliest case of an English top-flight team being mathematically unable to win a trophy. “They were knocked out of the League Cup on 28 August and the FA Cup in the fourth round on 26 January. Their inability to win the Premier League was officially confirmed in their 26th league match of the season, on 9 February, when a 3-0 defeat by Tottenham – coupled with a victory for the leaders Arsenal – made the gap between top and bottom insurmountable.”

Other countries start their main cup competition earlier in the season, which means many clubs have been forced to embrace their trophyless-ness before Christmas (realistically, if not mathematically). “The early rounds of the Coppa Italia are played at the start of the season,” writes Daz Pearce, “and therefore the weaker Serie A teams could easily crash out of it in September. That’s what happened to Lecce in 1993-94 and Brescia in 1994-95. They were never in contention for the title – Lecce won one of their first 23 games, Brescia none of their first 14. They also tumbled out of the Coppa Italia in round two, the earliest possible stage for a Serie A club at the time. I’m sure at some point, they would have clocked that the Scudetto was probably beyond them.”

We’ve looked into it and think that Lecce and Brescia were both mathematically out of contention after 22 of the 34 Serie A games. In Lecce’s case, that was 6 February 1994; in Brescia’s, 5 March 1995.

In last week’s Knowledge, we looked at players who ended their scoring droughts with a goal off their backside. Tom Clarke has one more to add to the list.

“I think there is in fact a case of a usually prolific striker enduring a barren run with a goal off their bum, at least partially,” he writes. “Late in the 2023-24 Championship season, Leeds’ automatic promotion push was stumbling due in part to Patrick Bamford’s goals drying up. He needed one to go in off his derrière, which is pretty much what happened during a 4-3 win at Middlesbrough. You could say it’s partly hip, partly backside, but surely it’s sufficiently rear-end to count! I recall saying to a fellow Leeds-supporting friend during the match how funny it was that he’d literally got one to go in off his backside and fulfilled the cliche.”

“Where and when was the term ‘shithousery’ first used, and do other languages have a word for it?” asked Brian in 2022.

Before we consider the contemporary phenomenon, we should probably look at how the word from which it is derived became part of the English language. According to our own John Ashdown, who wrote about the S-word during the 2018 World Cup, it can be traced back to Scouse slang used in the 1960s. The Concise New Partridge Dictionary of Slang has an entry for “shithouse”, with definitions “an extremely unpleasant individual” and “a coward”.

It had certainly reached the east Midlands by the 1970s. In Duncan Hamilton’s wonderful book Provided You Don’t Kiss Me, he talks about Brian Clough’s penchant for using the word. “The phone rang. ‘Where are you, shithouse?’ asked Clough. (He used the word ‘shithouse’ as frequently as other people use ‘please’ and ‘thank you’. ‘It’s an affectionate term,’ he’d explain – though he didn’t always use it that way)”. It also appears in most of the Clough stories told by Mark Crossley in his hilarious Undr the Cosh interview.

Jack Charlton was equally fond of the phrase. In 1990, during a prescient observation about how the media might ruin Paul Gascoigne, he said: “Journalists … they’re all shithouses, them”. A couple of years earlier, he said during an interview there was no room for “shithouses” in his Republic of Ireland squad.

John Hartson, then at Arsenal, was sent off against Middlesbrough in January 1997 after calling the referee, Mike Reed, “a shithouse”. But the neologism of shithousery only emerged in the 21st century. “The word does not (yet) feature in the Oxford English Dictionary,” writes the lexicographer John Williams, “but taking the ever-excellent Jonathon Green’s Dictionary of Slang as a baseline, we see that his earliest citation is from 2014, with Nicolás Otamendi as the alleged culprit.

“As this is a Twitter citation, I looked back further. The first football personality accused appears to be Arsène Wenger in 2011, the accusation coming from the Guardian’s own Daniel Harris.”

It started to become a wider part of the football lexicon in the 2010s, most notably when, according to one Arsenal fan, Crystal Palace “bantered us off for 90 minutes with shithousery”. Arsenal actually won 2-1, so goodness knows what he’d have said had they lost.

“AIK and Brommapojkarna contested an 11-goal thriller in the Allsvenskan league, with Brommapojkarna winning 6-5. Remarkably, all goals came in the second half. Is this the highest-scoring match where every goal was scored in the same half?” asks Kári Tulinius.

“As a Maidenhead United fan (National League South, the sixth tier of English football, since you ask), I was delighted when our marauding wing-back Jordon Ragguette recently received an international call-up for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines,” writes Adie Bradshaw. “Jordon was on the winning side in all four of their recent Concacaf Nations League games, which gives him a 100% win record in international football. This made me wonder: are there any players with 10 or more international caps who have a 100% win record?”

“In a Vietnamese league match against Nam Dinh in 2022, the home side Hai Phong had a goal ruled out for handball by video replay – even though VAR wouldn’t come to Vietnam until 2023. There was a giant TV screen in the stadium, and the referee happened to see an instant replay of the goal. Has there ever been another situation like this, where the referee didn’t have VAR, but another source of video replay helped them to reverse a decision?” asks Duc Tran Anh.

The former Liverpool and England midfielder ended up spending eight years at Newcastle

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jonjo Shelvey says he was given a get out of jail free card when he joined Newcastle United - but turned it down.

The former Liverpool midfielder made the move from Swansea City back in January 2015, just a couple of days after getting into an altercation with a Swans fan during an FA Cup defeat to Oxford.

Newcastle were not in a good way at the time, with Steve McClaren struggling to get the side into form and Rafa Benitez ending the season with an undefeated streak that was too little, too late to save them from the drop.

Shelvey told FourFourTwo: "The night before that Oxford game, I knew the deal had been done and I was going to Newcastle.

"I drove up there and never looked back. I was so excited."

Shelvey ended up spending eight years at Newcastle, making over 200 appearances for the club.

Along the way, Shelvey helped the club earn promotion back from the Championship and helped them to re-establish themselves in the Premier League - just like he had hoped.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"Me and Andros Townsend joined in the January window, and they gave me the option to add a relegation clause in my contract so I could leave.

"But I didn’t want that. I was there for the long haul.

"I’d always loved playing at St James’ Park, so I was going there to stay.

"The club paid a lot of money for me, so I felt it was my responsibility to get them back in the Premier League.

"It was the right decision, and I really enjoyed my season in the Championship.

"I loved living in Newcastle and we settled there as a family."

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. #494. Militão included for Sevilla as Real Madrid take cautious approach

Real Madrid have named Éder Militão in their squad for Sunday’s La Liga meeting with Sevilla, with the defender returning after recovering from an injury. Managing Madrid reported the club’s selection and cautioned that Militão should not be expected to play, although José Mourinho could consider giving him a few late minutes if Los Blancos have built a substantial lead.

His inclusion adds another senior option to the defensive group for the match at the Santiago Bernabéu. ESPN also reported his return to the squad, while stressing that Real Madrid intend to handle his involvement carefully.

The squad announcement confirms that Militão is available for selection again, but it does not point to an immediate return to the starting line-up. The expectation set out in Managing Madrid’s report is that any involvement would be limited, with a late cameo more plausible if the match situation allows it.

That distinction matters: being named in the group gives Mourinho another defensive option, but it is not confirmation that Militão is ready for a normal match workload. The report leaves the decision open to the flow of the game rather than presenting minutes as part of the plan.

ESPN likewise described his return as a notable addition to the squad and reported that the club are proceeding cautiously. The two accounts agree on the central point: Militão is back among the available players, but his presence does not guarantee an appearance against Sevilla.

Goalkeepers: Thibaut Courtois, Andriy Lunin and Javi Navarro. Defenders: Éder Militão, Dean Huijsen, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Ibrahima Konaté, Marc Cucurella, Álvaro Carreras, Antonio Rüdiger and Denzel Dumfries.

Midfielders: Jude Bellingham, Eduardo Camavinga, Federico Valverde, Aurélien Tchouaméni, Arda Güler, Bernardo Silva and Thiago Pitarch. Forwards: Endrick, Kylian Mbappé, Carlos Espí, Brahim Díaz and Yan Diomande.

The 23-player group includes a broad set of options across the defence and midfield, with Militão listed among eight defenders. His return is the clearest availability development in the announcement, though the list itself offers no further detail on how Mourinho intends to use him.

Real Madrid are scheduled to host Sevilla on Sunday, 18 October, at the Bernabéu. The match is listed for 21:00 CEST, and Mourinho will decide whether Militão is involved based on his assessment and the circumstances of the contest.

For now, the squad call-up marks a return to the match group rather than a confirmed comeback on the pitch. A comfortable scoreline late in the evening would create the clearest opening for the limited minutes described in the report.

#498. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Manchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the moment

The manner of Manchester City’s victory at Liverpool was an article of both vindication and vilification. Those gleefully wielding inflatable bananas in the Anfield away end could thumb their noses. Why not enjoy the dances of defiance until the music stops? The same went for City players, asked to perform under the darkest of clouds, able to focus, at last, on football, rather than legal argument and uncertain futures. Beyond City, the sight of a club found guilty of 100-plus charges laying waste to such rivals as Liverpool was deeply uncomfortable. The Premier League season and product are badly damaged until the matter is somehow resolved. What happened at Anfield should double the haste for a resolution. Chants of “cheat” whenever City players, the game already won, slipped the ball around, are bound to be repeated at other stadiums. Enzo Maresca has described his club’s plight as “noise” but his team’s victory did absolutely nothing to turn the volume down. John Brewin

Match report: Liverpool 0-3 Manchester City

Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool reboot will require patience. They showed plenty of drive and determination against Manchester City but also uneven edges, polish lacking. Iraola’s aim was to get his players in their opponents’ faces, deepening any doubts circulating in City’s players. Mission mostly accomplished during the first half. A flurry of chances at the beginning of the second half had City rocking only for Ryan Gravenberch’s dismissal to pull the rug. With Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo missing, Liverpool lacked the quality to cause the necessary damage. Lewis Koumas played well in the role of agitator as emergency centre-forward. Víctor Muñoz continues to be full of buzz but Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz, both players signed for £100m plus, are supposed to supply the cutting edge. Barcola has the mitigation of being a new arrival, while discussions about Wirtz border on football cliche. Once Gravenberch departed, and Trey Nyoni was required in midfield, the finger was always going to be pointed in the German’s direction. JB

For the second time this season, Pierre Sage watched his Crystal Palace side win a Premier League game despite not being at their best; the Frenchman was honest enough to admit they had been slightly fortunate against Nottingham Forest. But after overcoming Oliver Glasner on his return to Selhurst Park, Sage can look forward to a reunion of his own against Lyon in the Europa League on Thursday. He will know Palace must improve defensively. Axel Disasi will be available again after being suspended against Forest, although he will miss the trip to face Palace’s arch-rivals Brighton next weekend. “It’s not normal to concede as many chances as we conceded,” Sage said of the first 40 minutes against Forest, when Walter Benítez made a string of fine saves. “We need to be consistent but after the international break it’s a good result that can help us in our future games.” Ed Aarons

Match report: Crystal Palace 3-1 Nottingham Forest

Ainsley Maitland-Niles has some apologising to do. The right-back made two errors that ultimately cost Everton a first away victory in the league since February. The former Arsenal player contrived to botch what should have been an easy interception, gifting Sorba Thomas the chance to tee up Joe Gelhardt for Hull’s opener. With the visitors having turned the game around to lead, Maitland-Niles then got too cute defending against Elliot Stroud in the corner, allowing the Swede to find Mohamed Belloumi for the equaliser. With a squad short on attacking options, Everton cannot afford to score twice away from home and come away with only a point. Tom Bassam

With Manchester United so sluggish and shapeless, they did not serve as much of a barometer of Tottenham’s progress under Roberto De Zerbi. Though if anyone can take positives from Saturday’s clutter of a contest full of mistakes, it should be Spurs. “From a long time Tottenham played without this blood, this character, and I want it,” said De Zerbi. He has plenty to improve upon. Dominic Solanke wore the captain’s armband and got the late equaliser his team’s efforts with 10 men had threatened. If only Spurs’ finishing had not been so profligate in a first half when their energy made United fans mothball their jibes at Manchester City and resume worrying about the failings of Michael Carrick’s team. “Work together, stay together, have dinner together and get to know each other better,” is De Zerbi’s prescription for improvement. He continues to talk of a work in progress. Slow progress, slower than desirable, but Old Trafford offered hope. JB

Match report: Manchester United 1-1 Tottenham

A key topic of discussion for Arsenal fans before the Leeds match was who Mikel Arteta would pick on the left in the absence of the injured Christos Tzolis. Noni Madueke got the nod and the England winger, who was dropped from the latest Three Lions squad, proved a point. “He deserved the chance and he took it,” Arteta said of the wide man, who played out of position but whose pace was too explosive for Leeds’ James Justin and Jayden Bogle. Madueke’s deliveries were also consistently dangerous. He created the most chances in the game (three) and had the most touches in the box (eight). This was good news for a player who had looked to be receding from view at both club and international level. But it also cast a dim light on the range of attacking options available to Arteta after a summer in which Tzolis was the only addition to the forward line. Arsenal took a gamble on Madueke here and it worked out. How many more will they have to take over a long and arduous season? Paul MacInnes

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Chelsea have scored during the first 10 minutes in five of their six games this season. Xabi Alonso says the fast starts are nothing to do with him but Morgan Rogers had a different view after the 5-1 win against Bournemouth. “I put it down to the manager’s team talks,” Rogers said. “He gets us firing, gets us going. We always want to start off on the front foot. It’s about starting well and getting the lead. A lot of games, especially at home, we have won after jumping on the back of early goals – it’s a good trait to have. We need to keep going.” Jacob Steinberg

Home form has been a cornerstone of Unai Emery’s extraordinary success but a victory at Villa Park this season is proving elusive. It’s early days, of course, with Wednesday’s Champions League date at home to Fenerbahce offering another chance to get off the mark – but Emery recognises the value of a fortress. The stadium is different on the eye this season, the North Stand being rebuilt to take the ground’s capacity north of 50,000. Can a three-sided ground impact things? “I certainly hated it as a player,” said Brentford’s head coach, Keith Andrews, whose side remain unbeaten this campaign. “It just feels wrong, doesn’t it? When I was growing up as a kid, some Irish legends played here – Ray Houghton, Paul McGrath, Andy Townsend – so it’s always been a special place for me and you can feel the history of it. With a stand missing, it’s a bit different.” Ben Fisher

Six games in Ipswich are well ahead of the run rate on points required for survival. Gary O’Neil, the modern Premier League firefighter, has brought a doggedness to the Tractor Boys that they lacked when Kieran McKenna took them into the Premier League two years ago. The new Ipswich manager has been ruthless too. The summer signing Kjell Scherpen was dropped for a known quantity in Christian Walton after the win at Palace and, while it did not secure a first clean sheet of the league campaign, the veteran keeper does look a more assured presence. The goals against column will concern O’Neil – only two sides in the division have conceded more – but his side’s stamina will be pleasing. Ipswich have now have scored winners after the 90-minute mark three times. It is not a sustainable strategy but it indicates a team with the stomach for a fight. TB

Sunderland’s supposed summer transfer market priority was the acquisition of a specialist right winger. Ultimately they failed to recruit one and it is arguably costing Régis Le Bris’s team dear. They started Saturday’s deserved home defeat to an impressive Brighton with two natural right-backs on the pitch, the second, Thomas Meunier, operating in an advanced position. When Meunier, a far from shabby player, injured a hamstring, the industrious yet ineffective Nilson Angulo was shifted from his preferred left wing to the right. But a Sunderland XI lacking the hamstrung Brian Brobbey at centre-forward failed to threaten. Surely the moment has come for Le Bris to offer the talented but currently overlooked Chris Rigg or Chemsdine Talbi starting spots at Bournemouth next Sunday? Before that Sunderland travel to face Torreense in Portugal on Thursday. After collecting only four Premier League points this season, Le Bris is likely to rotate heavily for that Europa League engagement. With a Bournemouth trip followed swiftly by a game at Lech Poznan and a visit from Leeds, his task looks tricky. Louise Taylor

Nicky Butt took to his podcast to suggest that Michael Carrick had no desire to go into management before landing the United job

United face old foes Leeds with Carrick under increasing pressure after a run of four defeats and two wins in nine games this season.

His predecessor Amorim was sacked over a post-match meltdown at Elland Road in which he took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox but Carrick isn't worried about his future.

'I understand the reality. I accept where we are, but I don't feel that. I'm totally focused on what's best for this football club and what it's going to take to win games: get the boys playing how we know we're capable of, and we still don't think we're that far away.

'We can turn a few things in our favour, and we can move forward pretty quickly.'

#504. Barcelona eye outright La Liga record against Real Madrid

Barcelona beat Real Betis 5-2 in Seville on Saturday 17 October to win their first nine La Liga matches and equal Real Madrid’s record for the best start to a league season. MARCA report that Hansi Flick’s side can move clear of the mark in their next league fixture, against their rivals in the Clásico.

The nine consecutive victories match Real Madrid’s opening run from the 1968-69 campaign. Miguel Muñoz coached Los Blancos through that sequence, which ended when they drew 0-0 with Pontevedra on matchday 10.

Barcelona now have the chance to claim the record outright, with Real Madrid standing between them and a tenth straight league win. The run has grown match by match, including a comeback victory over Sevilla earlier in the campaign.

The achievement is a specific one: Barcelona have matched Real Madrid’s record for consecutive wins from the start of a La Liga season. The 5-2 result at La Cartuja brought the Catalans to nine; the historical comparison is the Madrid side’s nine wins before its draw with Pontevedra.

Barcelona’s next league opponent is Real Madrid, with the Clásico scheduled for Sunday 25 October at Spotify Camp Nou. That gives Flick’s side a direct opportunity to pass the record against the team whose 1968-69 start set it.

The meeting also arrives with the sides’ rivalry and the league campaign in view. The upcoming Clásico will be a key fixture in the La Liga title fight, according to MARCA’s report.

Barcelona have also won both of their Champions League matches so far, against Feyenoord and Galatasaray. Those European results add to the season’s strong opening, but the nine-win benchmark concerns league matches only.

Before the Clásico, Barcelona are scheduled to visit Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Tuesday 20 October. MARCA describe PSG as the current European champions, making the trip an immediate test between Barcelona’s record-equalling league result and the chance to extend the run.

Real Madrid follow at Spotify Camp Nou on Sunday 25 October. Barcelona can make the record their own with a victory, while a draw or defeat would leave the nine-win mark level with Muñoz’s side.

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola was left sweating over the fitness of two players despite an important comeback win at Brentford — and said his stricken duo could be out for 'some time'.

Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong both limped off during the Reds' win at Brentford, which saw them fight from behind after the Bees were reduced to 10 men.

Keane Lewis-Potter had put the home side ahead before Yehor Yarmolyuk's red for a head butt, then Victor Munoz and Alexander Isak scored.

'We need to look at ourselves first – we don't tend to look at what part they play in the incident. I think Liverpool were cute and clever – Yarmo needs to do better, and I can understand why that was a red.'

#514. Atlético make it five straight wins after Baena’s late strike

Atlético Madrid beat Espanyol 1-0 at the RCDE Stadium in La Liga on Saturday, 17 October, with Álex Baena scoring in the 89th minute to deliver a second consecutive late away league victory. Into the Calderón described a controlled but slow contest in which Atlético had to wait until the closing moments to turn their possession of the game into a goal.

Jonathan David, the Canadian forward who plays for Atlético, sent an early effort over the bar and later had another chance saved by Espanyol goalkeeper Ángel Fortuño. Marcos Llorente also came close after the hour, but Fortuño tipped his effort onto the top of the crossbar.

Fortuño made five saves and was named La Liga’s MVP of the match, according to Into the Calderón. He denied Julián Alvarez shortly before the Atlético forward set up the winner, while Baena had entered the game in the 62nd minute in place of Lee Kang-in.

The change brought greater urgency to Atlético’s attack. Into the Calderón noted that Baena began driving forward and taking on defenders almost immediately; Alvarez then teed him up outside the box, where the Spanish midfielder struck into the top-left corner. Alvarez’s assist was his first in the league this season, and he had three shots during his 45 minutes on the pitch.

Atlético had moved to within two points of Barcelona before the leaders played Real Betis. Barcelona later won 5-2 at La Cartuja, so that gap did not hold.

The victory made it five successive league wins for Atlético, a run the source says they had last managed between October and November 2025. It also extended a developing away pattern: in their last two league trips, the Rojiblancos have found late winners rather than dropping points in matches that had remained unresolved deep into the second half.

Baena’s goal added to a productive league season. He now has seven goal contributions, with five goals and two assists, two more than his total across the whole of the previous campaign. His late introduction against Espanyol gave Atlético another player able to carry the ball into dangerous areas when their earlier control had not produced a breakthrough.

The match account pointed to the attacking options around him, including David, Giuliano Simeone and South Korean Atlético midfielder Lee Kang-in, as a source of energy and initiative. Baena and Lee were not on the pitch together: the former replaced the latter, and his direct runs helped shift the pressure onto Espanyol in the closing stages.

Into the Calderón reported that Diego Simeone praised Baena’s progress after injuries disrupted the midfielder’s previous season, describing an improvement in his decisiveness, strength and confidence. The performance against Espanyol offered a clear match-day illustration: Baena came off the bench, registered three shots and supplied the defining moment.

For Atlético, the result was another narrow away win secured at the end of a match they had largely controlled. Their five-game league run is now established; whether Baena can keep turning late opportunities into goals will be a key part of the story as the season continues.

#515. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#517. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

#524. HIBS 1 FALKIRK 2: Losing habit hits Reedijk hard as Leith men hit rock bottom after defeat to Bairns

Published: 18:42 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 20:28 BST, 17 October 2026

Hibs manager Marink Reedijk isn’t particularly accustomed to losing. But with this lot at his disposal, he might have to get used to it.

Having gone unbeaten with Beveren in Belgium’s second tier last season, the new boss has been defeated twice in as many weeks in Scotland’s top flight. It couldn’t have gone much worse until this point.

They way in which Hibs gifted Falkirk a two-goal lead here at Easter Road was inexplicable. But not in the least bit surprising.

Shooting themselves in the foot is the norm in these parts. David Gray copped heavy flak towards the end – some of it deserved – but even his harshest critic would accept he was let down by individuals time and time again in big moments.

On early evidence, Reedijk is going to have the same issue. This team are toothless up top and incapable of keeping a clean sheet at the other end. It’s a recipe for disaster.

The Dutchman arrives with a reputation for getting his teams playing swashbuckling football, however that’s going to take time. Until then, the players have to help him out a bit by taking care of the simple things in order to start building some momentum. They can’t even do that.

Hibernian manager Marink Reedijk urges his players on from the sidelines

Falkirk striker Jacob Murrell celebrates his double against Hibernian

To be sitting bottom of the Premiership with nine games played is unacceptable. But as they say, the table doesn’t lie.

Unless Hibs get their act together pronto, they are going to be in a relegation battle. Too good to down? Nonsense.

Look, it wasn’t all bad. There were decent passages of play throughout, and at least they played much of the contest on the front foot. The brutal errors render everything else meaningless, though.

Reedijk said: ‘I think we are a thief of our own wallet. I think we gave away two easy goals.

‘If you dominate in this way, you can’t lose.

‘I’m just here for three weeks, so for me, we have to be careful in terms of what kind of conclusions I can get out of this. I think they are more than capable of what we are doing. Otherwise, we don’t do it in this way.

‘I have a sick feeling in my stomach. But I saw a better team today and I see progress.’

Reedijk would have been encouraged with his side’s start, at least.

Thibault Klidje was first to try his luck, curling wide of Scott Bain’s left-hand post from the angle of the area. He really should have hit the target.

The striker then made a mess of a promising counter attack at the end of a lovely move which started in Hibs’ own six-yard box, overhitting a pass down the line to the overlapping Adam Mayor with several better options available to him.

Reedijk bemoaned his team’s indecision in the final third following last weekend’s defeat at Dundee Utd, and it’s fair to say he wasn’t too chuffed with his frontman here either. Not that he was the only one to be on the receiving end of a steely glare from the sidelines.

Azeem Abdulai was next to cop it on 13 minutes as Falkirk took the lead against the run of play, letting a straightforward ball trundle between his legs in the centre circle and into the path of Ryan Strain.

His ball in behind was perfect for Jacob Murrell, who lashed beyond the reach of Raphael Sallinger.

Owen Elding pulls a goal back for Hibs in their 2-1 home loss to Falkirk

This was the home fans’ first proper look at Abdulai as he made his first start for the club following a summer move from Leyton Orient. Given that he hadn’t kicked a ball since the middle of August, his inclusion raised a few eyebrows ahead of kick-off. He didn’t particularly impress.

The visitors doubled their lead on 37 minutes courtesy of another Hibs howler.

Quite what went through Klidje’s mind as he attempted a backheel down at his own corner flag, only he will know, with the ball falling into the path of Murrell on the edge of the box.

The American’s finish high into the roof of the net was emphatic. Kamikaze stuff from a Hibs perspective.

Against the backdrop of a chorus of boos, Reedijk’s men somehow gave themselves a lifeline four minutes before the break.

Felix Passlack – not for the first time – was given acres of space on the right flank to pick out Owen Elding completely unmarked five yards out to bundle home.

The Irishman spurned a glorious chance to level the scores early in the second period after being played clean through. He should have burst the net, but opted instead to round Bain, who was having none of it.

Hibs dominated the ball but did precisely hee-haw with it until substitute Jamie McGrath forced a fine stop from Bain with a low drive from range with 10 to play. That came just seconds after Owen Eames had clipped the post for Falkirk at the other end.

Any hope of a late leveller went out the window in stoppage-time when Jason Kerr galloped across halfway and promptly passed the ball straight of out play in stoppage-time. It summed up Hibs’ performance perfectly.

Falkirk on the other hand were, to a man, outstanding. It wasn’t pretty, manager John McGlynn didn’t care one jot.

‘We’ve had a few sore ones recently with losing late goals,’ he said. ‘And we were potentially in that situation today.

‘I’m so proud of the players, they put in a helluva lot of work.

‘It was all about winning for us today. It’s a huge three points for us and from here, we want to kick on.’

HIBERNIAN (4-2-3-1): Sallinger; Passlack, Kerr, Ivezic, Mayor (Suto 76); Chaiwa (Cadden 76), Abdulai (McGrath 61); Boyle, Mulligan, Klidje (Matondo 60); Elding.

FALKIRK (4-2-3-1): Bain; Strain, Neilson, Henderson, Tanser (McCann 46); Spencer, Barbrook (Yeats 84); Ross (Fodrey 77), Krauhaus (Melniks 65), Eames (McMillan 85); Murrell.

#525. Real Madrid seek Tebas exit from LaLiga and RFEF roles

Real Madrid have demanded Javier Tebas resign as LaLiga president and vice president of the Royal Spanish Football Federation after he compared methods associated with Real Madrid TV to propaganda techniques used by Nazi Germany’s Joseph Goebbels. The club issued its formal response on Friday, October 16, rejecting Tebas’s remarks as unacceptable and arguing that his clarification that he was not referring to Nazi ideology did not lessen their seriousness.

In its statement, Real Madrid described the comparison as deeply offensive and said it was extraordinary for a person holding two senior positions in Spanish football to invoke Nazi propaganda methods to discredit the club, its management and its television channel. It also characterized the episode as another in a series of attacks by Tebas against the club, its president and its media outlets.

The club objected to Tebas attributing to Real Madrid actions by third parties for which it said it had no responsibility. Its response addressed not only the language of his comments but also what it presented as a wider dispute over the club’s public position on refereeing and football governance.

Real Madrid linked Tebas’s remarks to his criticism of the club and Real Madrid TV over their actions concerning the Negreira case. The club said it had approached UEFA seeking full clarification of payments made over the years by FC Barcelona to the vice president of the Technical Committee of Referees, as well as measures to protect the integrity of competitions.

It also called for a comprehensive overhaul of the refereeing system and of the structures responsible for governance, management, supervision and discipline in Spanish football. That should include replacing people who held positions of responsibility during the period in question, the club said. Madrid’s earlier call for Tebas’s removal had also placed his role in the governance dispute under scrutiny.

Real Madrid argued that Tebas’s repeated conduct showed a lack of neutrality, respect and impartiality incompatible with his institutional responsibilities. It said his attacks on the club and on those demanding transparency and regeneration disqualified him from continuing in either of his posts.

The demand covers both his LaLiga presidency and his vice-presidency at the RFEF. Real Madrid said it would continue defending its institutional standing, seeking clarification of the payments at the centre of the Negreira issue and pressing for changes to Spanish football’s structures.

#526. Why are some football shin pads so small?

Liverpool striker Lewis Koumas (second from left) sported low socks and small shinpads on his full Premier League debut at Anfield

Liverpool's Lewis Koumas made his full Premier League debut against Manchester City on Sunday.

While doing so, he sported some very low socks over what appeared to be a very small shin pad.

Last season, images of Burnley's Marcus Edwards went viral after the 27-year-old was seen wearing barely visible shin pads during a Premier League match against West Ham.

Two years ago, a picture of teenager Harry Howell celebrating with James Milner while they were Brighton team-mates also gained attention after fans noticed the visible difference in the size of their shin pads.

Howell's 'micro' pair were an obvious contrast to Milner's far more traditional-sized guards.

So what is behind the trend of extra-small shin guards, and why are they used instead of regular-sized pairs?

The simple answer is that players can choose what size shin pads they want to wear.

The International Football Association Board (Ifab), responsible for the laws of the game, say that shin pads are a mandatory piece of equipment players must wear while playing.

Be of an appropriate size to provide reasonable protection and be covered by the socks

And players are responsible for the size and suitability of their shin pads

The law does not define what an "appropriate" shin pad size is, but leave that decision to each individual player.

Shin pads provide vital protection for players to prevent serious injuries.

There has been a rising trend in younger footballers, as well as some big stars, wearing small shin pads during matches.

The reason for this could be for more comfort and to allow players to move around with greater ease.

Referees are only required to check that some form of shin guards are being worn, Ifab told BBC Sport.

Ifab said players - or the parents or guardians of youth players - must take responsibility for their own safety on the pitch.

While shin pad size is ultimately an individuals choice, any decisions around player safety would also be made in consultation with their club and medical staff.

Marcus Edwards last year was seen wearing very small shin pads for Burnley in the Premier League

Grassroots football teams have started to ban small shin pads for safety reasons.

There are concerns that small shin pads do not cover the shins properly, which can lead to an increased risk of injury - especially at non-elite level.

In August 2024, a football club banned small shin pads after a youth player suffered a double leg break.

Penistone Church player Alfie Collins broke his tibia and fibula in a tackle during a game. The teenager's shin pads, which were no bigger than a credit card, were similar to a size recently worn by some stars of the professional game.

Shin pads "play an important role in injury prevention as they are intended to protect the shin from injury", the Football Association said.

"'Micro' or 'mini' shin pads may therefore increase the risk of injury due to the smaller amount of shin covered compared to larger sized shin pads," they added.

#534. Bellingham set to stay at Real Madrid until 2031

Real Madrid have reached an agreement with Jude Bellingham on a five-year extension that would keep the midfielder at the club until 30 June 2031, Fabrizio Romano reports. The club has not yet made an official announcement, so formal confirmation remains the next step.

The agreement would extend Bellingham’s existing commitment by two seasons. It also represents a long-term decision on one of Madrid’s central midfielders and a growing presence in the dressing room.

Bellingham joined Real Madrid from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2023, signing a contract that was due to run until June 2029. The reported extension moves that expiry date to 30 June 2031, adding two years to his previous deal.

The new agreement includes an improved wage package, according to the account of the deal published by Goal, which attributes the contract details to Diario AS. Those reports also say discussions began towards the end of last season and progressed without major difficulty.

Madrid have also moved to secure other young midfielders on longer contracts, including Arda Güler and Aurélien Tchouaméni. Bellingham’s reported extension would further strengthen that continuity in the centre of the team.

Madrid’s report describes Bellingham as a key midfielder and a leader in the dressing room. It says he has returned to the level he showed in his first season in Spain after physical problems affected his performances, while continuing to contribute in both phases of play.

Under José Mourinho, Bellingham has been given freedom to operate behind Kylian Mbappé, according to the same report. His work is not limited to attacking: he is also cited for initiating the press and contributing defensively. The report puts his league return this campaign at three goals and three assists.

His position and responsibilities under Mourinho have been part of the discussion around his development at Madrid. The midfielder’s freedom in Mourinho’s system is relevant context for a renewal that would keep him at the club through the end of the decade.

The reports describe an agreement, not a completed public announcement from Real Madrid. The distinction matters: while the terms and end date have been reported, the club has yet to formally confirm the extension.

Once Madrid announces the deal, Bellingham’s new contract would run until 30 June 2031. Until then, the club’s confirmation remains the outstanding milestone in a renewal that would add two seasons to his current agreement.

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

#541. How much money do clubs get for Nations League players?

Several Premier League clubs are set to benefit financially from releasing players to represent their country

Uefa will pay clubs a total of Â£205m for releasing players to participate in the 2024-25 and 2026-27 Nations League tournaments, as well as both qualifying and finals matches for the 2028 Euros.

The majority of that fund is reserved for clubs with players released for the Euros finals, with Â£120m being distributed in this instance.

The remaining Â£89m is divided among clubs who have had players participating in either the Nations League or Euros qualifiers.

Of that total, a payment of Â£27m is due to be released this week to clubs which had players compete in the 2024-25 Nations League.

Uefa said in a statement that this will be the first payment under its Club Benefits Programme cycle.

The programme means clubs are paid on a per-player, per-match basis for the Nations League tournament and Euros qualifiers, changing to per-player, per-day for the Euros tournament proper.

A similar system was in place at the 2026 World Cup.

Norway goalkeeper Orjan Nyland's club RB Leipzig are receiving the biggest payout from Uefa for the 2024-25 Nations League tournament

Uefa has said 611 clubs will benefit from the current cycle of payments.

This will likely rise to more than 900 when including the full Euro 2028 tournament, as was the case in the 2024 competition.

The flat rate for each player named in a squad list per Nations League or Euro 2028 qualifying match is Â£3,285. This is a 5% increase on what clubs were paid in the 2020-24 payment cycle for the equivalent games.

According to Uefa, RB Leipzig are the club set to benefit most from the 2024-25 Nations League compensation, earning Â£302,000 after releasing 16 players for the tournament.

While it is not possible to calculate which Premier League clubs will benefit most financially from the current international break until after all Nations League and Euro 2028 qualifiers have concluded, a rough idea can be gathered from looking at how many players each club have released for the 2026-27 Nations League (not including those out on loan):

However, there is no guarantee every player called up will be named on a team sheet, which must happen in order for a payment to be made.

Most Premier League clubs have additional players who have been called for international duty in tournaments outside the Nations League, which will operate a different compensation system from Uefa (if any), as well as those attending under-21s matches.

And while there are obvious financial benefits to having multiple players released for international duty, many clubs sending fewer squad members will benefit from increased rest and training time for players remaining at home.

Uefa announced an equivalent compensation scheme for the women's game in 2022, in time for the 2025 Women's Euros.

More than Â£3.7m was allocated to 221 clubs across European national associations that had released players for the tournament.

Uefa states that the clubs given the financial compensation were "encouraged to use the funds for developing women's football".
