#544. Tebas’s Real Madrid TV comments draw CSD review

Spain’s Consejo Superior de Deportes (CSD) is studying whether to act on its own initiative over remarks by LaLiga president and Spanish federation vice-president Javier Tebas about Real Madrid TV, Mundo Deportivo reported on 17 October, citing EFE. The report describes an examination of possible action, not a confirmed disciplinary case or sanction.

The comments at issue were made on Friday 16 October, when Tebas compared Real Madrid TV’s communication methods with propaganda techniques used in Nazi Germany. He said the comparison concerned those techniques, rather than an ideology or Real Madrid supporters.

The CSD is considering whether to act ex officio, according to the report. It does not say that the council has opened formal disciplinary proceedings, referred the matter to the Tribunal Administrativo del Deporte or imposed a penalty.

Real Madrid responded by demanding Tebas’s immediate resignation from his positions at LaLiga and the Spanish federation. The club also criticised his remarks in strong terms. The dispute adds to the wider tension between Tebas and the Madrid club over his leadership, which has included calls concerning his position at LaLiga.

Tebas responded on X that he was surprised by the news that the CSD was studying possible action. He asked that any review begin with an examination of what he had written and take relevant precedents into account.

His response does not confirm that the CSD has formally begun proceedings. Rather, it addresses the reported consideration and asks the sports authority to assess the full context of his comments.

The immediate question is whether the CSD will move beyond its reported consideration and take further action. Mundo Deportivo’s account provides no timetable or decision, and does not report a formal referral to the Tribunal Administrativo del Deporte.

Until the CSD announces a next step, the matter remains at the review stage described in the report. No disciplinary outcome has been confirmed.

#548. How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it?

Cas has been involved in a number of high-profile cases across the world of sport in recent years

Manchester City's Premier League charges, the Africa Cup of Nations winner being overturned, and contested athlete bans at the summer and Winter Olympics - all very different sporting controversies overseen by different governing bodies, but all linked by one organisation: the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

Cas is the legal body that settles sporting disputes which require a legal resolution, with independent panels of accredited arbitrators (meaning legal experts appointed by both sides of the dispute to find a resolution) reviewing cases and reaching decisions.

Disputes can be down to governance, contractual or disciplinary issues.

More than 900 cases are filed to Cas every year, from more than 50 different sports.

Cas covers a broad range of sporting disputes, including:

elections and term rules for sports federations

recognition of national or regional sports bodies

The Cas headquarters are in Switzerland, but it can operate on-site teams for certain events.

One of the most high-profile cases involving Cas in recent years is the controversy surrounding the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) final.

Following a decision made by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) to overturn the result, meaning that Morocco became the winners despite being defeated by Senegal in the final, Sengal announced they would be appealing against the decision to Cas.

In July 2020, Manchester City themselves had a two-year ban from competing in European competitions overturned by Cas.

An independent panel of accredited arbitrators from Cas has been reviewing the case, with a hearing set for October.

At events like the summer and Winter Olympics, there is an on-site Cas team ready to handle all sporting disputes as quickly as possible.

For example, one of the biggest stories of the 2026 Winter Olympics emerged when Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych was banned from competing by the International Olympic Comittee (IOC) for wearing a helmet depicting images of Ukrainian athletes killed during Russia's invasion of his country - a decision which he appealed over to Cas.

An emergency ad-hoc Cas meeting saw his case dismissed during the course of the Games.

However, many cases cannot be resolved so quickly, and can in fact take years to resolve.

For example, at the 2022 Winter Olympics, Russian's team skaters had a gold medal dropped down to bronze by the International Skating Union after skater Kamila Valieva was handed an anti-doping ban. Russia appealed to Cas, but in July 2024, had their appeal dismissed.

And US gymnast Jordan Chiles may have her 2024 Paris Olympics bronze medal reinstated as Cas continues to examine evidence that she submitted a score appeal within the legal time limits.

Manchester City do not have the option to involve Cas in their appeal against their Premier League charges

An agreement made by Premier League sides means that all cases involving the league and its clubs are conducted in England and Wales and in accordance with English law.

Cas being based in Lausanne, Switzerland means it is not permitted to get involved in cases such as the Manchester City charges.

The Premier League has its own arbitration panel which can hear cases on a narrow number of factors as the last point of contest, rather than Cas, as stated in sections W97 and X.2.4 of the Premier League's handbook.

A similar agreement is in place for clubs in the English Football League, meaning legal issues in the Championship, League One and League Two must be settled domestically.

#554. Endrick’s Roma goal sharpens Real Madrid loan question

Endrick scored Real Madrid’s equaliser in their comeback against Roma, and José Mourinho has explained that he rejected a summer request from the Italian club to take the Brazilian forward on loan. Diario AS report that Mourinho’s decision was based on his belief in Endrick’s ability; the goal in Rome has sharpened the question of how the 20-year-old will earn regular minutes in Madrid.

“When Roma asked to take him on loan in the summer, I said it was impossible. I know what this kid is capable of,” Mourinho said after the match. Endrick came on with Madrid trailing and headed in the goal that made it 3-3, before Antonio Rüdiger scored the winner in a 4-3 victory.

Before the trip to Italy, Endrick had received only the final four minutes against Elche, also in a late change of plan, according to AS. The forward had been near the bottom of the squad’s minutes order, making his influence at the Stadio Olimpico a notable change in his immediate fortunes.

Mourinho had already said in August that Madrid’s No. 9 would not leave Valdebebas, while reiterating that stance when asked about Endrick’s prolonged muscle injury. The Roma match offered a vivid illustration of why the coach had resisted a loan: Endrick added urgency in attack, completed two successful dribbles and threatened the hosts beyond his equaliser.

The comeback gave Madrid a dramatic result in the Champions League, with their recovery from 3-1 down against Roma turning the contest late on. Endrick’s header was the pivotal intervention before Rüdiger completed the turnaround in the 90th minute.

AS report that Mourinho views Endrick primarily as a right winger rather than a conventional centre-forward. The coach wanted a different profile at striker and selected Carlos Espí from three options presented by Juni Calafat; he considers the Spaniard and Endrick compatible because they can feature together in that setup.

Endrick, for his part, said he trusted Mourinho to decide when he should play. “If I’m supposed to play, Mou will put me on. And if not, he won’t. He’ll do what’s best for me. I’ll be ready to help however I can.” The forward’s acceptance of that judgement does not settle the practical question: a place in the squad still needs to translate into opportunities on the pitch.

There is a different emphasis in reporting from Sports Illustrated, which says Endrick has left open the possibility of a January departure, while Mourinho’s position is that a loan is not necessary. Those accounts underline that the player’s openness and the coach’s preference are not the same thing. The immediate test for Madrid is whether the Roma display earns Endrick a more consistent role in the matches ahead.

AS describe the performance as a breakthrough and a starting point. Endrick’s next step will depend on the minutes Mourinho gives him, with his ability to operate wide offering one route to sharing the attack with Espí. The recent focus on Endrick’s return to training also places his squad involvement in context, but Rome is the clearest evidence yet of what he can contribute when called upon.

#555. Alvaro Arbeloa secures first Premier League win as Fulham boss and saves job for now: Fulham 1-0 Hull City

Published: 16:56 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 19:18 BST, 17 October 2026

Fulham finally got over the line to win their first match under Alvaro Arbeloa, earning precious breathing space for their under-pressure boss.

Arbeloa was facing serious questions over whether he was cut out for the role after six Premier League games without a win. Yet this was a confident performance that eased the pressure, with Fulham dominating Hull, who had lost just once before travelling to Craven Cottage.

In fact, the performance was best encapsulated by Hull manager Sergej Jokanovic: ‘It was men v boys out there. They ate us alive.'

Jokanovic was right. This was a transformative Fulham showing, a far cry from the team that has lacked balance and looked fragile. Fulham did not give Hull a sniff. They dominated possession, enjoying 76 per cent of the ball.

It was an entirely different Fulham side. Throughout the season, they have overcommitted and consistently caught in transition but that evaporated. Hull were limited to eight touches in the penalty area and were denied a shot on target or an attempt inside the box.

That said, there is a caveat: Hull were flat and did not offer much. Yes, Fulham were brilliant and outclassed their opponents but caution is required when hailing their defensive display. Hull were sloppy, which made Fulham look comfortable.

Alex Iwobi scored a scruffy goal in the 33rd minute to alleviate the pressure on Alvaro Arbeloa

The only negative for Fulham was the dismissal of Ryan Sessegnon in added time

There is also reason to be concerned in attack. Although Fulham were free-flowing and registered 18 shots, they lacked a clinical edge and missed four big chances.

Gonzalo Garcia, in particular, should have scored when Alex Iwobi put a delicious ball on a plate for him in the 74th minute but his header struck the crossbar from eight yards.

'I’ve seen this movie before,' Arbeloa replied when asked what he was thinking as Fulham squandered their chances. 'I never felt like we were in danger, but in football you never know. One moment and a goal can be scored.

'It was so important to see the players' commitment. For the players on the bench, not on the bench, they are so important for us, working for the group. We need to keep working, it's going to be a long season.

'I am happy because I think we deserved victories in games before, we lost some games where I didn't think the team was better than us. Today, was a perfect day where we dominated. We were almost perfect, I can't believe the game finished 1-0.'

On the whole, this was a drastic improvement from Arbeloa’s side and will keep him in the job for next weekend’s clash with Coventry City. He must now find a way to knit together the defensive and attacking performances.

Fulham played entertaining football with a strong defensive platform but if they do not take their chances, games like last weekend’s will continue to haunt them. Against Ipswich, they conceded twice in four minutes, throwing away three points having squandered three big chances. History will repeat itself if they continue to misfire in front of goal.

After all, the matchwinner against Hull was comical. Brooke Norton-Cuffy’s lazy clearance fell to Oscar Bobb before landing with Sander Berge, who spotted Alex Iwobi on the edge of the box and played the ball into his path.

Iwobi’s first-time effort went underneath goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis as it rifled in. Meanwhile, they failed to take the chances they were expected to put away.

Iwobi’s goal, though, was scored with over an hour remaining. Fulham had previously cracked in winning positions, dropping eight points. This demonstrated they do have the required mentality to see matches out.

With Arbeloa’s job on the line, this was an encouraging response.

Hull, meanwhile, were put back in their place after a positive start to the season.

The fans at Craven Cottage got slightly carried away, chanting about the Champions League after taking nine points from their first six games.

But the defeat against Fulham means they are now winless in four, which serves as a reminder of how difficult this season will be.

There were no positives in the Hull display. Fulham bossed them from the first minute until the last. They offered no threat and were bullied all over the pitch. Fulham have struggled this season yet looked a level above Hull.

If performances continue to tank like that, they will struggle to remain in the league. The manager put it down to a ‘bad day at the office’ - it must not become more than that.

#556. Who has scored against the most Premier League teams?

Erling Haaland (right) is one of two players to have scored against every team he has faced in the Premier League, while Frank Lampard (left) has scored against the most opponents in the competition

Manchester City striker Erling Haaland has become only the second player in Premier League history to have scored against every league opponent he has played against.

Haaland's second-half goal in City's 5-3 win over Sunderland means the Norwegian has scored against all 25 opponents he has faced. He could move to 26 this season, should he score against Hull City.

The only other Premier League player in history to have scored against every club they have faced (minimum two opponents) is England captain Harry Kane, who netted against all 32 clubs he played against.

However, neither player rank in the top 10 for highest number of opponents scored against in the competition.

That honour goes to current Coventry boss Frank Lampard, whose 178 goals between 1997 and 2015 came against 39 different opponents.

Former Manchester United striker Andrew Cole is second with 38, while ex-England duo Alan Shearer and Jermain Defoe managed to net against 37 different teams.

Wayner Rooney and Teddy Sheringham rank fifth and sixth with 36 and 35 respectively.

Completing the top 11 are Thierry Henry, Michael Owen, Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Ryan Giggs with 34 apiece.

#562. Registration doubts kept Nico Williams at Athletic, agent says

Barcelona’s failure to give Nico Williams sufficient certainty that he would be registered was decisive in the winger staying at Athletic Club, according to his agent Félix Tainta. Mundo Deportivo report that Tainta explained the breakdown of the summer 2025 discussions on the Los Fulanos podcast, with Williams ultimately renewing his Athletic deal through 2035.

Tainta said the negotiations reached a point where Williams could not risk moving to Barcelona and being unable to play. He also referred to the approaching World Cup as a factor in the need for the player to keep playing, while making clear that the concern was not simply whether Barcelona wanted him.

The agent’s account makes registration certainty a condition of the move rather than a detail to resolve after it. He said Barcelona did not provide the assurances Williams needed, and the forward stayed in Bilbao before agreeing a new contract with Athletic.

Tainta said Barcelona’s interest dated back to the summer of 2024, after the European Championship. He also named Arsenal, Bayern Munich, Liverpool and Paris Saint-Germain among clubs that had wanted Williams, but his comments do not establish that any of those teams made formal offers or agreed terms.

The representative said Athletic knew about the conversations with Barcelona because he kept the club informed. He described Williams as having wanted to explore a departure, while recognising the sporting limits of staying at Athletic; the eventual choice, however, was to remain.

Tainta also pointed to Williams’ earlier decision to renew in December 2023. He said that agreement was for three years and kept the same release clause, despite the possibility of the player becoming a free agent the following year.

The episode offers a specific lesson for Barcelona’s recruitment: interest in a player cannot settle a deal if the player’s camp is unsure he will be eligible to play. It does not, by itself, establish the cause of the registration uncertainty or support claims about a particular fee, salary-limit calculation or contractual safeguard.

For Williams, the outcome was a new long-term commitment to Athletic, running through 2035. Tainta’s account of the negotiations now places the registration assurance Barcelona could not provide at the centre of why the 2025 move did not happen.

#570. Vinícius to miss Barcelona clash after four-match ban

Vinícius Júnior has accused referees of treating him unfairly and called for greater protection for attacking players, speaking after Real Madrid’s 4-3 Champions League comeback win at Roma. The Brazilian forward’s comments, carried by Al Jazeera from an Associated Press report, came hours after he received a four-match La Liga suspension.

He named Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal and Atlético Madrid’s Julián Álvarez among the players he believes should be protected. The suspension will keep Vinícius out of league fixtures against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia.

The sanction followed Vinícius being sent off after pulling an opponent’s hair and protesting against the referee. He said he was surprised by the length of the ban and denied using offensive language towards the official.

Real Madrid coach José Mourinho also objected to the timing of the announcement, saying the team learned of the suspension on its way to the stadium before the Roma match. His complaint focused on the decision reaching Vinícius about two hours before kick-off.

Vinícius said he understood opposing supporters jeering him because he tries to score against their teams, but said he did not understand the referees’ approach. He argued that attacking players are booked despite taking repeated fouls.

Vinícius said he had seen statistics showing that he had received 500 fouls but that only five red cards had resulted. He argued that yellow cards often go to attacking players and said players who bring something different to the game, including Yamal and Álvarez, need protection. He also said defenders are allowed to foul him throughout a match while he receives the card.

He also said that, when it comes to Vini, it is all too easy, describing a disparity between the treatment he receives and the fouls he believes opponents commit against him. His appeal was not limited to his own case: he specifically included Yamal and Álvarez in his call for protection.

Mourinho questioned whether it was normal for a player preparing for an important match to learn of a four-game suspension only two hours before kick-off. “We were on the bus about to arrive at the stadium when we found out,” he said.

Vinícius has not scored for Real Madrid since August and had two goals for club and country this season at the time of the report. He acknowledged that he was not at his best, but said he was working to regain form and had no doubt the goals would return.

His suspension takes him out of four league games, including the away Clásico against Barcelona. He will next be available for Madrid’s league campaign after the fixtures against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia.

#573. Liverpool's victory at nine-man Brentford leaves more questions than answers as Florian Wirtz struggles again and Bradley Barcola fails to hit Champions League heights, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 17:07 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 18:42 BST, 17 October 2026

It was not a classic head butt that put Jeremy Jacquet down deep into time added on at the end of the first half. In other cultures, in other eras, it might have been interpreted as a nod of recognition from Yehor Yarmoliuk. But it was foolish and it was enough to seal his fate and cost his team. VAR intervened, Yarmoliuk was sent off and the game was changed.

Until then, Liverpool had struggled to assert themselves, even with a front line that cost more than £400m. Bradley Barcola had missed a gilt-edged chance, Florian Wirtz had spent another half fretting at the margins and Andoni Iraola’s team were soon to suffer two injury blows when both Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong were forced off.

But Brentford going down to 10 men wiped all Liverpool’s misfortunes away. By the time the dismissal of Vitaly Janelt reduced the home team to nine men in second half stoppage time, Liverpool were 2-1 up and heading towards fifth place in the table.

The statistics said that Wirtz had created nine chances, including the assist for Liverpool’s equaliser, more than any player in the Premier League this season. That flattered his overall performance but it was something to build on. There was time for one more glaring miss from Barcola but by then it didn’t matter.

It was hardly an emphatic victory. The questions about Wirtz are still getting louder. Barcola may have scored a hat-trick in the Champions League in midweek but he looks desperately short of confidence in the more testing conditions of the Premier League.

Liverpool will have been buoyed by the fact it was Alexander Isak who scored the winner after Victor Munoz had dragged them back into the game with a fine equaliser but even though Liverpool have only lost once in their opening seven league games, they are still searching for something.

Alexander Isak scored the winner on his return as Liverpool came from behind to beat Brentford

Victor Munoz had equalised; Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola provided the assists

‘He is disappointed,’ Brentford manager Keith Andrews said of Yarmoliuk and his indiscretion after the game. ‘He is an amazing young man. He will learn from this. We need to look at ourselves. They were cute and clever but he needs to do better.’

Andrews is as impressive a communicator as there is in the Premier League and his reaction fitted that pattern.

The game had got off to a slow start, notable only for Szoboszlai and Alexis Mac Allister blazing shots over the bar. But it suddenly came to life midway through the first half when a neat interchange between Michael Kayode and Dango Ouattara ended with Ouattara’s goal-bound shot being deflected wide by Jacquet.

A minute later, Liverpool should have scored. Brentford played themselves into trouble on the half-way line and Barcola, who cost £123m when he arrived from PSG in the summer, stole the ball away from Yarmoliuk and raced clear. Barcola lifted the ball over Caoimhin Kelleher but pulled it wide of the right-hand post. ‘What a waste of money,’ Brentford’s fans sang.

A fine challenge by Jacquet prevented Igor Thiago putting the home side ahead but Liverpool had other issues to deal with, too. Barcola was shown a yellow card for pulling back an opponent and then Szoboszlai had to be substituted with what looked like a recurrence of his hamstring injury.

The Hungary forward was distraught. He hammered his hand into the turf in frustration. Szoboszlai has been Liverpool’s most influential player for some time so his loss was a big blow. He marched straight down the tunnel, his expression set in a stony grimace.

Keane Lewis-Potter had put Brentford ahead not long before half-time with a header

The game changed going into half-time when Yehor Yarmolyuk was sent off for a headbutt

One misfortune followed another. Liverpool won a penalty five minutes before half time when Mac Allister fell under a challenge from Ouattara but VAR intervened and replays showed Ouattara had touched the ball before the Liverpool midfielder tumbled to the floor.

Two minutes later, Brentford took the lead. Igor Thiago curled in an inviting ball from the right and Keane Lewis-Potter ran on to it and leapt to power a brilliant header past the dive of Alisson.

Deep in injury time at the end of the half, though, Brentford indulged in an act of self-sabotage. In the routine jostling that takes place before a corner, Yarmoliuk bumped chests with Jacquet and then moved his head towards the Liverpool centre half. VAR intervened again and Yarmoliuk was shown a red card for violent conduct.

It was a classic ‘soft’ decision. In the press room at half time, I asked Ray Houghton if that would have counted as a head-butt in his day. ‘That would have been a friendly hello,’ he said with a smile. He was right, of course, but in today’s top-flight culture, Yarmoliuk moved his head towards Jacquet and opened himself up to the censure that followed.

More injury woes afflicted Liverpool after the break. Frimpong had come on at half-time but lasted five minutes before he was led off the pitch, limping. Liverpool’s frustrations grew. Jacquet was shown a yellow card for a foul. Mac Allister was booked for dissent.

Mac Allister brought a fine save out of Kelleher before Virgil Van Dijk drove a volley into the ground and watched it bounce just wide. Victor Munoz was involved in an altercation with Kevin Schade that saw Schade booked. The clash spurred Munoz on.

A couple of minutes after it, he escaped down the right and sprinted into the area. He turned inside Lewis-Potter and bent a low left-foot shot around Kelleher and into the Brentford goal to bring Liverpool level.

Liverpool finally looked as if they had the belief to win and eight minutes later they were ahead. Mac Allister lifted a deep cross to the back post, Barcola nodded it down and Isak got in front of his man, took one touch to control it and then rifled the ball past Kelleher. Lewis-Potter was on the line but he could only deflect it into the net.

Barcola hit the bar with delicate chip but when he had a chance to put the game out of reach in the dying minutes, he hesitated, tried to play in Lewis Koumas instead and the chance was gone. It was a good win for Liverpool but it still left more questions than answers.

BRENTFORD (4-2-3-1): Kelleher 7; Kayode 6, Van den Berg 5 (Hickey 71, 6), Ajer 6, Lewis-Potter 6 (Diouf 77); Yarmolyuk 4, Janelt 5; Ouattara 6 (Schade 46, 6), Jensen 5 (Sangare 46, 6), Anthony 5 (Damsgaard 78); Thiago 6.

Subs not used: Valdimarsson, Carvalho, Collins, Wilson.

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 6; Araujo 5 (Frimpong 46 (Ngumoha 52, 7)), Jacquet 7, Van Dijk 5, Kerkez 6; Szoboszlai 5, Mac Allister 7; Munoz 7 (Gomez 79), Wirtz 7, Barcola 8; Isak 7 (Koumas 79).

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Endo, Gakpo, Nyoni, Tsimikas.

#578. Barcelona’s 17-match clean-sheet drought clouds Champions League bid

Former Barcelona defender Abelardo believes Hansi Flick’s side still need a top-level centre-back to win the Champions League, despite their 4-1 victory away to Galatasaray on Tuesday 13 October. The win gave Barcelona two victories from their opening two European matches, but they have conceded in both.

Barcelona beat Feyenoord before the Istanbul trip, yet neither result brought a clean sheet. Their run without one in the Champions League has now reached 17 consecutive matches, according to the figures reported in the coverage of Abelardo’s assessment.

Abelardo’s concern is about the quality available at the back when Barcelona face the competition’s strongest forwards. He pointed to the need to win individual defensive duels against players such as Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Harry Kane, arguing that the squad still lacks top-level options in central defence.

That warning came after an emphatic scoreline, but the Galatasaray match itself offered a reminder that Barcelona can be tested before their attack takes control. The hosts scored first, and the Blaugrana had to recover before pulling away in the second half.

The former defender’s view is not that Barcelona cannot win the competition: he considers it possible, but believes they need a higher standard of centre-back to make a serious challenge. His comments were reported by Barca Blaugranes after the Galatasaray match.

Barcelona did not add a central defender in the summer window. The club’s recruitment choices left that position without the new senior reinforcement Abelardo says is needed; Barcelona’s summer transfer business therefore provides relevant context for his assessment.

The numbers capture the tension in Barcelona’s start: they have won both games convincingly, while the defensive sequence Abelardo highlighted has continued. A strong attacking display in Istanbul did not, in itself, answer the question he raised about the squad’s options at centre-back.

The next Champions League fixtures will offer more evidence of whether Flick’s defence can cope against a range of opponents. The challenge Abelardo identified is not limited to one match: his argument is that Barcelona must consistently win defensive duels against elite attackers if they are to go all the way.

For now, Barcelona have six points from six available in the league phase, with their next European test still to come. Their unbeaten start gives them a strong position, but the 17-match clean-sheet drought remains the clearest statistic behind Abelardo’s warning.

#579. How to become a football referee

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#584. Erling Haaland gives Man City an injury scare after starring in Ipswich victory and Enzo Maresca makes history as club keep winning in face of guilty verdict, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 17:02 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 18:12 BST, 17 October 2026

Enzo Maresca is statistically the best coach in Premier League history. Over seven games, anyway. Nobody has ever won their first seven in charge. Not Ancelotti, not Mourinho, not Wenger.

They’ll probably want that accolade wiped from the record books too, given how the conversation around City’s indiscretions is being shaped. Irrespective, it talks to a near-flawless few months to life at the Etihad Stadium for an Italian whose credentials were being written off before formally accepting the job and then again after a meaningless Community Shield defeat by Arsenal with an unfit team.

The public face of the guilty verdicts and the only management employee talking on record about ramifications and the club’s stance, this is a job far more difficult than merely succeeding the best to have ever done it. He’s passing everything with flying colours for City’s hierarchy, both on and off the pitch.

Six points is the gap between the leaders and Arsenal before the champions go to Nottingham Forest on Sunday. More strikingly, it is eight from Chelsea and nine down to Liverpool.

This, you have to say, is as awkward as it gets for Richard Masters and the Premier League board. As the world waits for the next stage of this bitter legal case, an appeal that is likely to bring down the grand old house of English football either which way, City just keep winning. Keep winning games with a load of jeopardy attached to them, nip and tuck, chances at both ends right until the end.

Ironically, they are dispatching the more established clubs with more ease than the upstarts, and Maresca keeps smiling in the face of ire. They are scoring heaps, giving up plenty of opportunities for the opposition with a daring style, and are eminently more watchable than anybody else in this division. To illustrate that, Gary O’Neil feels that Ipswich Town deserved far more from this and will have more than a few agreeing with him.

Erling Haaland netted twice for Manchester City as they beat Ipswich 3-2 on Saturday

The win means Enzo Maresca is the best manager in Premier League history, with no boss ever winning their first seven matches in charge before

Another Erling Haaland brace – four for the campaign – against a promoted team who are posing serious questions in this league and wasted decent chances at 2-1 just after the break, notably when Emersonn headed wide after Gianluigi Donnarumma flapped at a corner.

Haaland seemingly cannot stop – although went straight down the tunnel at full-time with what looks a knee injury having appeared as if he was unwell in the Mancunian cold – and the general merriment in the stands continued from Anfield last week. Maresca, though, seemed to suggest he was fine afterwards.

Some will instead label the merriment as defiance and others will ask what on earth do City supporters have to be defiant over. What is definitely the case is that the past few weeks have provoked a reaction from a fanbase that has been asked to swot up on matters no avid follower of any sport should have to.

And then there were the bananas. Eleven thousand of them hung over seats and many more sold outside. Word at the back end of the week was that chief executive Ferran Soriano had hoped to order in 60,000 to fill the stadium, only for constraints on supply putting paid to that.

Funnily enough, ex-striker Imre Varadi owns a business that trades in the sale of inflatable fruit. While not being the reason for the 1980s craze, Varadi is synonymous with it and City now do their banana business with him. He was invited into a box for the day to see them waved as each goal went in.

None more so than when Haaland thought he’d completed his hat-trick late on, callously volleying into the roof of Christian Walton’s net, only for Enzo Fernandez to have been ruled offside in the build-up, cleared up by VAR.

Marc Guehi has a tough game - and Gary O'Neil felt his Ipswich side deserved more

Former director Txiki Begiristain (left) was in attendance to show support for his old club

Then the game turned heading into stoppage time. Marc Guehi – who had been culpable for Ipswich’s earlier equaliser, when Daizen Maeda wriggled clear from a routine ball in behind – was caught wrong side of Abdul Fatawu. Guehi nicked the winger’s calf as he strode towards goal. Referee Farai Hallam waved away the appeals when the decision seemed clear and needed calling back by VAR again to overturn it.

Zian Flemming hammered the penalty down the middle, Ipswich now within a goal and Hallam – who became exceptionally unpopular in a game against Wolves here last January – then somehow ruling 12 minutes of injury time to incredulity.

Still end to end, still City desperate to find a fourth and not hold what they had. Donnarumma tangled in his own netting while punching away a corner. Sharp intakes of breath, more gasps.

Maresca loves this entertainment but doubtless wants a tad more of the control with which this club had become accustomed. Former director of football Txiki Begiristain, sat next to Hugo Viana as another show of support for the club from the old guard, will not have seen much of this helter-skelter stuff under the previous incumbent.

Begiristain witnessed a positive afternoon for Phil Foden, sweeping in the 19th-minute opener beautifully from Jeremy Doku’s pass in a way we have seen so often down the years. He went off to a standing ovation and with a huge grin for the first time in a long time. Maheda struck back two minutes later before Haaland’s powerful header proved too hot for Walton just after the half hour.

It prompted ‘Dave from Liverpool’ to send a message into the BBC’s live text service to suggest that ‘City are just a midtable team without Haaland,’ which feels indicative of the collective loss of perspective in recent weeks. As it was, the goal was greeted by chants of ‘we are staying up’ before they completed fine renditions of a future spent travelling to Stockport County for league fixtures. That should stir some enthusiasm given the bounty of ale choices behind Edgeley Park’s Cheadle End and the town’s general upturn. It’s a pretty strong away day.

Haaland’s second – 12 for the season – saw him muscle Ouattara out of the way from the industrious Iliman Ndiaye’s pass and appeared to put the game beyond doubt, only for Ipswich to wrestle back in for what became a ridiculously nervous final passage. Say what you like about City but they are certainly not boring.

Man City (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 6; Nunes 7 (Khusanov 76), Dias 6, Guehi 4, O’Reilly 5 (Gvardiol 61, 5); Bouaddi 7, Kovacic 7 (Fernandez 50, 7); Ndiaye 7, Foden 7 (Anderson 77), Doku 7 (Semenyo 77); Haaland 8

Subs not used: Rulli, Air-Nouri, Cherki, Allan

Ipswich Town (4-2-3-1): Walton 6; O’Shea 6, Diop 5, Greaves 6 (Clarke 90), Davis 7; Florentino 4 (Matusiwa 71, 6), Palacios 7; Outtara 6, Enciso 6 (Akpom 78), Maeda 7 (Fatawu 71, 7); Emersonn 6 (Flemming 78)

Subs not used: Scherpen, Kipre, Furlong, Philogene

#588. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#593. The fact Man United cannot drop Lisandro Martinez after his outburst just goes to show he was spot on about Sir Jim Ratcliffe's politburo of under-qualified, over-protected advisors, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

By RIATH AL-SAMARRAI, CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 23:35 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 17:57 BST, 17 October 2026

Lisandro Martinez will be in the Manchester United squad when they face Leeds on Sunday. And of course he will, because he was right about that shambling wreck of a club.

If he was wrong, and United were indeed a functional, intelligent organisation, he wouldn’t be anywhere near the bus for Elland Road. Not after what he said the other night.

A proper recruitment system would have meant there was enough defensive cover to drop a dissenting voice in questionable form. But United don’t have that. Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s politburo of under-qualified, over-protected advisors messed up another transfer window, so kicking Martinez into the long grass wasn’t an option.

In other words, if Jason Wilcox was better at his job then Martinez would have lost his and here’s a little list to support the point: Cristiano Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho, Marcus Rashford.

In the past few years, all of them have spoken out about those above them at United. And with the exception of Rashford, their feet didn’t touch the ground. Straight red. Rashford got put in the freezer for 18 months.

Martinez’s comments were slightly different, of course. He didn’t go after his manager, like Ronaldo and Sancho, and he didn’t turn up late and then flash some leg to potential suitors, like Rashford.

But he did sing a similar song by tearing strips off the regime in public. That used to be a hard no-no at Old Trafford, irrespective of how much truth was in the pudding.

We know that everything Martinez said about Wilcox and the club’s lack of ambition was accurate. We also know that his performance at the microphone was better than anything he has shown on the pitch in quite some time. No one could score points off him for accuracy, only his wisdom in stating the obvious and his reliability as a witness.

Michael Carrick says the club have moved on from Lisandro Martinez's comments after the defeat by Atletico Madrid on Tuesday night

Sir Jim Ratcliffe brought in Jason Wilcox from Southampton in 2024

Michael Carrick’s position in all of this is quite interesting. Unlike Wilcox, he has to answer questions about rogue speakers, limited options and poor results and the links between them.

When the Martinez situation was put to him on Friday, he dealt with it the way he used to play, by taking the least fussy option – he managed upwards by not slapping his bosses and he limited his criticisms of Martinez to saying he made a ‘mistake’. Pinned into a tight space, he found a sensible pass.

Carrick couldn’t have done much better in that no-win scenario. But on some level, and in thoughts best kept to himself, he might even wish to thank Martinez. Because who else in-house has pinned United’s difficulties to the lapels of those who are largely responsible for this mess?

It won’t count for much in the long run, as it’s always the manager who carries the can. And some of the flak he has drawn in recent weeks is justified, of course. Same goes for the players.

But it is inconceivable to think Carrick, a smart man, would have supported the thinking behind a summer window in which United prepared for a return to a European workload by signing three midfielders and a back-up goalkeeper.

A window that offered no cover for a left-back in Luke Shaw, who has managed 25-plus Premier League games in four of his 12 seasons at United. A window that left Martinez and Harry Maguire as the first-choice centre-back pairing. A window that marked two years since they last signed a senior defender, the entirety of which has been spent under the watch of Wilcox, the director of directionless football.

Those are the decisions that shape seasons and what we are seeing from United is no surprise. We all called it a mile off. And we can all see Carrick’s points of exposure when Leeds are in the opposite corner.

Wilcox brought in Carlos Baleba from Brighton to complete United's transfer business this summer - he was the third midfielder they signed, after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans

In many ways, they are the last thing he needs right now. They are a club that, for a number of reasons, highlight his shortcomings and those of United’s executive tier.

I was at their game against Arsenal and left with three main thoughts – Leeds dominated the champions for an hour, they are brilliantly organised by Daniel Farke and they know the value of a good defender.

Leeds didn’t have a spectacular window, but it was key to the building of a backline that is jointly the best in the Premier League so far. Nico Elvedi has been a good signing and Tarik Muharemovic an exceptional one; between them, they cost roughly the same as Youri Tielemans, with the difference being that Farke had a clear idea of how to use them.

It’s possible that Carrick will crack that code on Sunday – his team are good for attacking moments, if nothing else.

But it is also possible that Elland Road will prove the worst possible place for him to be, because so many of the areas where his side have under-performed are those where Farke has excelled.

A solid, physical midfield, a reliable defence, and a collective that operates with a detailed, well-understood plan has been shown so far this season by only one of the two clubs in the fixtures.

For Carrick, there is some blame to be swallowed there. But only some. The vast majority goes to higher planes, where the responsibility truly lies for United’s problems.

I would doubt Lisandro Martinez’s judgement in designating himself as the man to point it out. But he wasn’t wrong.

#594. Ten unusual jobs in football

Player, manager, referee, coach â if you were asked to name a job in football, we reckon you might be able to reply quickly with one of these. But what about private chef, bodyguard, or barber? These are just three of the many, many, slightly more unusual roles that exist in the game. After all, someone has to make sure players eat well, are kept safe, and captured creatively for the âgram, while fans also want to have an amazing match-day experience.

BBC Bitesize Careers caught up with author and creator of Jamie Johnson Dan Freedman, who like many people finds himself working in the world of football without being a player on the pitch. Heâs written the book 50 Ways Into Football: Dream Jobs on and Off the Pitch and we couldnât help but get stuck in and select a few of our favourites.

Take a scroll through the carousel and see how many of these roles you already knowâ¦

For some of the games most elite players, security is an absolute priority such is the level of stardom. Take Lionel Messi for example, he has a full-time bodyguard. Yassine Cheuko, who has a background in Mixed Martial Arts, is never far from the Argentinian playerâs side! Job requirements: A good level of fitness, eyes on the back of your head.

Keeping the vibe going on match days can be a tricky task, especially if the home team isnât performing at their best. But when it comes to a fanâs match-day experience, away from the action the pitch, the stadium announcer is often the unknown star of the show. From pre-match hype-building, to making sure everyone know which players are being substituted, itâs all in the day job. Job requirements: A commanding voice and a decent playlist!!

Tournaments like the UEFA Champions League capture the imagination of fans around Europe and beyond, itâs where the best meet the best. But logistically these tournaments are huge operations, from scheduling to staffing, planning epic ceremonies to keeping on top of player appearances. It all falls on the shoulders of the often unspoken about Tournament Organiser. Job Requirements: An encyclopaedic knowledge of the tournament, some space in your passport for stamps.

If tactics and formations arenât for you but you reckon youâve still got some impressive talent when it comes to ball skills, football freestyling might be for you. Itâs a continually growing area of the game, complete with annual world championships. Great Britainâs Liv Cooke is a former world champ! Job Requirements: Top tekkerz, and then some more top tekkerz.

Imagine getting to be in the dressing room when your team gets the big win, or when a new player arrives at the club, capturing the moment for fans can often fall to the clubâs own photographer. Always ready, with camera in hand, they need to expect the unexpected, including turning from being the photographer to being the subject of the photograph. Just ask Martin Ãdegaard. Job Requirements: A good knowledge of the âgram, plenty of charged batteries.

Footie video games are big business. Keeping them as accurate and representative to the game on the pitch is vitally important for the people that design and work on making them (and of course for the people who play them). We know the team at EA Sports will be busy doing all of that right now, their next release is expected to drop November this year. Job Requirements: An eye for detail, a willingness to spend a lot of time playing and testing video games.

From Cole Palmerâs high fade, to Marcus Rashfordâs latest braid design, itâs often claimed that when players feel and look their best, they play their best too. Whether thatâs exactly true or not weâll leave it up to you to decide. But when it comes to looking sharp, or trying out something a little different on top, one thing is for sure, footballers all have their go-to guy or girl! Job Requirements: Some creative clippers and good chat for when the client is in the chair.

From jetting off to world cups in far flung locations to needing to make dramatic transfer deadline day journeys footballers cover the miles, and not always on the team bus. Thereâs often a need to fly, and where thereâs a private plane, thereâs a private pilot, like this uniformed chap who flew Granit Xhaxa to sign for Sunderland FC in 2025. We reckon it's some way to see the world. Job Requirements: Solid flying skills and a professional attitude, no head in the clouds here.

When it comes to admin, footie stars leave all of that to their agents, they help strike the best contracts and deals for players and can end up with an impressive amount in their own bank accounts as a result! "Super-agent" Jorge Mendes currently represents Lamine Yamal but has also worked for Ronaldo and Jose Mourinho among others. Job Requirements: A business brain and an eye for deal.

While many pros work closely with nutritionists and chefs during the lead up to match day, eating well doesnât just stop at the training ground. For those players that are more confident in the box than kitchen, a private chef is often the answer. Itâs another role that gets a really unique view into the private world of footballer lives, and another thatâs growing in popularity on social searches too. Tasty! Job Requirements: A passion for meal-prep, a decent chopping board or two.

With Jamie Johnson being a hugely popular series of books (and TV drama) we wanted to asked Dan for his top tips for working as an writer in, or out of, the world of football. Hereâs what he suggested:

Read lots, especially about subjects you're really interested in: Dan spent loads of time reading football newspapers as a teenager, studying match reports and articles all the time.

Learn to accept rejection: Dan spent three years being rejected by publishers before getting his first break in the industry. Although it was hard, he decided that he would always try to âfail betterâ each time â looking for feedback for next time.

Know your characters inside out: This one is particularly important if youâre writing fiction Dan recommends knowing your characters so well that they almost feel human.

Bitesize Careers, in partnership with The Open University, has launched the Follow Your Passion campaign, exploring how you can draw on your passions and interests to find your future jobs.

From content creation to computer game design, nutrition to number-crunching, check out the full Bitesize Careers Follow Your Passion collection for loads of inspiring careers content.

#600. Former Man United star Ander Herrera reveals he is now 'playing for free' after choosing to donate weekly wage to his boyhood club - having cashed in on £53m at Old Trafford and PSG

Published: 12:28 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 17:00 BST, 17 October 2026

Ex-Manchester United midfielder Ander Herrera has revealed he is playing for free at his boyhood club Real Zaragoza.

The 37-year-old who has two caps for the Spanish national team was, until very recently, living out the final years of his storied career in Argentina with Boca Juniors but has now decided to ply his trade in the Spanish third division with Real Zaragoza, in hopes of bringing the historic club back to the big time.

Herrera is reportedly earning £5,500 per week, a far cry from the £150,000 he earned while playing for European giants Paris Saint-Germain. But in an interview with Manchester United legend Rio Ferdinand on the former centre-half's YouTube channel, Rio Ferdinand Presents, the Spaniard revealed that every penny of his wage will be going to the club's foundation.

The six-time Copa del Rey and one-time Europa League winner said: 'Now in a difficult moment for the club, I think we all, we the fans, we have the responsibility to help the team and the club. And I feel so proud of my career.

'I feel so proud about what I have achieved in terms of football and also in terms of money. So I don't need it. I wanted to play for free. I wanted to help for free.

'At home, my city, where I grew up, and hopefully, as I told you before, helping the club to come back to professional football.'

The Spaniard revealed the motivation behind his decision to return to Real Zaragoza in an interview on Rio Ferdinand Presents source: RioFerdinandPresents/YouTube

Herrera spent five years with Manchester United winning four major trophies but is now hoping to bring his boyhood club back to the professional game

Real Zaragoza, slipped into the third division of Spanish football, officially a semi-professional division, at the end of last season in one of the most shocking declines a big European club has experienced in recent years.

Herrera also stressed the importance of his decision: 'I think we also have to give something back to football, you know, and I wanted to do this because I am not only a professional football player, I am also a football fan and I love what I do.

'And one day, probably soon, when I am retired, I want to feel proud of what I have done during my career.'

Ferdinand took Herrera's candor as an opportunity to pile more criticism onto Manchester United's rivals, Manchester City, saying: 'In a world where Man City have these charges hanging over their head, it's so good to hear about a gesture like this still in the game of football.'

The pair continued to joke about the potential re-attributing of Premier League winners medals following the bombshell Manchester City verdict.

Ferdinand began by saying: 'I'm waiting for my medal as well, so you can have one and I can have another one as well.' Herrera gave a classy response saying: 'I don't know if we deserve the trophy, but for sure they don't deserve to win it.

'If the Premier League want to keep being respected all around the world they have to do something.'

Herrera could potentially be entitled to a Premier League winners medal as he was a key part of Jose Mourinho's 2017-18 Manchester United side that finished second to City, although they were 19 points off the pace.

The one-time Europa League and FA Cup winner with Manchester United did express some sympathy for the Manchester City players during his interview, saying: 'I don't know if you will agree with me but if I was a Man City player I would be angry with my owners, I would be angry with my board, because they have put all that I have done during these years in doubt.'

#610. The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?

You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.

Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.

The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times â including those three on the trot.

And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.

Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.

It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.

His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.

After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.

Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.

"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.

"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.

Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career

Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.

"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.

"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."

Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.

After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.

"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.

"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."

A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.

Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east â including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.

Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.

"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."

And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.

"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.

Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.

"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.

"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."

Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.

Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.

"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.

"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."

Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final

Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.

And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.

They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.

"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.

She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".

"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.

"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."

Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.

But even the best laid plans can go awry.

"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."

By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.

"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.

"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."

Thousands of fans travelled from Whitley Bay to London across the three finals

Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.

"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.

"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."

And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.

After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.

The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.

The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.

In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.

After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.

"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.

"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"

The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.

"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."

Whitley Bay lift the trophy in 2010, joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor (left)

Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.

Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.

"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.

"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."

Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".

"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.

"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"

Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.

But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.

"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.

"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

#611. Jose Mourinho admits Vinicius Jr should have LEFT Real Madrid last summer 'to a country where he is respected' as boss lavishes praise on former Arsenal target

Published: 13:00 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 16:58 BST, 17 October 2026

Jose Mourinho thinks Vinicius Junior should have left Real Madrid in the summer to go somewhere he is 'respected'.

Arsenal enquired about the Brazilian superstar and reports suggested they were willing to offer him a mammoth £18.5million per season - more than any player at the club.

His contract expires at the end of the season and the club's position is that he must lower his demands if they are to agree an extension. They would still be willing to make him their joint-highest earner alongside Kylian Mbappe.

Vinicius Jr has often been a target of racism in Spain - there have been more than 20 such cases of alleged abuse towards him since he joined from Flamengo in 2018. The situation has reduced him to tears before, but he has insisted on staying in La Liga so that he doesn't 'give the racists what they want'.

His future has come under more scrutiny in recent times as he has had a slow start to the season - one goal and three assists in ten outings - and is now serving a four-match ban for pulling Villarreal star Nathan Saliba's hair.

Mourinho said: 'If I were in his shoes, I probably wouldn't be here. I would have forced a move to a country where he'd be respected, but out of loyalty to Real Madrid and love for the club, he stayed.

Jose Mourinho says he would've left Real Madrid in the summer if he were Vinicius Junior

'I would have forced a move to a country where he'd be respected,' said Mourinho, of the star who has suffered persistent racial abuse in Spain

'He believes things can improve, and he still has that smile. Nothing and no one can take it away from him.

'He's a fantastic guy, and it's easy to get along with him. I spend a few minutes alone with him every day.

'I value him immensely because he always manages to live and survive with a smile.'

Vinicius has been a phenomenon at Real Madrid, scoring 129 times in 386 games from the wing.

But the balance of power shifted to Mbappe when he joined from Paris Saint-Germain in 2024 and talk of his future has increased.

There is a chance that, if Madrid go a third season in a row without significant silverware, they choose to rebuild and go in a different direction.

Moving away from the heavy 'superstar' model has worked for PSG and rewarded them with two Champions League titles in a row.

Vinicius had a tricky summer, being knocked out of the last 16 of the World Cup with Brazil and then missing his pre-season return date as his representatives tried to revive talks over a contract extension.

If an agreement cannot be found on a new deal, Madrid could be open to selling in January, rather than lose him for free next summer.

Last year Al Ahli were willing to offer a €1bn five-year contract offer for the 2024 Ballon d'Or runner-up.

Liverpool were also credited with interest earlier this window but are not in the mix for a player who earns around £520,000 a week.

Mourinho has been a strong defender of Vinicius and recently insisted to TNT Sports that he is going to get back on track.

'He is going to emerge,' the Portuguese promised. 'It is just a question of when.'
