#638. Chelsea climb into the top four and end NINE-MONTH wait for a clean sheet - as Mike Penders proves he is ready to seize his chance after Emiliano Martinez's brual injury at Everton

Published: 14:35 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 16:20 BST, 17 October 2026

At first, a few Everton fans suspected Emiliano Martinez was time-wasting. Then the seriousness of the situation sank in. Chelsea's goalkeeper was faking nothing.

He had collided with Jarrad Branthwaite, who is a hulk of a man, when bravely coming to clear a set-piece after 67 minutes.

Everton might have scored had he not, but it floored him as his Chelsea team-mates immediately signalled for help. What followed were almost ten minutes of no football; just concern for Martinez as Joao Pedro called on the paramedics to hurry up with the stretcher.

Bizarrely, there were some boos when the concussed Martinez was carried away to be taken to hospital. It was perhaps in riposte to Chelsea fans singing the offensive 'sign on' song and chanting 'we pay your benefits' while their goalkeeper was receiving treatment.

Two wrongs do not make a right but thankfully, the majority of those inside the Hill Dickinson Stadium applauded Martinez as he was replaced by Mike Penders.

This was hardly how Penders – Chelsea's 21-year-old goalkeeper whose potential is extremely high – wanted to make his Premier League debut. Penders had hoped to earn his opportunity eventually, but not at the expense of Martinez's wellbeing.

Pedro Neto broke the deadlock inside the first minute of the second half

Morgan Rogers got in to another off-the-ball bust up this time with the Everton's James Tarkowski, both recieved a yellow card for their antics

Rogers was lucky not to receive a second yellow moments later after colliding strongly with James Garner

Still, it was with the help of their two goalkeepers that Chelsea finally secured their first clean sheet since January. They had conceded in each of their last 22 league games. They had waited nine months to stop an opponent from scoring – and 11 months to do that away from home.

Martinez thwarted Everton as he denied Thierno Barry more than once in this match, and then Penders took over from there with ease, even seeing through the 11 minutes of stoppage time slapped on to the end.

Everton (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Maitland-Niles 5 (George 55, 6), Tarkowski 5, Branthwaite 5, Mykolenko 6; Armstrong 5 (Norgaard 85), Garner 5; Rohl 5, Dewsbury-Hall 6, Grealish 5 (Johnson 85); Barry 5

Subs not used: Travers, O'Brien, Dibling, Alcaraz, Hackney, Graham

Chelsea (3-4-2-1): Martinez 7 (Penders 75, 7); Acheampong 7, Lacroix 7, Colwill 7; Neto 8 (Quenda 90), Caicedo 7 (Lavia 90), Henderson 7, Hato 7 (Palestra 90); Palmer 6, Rogers 6; Joao Pedro 6 (Welbeck 90)

Subs not used: Fofana, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao

This was a major milestone for Xabi Alonso. At last, his side showed some solidity, and proved they do not only need to outscore the opposition in order to win.

'We needed to show that we can win in this way,' Alonso said afterwards. 'We looked solid. We played solid. We were strong and we stayed in control. In the first half, there were difficult periods with throw-ins, corners, pressure from Everton. You have to overcome those moments.

'In the Premier League it is very hard to have complete control in an away game, but you cannot lose your shape or your conviction. We spoke about that at half-time. We felt the first goal would be crucial. It could have sent the game in either direction. It went our way.'

Indeed, Chelsea opened the scoring via another kick-off glitch. The visitors got the second half going, and scored within a minute. It was Pedro Neto with the goal, Jorrel Hato with the assist, and Morgan Rogers with the inventive back-heel in the build-up.

With that, Chelsea led 1-0, just 43 seconds after kicking off.

Hato was not even supposed to be starting. Pep Chavarria was earmarked to be Chelsea's left wing back. But he picked up a problem despite travelling to the Hill Dickinson Stadium and so had to drop out of the squad. Hato replaced him, and was crucial in this opener being scored, setting up his opposite wing back after he had drifted into space in the box.

Neto added Chelsea's second goal just as the 11 minutes of stoppage time were announced. That was timed well, and originated from a 25-yard free-kick. Chelsea's supporters had been chanting 'Hendo again, ole, ole'. They wanted a repeat of his strike from last weekend against Bournemouth. Jordan Henderson tried but struck the wall. The ball fell kindly to Neto for 2-0, however.

Everton tried sending balls into the box, but Penders was clean enough in collecting them, which will give him confidence if he is to now face Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge next weekend, and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup's fourth round thereafter.

Emi Martinez suffered a nasty blow to the head half way through the second half that forced the Argentinian to leave the pitch on a stretcher

Neto put the game to bed with an calm finish in stoppage time

Per sources, Penders was confident of succeeding Robert Sanchez when the 28-year-old Spaniard went into this season as Chelsea's No1.

Even Liam Rosenior preferred Filip Jorgensen to Sanchez for a while during his doomed tenure in charge of the club, so Penders believed he was capable of taking over as first choice at some stage in 2026-27.

Yet Daily Mail Sport has heard how Penders' confidence waned when Martinez was then signed for £7.5million from Aston Villa on a two-year contract with the option of a further year.

The 34-year-old Argentinian replaced Sanchez, who was sent to Como after a poor performance in Chelsea's season-opening win at Fulham. That is a dry loan with no option or obligation included, and Sanchez is currently second-choice to Jean Butez under Cesc Fabregas.

Martinez's arrival surprised Penders, who had spent the summer hearing Alonso say he was happy with his set-up and would not be signing a new No1. According to a source close to the goalkeeping situation at Chelsea, Penders felt the sudden signing of Martinez pushed him further away from a starting place and changed the complexion of his coming campaign.

Yet Martinez's injury here gave him his first opportunity in the Premier League, and more chances are likely to follow depending on how long his competition will be sidelined.

For Everton, this was a frustrating afternoon. They were unbeaten under David Moyes in the Premier League this season, but never truly tested Chelsea with Josh Acheampong preventing Jack Grealish from having any joy. Moyes tried bringing on Tyrique George, who may have had a point to prove against his old club, but Everton could never beat Martinez nor Penders.

It was a performance which Chelsea can build on. This was their first game outside of London this season, and while they have an awesome attack, they showed they can win ugly with a little nastiness thrown in. 'Sometimes it is not about playing nice,' Alonso summed up.

#645. Revealed: Arsenal's plans to revamp London Colney training ground in arms race with Big Six rivals - from new gyms to state-of-the-art 'hub' and why they wanted 'mini-stadium' for academy teams

Published: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 16:20 BST, 17 October 2026

Evolve or be left behind is the mantra ingrained at Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal.

From their commercial operation to recruitment, the champions are hellbent on revamping whatever they can to capitalise on a first Premier League title in 22 years and cement their place in Europe’s elite.

Next in their sights is their London Colney training base. Sources say there is an acceptance that Arsenal’s training facilities lag behind some of their Big Six rivals, which the club are focused on rectifying.

In February 2024, Arsenal made Dubai-based real estate developers Sobha Realty their first training ground sponsor. The club said the relationship would also help them explore development opportunities at the site, which are now kicking into gear with Sobha involved in the plans. But since that deal, the rest of the Big Six have left Arsenal behind.

Manchester United spent £50million on their Carrington redevelopment in August 2025, with improved gym and rehabilitation areas, nutrition facilities, an altitude-training room, sleep pods and dry-floating recovery equipment.

Chelsea are exploring further redevelopment of their facilities, while Liverpool’s AXA base remains state of the art after opening six years ago. Spurs began further upgrades to the first-team gym at their Hotspur Way training ground in July this year.

Arsenal are desperate to stay at the top of English and European football - and next in their sights to achieve that is revamping their Sobha Realty training ground

Tottenham's Hotspur Way facilities are some of the best in the world, and are regularly used by England for training camps

It’s understood Arsenal have undergone a refurbishment of their first-team gym and treatment amenities and also been granted planning permission for a temporary women's gym, which will kickstart the wider revamp.

Longer term, Arsenal are understood to be assessing whether they can build a new state-of-the-art men’s hub which would put their facilities among the best in Europe.

The women’s team would be able to train in the temporary gym for a maximum of three years and then – if a brand new men's hub is built – move into the facility that the men's team currently use.

It is understood that last season Arsenal were considering plans to erect stands around a pitch at Colney, to in effect create a mini-stadium for the Under 21s and Under 19s. It is believed the club had an informal talk with the local council before deciding not to pursue planning permission.

The Under 21s play at Meadow Park, the home of National League leaders Boreham Wood FC. The new stadium would have ended those journeys to Boreham Wood for youth-team players and their parents.

The pivot towards focusing on the training ground comes after resolving their more pressing matter of the Emirates Stadium, built in 2006. At the time, it was widely regarded as one of the most advanced football arenas in Britain, a benchmark for modern stadium design.

Since then, competitors have built or redeveloped stadiums with increasingly sophisticated hospitality, entertainment, retail and non-matchday offerings – none more so than their north London rivals Tottenham.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport in November 2024, options to expand the Emirates were keenly explored with architects from Populous – the firm which designed Arsenal’s stadium – consulted on the options available. Yet, earlier this month, Arsenal confirmed they had decided to pursue a ‘continued evolution’ of the stadium rather than an expansion.

Arsenal's Under 21s currently play at Boreham Wood FC, but plans were in the works to build a mini-stadium for them at Colney

Arsene Wenger oversaw the project to build London Colney back in 1999 and then the major upgrades from 2015 to 2017

Attention has instead turned to Colney. Built on a 143-acre site back in 1999 in a project overseen by Arsene Wenger and largely financed by the £25m sale of Nicolas Anelka to Real Madrid, the previous major upgrades began in 2015 and were completed ahead of the 2017-18 season.

This included a new player performance centre, which brought together fitness, medical, rehabilitation and player-support facilities for the women’s and academy teams. Recovery technology such as ice baths and a cryotherapy chamber were brought in, as were a 40-metre running track and dedicated analysis and scouting suites.

For Arsenal, the latest plans underline a growing recognition that staying competitive off the pitch is just as important as the results on it.

With rivals continuing to invest in their infrastructure, the challenge for Arteta and the club’s hierarchy is to ensure London Colney can keep up with their title-chasing ambitions.

#646. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

#656. Is this the worst penalty decision ever?

Published: 22:35 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 12:47 BST, 17 October 2026

Viewers were calling it the 'worst penalty award' they'd ever seen. Former Scotland star James McFadden could only say 'wow'.

FIFA referee Matthew MacDermid certainly won't want to watch the highlights back on Saturday morning.

MacDermid awarded a penalty to Partick Thistle when Seb Drozd dropped to the ground theatrically, with no apparent contact from Ayr defender Kevin Holt.

Smyth converted from 12 yards to give Thistle a 1-0 win and even Partick boss Mark Wilson admitted afterwards it was not a penalty.

Seb Drozd lies smirking on the ground after winning a contentious penalty for Partick Thistle

🗣️ "Wow"James McFadden is in disbelief as Partick Thistle take the lead against Ayr United from the penalty spot through Oisin Smyth.⌚️ Watch the second half on BBC Scotland pic.twitter.com/vnjbMHWF84

A fellow Jags fan had a slightly different take when he posted: 'As a thistle fan its 100% a dive but overall we have been all over you.'

#663. Poppy protest footballer James McClean claims former club 'hung me out to dry' over political stance - and opens up on death threat that left him needing police protection

Published: 10:58 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 12:25 BST, 17 October 2026

Poppy protest footballer James McClean says his former club Sunderland 'hung him out to dry' over his stance.

And he has opened up on the death threat which saw his house guarded by police after he first went against the grain in 2012.

McClean, 37, is remembered in English football for his refusal to wear the poppy because he feels it shows disrespect to people who died during the Troubles in his home nation of Northern Ireland. He also played in the Premier League for five seasons with the Black Cats and West Brom.

His hometown, Londonderry, known to Republicans as Derry, was the scene for the infamous 1972 Bloody Sunday massacre, in which British soldiers shot 26 unarmed civilians during a protest march, with 14 killed.

'Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen,' he told The Guardian.

'It was a very difficult year and I felt a lot of that could have been handled better by the club. But Sunderland came out with a statement before the game which drew all eyes on me. It was there to protect the club. They basically said this is James’s personal decision but we, as a club, wholeheartedly support the poppy appeal.

James McClean says Sunderland 'hung him out to dry' over his poppy protest stance

The star, who was born in Northern Ireland, has always refused to wear the poppy as he feels it shows disrespect to people who died during the Troubles

'I wanted to make my own statement but I was constantly told by the club that: "No, no, it’ll die over. Just leave it."

'I’d just turned 23 and I thought the club had a duty of care to look after me and that’s what they were doing. I’d won the player of the year the previous season but I felt they hung me out to dry.

'The next game was away to Fulham on a Sunday, on Sky. A threat was made that I would be shot if I came on to the pitch. I remember Erin [his wife] panicking. It sounds extreme and people might say: "Oh, wise up, you’re not going to be shot on TV." But the night before the game I was assigned two police officers to stand outside my door. So the Met police took it seriously and that made it more real.'

McClean has followed his stance ever since, despite the intimidations. In 2024, he even stood separately from the Wrexham and Mansfield players as they observed a minute of silence for Remembrance Day.

He has previously stated that if the poppy was only used to memorialise those who died solely in WW1 and WW2 then he would be happy to oblige with the show of respect.

His decision has previously seen McClean suffer torrents of abuse from angry supporters that view his poppy snub as an insult to the memory of armed forces personnel who have lost their lives in combat.

The Republic of Ireland international is a divisive figure in professional football having previously issued calls for a united Ireland, refused to wear a poppy as is tradition in fixtures throughout November and once posed IRA-style in a balaclava in front of his children for a 'school history lesson'.

In September, he clashed with Birmingham City supporters when being substituted and later called a fan at the match a 'smelly fat gammon' after catching a cup of Bovril that had been thrown at him.

He says he would sometimes go 'looking for conflict' during his career - and even suffered from death threats

He is back at hometown club Derry City but is not playing and says they fed him 'b*******'

He admits to the Guardian that sometimes he riles people up deliberately.

'There were days where I went looking for the conflict,' he says.

McClean has been back in the headlines recently after moving to his hometown club Derry City.

Derry attempted to bin off McClean in August – despite signing him in January on a multi-year deal – reportedly claiming he is unable to fulfil his contract's terms because he is not fit enough to play or train.

He has branded it 'incomprehensible' and a 'dangerous precedent' for the club to try and terminate his deal due to his physical issues.

And he told the Guardian: 'I was meant to be coming home for the fairytale ending. But you quickly realise the promises are just b*******.

'It’s not good. It’s a player against owner and there’s only one winner. I think that’s it in terms of Derry City. You never think you’ll be betrayed by your own so it’s painful.'

#670. Marcus Rashford settles into Barcelona life with surprise IKEA trip

#686. How Fabian Hurzeler turned Brighton from 'nice guys' to Champions League contenders: His ruthless pre-season edict, the Austrian boot camp, an All Blacks guru, Bart Verbruggen's coffee club and the 'best squad ever'

Published: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026

It's only eight months since the low point not only of Brighton's season but also head coach Fabian Hurzeler’s tenure. A dismal 1-0 home defeat by rivals Crystal Palace was played out to chants of ‘sacked in the morning’ from Seagulls supporters after a run of one Premier League win in 12.

Sacked in the morning? As Daily Mail Sport revealed at the time, that was never going to happen. Owner Tony Bloom stood by his man, Hurzeler went back to basics and recalled James Milner, and Brighton won seven of the next 11 to climb from 14th to eighth and qualify for the Conference League.

On Sunday they welcome Palace again, this time third in the table after winning four and drawing one of their first six games. They have won their last three by an aggregate score of 10-0, including a complete domination of champions Arsenal.

Hurzeler was Manager of the Month for September, Pascal Gross Player of the Month and captain Lewis Dunk winner of Goal of the Month for his audacious 30-yard screamer in the 5-0 rout of Coventry. So how have they done it?

It all began with a pre-season like no other, partly spent in Austria, partly on the south coast. Club insiders rate it as 'elite level', not just on the grass but with every spare minute used for meetings and discussions with Hurzeler and senior staff.

The summer transfer window was also key. Brighton brought in players high in character who were already disciples of the Hurzeler way of playing and a work ethic that has required a serious buy-in from all.

Fabian Hurzeler celebrates another Brighton win with Ferdi Kadioglu in what has been a fantastic start to the season for the club

Brighton have scored more goals than any other team in the top flight, netting 18 times in their first six games

They also decided to introduce a ‘no more Mr Nice Guy’ attitude. Hurzeler wanted the team to be difficult to beat, ruthless in personal duels and Brighton to no longer be perceived as a 'nice' club. He relayed this to all staff.

Brighton have also been ruthless in front of goal and are the league’s top scorers with 18, despite selling their own top scorer last season, Danny Welbeck, to Chelsea. 'Who is going to score the goals?' was an oft-heard refrain after Welbeck’s departure, which the club did not seek out. The answer? Everyone else. Algeria left-back Jaouen Hadjam, a £10.3million summer signing from Swiss side Young Boys, became Brighton’s 12th different scorer this season in the 2-0 win at Sunderland on Saturday.

A visit to the club’s training ground helps to explain the feel-good factor. There is a coffee wagon parked up and goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen makes a point of buying everyone a hot drink whenever he keeps a clean sheet. He already has seven those this season of those in nine appearances in all competitions.

There is also new padel court for staff use, and next to go in might be a crown green bowls arena after the success of a staff tournament on Hove seafront. It was held as a way of building connections among staff and for Hurzeler – who didn't win the tournament – to say thank you to the people in the background at the club.

It was organised by Mike Anthony, the club’s head of player development and high performance. He spent 14 years with the All Blacks rugby team, filling a variety of senior performance roles in strength and conditioning, performance science, player development and elite culture building. In fact, 'culture' is a word you hear everywhere at Brighton.

'Bowls is more a game for, I would say, experienced persons, older persons,' Hurzeler said, 'and when we were there, we took the average age down a little bit.'

Bloom has hinted that he regards a top-five finish, and with it Champions League qualification, as within reach and says Brighton have their best-ever squad. Its depth will be tested in the coming weeks by the Thursday-Sunday grind of the Conference League. But Hurzeler could field two different teams of good quality and Brighton's starting XI against Palace may well bear little resemblance to the side they put out in a 4-0 win over Lithuanian outfit Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday.

Welbeck leaving allowed Greek striker Babis Kostoulas, 19, to move from bit-part player to main man. Injured wingers Yankuba Minteh and Kaoru Mitoma are yet to feature this season, but Belgium left-back Maxim De Cuyper has stepped forward into Mitoma’s berth on the left wing with two goals and two assists, while Paraguay forward Diego Gomez has taken Minteh’s place.

Bart Verbruggen buys every Brighton player a drink from the coffee wagon outside the training ground when he keeps a clean sheet - that's seven rounds in his nine appearances this season

Babis Kostoulas has been able to become the main man up front after Danny Welbeck's exit, and the Greece striker smashed in a fine goal in the hugely impressive 3-0 win over Arsenal

Maxim de Cuyper (left) has been converted from left-back to left winger and has proved a revelation, scoring twice and adding two assists

Few complained about the sale of Carlos Baleba to Manchester United for £70m after they saw his replacement, Spain Under 21s midfielder Chema 'Baby Rodri' Andres, signed from Stuttgart on deadline day for a fraction of the Baleba windfall.

It would be an exaggeration to claim that most Brighton signings are from the bargain basement. But for every £44m Luka Vuskovic, there is a £3.5m Yasin Ayari, while Andres (£15.5m), Gomez (£11m) and De Cuyper (£17.5m) hardly broke the bank by Premier League standards.

Players who struggled for game time last season, such as French defender Olivier Boscagli, are now regulars, while Malick Yalcouye has been a revelation in midfield after two years out on loan, earning an Ivory Coast call-up.

And of course, there is always Gross. The 35-year-old continues to defy Father Time, stepping seamlessly into Milner’s role since the latter’s retirement during the close season.

He still looks like the Premier League’s all-time bargain buy at a total profit to Brighton of £3.5m. They signed him from Ingolstadt for £3m in 2017, sold him to his boyhood club Borussia Dortmund for £8m in 2024 and bought him back last January for £1.5m. Last weekend he became the oldest player since Ryan Giggs to provide an assist in three successive Premier League matches, and along with Kostoulas and Andres, found the net in the 3-0 win over Arsenal.

Gross’s example inspires the relentless pressing of opponents that drove both Manchester United and Arsenal to distraction before the international break. For the press to work so well so often, everyone has to be committed.

'You have to be intense,' said Sweden midfielder Ayari recently. 'To play the way we play, you have to be fit. We emphasise this every day and we train hard to be able to play like this. Everyone knows the standards. When we started this summer, everyone was fit and had been doing their own training.'

The willingness to keep pressing until the final whistle depends on a team spirit and togetherness that appears to be off the charts. The substitutes and coaches rose as one to applaud Dunk’s goal at Coventry, and the bench cleared at the Stadium of Light as team-mates rushed to congratulate Hadjam on his first goal in English football.

Chema Andres, 21, celebrates scoring against Arsenal. The Spain Under 21s midfielder is known as 'Baby Rodri' and signed from Stuttgart on deadline day

The bench cleared at the Stadium of Light last weekend as team-mates rushed to congratulate Jaouen Hadjam on his first goal in English football

Pascal Gross looks like the Premier League’s all-time bargain buy at a total profit to Brighton of £3.5m

Not everything has been perfect. Chaos reigned at the back as Brighton went 3-0 down at Chelsea in a 4-3 defeat. Blooding several new faces all at once caused early confusion in a Carabao Cup tie away to Manchester United, but once a much-changed team had settled down, they recovered from 2-0 down to win 3-2.

And you have to wonder how many analysts at the other 19 clubs spent the international break working out how to beat them. Does Hurzeler have a Plan B if so?

'If you think you are perfect, then you are done,' he has said. 'It's about finding other solutions, it's always finding different approaches.

'There will always be some non-negotiables in our game but there are always different elements and different adaptations we need to do to stay competitive. You can never be satisfied, you can never stop.'

#691. 'He's a dead man strutting': Inside Fulham's divided dressing room - as we reveal how Alvaro Arbeloa alienated his own players from day one, the 'disconnect' splitting stars and staff and why 'worried' owners don't want to pull trigger

Published: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 02:00 BST, 17 October 2026

After just six Premier League matches as Fulham manager, Alvaro Arbeloa is a dead man walking. Or in the words of one source close to the dressing room, a ‘dead man strutting’.

It was always an extraordinary gamble for a mid-table Premier League club operating on a limited budget to hire a man who had only previously coached within the confines of the world’s mightiest club, Real Madrid, and then to purchase him three young products of the Spanish club’s La Fabrica academy.

So far that high-risk strategy is failing alarmingly. Fulham are bottom of the Premier League and winless, having tossed away the lead in three of those six matches.

Most glaringly at Ipswich Town last Saturday when Arbeloa’s team led until the 88th minute, only to concede twice after their manager made a series of baffling substitutions.

As a result of that ‘Farmageddon’ against the Tractor Boys, today’s home fixture against Hull City is pivotal for the Spaniard. Lose it and he will surely be sacked – with former Premier League managers Thomas Frank and Vitor Pereira in the running to replace him. Although Pereira is believed to be keener on the role than former Brentford and Tottenham boss Frank.

Draw and Arbeloa may limp on until next weekend’s trip to Coventry City – a third consecutive fixture against a newly-promoted club. That all three of those teams have all made decent starts only adds to the current sense of dread around Craven Cottage.

Alvaro Arbeloa has been described as a 'dead man strutting' by a source close to the Fulham dressing room

Fulham are bottom of the Premier League after six games and still waiting for their first win

Fulham owner Shahid Khan and his son Tony – who, while juggling other roles in wrestling and the NFL, is the club’s controversial director of football – are said to be ‘worried’ but also reluctant to make any early managerial change.

Especially given that they took such a leap of faith on Arbeloa, along with his three Real recruits – striker Gonzalo Garcia and the lightweight midfield duo of Cesar Palacios and Manuel Angel.

In the post-match press conference at Portman Road, Arbeloa further enraged large sections of the Fulham fanbase by playing the Real card.

Asked about the pressure of his predicament, he responded: 'Maybe you don't know me, but I have played for the best team in the world and I have coached the best team in the world. Maybe you don't know, but just to let you know that pressure is part of my life since I was a kid.'

Such confidence – bordering on arrogance – has been noted by his players, hence the ‘dead man strutting’ comment. While a struggling side need a manager to show self-belief, some players feel Arbeloa is covering up for the fact he is simply unsuited to the job at hand.

At Friday morning’s pre-match media conference, however, Arbeloa was far more contrite – insisting the Hull match is ‘not about me’ and admitting to his own errors against Ipswich.

Some senior players have had serious misgivings about Arbeloa’s tactics and training since the off – and these have only grown during a dismal start to the season.

Three players expressed dissatisfaction with the club on social media after the Craven Cottage crowd turned toxic in the aftermath of last month’s 3-2 home defeat by Crystal Palace, when Fulham twice squandered leads and conceded two shambolic second-half goals before supporters on the Hammersmith End erupted into cries of ‘what the f***ing hell was that?’ at the final whistle.

There is a general sense of dread at Craven Cottage at how the season is going to unfold

Fulham's players have not been impressed by Arbeloa's tactics and training methods

Alex Iwobi was booed by Fulham fans when he was withdrawn late on. He and fellow former Arsenal player Emile Smith Rowe took down all Fulham mentions from their Instagram accounts, while Brazilian winger Kevin posted a cryptic message of the three wise monkeys with the words ‘no hear, no speak, no see’. This post, in particular, is said to have angered Arbeloa.

A former Real and Liverpool defender, Arbeloa was part of Spain’s all-conquering side which won three straight major international tournaments between 2008 and 2012. His playing credentials were beyond doubt.

Yet as a coach, he progressed through Real’s age-group teams to manage second-string Castilla – who compete in the third tier of Spanish football. When Xabi Alonso left the Bernabeu in January, Arbeloa stepped up as manager for a four-month stint, yet Real ended the season without silverware, finishing eight points adrift of champions Barcelona and knocked out of the Copa del Rey by lower-league Albacete.

At Castilla, Arbeloa helped nurture Garcia, Palacios and Angel, who all played under him during his brief spell as Real’s first-team boss. There is a feeling among some Fulham players that he has shown too much faith in that inexperienced trio since arriving in west London.

Garcia, who is quick and strong but not a target man, has started every league match. He scored on his debut, a 3-2 home defeat by Chelsea, but has missed several decent chances while failing to find the net since.

Palacios, a slightly-built, technically-gifted midfielder, started the first three league matches – which all ended in defeat. Yet after a man-of-the-match display in a Carabao Cup win at West Ham, he has not featured in Fulham’s last two games.

The tiny Angel – officially 5ft 7in – was handed his Premier League debut as a substitute in the 71st minute at Ipswich, replacing the impressive and physical Shea Charles with Fulham attempting to defend a one-goal lead.

If that move was met with incredulity, then the subsequent decision to bring on a second striker, Rodrigo Muniz, and swich to a 4-4-2 formation while clinging to a slender lead, was even more difficult to fathom.

Fulham's Kenny Tete looks broken after his side conceded two late goals against Ipswich last weekend to lose 2-1

Cesar Palacios (right) put in a man-of-the-match display in a Carabao Cup win at West Ham but has not featured in Fulham’s last two matches

Fulham had been ahead on every metric until those changes, which led to their late collapse and have caused widespread alarm about Arbeloa’s in-game decision-making, including among some members of his squad.

After the match, goalscorer Ryan Sessegnon damningly spoke of a problem with the team’s ‘mentality’.

When asked about these substitutions on Friday, Arbeloa admitted: 'Maybe I was wrong. Maybe it was my fault that we lost the game – not because of the players but because of me, I can accept that analysis.'

Fulham had already surrendered leads against Palace and given up a late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Manchester United.

All of Arbeloa’s senior coaching staff are Spanish and arrived at the club with him. Some speak of a ‘disconnect’ between them and Fulham’s players, staff and supporters. They trained the players especially hard in pre-season, with an expectation that Fulham would be one of the fittest, hardest-running and highest-pressing teams in the League.

That energetic, attacking style was apparent in the opening three matches but Arbeloa’s side were wide open defensively. A goalless draw at Anfield showed a willingness to compromise on his attacking ideals – but the Ipswich defeat has turned the majority of Fulham’s fanbase against the Spaniard.

Arbeloa succeeded Marco Silva, one of the most successful managers in Fulham’s recent history – who apparently blindsided the Khans by leaving to take charge at Benfica in June when the owners claim they had expected him to sign a new contract.

Alex Iwobi has taken down all Fulham mentions from his Instagram account after being booed by the fans

This is Fulham’s eighth Premier League campaign since the Khan takeover of 2013. In four seasons under Silva, they enjoyed four comfortable mid-table finishes. In the first three seasons under other managers, Fulham were relegated by a distance. In the fourth, they are winless and bottom.

In all four top-flight campaigns under Silva, Fulham threatened to qualify for Europe only to dip from March onwards and miss out. The Portuguese valued experience over youth and consistently fielded the oldest starting line-up in the Premier League.

And his three most expensive signings – Smith Rowe, Kevin and former Manchester City wide player Oscar Bobb, signed for a combined £94million – have all struggled to make an impact. Last season’s leading goalscorers, Harry Wilson and Raul Jimenez, left on free transfers in the summer.

So a refresh was certainly needed but a revolution based on the idea of turning London’s oldest professional football club into Real Madrid Lite always felt like a reckless punt.

Dave Kidd is the editor of Fulham site Saturday White Fever. Go to: saturdaywhitefever.counterpress.media

#710. Former Man United striker Fraizer Campbell reveals crippling snus addiction during his Premier League playing days that left him 'constantly fatigued'

Published: 19:26 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 17:32 BST, 17 October 2026

Former Premier League forward Fraizer Campbell has revealed snus left him 'constantly fatigued' after becoming addicted during his playing career.

Campbell played for Manchester United in the Premier League after coming through the club’s academy, while he also spent time at Tottenham, Hull, Sunderland, Cardiff and Crystal Palace during his career.

The forward told the Sports Agents he was first introduced to snus – a tobacco-based nicotine product that users place between their upper lip and gumline – during his time at Palace, who he represented from 2014-17.

Campbell explained that he was initially introduced to snus by a team-mate and began using it to try to relax after matches.

'I felt relaxed, and it just chilled me out more than anything,' Campbell said.

'It was after a game as well, and after a game is, you know, it's one of them things that it's quite hard to relax after.

Ex-Man United star Fraizer Campbell has revealed he was addicted to snus during his career

'It started off just after games, then training sessions, but that is how it starts and then you have the addiction and you are having them more and more.'

Campbell admitted that he would regularly suffer a 'slump in the afternoon' when he felt exhausted after becoming addicted to snus.

The former forward, now 39, explained that while he initially used snus to relax after matches, he increasingly began using it before training sessions.

'I definitely was addicted, but yeah, obviously, when I had more time on my hands when I retired, I had more time to have the snus,' Campbell said.

'So obviously, in the morning, while I was playing, I might have one in the morning or two in the morning and then for the next couple of hours I'd be out on the training pitch.

'I would never have them on a match day. Because, you know, it chilled me out too much, and I was someone that I'm pretty chill person as it is. If I was more chilled, I'd struggle to get into a jog.

'It got a lot worse after I finished playing football, but I didn't really see the negative side of it while I was playing.'

Campbell added that he is now 'six months clean' after tackling his addiction after feeling 'constantly fatigued'.

Campbell said he first tried snus while at Crystal Palace as he tried to relax after matches, but gradually began using it before training sessions as he became addicted

A study commissioned by the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) in 2024 found that one in five top-level players were using snus, nicotine pouches or both.

There are concerns that the use of both substances has been linked to a variety of health issues, with the report claiming that users can develop nicotine dependency, 'an increased risk of oesophagus and pancreatic cancer compared to non-smokers', as well as oral health issues and cardiovascular problems.

The PFA earlier this month launched a confidential support pathway to help its members overcome reliance on snus, nicotine pouches and vapes.

'Nicotine use is a growing trend among players right now. We know because we worked with Loughborough University on a world-first study to assess the scale of the issue in professional football,' the PFA said.

'Our research found that while the use of snus and nicotine pouches is high among players, most who use them would prefer to stop.'

#716. Celtic boss O'Neill insists a future Hearts title triumph would be a shot in the arm for Scottish football

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 22:30 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 22:57 BST, 16 October 2026

MARTIN O'NEILL believes it would be a huge boost to Scottish football if Hearts were to win the league title in the near future.

Hearts were top of the league for much of last season and came within minutes of making history and clinching a first title in 66 years.

They were ultimately denied on the final day by O'Neill's Celtic on what proved to be the most incredible - and controversial - finish to the campaign.

Hearts investor Tony Bloom spoke earlier this week and reaffirmed his belief that the Tynecastle club should win the league within the next 10 years.

Now into their second season working with Bloom's Jamestown Analytics firm, Hearts have once again made a good start to the campaign.

They sit third in the table ahead of tomorrow's grudge match with Celtic which sees them return to Parkhead for the first time since that infamous day last May.

O'Neill insists he is full of admiration for what Hearts are doing - and agrees with Bloom that they are likely to be champions at some point in the next decade.

O'Neill hoists the Premiership trophy aloft after beating Hearts on the final day of last season

Callum Osmand completed Celtic's turnaround to spark wild celebrations at Parkhead

Asked whether he felt it was possible, O'Neill said: 'I do, yeah, I do. I think their recruitment is really good. I think that what they've done has put pressure on Celtic and Rangers. They're a definite challenge.

'They kept going all last season. That was a big, big effort. They kept going and they took it right to the last couple of minutes. Are they capable of doing it? Yeah.

'I think that they've got a certain system in place at this minute, which has been used down at Brighton. They used it there and they're scouring the European scene for these things.

'I thought in the opening game of the season against Aberdeen there might have been just a bit of a hangover from last season.

'I think they've put that to bed and I think they've come roaring back. I think they're capable of winning the league even before that.

'If you're looking at it from a neutral viewpoint I think it's only a great thing for Scottish football, that the Old Firm is being challenged in a big, big way.

'Rightly so. So it should be as well. Hearts have taken on that and I think they're here to stay.

'I have a lot of admiration for it. I really do. I have a great admiration for the way they stuck at it last season, the whole way through.

'Considering that they were up there all that time. You're up there, you're looking down, you feel as if: "Oh gosh, could it happen". They kept it going right to the end.

'Okay, so they've lost the manager (Derek McInnes) and lost a couple of players as well. But I genuinely feel that they're a strong challenge. I think that can only be good.

'They went so, so close. I think inevitably they were going to lose a couple of players. If you're thinking about the big centre-forward (Lawrence Shankland) that has gone to Rangers and things like that.

'But I think they've recruited really well and I just think they're physically very strong, again, which they were last season. Yeah, they are definitely challengers.'

Tony Bloom's investment and analytics have helped make Hearts into title contenders

Following Celtic's title win on the final day last season, O'Neill came under fire for comments he made about the subsequent pitch invasion.

He and Bloom were locked in a war of words at one point over allegations that some of the Hearts players had been assaulted.

O'Neill was asked whether his views on it all had changed in the months that have passed or whether he stood by what he said at the time, despite the widespread condemnation of the pitch invasion.

It was confirmed last month that Police Scotland had charged a man over an assault that took place at the match, with another Celtic fan also handed a two-year ban for accosting Shankland.

Asked for his own reflections on it all, O'Neill said: 'I've often said about how it finished and the answer is I'm happy how it finished. Listen, we won it. We won it.

'And Derek's comments when the sound thing was picked up, he said he told the referee to blow it up.

'So I was asked by Jim White "did it tarnish things?" Well, not for me. It didn't, honestly. I thought it was fantastic.

'We cleared the pitch. People thought it was half an hour before we cleared the pitch but it was in less than three minutes at the end of it all.

'If I turn around and say to you one more time, if this is the last time that the crowd invades the pitch for a moment like that, anywhere in the world, I'll be really surprised.'

Celtic fans invaded the pitch at full time but O'Neill defended them afterwards

Pressed on the fact he took criticism for his comments on the pitch invasion, O'Neill replied: 'I don't care. I couldn't care less.

'I think I say too much at the end of the day. But absolutely not. If Hearts had won and their fans had come onto the pitch - I'm telling you now, and it's easy for me to say this - I would have accepted that.

'Because it's the first time they would have won the league for years and years and years and the euphoria of doing that there would have been there. Of course.

'And would we have been disappointed? Absolutely, to lose on your own pitch as well. All of those things.

'But if you take the bigger picture at the end of the day, if they had won - and they were very, very close to doing it - and their crowd had come on to celebrate with their players that is something I would have accepted. It's easy me saying that, but that's how I feel.

'I think it was one of the great days. Listen, whatever happens this year, you can't take that away. It was fantastic and to me it was up there with any moment in my managerial time.'

Celtic will be wounded on the back of a 4-1 thrashing against Benfica in the Europa League in Lisbon on Thursday night, with Hearts drawing 1-1 at home to Nordsjaelland in the Conference League.

O'Neill was determined to take the positives from an improved showing in the second half, despite the fact his team were 3-0 down after little more than half an hour.

O'Neill insisted he has no concerns over Kasper Hogh's form after the £11million striker endured another difficult night.

Hogh hit the post from close range against Benfica as his struggles continued

Hogh has been a disappointment so far and missed a glorious chance at the back post against Benfica when he hit the post from barely a yard out.

'It was always going to be a difficult game,' said O'Neill. 'We could have crumbled and we didn't. I take encouragement from that.

'I really do, genuinely, from the way the side played in the second half. It was more like us. It was tough. I knew it was going to be a tough game.

'It's not bravado, I just feel as though we can still make it, if we win our home games.

'It would have been nice if he (Hogh) had scored that goal. Because at the end of it all centre-forwards or strikers live or die by goals. They really do. And if you've not scored for a while and you miss the opportunity...

'That was a good chance to score on Thursday night. But overall, over the course of the season, I think he'll be absolutely fine. At this minute, he just needs a goal because it does give you a big boost of confidence.'

#728. Peter Schmeichel explains 'clumsy' Lisandro Martinez interview after Man United fans claimed he 'tried to shift the conversation' to 'the good news' after Argentine's explosive outburst

Published: 20:54 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 21:03 BST, 16 October 2026

Peter Schmeichel has conceded his interview with Lisandro Martinez was 'clumsy' following criticism from Man United supporters, after admitting he was caught by surprise when he was presented with the chance to speak to the defender.

Martinez delivered an extraordinary outburst to Amazon Prime accusing Manchester United's chiefs of lacking ambition in the transfer market after his side suffered a 2-0 defeat against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday night.

After his explosive post-match interview, Martinez had joined Man United legend Schmeichel on American network CBS Sports and continued to hit out at the board for failing to build a suitably competitive squad for the season.

Several Red Devils fans were unimpressed by Schmeichel's line of questioning during the interview, disappointed that he appeared to try and find a 'positive' to soften Martinez's attack on the board.

Speaking on the Overlap, Schmeichel revealed he had not been due to interview Martinez post-match and that the defender had been presented to him moments after giving his explosive comments.

Peter Schmeichel has admitted his interview with Lisandro Martinez was 'clumsy' after the former Man United star was criticised by supporters for his 'positive' approach

Schmeichel revealed he had not been due to interview Martinez and was caught by surprise, while admitting he was unaware of his explosive comments moments before to Amazon

'It’s a little bit of a weird one. When I do my job in the Champions League, I do a couple of pieces to camera from the touchline about the atmosphere, and afterwards I go to the flash zone and do interviews,' Schmeichel said.

'You build relationships with the media people from the different clubs, and you can say you want to speak to him or him, but at the end of the day they’re not solely in charge of who you get to speak to, because the UEFA also has media people on.

'There’s one responsible for every team, then there’s one above them, and everything has to go through them.

'When this happened, I was next to TNT Sports, and Gabriel [Clarke] interviewed Martínez. That interview is where everything came out. I knew he was there, but he wasn’t on my list. I wasn’t interviewing him at all. I’d asked for somebody else.

'That interview finished, and they pushed him into mine. So, when you look at the interview, I’m a little bit surprised. At that point I didn’t know what he’d said.

'Then in my interview he says, "We should do a lot better." He’s carrying on from that interview, but I don’t know what he’s saying. Because he’s speaking to a former player, I thought he was saying that we, as players, should do a lot better.

'I had no clue he was on the attack the way he was. I didn’t understand that he was saying all that, so in a way my interview became a little bit clumsy in the greater scheme of things.'

Schmeichel, who won the Champions League in 1999 during Man United's historic Treble-winning season, had begun his interview by asking Martinez to explain the team’s poor run of form having gone five games without a win.

Martinez will be in Man United's squad on Sunday after apologising to Man United chiefs for his comments

Martinez responded by again taking aim at the board by criticising the size of United's squad, insisting a lack of depth makes it difficult to compete.

'The rotation in the team, we have many games and have to rotate players. For me, we don't have the best squad,' Martinez said. 'For sure, when you watch the television, you see the player and the manager and you point the finger, which is right - we take responsibility - but also as a club I expect more.

'I'm not going to close my mouth. We need more ambition, we need to talk more about winning Champions Leagues, winning Premier Leagues.'

To that, Schmeichel responded: 'But the good news is that we're only in October, there's a long way to go.' Cutting him off, Martinez interjected: 'Yes, but every season we are saying the same thing. If we don't say the truth, nothing will change.'

Martinez will be in United's squad to face Leeds at Elland Road on Sunday after he apologised for criticising director of football Jason Wilcox and club bosses in a television interview which landed the 28-year-old defender with a fine.

On Thursday evening, after talks with United, Martinez shared a social media post apologising.

'Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager,' he said: 'It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday's game.

'Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity.

'The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.'

#732. McInnes thrilled at hunger of his Rangers squad as he reveals that players turned down chance to take a day off after international break

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 18:39 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 18:42 BST, 16 October 2026

IT'S always easy for players to talk about their unstinting commitment to the cause and being prepared to go the extra yard. Proving it is a different matter.

When Derek McInnes addressed his squad following last week's victory over Kilmarnock, he recognised that, for the majority in the room, the international break had been anything but a chance to rest up.

Hard miles were travelled and tough matches were played across the globe before they reconvened and got back down to club business.

Sensing that a belated day off at the start of this week might be welcomed by all concerned, the Rangers manager anticipated the offer being taken without debate. The response was not what he was expecting.

'I gave a lot of them the option to take Monday off because they had been travelling,' he explained.

'And not one of them took it. They all came in.

'They came in, did the work and did the recovery. We thought it was an opportunity for them just not to think about football, be with their families and all the rest of it.

'But they all came in, barring one or two who had felt the effects of the bug that was going about.'

McInnes was delighted to see his players refuse a day off following a long international break

The Rangers boss won the Premiership's Manager of the Month award for September

Players voluntarily forgoing a day off because they enjoy being at their place of work so much? Something that must surely be encouraging?

'Yeah, unless their family lives are not great and they want to come into work. I've played with plenty of players like that,' McInnes smiled.

'They had the option to come in. It wasn't a test. For me, it was genuinely about taking the time off if they wanted it.

'They all responded on Sunday to the message in the group chat saying they wanted to be in, which was good. We've tried to look after those ones because they have been away for so long.'

It's this buy-in to McInnes' ideas which has helped to turn things around. At the end of August, with league points being spilled and two European defeats chalked up, a new-look squad was in a dark place.

They travel to Dens Park this evening seeking to claim a seventh straight league win for the first time in three years with optimism steadily growing around the club.

The improvement has been fuelled by the desire of the raft of new faces to succeed in a new environment.

For those who saw the side rally after a poor start last season then collapse after the split, there's also a motivation to atone for what happened.

McInnes hails Ryan Naderi after his winner at Celtic Park just before the international break

Not normally the most vocal of characters, Dujon Sterling recently laid bare his angst.

'When I first came in, I had conversations with a lot of the lads who were here last season,' said McInnes.

'He was one of the lads who still had a grievance about how last season played out. He was still annoyed at how Rangers had allowed themselves not to be right down the line and go to the last few games.

'He was honest enough about that and said it was down to them as players.

'I would like to think that the players coming back for pre-season had that grievance and were ready not to let it happen again. They had to be ready to step on.'

After an inauspicious start, the road to redemption began with a scrappy win at Aberdeen.

Three further narrow victories over Falkirk, Motherwell and St Mirren duly arrived. Then came that thumping 3-0 win over Celtic in the League Cup - a display which came with bells and whistles attached.

A follow-up win in the league at Parkhead was no less impressive for the tighter scoreline. Any fears that the international break would prove to be a rude interruption on the progress were washed away with a comfortable win over Kilmarnock last weekend.

Seven wins on the spin with six coming in the Premiership. The best league run since the early days of Michael Beale's tenure when 10 victories were chalked up at the start of 2023.

Kevin Kelsy celebrates making it 2-0 as Rangers cruised to a win over Kilmarnock

A far cry, certainly, from those early weeks of McInnes' reign when you wondered where all of this was going to end up.

'We've got to make sure we're maximising the effort and the mindset all the time, ready to go for the next challenge,' the manager stressed.

'The next challenge is just around the corner tomorrow in Dundee and the game is going to need our full attention.

'We were pleased that we managed to have a home game last week on the back of all the disruption.

'We've got to understand now that when we go away from home against a team in good form, who have started well, we have to be ready for it.

'Having the players in this week has allowed us to go into the game in better shape. It doesn't guarantee anything, of course, but once the game starts, hopefully we can deliver a big performance.

'We can't have the performance we had in the second half last week. The drop-off was too big, although there were maybe a lot of reasons for that.

'There will be no reason for that this week. It's up to us to deliver a big performance and recognise that we need to get more. We need to keep stepping on the gas and deliver the big performances we're looking for.'

While Dundee haven't beaten Rangers at Dens Park since 2017-18, the Ibrox men have drawn three times in that corner of Tayside since.

Despite a crippling injury list, Steven Pressley's side have been the surprise package of the season to date, defeating Motherwell and Falkirk either side of the international break.

Sitting in fourth spot after eight matches, they have good reason to believe that a famous night awaits.

'Very good,' McInnes said of the Dark Blues' campaign so far. 'I know a lot of the staff there and I know how they work. They look like a good staff and I think they've got a good thing going.

'I had Yan Dhanda on loan there last year and he spoke really positively about how they worked.

'What they've done is cope with injuries themselves. It was mentioned earlier that we've had major injuries, but I think they've had six, seven or eight out at a time in recent weeks.

'They still managed to go to Falkirk and win the game, and they were strong in the game.

'They've committed to a system this season with two strikers, two wide players who work off shape, two sixes and two overlapping full-backs. You can see what they're trying to do.

'They also have the ability to mix the game up. They've got good physicality, decent strength and experience in the right areas.'

Real Madrid have called for the resignation of La Liga president Javier Tebas after he compared methods used by the club's management to Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.

Real Madrid have called for La Liga president Javier Tebas to resign after he suggested the club have employed techniques used by Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels

'The comparison is with those propaganda techniques, not with an ideology or, of course, with the Madridista fanbase. Real Madrid TV is a central piece of that machinery. Where is the full match analysis for each round of games?

'Where are the possible errors that harm other clubs or those that favor Real Madrid? If they applied the same magnifying glass to every match, the result might ruin their script. But the script demands that Real Madrid always appear as the victim.'

Real Madrid responded in a lengthy statement with the club declaring Tebas's reference to Goebbels, who served as the Third Reich's Minister of Propaganda between 1933 and 1945, was 'deeply offensive' and 'morally repugnant.'

Barcelona have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, claiming the money was paid for scouting and technical reports provided by a company belonging to 81-year-old Negreira since the story broke in 2023.

La Liga claimed they were unable to investigate because of the time elapsed since the alleged offences were so far in the past, but UEFA did launch an investigation which remains ongoing.

Real Madrid and Tebas have frequently clashed in the past, with the latest incident coming with the Spanish giants having complained about refereeing decisions in recent matches.

Tebas had claimed last month the club were creating a 'permanent conspiracy' about officiating.

'I've lost count of the times that, in thirteen years, Real Madrid's leaders have demanded my resignation or tried to disqualify me: complaints to the CSD, directly or through third parties, criminal lawsuits… Today's is just another one,' he wrote.

'What still hasn't arrived are the responses. They confuse neutrality with independence. My position demands independence, not passivity in the face of injustice or silence in the face of the continuous, disproportionate, and insulting attacks from Real Madrid TV and its lapdogs on our competition.

'The LaLiga president must defend it. Including against Real Madrid's leaders.

'My conclusion: they seek to DESTROY the national competition. What they haven't achieved so far with the Superliga, they're trying with a distorted narrative from their media and their lapdogs. They call it regeneration while attacking the prestige of the competition they participate in.'

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 16:52 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 17:53 BST, 16 October 2026

Derek McInnes says he shares Andrew Cavenagh's desire for a calm January transfer window at Rangers.

The Ibrox chairman met with the Fan Advisory Board last weekend and informed supporters that he didn't expect any significant activity – unless unforeseen circumstances forced the club to go into the market.

After a busy summer which saw 14 new faces arrive at the club, McInnes has a handful of players presently injured including Lawrence Shankland, Cammy Devlin, Daisuke Yokota and Youssef Chermiti – with Ross McCrorie also now out for a few weeks with a hamstring issue.

But with all of those apart from the Portuguese forward set to return before the end of the year, the Rangers manager concurs with Cavenagh's view that further wholesale changes won't be needed.

'I think we can cope in terms of numbers,' he said.

'The conversations I've had with both Andrew and Jim (Gillespie, chief executive) separately were a couple of weeks ago, after the Celtic game.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes insists he is happy with his squad

Rangers are in fine form ahead of their trip to face Dundee on Saturday night

'We spoke about the need for January to be calm and not to become an unsettling month for us. We spoke about the importance of keeping the squad together. We feel that, by the beginning of December, we could have the boys I've just mentioned back fit.

'That will feel like signing three new players with Cammy, Daisuke and Lawrence bolstering the squad. What the chairman said reflects the conversation we've had. We don't expect to be busy in January at all.

'For me, that's really good to hear and good to work towards. Hopefully, the players can just work towards this season and we can be as strong as we can.

'Obviously, the window gives you the opportunity to deal with injuries, loss of form or whatever. These things are always there.

'But unless there's a figure that comes in way over the top for any of the players, I think there's a feeling from everybody, and obviously the chairman has said it, that we want to maintain what we've got in the building.'

Rangers take on in-form Dundee at Dens Park on Saturday evening with McInnes' men again having the opportunity to move to the top of the table before Celtic and Hearts play at Parkhead on Sunday.

Now without European football, Rangers will again play first next weekend against St Johnstone with Celtic and Hearts travelling to face Hibs and Motherwell, respectively.

But with the first lap of the track still to be completed in the Premiership race, the Rangers manager feels it's much too early to be talking about applying pressure to title rivals.

'For me, you've still just got to win your game at the weekend,' he added.

'Whenever you're asked to play, whether it's a Friday, Saturday, Sunday or Monday, you've just got to try to win your game. It's a bit early in the season to be looking too much into that. I think we're all kind of used to it.

'Of course, we would rather be in Europe. There was a wee bit of envy watching last night.

'At the same time, the only real benefit from not being involved, and the only time you feel good about yourself, is if we can be successful domestically.

'It gives us longer to prepare for games, but it doesn't guarantee anything. The fact that we're playing first this time around, I won't even mention putting pressure on our opposition.

'I'm more focused on the fact that we need to improve, win more games and concentrate on trying to get another three points.

'I think that approach serves us well. It has done in recent weeks. It's about taking small steps, winning your game and not being too obsessed with what's happening elsewhere.'

A recent addition, the Saturday night fixture slot in the top flight isn't to everyone's liking.

But McInnes said: 'I like them, to be honest.

'I think the atmospheres are always good. It can be a long day waiting for it, but we know it's there. We'll travel up to Dundee in the morning, Saturday night under the lights, live on TV, a full house and Dundee going well ... we've got our work cut out to get a result.

'I think you enjoy all these night games, whether it's a Friday night or a Saturday night. In the past, they've been good occasions, but you're only going to enjoy them if you win.

'It's important that we're ready for it, but I'm looking forward to it.'
