Christian Horner has opened up on his 'brutal' Red Bull sacking and reflected on the support of wife Geri Halliwell during his 'sex texts' scandal.

Horner, 52, was dismissed as CEO and Team Principal in July 2025 after 20 years in the role following an internal power struggle and a decline in form.

He received a £67million severance payment, as Daily Mail Sport reported last week, with his exit coming a year after he was cleared of misconduct amid a texting scandal with a female employee.

Horner has always denied the claims and was twice cleared of any impropriety in internal investigations at Red Bull, despite a tranche of supposedly intimate text exchanges between the pair – including messages and photographs – being made public in an explosive email sent to F1 figures before the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

His sacking was unrelated to that, but speaking to The Guardian after Max Verstappen made it back-to-back Grand Prix victories for Red Bull in Malaysia and Singapore over the past two weeks, Horner opened up on the pain it caused.

'It felt particularly brutal and sad to finish in that manner,' Horner said. 'But I now have a reasonable relationship with Oliver Mintzlaff [the CEO of corporate projects at Red Bull]. He rang the other day and thanked me for all I’d done for the engine.

Christian Horner has opened up on his 'brutal' sacking as Red Bull Team Principal last year

Horner, pictured with wife Geri Halliwell, was embroiled in a sex texts scandal in 2024. He was cleared of any impropriety in two internal investigations and always denied the claims

'It was very strange because that group became your extended family. So the tears on grown men’s faces was deeply moving.'

Horner also revealed outside circumstances made his departure 'very painful', with his ex-wife Beverley Allen having passed away due to eye cancer just a week before.

The 52-year-old shared a daughter, Olivia, with Beverley, and the pair had remained on good terms after splitting.

He added: 'I didn’t really process it (my departure) until a month later because, in the immediate aftermath, I focused on supporting my daughter through a hideous period.'

In some ways though, the exit brought 'relief' to Horner, who is now married to former Spice Girl Geri Halliwell.

'The last two years had been pretty tough but it was a particularly sensitive time, with the bereavement of my daughter’s mum the previous week,' Horner said. 'I had an 11-year-old child grieving her mother. Nothing was more important than that.'

He also insisted his dismissal 'was more focused on performance and the future' after 'coming through' the 2024 allegations, but was full of praise for Halliwell's role throughout that saga.

'My wife was a pillar of support throughout and I just had to believe in the process,' he added.

Horner went on to express his pride at what he achieved at Red Bull over 20 years, with the constructor winning six championships during that time, while Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen both won four world titles in a row.

But, things became more difficult after the death of Red Bull founder Dietrich Mateschitz in 2022.

Mateschitz had always been a big supporter of Horner, but the 52-year-old then appeared to be regularly undermined by Helmut Marko, a key consultant for Red Bull, and Jos Verstappen, father of Max, amid a power struggle at the team.

During Horner's 20-year stint at Red Bull, the team enjoyed an incredible run of success

Horner refused to criticise Jos, but expressed his disappointment at Marko for giving 'no indication this was coming' in relation to his dismissal.

Horner's arrival back in 2005 had also come after the shock dismissals of then-Red Bull Team Principal Tony Purnell and Managing Director David Pitchforth.

When asked about the comparison with his own exit, the 52-year-old added: 'History repeats itself. Not all teams act in that way. A lot of teams haven’t delivered over the years but you don’t see the same brutality as when I left. We had pole position at the previous race.'

Horner insisted he remains excited by Formula One and would be attracted by a return to the sport, but insisted he would only come back 'for the right opportunity with like-minded people that want to win'.

#764. There is a fine line between defiance and delusion ... Anything less than a win against Hearts will make O'Neill's continued presence as Celtic manager increasingly difficult to defend

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 15:01 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 15:06 BST, 16 October 2026

Deep in the bowels of the Estadio da Luz, Martin O’Neill took his seat in his media conference, cleared his throat, and tried to pick the bones out of another chastening night in Europe.

The language and tone used by O’Neill didn’t really square with a team who had just been hammered 4-1 by Benfica and now sit without any points after their opening two matches in the Europa League.

Nor did it really tally with the reality of what happened on a night when Celtic folded like a pack of cards during a dismal first half and were 3-0 down after 36 minutes in Lisbon.

O’Neill insisted that he took solace from his team’s performance in the second half and encouragement from the fact they fought back and tried to make a game of it.

‘We could have capitulated, but I thought in the second half we were terrific,’ claimed O’Neill. ‘We created chance after chance. It’s not bravado on my part, I genuinely do believe we can still qualify.’

Granted, Celtic were better in the second half. That much was true. But it wasn’t an especially high bar given how atrocious they had been in the opening 45 minutes.

O’Neill sounded like a man clutching at straws, desperately trying to put a positive spin on what had been another damaging night in Europe.

Manager Martin O'Neill and assistant Shaun Maloney look on as Celtic suffer in Lisbon

Whether or not he truly believes Celtic were ‘terrific’, only he will know. But the fact he chose to say it publicly only demonstrated how standards have fallen.

This is a manager who once elevated this club to the most extraordinary heights in Europe, now reduced to finding comfort in a belated response from his players after the contest had already been lost.

Benfica were three goals up by half-time. Jhon Duran converted a fifth-minute penalty after Dane Murray’s clumsy foul, Alexander Bah was left unmarked to make it two, and Duran added a third before the break.

Celtic’s defending was soft, reactive and all too familiar. Only then, with the game effectively over, did O’Neill’s side begin to play with any real intensity or purpose.

Camilo Duran headed a consolation just after the hour and struck a post. Substitutes offered energy. Chances came and went.

Having taken their foot off the gas, Benfica still scored a fourth late on through Vangelis Pavlidis. The final score flattered the visitors only in the sense that it could have been much, much worse.

Former Celtic striker Chris Sutton branded his old club ‘flat-track bullies’. The contrast between those words and those of O’Neill were stark and instructive.

It is easy to start playing when you are already three goals down. The pressure has eased off. Benfica were coasting. The fear of further embarrassment is replaced by the freedom to swing.

The simple reality is that Celtic are yet to win a big match this season. Both meetings with Rangers ended in defeat.

The European campaign opened with a home loss to Ferencvaros and has now continued with this heavy defeat in Portugal.

O'Neill was quick to emphasise Celtic's improved second-half performance against Benfica

They have conceded the most goals of any team in the Europa League so far this season. In their last three European matches taking it back to LASK Linz, they have shipped 12 goals.

Most damningly for O’Neill and his players, every high-stakes fixture this season has produced broadly the same outcome.

The league table may still offer some insulation in the sense that Celtic are still top, but the character of the performances in the games that matter most does not.

Standards have fallen dramatically. That is not hyperbole. Rather, it is the measurable truth of Celtic’s recent European record and their repeated failure to deliver when the opposition is organised, technically proficient, and clinical.

O’Neill’s first tenure at Celtic was built on raising those standards. His teams were hard to beat in Europe for a reason.

They did not wait until the game was gone before deciding to compete. They did not require the opposition to take their foot off the gas before showing their quality.

This current version of Celtic under the same manager appears to have inverted that principle. They can produce moments against lesser domestic opposition, such as against Motherwell last weekend.

They can respond when the scoreline has already condemned them to defeat. What they cannot do, so far, is impose themselves when the match is still there to be won or lost.

That is the definition of a side whose standards have slipped. O’Neill’s claim that the second half was ‘terrific’ only highlights the issue.

No manager should ever seek to excuse his players and give them credit for recovering from a hole they dug themselves with basic errors.

There is a fine line in these situations between defiance and delusion. O’Neill’s words on Thursday night in Lisbon sat uncomfortably close to the latter.

Praising a second-half display that arrived only after the contest was decided risks normalising the collapse that preceded it.

It risks telling the players that the real examination starts once the damage is done rather than before it. It is fundamentally not good enough.

Sunday’s home game against Hearts is no longer just another run-of-the-mill league fixture. For O’Neill and his players, there is now real jeopardy attached to this.

Hearts are not at the same level as Benfica. Then again, neither were Ferencvaros. Or Rangers. Or, indeed, LASK Linz for that matter.

Celtic need a win tomorrow and they need a performance which signifies some degree of progress is being made.

Auston Trusty despairs after Jhon Duran scores Benfica's second goal on Thursday night

Anything less will make O’Neill’s continued presence as manager increasingly difficult to defend. The 74-year-old would not be human if he didn’t have cause to reflect on his decision to stay on this season.

He remains a figure of genuine stature at Celtic Park. Only Jock Stein stands above him in the pantheon of the club’s all-time greatest managers.

But stature alone does not excuse results. It does not rewrite the record of repeated big-game failures this season. And it most certainly does not turn a 4-1 thrashing into some kind of positive PR spin.

O’Neill is entitled to take whatever encouragement he can from the second half in Lisbon. Managers always do.

The rest of us are entitled to notice that it only arrived once the game was gone, that Celtic remain without a win in a meaningful fixture this season, and that another failure against Hearts would leave precious little case for the defence of the current regime.

Defiance has its place. Delusion does not. Celtic and O’Neill are running out of room to tell the difference.

Published: 09:53 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 13:58 BST, 16 October 2026

Reece James is set to be out of action for around three months after having surgery on a knee injury sustained in training.

James, 26, missed his side’s 5-1 Premier League win over Bournemouth after the international break.

While he usually still travels with the squad on the team coach when injured, he did not do so for that victory, sparking concerns that there was more to his latest setback.

Now, Chelsea have confirmed that James has had a ‘successful minor’ operation, and will be without him for their league trip to Everton on Saturday and beyond.

In a statement, Chelsea said: ‘Captain Reece James has undergone successful minor knee surgery.

'The 26-year-old was absent from Saturday’s 5-1 victory over Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge while medical assessments took place following the injury suffered in training.

Reece James has undergone knee surgery after missing Chelsea's 5-1 win over Bournemouth

‘Those assessments confirmed surgery would be the required course of action. Reece has already begun his road to recovery and will be supported by the club's medical department at Cobham during this rehabilitation phase.

‘Everyone at Chelsea wishes Reece a speedy recovery and will support him on his road to return.’

Levi Colwill captained Chelsea against Bournemouth in James’ absence.

Xabi Alonso said on James: 'It's not going to be short. It's not going to be two or three weeks. It's going to be longer. We will see. Before Christmas, after Christmas, time will tell.

'But things have to be done properly, so that he feels right, and that means in the best possible condition. Yes, is it a disappointment for everyone, for him. But we have a squad for that to deal with injuries.'

On whether James' injury will force Chelsea to use the January window, Alonso added: 'No, I don't think so. We expect for that time that he is back. It doesn't affect (transfer business).'

James has an unfortunate history of injuries, largely due to hamstring issues. With that, Alonso had been morphing him into a midfielder rather than a right back.

In fact, James has missed 842 days of action, as per Transfermarkt, since he broke into Chelsea's first team during the 2019-20 season. That is the equivalent of 2.31 years or 99 games for club and country.

Given that record, Daily Mail Sport understands that Chelsea won't rush the 26-year-old back prematurely and will ensure he recovers fully before returning to action.

James suffered the injury in training and is set to miss around three months of action

James’ new problem robs Alonso of another midfield option, at a time when there were already concerns surrounding numbers in that central area.

Moises Caicedo is now back from being sidelined, which should help until January, when Chelsea are likely to try to add at least one reinforcement.

They are known to admire Alex Scott, though Bournemouth say they want more than £100million to sell him this winter.

Other midfield options for Alonso include the injury-prone Romeo Lavia, Valentin Barco, Jordan Henderson, full-back Malo Gusto and youngster Reggie Watson.

The Blues face Everton on Saturday lunchtime, before league games against Tottenham, Man United and Sunderland ahead of next month's international break.

#772. Burn down the mission: Inside the Watford 'circus' as Elton John leads irate fans in revolt - 'crazy' meddling from on high, players turning on executives, staff leaving 'unrecognisable' club and why Gino Pozzo is struggling to sell

Published: 12:30 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 12:41 BST, 16 October 2026

'Burn down the mission. Burn it down to stay alive. It's our only chance of living' -Elton John, Burn Down The Mission.

The pitchforks are out at Watford. The torches are lit. There’s no turning back now as they march to Vicarage Road. The mission is in their sights and they are, figuratively speaking, ready to burn it to the ground. For them, now, it’s their only chance to survive.

Over the past few days, Watford have come to discover that when it comes to his beloved football club, if Sir Elton John speaks out, soon does everyone else. They rise up and make their voices heard.

After the Hornets’ 4-0 defeat by Burnley at Vicarage Road, a team previously 241 days without a win, the legendary singer and former Watford chairman made his feelings known.

‘As a lifetime supporter of Watford FC, I am very upset and disappointed at the decline over the past few weeks,’ wrote Elton in a now-deleted comment to a club post on Instagram. ‘I really feel for the other supporters who have to watch this.’

In doing so, he lit the fire. Elton made no reference to the club’s ownership in his comment – and Daily Mail Sport understands he has been in contact with chairman Scott Duxbury since making it – but, suddenly, a fanbase that had long been simmering with malaise and discontent towards Gino Pozzo and the Watford board heard the rallying call they needed.

Sir Elton John lit a fire around his former club Watford this week, after another damaging defeat saw the Hornets slip into the Championship relegation zone

Watford have lost four games in a row, conceding 12 goals in the process and raising the heat on their owner Gino Pozzo

Out they came. Former captain Troy Deeney said the ‘writing was on the wall’. The Watford Supporters Board called for owners to give ‘urgent attention’ to the ‘deep concern’ fans had about their leadership. The club’s Supporters Trust backed their statement. Even the mayor got involved. The 1881 Movement, the supporters’ group behind the singing section in the Rookery Stand, issued an open letter of no confidence in Pozzo.

‘For too long now, Watford has been treated as a revolving door of managers, a testing ground for short-term decisions, and a vehicle for constant upheaval,’ it read. ‘The endless cycle of appointments and dismissals has reduced a once-proud club to a source of ridicule.’

Pozzo is due to meet Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement at the training ground today after the Watford owner became aware of the open letter and reached out via the club. Moore agreed on the proviso he could report back to supporters what was said. ‘Full transparency was the price of acceptance,’ he said.

Only three days earlier, Watford lost 5-1 to Cardiff, a fourth straight defeat that dropped them into the Championship relegation zone. By then, the supporters were already in full revolt.

In response to every club post on X, hundreds of fans replied with bright yellow squares with the words ‘Pozzo Out’ emblazoned across them. Streams and streams of them, forming their own yellow brick road.

Supporters in the ground sung anti-Pozzo chants. They will do so again at Vicarage Road on Saturday against Charlton, turning their backs and raising their scarves in the 14th minute in protest against 14 years of Pozzo ownership. They feel it is the only way to save the club, in the words of the final track of Elton's 1970 album Tumbleweed Connection, about a settler starting a revolt against the wealthy establishment, is to Burn Down The Mission.

The defeat in South Wales looked as if it might prompt that managerial door to revolve once more. Reports emerged mid-match that Alessio Dionisi, who only arrived in the summer, was for the chop and the Hornets would be looking for a 24th manager since Pozzo bought the club in June 2012 and their 14th since 2021. Their former manager Tom Cleverley, by the way, is currently top of League One with Plymouth.

As it happens, the club are sticking by Dionisi for now and he will take charge against Charlton on Saturday. The owners are said to recognise they have been too hasty with hirings and firings in the past and so will give the Italian more time.

That’s always the thing with Watford, though, you never know quite how much time that will be. It’s believed Pozzo was scouting out potential replacements over the weekend.

Two days after a supporter group published an open letter of no confidence in Pozzo, Watford lost 5-1 to Cardiff

Reports emerged mid-match that manager Alessio Dionisi was for the chop but Watford are sticking by the Italian... for now

Daily Mail Sport understands players and staff held a big meeting on the Sunday after the Burnley defeat at the club’s training ground to air their frustrations. While club sources were keen to play down the idea of ‘showdown’ talks, it’s understood senior players led by captain Mattie Pollock spoke up about the current form and launched a staunch defence of their manager. Dionisi is well-liked around the dressing room.

There were believed to be pointed comments made, too, towards Duxbury about his glowing remarks on Watford’s official podcast about young midfielder Jack Grieves – despite the 21-year-old only making a single matchday squad all season.

Grieves’ brother Ben even called into a phone-in on Watford fan podcast Do Not Scratch Your Eyes after the Cardiff defeat to complain about his lack of match action and to add his voice to calls for change.

‘Some players care, some players don’t,’ he said. ‘There is something seriously, seriously wrong with our football club at the minute and there has got to be something that changes.’

For the fans, it is clear what should change – the owner. Pozzo, who took over the club with his father in 2012 before having sole ownership two years later, has enjoyed great success in his time with six seasons in the Premier League and four trips to Wembley, including an FA Cup final. It was the club’s best run of success since the days of Graham Taylor, under Elton’s stewardship, in the 1980s.

And yet, since that historic day against Manchester City in 2019, the cracks have begun to appear and widen. The player trading model on which Watford is based, and previously led to huge profits on players like Richarlison and Joao Pedro, has gone stale. Recent signings from Udinese, Pozzo’s other club, haven’t fired as they once did.

The constant churn of players and managers leaves a place that describes itself as ‘the original family club’ feeling more like a hotel lobby which bodies merely pass through. Members of staff have left, with a heavy heart, a club they no longer recognise.

Gino Pozzo at the 2019 FA Cup final, which Watford lost 6-0 to Manchester City. Since that day the club has been on a gradual decline

The club’s summer business was described by recently departed midfielder Tom Ince as ‘soulless’

Watford's summer business, described by recently departed midfielder Tom Ince as ‘soulless’ in another incendiary interview by a former player, saw players arrive late in the window, miss chunks of pre-season, and soon pick up injuries.

The club barely spent a penny on their 12 summer transfers as they look to tighten the purse strings even more now that the parachute payments have dried up. The most recent accounts for 2024-25 showed Watford to be spending more on wages (£28m) than revenue (£26m), though the club are now understood to have one of the lowest wage bills in the Championship at around £14m.

Watford were in talks with former West Ham striker Michail Antonio throughout the summer but felt they couldn’t do a deal due to wage demands, only to bring him in on September 11. Antonio is yet to play a single minute.

The signing of former Monaco defender Krepin Diatta was seen as a huge coup for the club – ‘our point of difference, which other clubs don’t have, is our scouting network,’ said Duxbury on the club’s official podcast – only for the player's agent to suggest he’d had to settle for the Hornets after being rejected by clubs all summer for asking for excessive wages.

Ince’s comments poured yet more fuel on an already raging furnace. ‘From the outside you see Watford is a circus, but when you’re in it you kind of feel it too,’ he said on the BBC’s 72+ podcast. 'Circus' was the word used by another former player to Daily Mail Sport this week.

‘Players knew the manager wasn’t important,’ added Ince. ‘They would almost bypass the manager (and speak directly to the owner) as we knew he had no control.

‘Watford is built to be a Premier League team but they need to think, "Are we more bothered about profit or building a successful football team?" and not hire yes men who are told who to play, what systems to play, how training goes.’

There’s always been stories like that around Watford, of envelopes slipped under hotel room doors with team changes sent from on high. One source close to a former manager recalled players being signed without their knowledge. Daily Mail Sport heard a perhaps far-fetched tale this week of senior players receiving WhatsApp messages in the dressing room at half-time with substitute recommendations to pass on to the coach.

‘It’s crazy at that place,’ another former player told Daily Mail Sport this week. ‘I only expect it to get worse, sadly.’

Krepin Diatta was seen as a huge coup for the club, only for the player's agent to suggets he’d had to settle for the Hornets after being rejected by clubs all summer over wage demands

Burnley had not won all season when they turned up at Vicarage Road last week. They ran out 4-0 winners

As always with clubs in a downward spiral, it’s issues off the pitch that trickle on to the grass.

The club's ownership are understood to be open to offers. They have sold the women’s team to a US investment firm. The academy has been downgraded to Category 3 and its director, club legend Richard Johnson, has just left.

One agent told Daily Mail Sport they had been approached multiple times by interested parties asking for the best way in. However, the £175m valuation placed on the club, when it sought out £17.5m for a 10 per cent share a few years ago, seemed far too high. As the club is in a worse position now than it was then, such a figure is surely unrealistic now.

According to football finance analyst Swiss Ramble, Watford have repaid a Championship-high net £34m to their owners in the six years to 2024-25. The £53m still owed to them carries interest of up to 8.75 per cent, with £7.7m built up so far. The club's available cash appears to come almost entirely from player sales.

Watford were forced to pay out to a stewarding company in the summer, who had hit them with a winding-up petition. The club is also understood to have recently threatened legal action after questions were raised about its finances.

There’s still the uncomfortable relationship Watford has with agent Mogi Bayat, who they continue to do business with despite him awaiting trial in Belgium over charges including money laundering and fraud. Bayat denies all wrongdoing.

And then there’s Pozzo’s own court case in Spain next month, where he stands accused of evading more than £7.5m in tax on transfers while at Granada. A guilty verdict would see him fall foul of the Football League’s owners regulations. Pozzo's lawyers have said he 'refutes in the strongest possible terms that he has breached Spanish tax laws in any way'.

The message from the club is that patience is required and there’s no need to panic. Results will come and they always change the mood. For supporters, it’s too late for that. For them, they only have one way left to stay alive. Their only chance of living.

#776. Fixing Florian Wirtz: Why Liverpool's £116m man is making poor choices, the midfield rejig that could be the answer, the signs he's gelling with Alexander Isak and why insiders think Jurgen Klopp holds the key

Published: 12:10 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 12:35 BST, 16 October 2026

The last decade at Liverpool was all about making bargain signings look like £100million world-beaters. Recently, the problem for both Andoni Iraola and his predecessor Arne Slot has been the £100m-plus supposed world-beaters struggling to live up to their billing.

The Reds have broken the nine-figure barrier three times in the last 18 months, welcoming Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola for a combined £364m including add-ons. Between them, they have made 92 appearances and returned just 18 goals, which is admittedly a stat that – like most things in English football at the moment – needs a rather large asterisk alongside it.

Barcola’s midweek hat-trick showed signs he is trending upwards after a slow start, while Isak was in and out last term through injury and has already matched his goal tally this time around after a proper pre-season.

But what about Wirtz? He has featured in 39 of 44 possible league games since his arrival so cannot blame injuries and the German is not the new kid on the block anymore.

On Wednesday night he flourished at Austrian champions LASK in a 6-3 win. During the last Champions League round he gave another eye-catching performance against Atletico Madrid.

So why can't he translate his European form to the Premier League? How are Liverpool coaches planning to unlock Wirtz’s talents? And what do the experts back home in Germany, including a certain Jurgen Klopp, make of the conundrum?

Liverpool's £116m midfielder Florian Wirtz looks lost for answers against Manchester City as he puts in another ineffectual display

Wirtz was better against LASK in the Champions League in midweek but can't translate his form in Europe to the Premier League

The 23-year-old has shown glimpses of class in nearly every game he has played but the reason he is often chastised by pundits is a lack of consistency.

‘Wirtz never looks like scoring a goal,’ said Reds legend Jamie Carragher after last weekend's 3-0 loss to Manchester City. ‘You don’t come away thinking he missed chances or he worked the goalkeeper.

‘There was absolutely nothing today where you thought he put someone through, or nearly scored. There’s absolutely no goal threat whatsoever.

‘He needs to come out of the team. Liverpool played well for a lot of the game before the (Ryan) Gravenberch red card, but they didn't create a chance... and that's what you bought Wirtz for. He's not giving you anything defensively, and he's not giving you anything going the other way.’

When a player costs £116m, this criticism is natural. Since his Reds debut, 87 players have created more 'big chances' (as defined by Opta) in the Premier League. Wirtz has created just five in the league, or one every 7.8 games.

For comparison, Bruno Fernandes has created 34 big chances since Wirtz arrived in England. Rayan Cherki – who Liverpool also looked at but went to Manchester City for £81m less than Wirtz’s fee – has 22.

Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher has called for Wirtz to come out of the team

At Bayer Leverkusen, albeit in a weaker league, Wirtz scored 16 goals and assisted 15 more in his final season of 2024-25, with 18 goals and 20 assists in the title-winning season of 2023-24. He was the main man as Xabi Alonso’s side went unbeaten in domestic competitions.

‘He can control the game and the rhythm,’ Maximilian Koch, chief reporter for Abendzeitung told Daily Mail Sport at the time. ‘He reminds me of Andres Iniesta, a very intelligent and creative player. He can also score and assist, which makes him a complete player.’

Liverpool fans have not seen that yet and his confidence is clearly shot, with Wirtz often going through the motions in games and all too often making the poor choices. When a pass looks on, he will shoot; when he should pull the trigger, he looks for support.

The perfect example of this came in the loss against City when Wirtz took a shot that missed the target and prompted his team-mates to vent their fury. Milos Kerkez punched the air, Bradley Barcola stretched out his arms and Gravenberch puffed out his cheeks.

Not getting the best out of his big-money assets was the undoing of Slot. Had he not spent £446m after winning the title, fans – the majority of whom turned on the Dutchman and wanted him gone by the end – would have been more forgiving.

His replacement Iraola has impressed in many respects so far but has still not cracked the Wirtz code. So how does he plan to do it?

One option could be to alter the two who play behind him. The Basque manager’s system has one No6, one No8 and one No10 (Wirtz) but the deeper-lying duo have got in each other’s way at times this season.

Against LASK on Wednesday, with both of the usual duo Alexis Mac Allister and Dominik Szoboszlai not starting (the former rested, the latter injured), Liverpool’s midfield looked much more balanced – and Wirtz could thrive more than usual.

Against LASK, with neither Alexis Mac Allister nor Dominik Szoboszlai playing, Liverpool’s midfield looked much more balanced – and Wirtz thrived more than usual

To truly get the best out of Wirtz, manager Andoni Iraola (right) has to build his team around him. At Leverkusen, he was the main man

Many will discredit this argument based on the fact it is only LASK, but the duo of Trey Nyoni and Gravenberch seemed to sort out a balance issue. Nyoni is in firm contention for his first league start this weekend when Liverpool visit Brentford on Saturday but Gravenberch is suspended.

‘There is one big difference between the Bundesliga and the Premier League and that is the space he gets,’ explains Heiko Niedderer, chief reporter at German newspaper Bild. ‘He would often get more space at Leverkusen to dribble and take great shots.

‘He will adapt to it but it is taking more time than we all thought. Maybe with the new coach he has to get into that style of play. The big advantage he has is that he is very clever and a very good one-touch player.’

To truly get the best out of Wirtz, then, Iraola has to build his team around him. At Leverkusen, he was the main man in a 3-4-2-1 system. Think of the roles played by Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers at Chelsea under Alonso now. Now, team-mates get in his way.

It is the same in Germany, with a big debate in the country over why Wirtz is so much better when Bayern Munich star Jamal Musiala is not in the side. It is because they do not step on each other’s toes and neither is forced out to the left wing.

Iraola has asked Wirtz and Isak to play in tandem. There were signs the duo were clicking until the Swede’s recent injury. He wants Wirtz to be tight to Isak, occupying defenders and creating spaces while also enjoying link-up play in an old-fashioned way.

The player has bulked up to cope with the physical demands of the Premier League, putting on around 9lb last season. There is a strong belief that, with time, it will all start to click and he can show England why he was so in demand 18 months ago.

‘Sometimes we focus only on the numbers,’ said Iraola this week. ‘With Bradley, the other day, he had good situations and we did not finish them. Bradley and Flo are players that I trust 100 per cent.’

Iraola has asked Wirtz and Alexander Isak (left) to play in tandem. There have been signs that the duo were clicking until the Swede’s recent injury

‘At Leverkusen, he did not think about much, he just played – but now he has lost his confidence, maybe he is overthinking'

The most simple but realistic reason for Wirtz’s struggles is psychological.

He has gone from being the star of Germany to just another player in England – and let’s not forget he walked into a dressing room grieving the devastating loss of Diogo Jota, which made it hard for new players to settle.

Wirtz, like many in a Liverpool shirt, had a poor season last term and is struggling to rediscover his confidence. He has only played 1,084 minutes with Isak so their partnership remains a work in progress, while an understanding with Barcola will only grow with experience.

The signs are that Wirtz is slowly getting better – but Reds fans still demand more consistency.

It is believed that Klopp and Wirtz are in regular contact and the Germany manager is said to send messages to the midfielder after every Liverpool game.

Bild reporter Niedderer explains: ‘Wirtz and Klopp are very close. Klopp sees Wirtz as a big project. They spoke a lot in training, arm in arm and Klopp helped him a lot and publicly said he wants to develop him.

‘The style of Klopp’s play is very good for Wirtz and will help Liverpool because it is obviously the same, he tries to implement that as well. Pressing and stuff. For that game and that style, Wirtz is a great player.

‘The match against Serbia where he had a goal and assist, you can see: if he has the space, the freedom, he can be a great, great, great player. He will show that at Liverpool too, you just need to give him a little more time. Klopp being the national coach will boost it a bit.

'The style of Jurgen Klopp’s play with the German national team is very good for Wirtz and will help Liverpool because it is obviously the same'

It is believed that Klopp and Wirtz are in regular contact and the Germany manager is said to send messages to the midfielder after every Liverpool game

‘At Leverkusen, he did not think about much, he just played – but now he has lost his confidence, maybe he is overthinking. The two of them are talking on the phone when there is no national break. We will see a better Wirtz in the future. It will come.

‘It is not a Wirtz alone problem, they all have to develop together and know how to play with each other. Wirtz is a team player, he does not want to do it all alone. I am confident he will be a big thing in Liverpool.’

For what it is worth, Liverpool coaches believe the same. He was signed on a five-year deal and by the time that expires in 2030, they think, everyone will see just why he came with a superstar reputation and mega price tag.

#785. 'Angry' and 'very sad' Antony has home burgled while he plays in Champions League - as former Man United star bemoans 'unease in my family's eyes' in emotional message

Published: 08:09 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 08:20 BST, 16 October 2026

Former Manchester United star Antony has revealed his house was burgled while he was playing in the Champions League this week.

The Brazilian, 26, was substituted late on during Real Betis' 3-2 victory over Porto on Tuesday after providing an assist for Cucho Hernandez's equaliser in the clash.

It proved to be a great night for Antony's side after Isco's late winner as they made it two wins from two on their return to the Champions League for the first time since the 2005-06 season.

However, on Thursday he took to social media to share the horrifying news that during the match, his house had been broken into.

Antony added that although he was frustrated at what had been taken, he was more concerned about the fear the ordeal had struck into his family.

In a post on his Instagram story, he said: 'Today, I want to talk about something that made me very sad and angry.

Former Man United star Antony revealed his house was burgled while he was playing for Real Betis in the Champions League this week

Antony pictured celebrating after the match, which was Real's second win in a row in Europe

'What should have been a beautiful night ended in anger and frustration. My house was robbed.

'It's hard to describe the feeling of having your home broken into. Everything we worked so hard for and poured our hearts into obtaining was taken by someone who has no idea how much hardship we went through to get it.

'The most infuriating thing is not just the loss of belongings, but the loss of security in a place where we should feel most protected, and seeing the unease in my family's eyes. But after all this, one thing makes me even more certain: in this world, no possession is more precious than the lives and safety of my family.'

Antony's post continued with an inspiring message and a determination to bounce back from the setback.

He added: 'What was lost, we can earn back. The effort will not stop, the dream remains, and the determination to win has not diminished in the slightest.

'What truly matters is that when I look at my family, I know we are still together, united, and have the strength to overcome this difficulty.

'The unease and anger still linger, but I am also more certain: our greatest wealth has never been the items in the house, but the loved ones who make it a home, because ultimately, my greatest achievement in life will always be my family.'

Antony grew up in poverty in a favela in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and during his time at Old Trafford, he opened up on his traumatic upbringing.

'It's difficult for me to talk about my background,' he said in 2024. 'It's not by chance I have the favela where I grew up tattooed across my back and always play with "favela" written on my boots. The favela is always with me.

'I'll never let anyone else write my story or let people put me down as I genuinely know what it's like to be at the bottom.

'There were times when I didn't have boots to play football in, times when there wasn't enough to eat. I didn't have a bedroom - I slept on the sofa in the living room. My house would flood when it rained heavily.

'I saw a lot of friends go down another path and some of them lost their lives. I know what I went through; I know what my mother, father, brother and sister suffered together with me.'

Antony shared the horrifying news and the impact that the ordeal had on his family

Unfortunately, Antony is not the first high-level footballer to suffer a robbery while in action.

A similar fate befell Man City captain Ruben Dias in January of this year when his home was burgled at the same time City were playing Galatasaray in the Champions League.

Real Madrid icon Karim Benzema also saw his home targeted by burglars during matches in 2019 and 2022, while Raheem Sterling's property was robbed in 2022 when he was at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar representing England.

The Premier League is set to introduce a new LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, launched in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences."

Despite Stonewall's efforts, recent reports from Kick It Out reveal an alarming increase in discriminatory incidents in football, including rises in sexism, transphobia and faith-based abuse, with racism continuing to be the most prevalent issue.

Controversies around playersâ attitudes to rainbow armbands have also made headlines. Last season, Ipswich captain Sam Morsy declined to wear one due to religious beliefs, while Crystal Palaceâs Marc GuÃ©hi faced criticism for personalising his armband with the phrase âI Love Jesus.â

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped plans for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players currently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

Details of the Premier Leagueâs new campaign are still under wraps, but as the league presses âreset,â thereâs hope it will introduce a meaningful and effective initiative that advances equality rather than undermines it.

#789. Revealed: The death of possession football as Premier League teams are winning games with less of the ball than ever before... and goalkeepers are going longer instead of playing out from the back

Published: 07:01 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 08:03 BST, 16 October 2026

It was after a Champions League victory over Arsenal in 2015 that Pep Guardiola, then Bayern Munich manager, made clear his idea of a football utopia: 'What I want, my desire, is to have 100 per cent possession.'

Bayern had only enjoyed 66 per cent that night in a 5-1 victory over Arsene Wenger's side but even that wasn't enough to satisfy Guardiola's unquenchable pursuit of perfection.

After all, as his idol Johan Cruyff once said, 'if you play on possession, you don't have to defend, because there's only one ball.'

If the opponent doesn't have it, bar calamity or self-sabotage, they can't score.

It was this philosophy that Guardiola brought with him to Manchester City and the one that has since permeated every corner of the English game over the past decade. Who can forget that viral video of Rochdale, then in League One, scoring a sweeping team goal, playing out from the back, with the accompanying caption: 'Right, so f****** ROCHDALE scored this goal and you're telling me Pep Guardiola isn't having an influence on English football?'

Only, now, the pendulum has swung the other way. Football embraced the possession obsession, then began to rebel against it and, at last, is thriving in the face of it.

Pep Guardiola made clear his idea of a football utopia: 'What I want, my desire, is to have 100 per cent possession' back in 2015

Last season was the first since before Guardiola came to the Premier League that the average possession figure for winning matches dropped below 50 per cent and the first time it's happened since Opta records began in 2003-04. That has fallen again across the first 60 games of this campaign.

Over the weekend, only two of the 10 sides that had more than 50 per cent possession came out on top (and one of those was Manchester City so does that really count anyway). Five teams won with less than half of it.

Coventry thumped Newcastle on Monday night with only 33 per cent of the ball. Earlier in the season, Chelsea beat Brighton with just 26 per cent.

Last season, too, was the first since 2005-06 that clubs won more matches (139) with less than 50 per cent of the ball than with more of it (137). The current count is 22 to 19 in their favour again.

Beyond that, the days of teams wanting to completely dominate possession are gone, too, for now. Probably because when they do, they don't win as much as they once did.

Just three seasons ago, in 2023-24, there were 66 matches across the entire campaign in which a team had more than 70 per cent of the ball. Only 14 of them were by Guardiola's City. In all, 12 different sides managed it and one of them was Luton. Fifty-five per cent of them went on to win.

Then, it stopped. In 2024-25, there were just 29 matches where a team had 70 per cent possession and only 11 of those teams won. Last season, it happened just 19 times and only six of them won.

By this point, even Guardiola knew the game had changed. In January last year, he famously remarked that 'Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton and Liverpool play. Modern football is not positional. You have to rise to the rhythm.'

But Premier League teams are winning games with less possession than ever before, including promoted side Hull, who are thriving in eighth place

This season, teams boasting 60 per cent possession have won just 35 per cent of their matches. In 2023-24, it was 54 per cent. Teams with less than 30 per cent of the ball now win a third of their games. Five seasons ago, they won less than 10 per cent of them.

We've seen it creep in over recent seasons, as more sides like Bournemouth under Andoni Iraola, now Liverpool manager, embraced fast, direct football as an antidote to death by 1,000 passes. Teams are quicker, stronger, better at man-to-man pressing and able to harangue and harass outfits who previously felt they had the divine right to play out from the back.

When they did, they could punish them. As those possession numbers dropped, so too have those for counter attacks soared. According to Opta, this season is the highest on record (since 2006-07) for fast breaks, shots from fast breaks and goals from fast breaks. Teams soak up pressure and then strike.

Teams also now look to beat the press by going over the press. The average length of goalkeeper passes from open play is on the rise again as it dropped considerably during the Guardiola years.

Gone, too, are the days of promoted sides battling to win their place in the Premier League only to try to play like Guardiola when they get here. Vincent Kompany did it with Burnley and went straight back down, Russell Martin tippy-tapped an instant return to the Championship with Southampton.

Not anymore. Coventry, Ipswich and Hull are averaging the lowest possession of any three promoted teams since Opta records began, with the Sky Blues having 38 per cent of it and eighth-placed Hull the lowest of any side in the division on 32 per cent. Hull sit in the top 10 of the Premier League, having beaten Manchester United and taken a point off Chelsea, while Coventry are level on points with Michael Carrick's side.

'Sergej knows what it takes to win, and having the ball is not that important to him,' one Hull dressing room source told Daily Mail Sport. 'Anybody that knows the game knows there are different ways to win and he plays completely to the strengths of the players that he's got.'

It's not the only barometer for success, of course, with the current top three sides in the division also the top three for possession. The difference, though, is that it's not the only way to win and teams will use whichever method is best. Pragmatism is thriving once again over principles. Teams no longer need to pretend to be something they are not.

Possession does not remain the same throughout a game, of course, and forever fluctuates depending on who's holding on to the lead, who's chasing it and who is pushing for a winner. It is never as simple as saying that the less possession you have, by itself, makes you more likely to win.

Yet what does appear to be becoming clear is that some sides, even when chasing a goal, are content to give up more of the ball because they know they can create more chances when they do.

When Everton came from behind to draw against United, their possession dropped from 47 per cent in the first half to 44.5 per cent as they went searching for an equaliser. It did the same when they snatched a point against Bournemouth, dropping from 42 per cent until the opening goal to 40 per cent until they went level and 37 per cent in the 10 minutes before their stoppage-time equaliser.

Football is often cyclical and the trend has, for now, shifted the other way. In Guardiola's old dream world, he longed for 100 per cent of the ball. In football's latest cycle, it would be the wish of many to let him try.

#792. Lions to lambs in Lisbon ... but Martin O'Neill insists Celtic can still qualify for knockouts despite 4-1 defeat

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 23:41 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 00:05 BST, 16 October 2026

Martin O’Neill remained defiant and insisted Celtic can still qualify for the Europa League knockout stages despite a bruising 4-1 defeat to Benfica.

Already reeling on the back of losses to LASK Linz and Ferencvaros over the past couple of months, O’Neill’s side were given another brutal European lesson in Lisbon, a city which holds such historical significance for the club.

Celtic have now conceded the most goals of any team in this season’s Europa League – and have shipped 12 in their last three European matches.

Without a win or even a point from their opening two games, they fell behind after only five minutes at the Estadio da Luz when Dane Murray gave away a penalty which was converted by Benfica striker Jhon Duran.

Threatening to run riot every time they ventured forward, Benfica were 3-0 up by half-time thanks to another goal from Duran and one from Alexander Bah.

O’Neill had asked his players to channel the spirit of the Lisbon Lions in their efforts to cause a shock.

O'Neill's team fell to 4-1 defeat but he still feels they can qualify for knockout rounds

They fell a long way short but the manager claimed he was proud of his players for not capitulating and showing some fight in a second half which saw Camilo Duran pull a goal back.

‘Last thing you want to do is concede so early on,’ said O’Neill, whose side now face a huge game against Hearts on Sunday before taking on Celta Vigo in Glasgow next week.

‘We could’ve capitulated, but I thought the second-half performance was terrific. We created chance after chance.

‘The second-half performance gives me the determination. I think we can still qualify. We can still do it. It’s not bravado on my part. I genuinely believe we can still do it.

‘We came roaring back, the subs came on and did brilliantly. We could’ve scored a number of goals. It changed because two wide players really wanted to get at people.

‘I accept on the break they (Benfica) could have scored themselves, as they did with their fourth goal. But I thought the second half was really terrific.

The Celtic players look dejected after the final whistle sounds in Lisbon on Thursday

‘I take great encouragement from this and even though we’ve lost two games, I genuinely believe that we can make it.

‘Benfica are a very fine side. I think they’ve spent about £100 million, they’re one of the favourites for the competition.

‘We know we can defend better and hopefully we can look to eradicate that over the course of the season.

‘We could have crumbled after going 3-0 down, but we didn’t. We have to take encouragement from that and use that second half performance going into Hearts on Sunday.’

During O’Neill’s first stint as Celtic manager, the club could hold their own in the Champions League and also reached a UEFA Cup Final.

It now looks like another European season could be on the verge of going down the drain after opening their account with two straight defeats.

Vangelis Pavlidis scores the fourth goal for Benfica on a tough night for Celtic

Pressed on why there has been such a decline in the club’s European fortunes, O’Neill replied: ‘No, that’s a big, big question.

‘I haven’t seen all the things that have happened over the last 20-odd years. What I do know is Benfica are a fine side, maybe unfortunate not to be in the Champions League.

‘There are some serious teams in the Europa League. But, that aside, your question demands a longer answer than I can give at this minute.’

Meanwhile, Celtic skipper Callum McGregor admits the team were architects of their own downfall during a dismal first half.

‘It is a disappointing result,’ said McGregor. ‘We were here to get points and win.

‘We were playing against a really good side with with really good quality in final third. First half we didn’t help ourselves.

‘Second half we score one, probably could score another. Bit of a game of two halves.

‘Unforced errors lead to the second and third goals and you have a mountain to climb.

‘We know at this level if you don’t look after the ball you’re going to get punished.’

#793. Cherries on top! Bournemouth make European history as Sunderland score last-gasp winner and Brighton enjoy easy win... but Crystal Palace fall to defeat in five-goal thriller against Lyon

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER and MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER and JAMES SHARPE and KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER

Published: 21:14 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 23:24 BST, 15 October 2026

This was a night for Bournemouth to look back as much as it was to look forward.

A night to reflect on how far they’ve come, from navigating a 17-point deduction that put their Football League status at risk in 2008 to playing – and winning – their first ever European home game, thanks to a sublime treble from Evanilson, Rayan and Alvaro Rodriguez, who added the cherry on top with a late penalty.

There was a special tifo behind one goal to mark the historic night, with a record crowd of 12,010 packed in to witness it.

It was Adam Smith, who has been with Bournemouth since 2010 when they played in League One, leading them out as club captain.

Here was owner Bill Foley, seeing his vision to get Bournemouth into Europe, a target he ambitiously but explicitly set back in December 2022, occurring a year ahead of his five-year target.

But when Smith’s cross in from the right was expertly flicked up into the air by Evanilson, looping over Sturm Graz goalkeeper Daniil Khudyakov, it was a moment for Bournemouth to look forward, too.

Tournament favourites before they beat Real Sociedad in San Sebastian last time out and back-to-back European wins has done little to rubbish that label. Bournemouth have had to take the long way to the top but now they are here, they are showing just how much of a punch they pack.

Evanilson scored Bournemouth's first European goal at home in their 3-0 win over Sturm Graz

Bournemouth fans celebrated the club's journey pre-match, with the club now among the leading contenders to win the Europa League

Boss Marco Rose, who made five changes for this one, described the weekend’s 5-1 drubbing at the hands of Chelsea as a ‘good slap’.

Bournemouth were ruthlessly dismantled in south-west London. But to paraphrase the iconic ‘Tubthumping’, a song by British band Chumbawamba, when you get knocked down, you get up again, and that’s exactly what Rose’s side did.

It was a suffocating first half for a Sturm Graz side that started with a back five before pivoting to a back four at the interval.

Bournemouth had 10 efforts on goal to the visitors’ zero, with Ben Gannon-Doak and Evanilson a constant threat down the Bournemouth right.

Good sides ride their luck at times, too, and Bournemouth are no different. Sturm Graz wanted a penalty just before half-time when Belmin Beganovic was clumsily felled by Smith, only for the referee to adjudge Beganovic to have dived.

In a much improved second half, Graz struck the post when Jurgen Heil was picked out in the area.

But when you’ve battled back from the brink of minus-seventeen in League Two, and all the perils that come with trying to gatecrash the Premier League elite from a starting base in the fourth tier, adversity in Europe is light work.

Second halves have been an issue that have pockmarked Rose’s tenure on the south coast so far, coming into this one having led in six out of eight, only going on to win two of them. It was an irritation away to Sociedad, and here was proof that Rose and his players are learning lessons on the fly.

Marco Rose wants his side to take their performance against Sturm Graz into the Premier League

Justin Kluivert, Rayan and Ryan Christie all formed part of the cavalry sent on by Rose in a bid to settle the game and allow the party atmosphere to kick into another gear and that roll of the dice paid off with 15 minutes to go.

Khudyakov dealt poorly with a Bournemouth corner and after dropping it in his six-yard box, Rayan smashed in as Rose threw both arms into the air in celebration.

Rose is already looking ahead to how they can now secure their first league win of the season - starting on Sunday, when Sunderland visit the Vitality.

'Performance-wise, clean sheet, attitude, effort - a deserved win and now we have to continue, have to get consistent in these things and Sunderland is the next challenge,' said Rose.

'I believe in this team and know they are always confident despite a difficult situation. The squad is working, everyone is keen to play, everyone deserves to play and its good for us for the busy weeks to have a competitive squad.

'If we stick together and play like this and we have our fans then we are hard to play and it's hard to beat us. That's what we should take into the next game.'

For all the fireworks, tifos, light shows, and noise that lit up the night sky, here was proof of just how far Bournemouth have come… and how much further this ascending group can go with Champions League football in their sights.

Regis Le Bris was forced to call on the cavalry to rescue his side as Sunderland came from behind to win their first European away match in 53 years in stoppage time against Portuguese second division side Torreense.

Noah Sadiki struck in the dying minutes prompting wild celebrations from the near 4,000 travelling supporters, who had earlier seen summer signing Jules Ahoka cancel out a spectacular opener from Torreense defender Volnei Feltes.

The winner owed much to the creativity of Enzo Le Fee and Granit Xhaka as the pair, who began the night on the bench, underlined their importance to the Black Cats.

Having watched their team-mates struggle to break down Torreense, Le Fee produced a delightful dinked pass into the penalty area to find Xhaka, with the Swiss flicking the ball first time into the path of Sadiki to score his first goal for the club.

‘When Granit touched it I heard him scream shoot and I didn’t think twice,' Sadiki said. 'I just hoped it was going in and the keeper wouldn’t save it. I’m really happy. It was a beautiful moment.’

Le Bris had taken the understandable risk by deciding to make seven changes for the fixture against arguably their weakest Europa League opponents, with Torreense currently lying 15th in the Portuguese second tier.

Noah Sadiki scored a stoppage time winner as Sunderland beat Portuguese side Torreense

Sunderland were forced to fight back following a stunning opener from Volnei Feltes

With just four points in the Premier League and five matches left to play this month, this was the match to give an opportunity to fringe members of the squad.

Torreense, though, have proved they are more than capable of springing a surprise. Their journey to the Europa League is one to rival Sunderland’s own having stunned Sporting Lisbon in last year’s Portuguese Cup final to qualify.

Their opening goal proved just as unexpected as that triumph.

Feltes was well inside his own half when he received possession and opted to embark on a forward run. After driving towards the Sunderland box, the Brazilian defender chopped between the challenges of Malick Fofana and Nilson Angulo and curled magnificently into the top corner.

Whatever happens to the minnows, they will come away with one of the best goals of this year’s competition.

Sunderland were forced to be patient when trying to break down their opponents, who dropped deep in the second half.

Le Bris turned to his bench moments after Nilson Angulo saw a header superbly kept out by goalkeeper Lucas Paes, with Omar Alderete failing to convert the follow-up.

His quadruple change of Xhaka, Le Fee, Reinildo and Nordi Mukiele proved crucial. The latter's cross for Ahoka to equalise with a header while Xhaka and Le Fee were central to Sadiki's winner.

'Winning this game just at the end is really special,' Le Bris said. 'It’s important for the club and the fans – they were fantastic once again.

'We are growing and we need experiences and I think the team showed the belief until the end which is really important for us. We showed again we have this mindset.'

Now Pierre Sage knows how Oliver Glasner feels. He knows how it feels to return to your old stomping ground, one where you achieved great things, and come away with nothing.

Just as Glasner took his new Nottingham Forest side back to Selhurst Park at the weekend and lost, so too did Sage as Crystal Palace endured a frustrating night in Lyon where he once helped save the French side from relegation.

In truth, a night like this has been coming. Palace cannot keep defending like this, be so open and unorganised, and expect to win matches. Sooner or later, you leave yourself with too much of a hill to climb.

It took Forest just three minutes to open the scoring at the weekend and Lyon needed only seven minutes and 31 seconds here. As always, it was all too easy.

A bog-standard corner into a crowded six-yard box and, despite the hordes of black Palace shirts, the ball still dropped to Lyon captain Corentin Tolisso.

Only this time, Lyon didn’t miss the rest of the chances that came their way like Forest did. On the stroke of half-time the hosts cut through Palace with simple passes and Keito Nakamura squared for Ernest Nuamah, who darted ahead of the defenders to finish. Tyrick Mitchell, for all his goalscoring exploits this season, made little effort to track his run.

It was this leakiness that caused a few shudders in the Palace boardroom, letting in 11 goals in their opening four matches, and sparked rumblings that Sage could be the first Premier League managerial casualty of the season.

Pierre Sage saw his Crystal Palace side fall to a 3-2 defeat against his former club Lyon

Ernest Nuamah was among the scores as Lyon capitalised on poor Crystal Palace defending

If there is a saving grace to which Palace can cling, it’s that when they do get it right under Sage, they do look menacing. There was little of that in a dreadful first half but, after the break, they clicked into gear. They are just, as yet, unable to find the balance.

Having wantaway forward Ismaila Sarr back in the line-up always helps with his directness in the final third.

And when you have the precision of Adam Wharton in your midfield, you will always stand a chance. It was his delightful first-time through ball to Yeremy Pino after a fine short corner routine that helped fire Palace back into the game.

The introduction of Daichi Kamada swung momentum further Palace’s way. He was bundled over inside the box but Palace’s furious protests fell on deaf ears. He had a shot from close range saved and, eventually, found the net after some chaos inside the box.

The only problem was that, by then, Lyon had already added a third courtesy of Pavel Sulc’s cheeky backheel flick.

Palace kept pushing as Chris Richards saw a late header from a corner saved but, ultimately, in vain. This time, it wasn’t enough. This time, they didn’t get away with it. This time, they gave themselves too much to do.

'I’m really frustrated about the result but really frustrated with the way of playing in the first half,' Sage said.

'Our game started at half-time and it was too late.

'We play too quickly sometimes with the idea to play out the back quickly in transition but we are not a team like this, we have only one or two players able to run and make the difference with the speed.

'That’s why we have to move with the ball, travel with the ball, and we did that in the second half.'

It must be up there with the finest feelings in football – the relief that washes over when your team finally finds a way through that dastardly low block in front of them.

For Brighton, that arrived just before half-time. There was no blaming Kauno Zalgiris for their tactical approach. Hardly anyone other than Fabian Hurzeler, who was perhaps being polite when listing the Lithuanian side’s attributes before kick-off, gave them a hope in hell of escaping their first-ever fixture in the main stage of a European competition without losing.

Once Georginio Rutter found that first goal after 41 minutes, this turned into a much more enjoyable evening at the Amex Stadium. Even more so when Jack Hinshelwood, back from his ankle injury and appearing for the first time since August, added a second before the break.

With that, the floodgates opened, Brighton started their Conference League campaign in style, and truthfully, this competition should sit high on Hurzeler’s priorities this term.

Georginio Rutter scored the opening goal as Brighton overcame Lithuanian side Kauno Zalgiris

While we often praise Brighton for the way in which they work – including in the talents they find that the richer clubs then seek to steal – all that is missing is the silverware to complement it all.

Despite being brilliantly run, they have never won a major trophy in their history, and the Conference League is an opportunity to correct that. Other English clubs such as West Ham and Brighton’s rivals Crystal Palace have used it well. To sides such as Kauno Zalgiris, these are giants they are competing with, opponents competing on an entirely alien level to their own.

While Hurzeler had explained why Kauno Zalgiris would be confident – he warned us they were the champions of Lithuania and that they had won the Lithuanian Cup at the weekend – Brighton are in a happy place, too. This made it five successive victories for them in all competitions.

They are third in the Premier League behind only Manchester City and Arsenal, and into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup after winning away at Manchester United – a club now linked with liking Hurzeler in case they move on from Michael Carrick.

With that, we had an inkling as to how this game would go. Brighton would attack, and Kauno Zalgiris would defend, and the opening 30 minutes was all about blocks. From Anton Tolordava, from Nosa Iyobosa Edokpolor, from any Kauno Zalgiris player with a body for throwing at the ball.

But then arrived the breakthrough. It was a nice finish from Rutter despite the on-field officials thinking the ball had gone behind for a goal-kick in the build-up. It had not, and VAR overruled to award Brighton their opener. Hinshelwood added a second before the break before Rutter grabbed the third goal and Matt O’Riley the fourth.

‘We want to keep improving every game,' said Hinshelwood. 'What’s happened in the past has gone now. We want to look forward to the future.’

It was a good way to warm up for Palace in the Premier League on Sunday, though Brighton may be reminded by the Amex’s away end which side have won a trophy of late. Hurzeler should be embracing this European competition as a way to give his supporters a season to cherish.

#794. FA pile pressure on Gianni Infantino - with chair saying he 'is not fit to be FIFA president' if he refuses to answer questions over World Cup sell-off

Published: 23:18 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 23:19 BST, 15 October 2026

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt says Gianni Infantino is 'not fit to be FIFA president' if he does not answer questions about his World Cup sell-off plan or the Folarin Balogun case.

Hewitt, also a FIFA vice-president, was one of the FIFA Council members who tried to hold Infantino to account in Zurich on Thursday at its first meeting since the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan came to light.

Infantino apologised in the meeting for what he called 'mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process'.

Hewitt said Council members had not received answers to 'anything we had specifically requested' regarding FFE or the Balogun incident, where the USA striker’s one-match ban was suspended following a call to Infantino from US President Donald Trump.

Hewitt told reporters in Zurich: 'The man has to answer those questions, and if he doesn’t answer those questions, no, he’s not fit to be FIFA president, and that was what was shared in the meeting.

'He’s told us to submit those questions. There were so many of them, and now it’s up to him to do that, and do that in the open way.

Debbie Hewitt has called for Gianni Infantino to answer questions over his World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair ahead of FIFA's presidential elections

'The minimum is having the papers from FFE, because if there’s nothing to hide, then share them with us.'

The FFE plan first became public knowledge in July. Infantino sought to create a company to manage the commercial interests of FIFA’s competitions, including the World Cup, but wanted a minority stake to be made available to private investors.

The lead investor was set to be Thrive, a company founded by President Trump’s son-in-law’s brother, Josh Kushner, but the plan was abandoned on August 1 after three continental confederations rejected it.

Among those within to publicly disagree with Infantino's plan were FIFA general secretary Mattias Grafstrom, senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro, chief operating officer Kevin Lamour and Arsene Wenger, who serves as FIFA's Chief of Global Football Development.

Hewitt has previously written to Infantino demanding the release of documents related to FFE, while European football’s governing body UEFA has also submitted legal applications in the US seeking disclosure, which FIFA has challenged.

Hewitt’s September letter to Infantino is also understood to have requested information on how the Balogun ban came to be suspended. Infantino has always maintained the decision was made independently of him by the FIFA disciplinary committee.

Trump bragged about calling Infantino in the wake of Balogun's red card in the build-up to the USA's next game against Belgium, confirming that he 'asked for a review by FIFA'.

'I'm good at this stuff,' Trump added. 'That wasn't a foul. That wasn't even an infraction.'

Hewitt said it was 'reasonable' for Infantino to request the submission of questions in writing, adding: 'He gave us the opportunity to say what we felt, and I think anybody that didn’t say what they felt in there, they’ve missed their opportunity.

'I have no new information that makes me feel any differently about how I felt when I went in, other than we do have a president of FIFA who is apologetic about what has happened, and secondly, a promise again that we will get the information that we’ve requested.'

Infantino said 'everyone had the opportunity to ask questions and express their views' on FFE.

He added in a video released by FIFA: 'I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project which then led to many consequences.

'But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal, so in no way a done deal. Just a proposal that actually intended to enable FIFA to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources.'

UEFA has vowed to identify a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in next March’s presidential elections, having declared its loss of confidence in him in August over the FFE plan.

The deadline for candidacies to be submitted is November 18.

#795. Arsenal star Mikel Merino admits he's 'fortunate to be alive' after 'an angel' saved him during Borussia Dortmund bus bombing

Published: 22:54 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 23:19 BST, 15 October 2026

Arsenal midfielder Mikel Merino has admitted he is 'fortunate to be alive' after 'an angel' prevented him from being injured in the 2017 Borussia Dortmund bus bombing.

The football world was shaken when the German side were victims of an attack by Sergej Wenergold, which saw three pipe bombs detonated near the bus when it was on its way to a Champions League match.

Dortmund defender Marc Bartra was left hospitalised with a wrist injury following the attack, while a police officer was also treated for injuries and unable to return to work.

Merino, meanwhile, escaped unscathed – but that may not necessarily have been the case.

'I think I have an angel on my shoulder,' Merino, who was 20 at the time, told The Players' Tribune. 'I'm actually fortunate to be alive at all.

He added: 'There was a deafening noise, and then I remember the bus nearly tipping over. I looked behind me and saw blood on the floor. Smoke, screams. I remember being at the hospital later that night, waiting for Marc Bartra, who had his wrist badly cut up.

Arsenal's Mikel Merino has said he is 'fortunate to be alive' after being onboard Dortmund's team bus during a bombing

The Dortmund bus was targeted in 2017 when on its way to a Champions League quarter-final

'The next day, someone told me that a huge piece of shrapnel was lodged in the headrest of the seat next to Marc. My usual seat. That day, the seat was empty.

'My legs were feeling a bit tight, and the seats in the front reclined. So I sat up there instead, and it may have saved my life. So yeah, I just have this belief that things happen for a reason.'

The pipe bombs were hidden in hedges by the side of the road and detonated at around 7.15pm local time. Dortmund were on the way to their stadium to face Monaco in the Champions League quarter-finals.

The bombs were filled with metal pins and had a reach of around 100 meters.

After a lengthy investigation, Wenergold, then 29, was charged with 28 counts of attempted murder for the attack. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison.

He said during the trial that he did not intend to kill any of the players but make money by betting on a fall in Borussia Dortmund's stock market price.

The match against Monaco was postponed but played the following day - a decision led to some heavy criticism of UEFA.

England coach Thomas Tuchel was manager of Dortmund at the time and after the match branded the decision to play the game 'absurd'.

'We were informed by text message that UEFA was making this decision,' he added. 'A decision made in Switzerland that concerns us directly. We will not forget it. It is a very bad feeling.

'There is a feeling of helplessness. What we think has not interested anyone. We weren't asked about playing the game.

'Everyone has their own way of reacting to events. The players had the choice not to play, but no-one chose this option.'
