#796. Louis van Gaal insists Man City's scandal contributed to 'all the consequences and suffering' that followed his Man United exit - as ex-boss believes 'for sure' his reign would've ended better

Published: 23:00 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 23:02 BST, 15 October 2026

Louis van Gaal has blamed Manchester City's financial doping for the 'suffering' that he endured in his torrid 2016 Man United exit.

The Dutch manager was given his marching orders on the heels of the 2015-16 season, which saw the Red Devils narrowly miss out on a place in the following term's Champions League.

Both Man City and Man United wrapped up with 66 points, but the Cityzens, playing their final season under Manuel Pellegrini had the superior goal difference which secured their spot at Europe's top table.

Van Gaal was despatched despite ending the season having won the FA Cup, and in correspondence with the Athletic, stressed that he believed that failing to qualify for the European top flight had prompted the club's Glazer ownership group to swing the axe.

'For me, at the time, that (missing out on the Champions League in 2016) was probably the deciding factor in my dismissal from Manchester United and all the consequences and suffering this entailed,' he stated.

The former Barcelona boss added that 'for sure', things might have been different if he had been playing in a fair competition.

Louis van Gaal admitted that he believes his time at Man United might have ended differently if not for Man City's financial manipulation

The former manager was dismissed at the end of the 2015-16 season after missing out on a spot in the Champions League, despite finishing level on points with City

Van Gaal subsequently took a hiatus from management, which he described at the time as being a 'sabbatical'.

He only returned to the dugout in 2021, when he was appointed as head coach of the Dutch national team.

Van Gaal's tenure at Old Trafford fell during the period between 2009 and 2018 that Man City have been found guilty of artificially inflating revenue made through sponsorship.

City were found to have used 'sham' contracts and agreements to cook their books by around £900million over a nine-year period, claiming a commercial income of £949.94m of which only £119.25m had come from sponsors.

The Premier League said the panel found City arranged ‘sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on ‘sham’ agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs’.

Deals with a number of sponsors were part of ‘a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees’, the statement added, saying that ‘the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club’.

The result was that the club had ‘filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators’.

Man City have doubled down on their innocence and appealed the verdict, with the club underscoring that they are in possession of 'irrefutable evidence' which will clear their name.

For Van Gaal, he admitted that there was little he could do as he 'cannot turn back history now.'

'Not even the English Football Association can (do that),' he added.

But the 75-year-old is not alone in wondering what might have been had Man City not been able to inflate their revenue and in turn, invest in some of the players fundamental to their multi-year successes.

Former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard admitted that he wanted the club to 'suffer' after 'stealing memories', with the Reds icon going without a Premier League medal during their era of dominance.

Liverpool came second to Man City when they claimed the title in 2013-14, and although Gerrard was circumspect last week as he discussed Man City's potential punishment, he ultimately called for the club to be sanctioned heavily.

'I think I have come to terms with that I have never won the Premier League, that I was short in that department in terms of winning it,' Gerrard said last week. 'I have come to terms with the incident that happened to me at the back end of that season and I have heard a lot of City players, a lot of City fans, and celebrity fans say "you can't take those moments away from us".

'What about the memories they have taken away from not just possibly me, and the team that I played in but over that period of time, nine, ten years?

'Spurs fans, United fans, Everton fans, teams at the bottom, teams in the cups? City, ex-players, current players, and City owners, everyone connected with City have got to think about the memories they have stolen away from everyone else.

'Multi-year punishments, that would be my opinion,' he added when asked what was deserved. 'I'm not saying that's the right opinion, but that's just how I feel sitting here in this chair.

'I think putting them down to the Championship is not fair on the EFL. I don't think it's enough, because they'll bounce back. You look at that team yesterday. Can you imagine that in the Championship? With all due respect, it's not fair on the teams playing against City week in, week out. It's not fair on the potential team that could be the third team to come up.

'I think it needs to be a transfer ban. I think it needs to be points over a period of time. And make them suffer like they've made everyone else suffer for the nine, ten years that they've done it for. That would be my opinion. But there needs to be an example set.'

#800. Hearts 1 Nordsjaelland 1: Agony for Vrancken as Danes hit back with late equaliser

Published: 22:14 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 22:29 BST, 15 October 2026

Hearts had to settle for a point from their Conference League league phase opener as they conceded a sickening late equaliser to Nordsjaelland substitute Nicklas Rojkjaer.

Oisin McEntee looked as if he had given Wouter Vrancken’s side the perfect start to their campaign when he put them ahead in the first half.

The Irish midfielder, catapulted into Vrancken’s starting line-up after club record signing Eduardo Ageu suffered yet another injury which forced him to be withdrawn from the European squad on the eve of the match, made the most of the unexpected opportunity.

In truth, however, a share of the spoils was the least Nordsjaelland deserved from a contest in which the Danish Superliga outfit looked the more dangerous for long spells.

Hearts will still feel hugely frustrated at not being able to see out the win, however, especially as Rojkjaer’s 86th minute leveller took a hugely fortunate deflection to beat Beau Reus.

Hearts boss Wouter Vrancken urges his players on against Nordsjaelland

Oisin McEntee celebrates after giving Hearts the lead against Nordsjaelland

It doesn’t get any easier for Hearts who face a trip to face Trabzonspor in Turkey on matchday two next week. They may come to rue their inability to make home advantage count last night.

Nordsjaelland arrived in Gorgie with a reputation as a technically sound and dangerous counter-attacking side and they didn’t take long to show both of those qualities.

Hearts, whose own willingness under Vrancken to commit as many players forward as often as possible can leave them vulnerable at the back, were certainly fortunate not to find themselves behind in the opening stages.

Ghanaian winger Prince Amoako provided the visitors’ biggest threat as he regularly took advantage of Hearts’ propensity to give the ball away cheaply at times.

Not even 60 seconds had elapsed when Amoako burst clear down the left for the first time and his dangerous cross was headed behind for a corner by the back-pedalling Harry Milne.

Hearts were initially unable to heed the warning signs and Amoako continued to torment them down their right flank. It needed a lunging intervention from Malachi Fagan-Walcott to deflect Amoako’s next effort wide of the target.

Calvin Miller produced the first significant attacking threat for Hearts with a superb turn and cross from the right. With Nordsjaelland goalkeeper Andreas Hansen static, the ball agonisingly eluded both Claudio Braga and Josh McPake as they stretched to try and connect with it at the back post.

Rather than spark Hearts into life, however, it was Nordsjaelland who continued to look the likelier side. There was a real let-off for Vrancken’s men in the 23rd minute when they coughed up possession yet again in a dangerous position.

Alexander Lind pounced to feed a pass to the ubiquitous Amoako who had the goal at his mercy but sent his low shot against the left hand post of Reus who was clearly beaten had it been on target.

When Milne then had to make a timely block to keep out a shot from Lind, the portents weren’t looking good for Hearts.

That all changed in the 33rd minute when McEntee made the breakthrough. Milne flashed the ball across the face of the penalty area where it was deflected behind.

Miller took the corner from the right and Nordsjaelland struggled to cope with the physicality of the Hearts players as the ball ricocheted into the path of Jamie McCart who headed it towards the six yard box. McEntee was the quickest to react as he stretched out a boot to stab a shot beyond Hansen and spark wild celebrations inside Tynecastle.

Suddenly, the momentum was firmly with the hosts who piled on the pressure in search of a second goal before the break.

James Wilson had what looked like a decent shout for a penalty when he was wrestled from behind by Victor Nelsson inside the box but after a quick VAR check, Polish ref Damian Kos was cleared to stick by his on-field decision to wave away the claim.

Christian Borchgrevink’s inclusion at right-back in place of Jordi Altena was something of a surprise selection for Hearts but the Norwegian justified his manager’s faith in him.

Borchgrevink got forward to good effect and conjured up a delightful pass to send Braga free in the 43rd minute. It was a glorious opportunity for the Portuguese forward but he lacked his customary composure as he blazed his shot over the top.

Hearts players are dejected after Rojkjaer's late deflected strike denies them victory

Nordsjaelland were creaking at the back now and were fortunate to survive a real barrage from Hearts on the stroke of half-time which saw McEntee have a shot blocked before Hansen made fine saves to deny both McCart and McPake.

The visitors recovered their poise after the break but the first clear chance of the half fell to Hearts when Miller sent McPake clear on the counter attack, only for the winger to wastefully drag his shot wide from around 14 yards.

Reus, the man whose heroics in the penalty shoot-out against Rapid Vienna in the play-off round took Hearts into the league phase, has quickly cemented himself as a hugely popular figure among the Gorgie support.

The Dutch keeper earned their approval again with a superb reaction save to deny Lind what looked like a certain equaliser in the 55th minute. As Nordsjaelland enjoyed another dangerous spell, Lind was confounded again by a brave block from Milne just as he was about to pull the trigger inside the penalty area.

The tension inside the stadium was increasingly palpable and Reus displayed outstanding reflexes once more to somehow claw away another Lind effort which had taken a wicked deflection.

How Hearts craved the insurance of a second goal and it should have been delivered by Fagan-Walcott in the 74th minute. The big defender rose brilliantly to meet a Miller free-kick, only to send his header wide of Hansen’s left hand post from close range.

It duly came back to haunt Hearts with four minutes of regulation time remaining as Nordsjaelland were rewarded for their pressure when Rojkjaer’s shot was deflected past the helpless Reus.

Hearts (4-2-3-1): Reus 8, Borchgrevink 7, Fagan-Walcott 7, McCart 6, Milne 7 (Kingsley 87); McEntee 7 (Altena 87), Mendy 6; Miller 7, Braga 6 (Kerjota 70), McPake 6 (Mato 87); Wilson 6 (Williams 77).

Harry Kane has agreed a new contract that will tie him to German champions Bayern Munich until 2029.

#802. Benfica 4 Celtic 1: Return to Lisbon only serves to show Bhoys how far they've fallen

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 21:54 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 22:00 BST, 15 October 2026

In the moments before kick-off, the Estadio da Luz was briefly plunged into darkness before a spectacular light-show illuminated this magnificent arena.

As the names on the Benfica team-sheet were read out on the tannoy, and the home crowd belted out the official club anthem, all manner of strobe effects and disco lights dazzled the eyes.

With enough electricity surging through this place to blow the national grid in Portugal, it made you wonder whether half of Lisbon had been left without power for a couple of minutes.

Yet, when the match started, it took only five minutes for the lights to go out on Celtic. They fell behind to a Jhon Duran penalty and a wretched first half would see them 3-0 down by half-time.

On nights like this, Martin O’Neill wouldn’t be human if he didn’t feel cause to reflect on his decision to stay on as manager this season.

Having lost their opening match against Ferencvaros in Glasgow by a scoreline of 3-1 a few weeks ago, the painful reality is that Celtic have turned into Europa League also-rans.

There are, of course, still six matches in which to try and mount some sort of comeback and progress to the knockout stages.

Sinisalo is helpless as Jhon Duran dinks home Benfica's first from the penalty spot

But there is simply no evidence to support any theory that this Celtic team would be capable of going on such a run.

In this fabled city which holds such historic links to Celtic, O’Neill had asked his players to channel the spirit of the Lisbon Lions in their efforts to cause a shock.

But they were lambs rather than lions. This cavernous arena had the distinct feel of an abattoir during those opening 45 minutes when Celtic were thrown to the slaughter.

Credit to Celtic for at least showing some fight and making a game of it in the second half, with Camilo Duran pulling one back, but giving a team like Benfica a three-goal start was never likely to prove fruitful.

This was another chastening night in Europe for O’Neill and his players, who must now regroup ahead of another huge match against Hearts at Parkhead on Sunday.

O’Neill sprung a couple of surprises with his team selection. Auston Trusty came in to replace Liam Scales at centre-back and Dane Murray also kept his place in the heart of defence.

A loan signing from Parma in the summer, Danish midfielder Oliver Sorensen came into make only his third start of the season for Celtic.

After making a late dash from Glasgow to Lisbon following the birth of his child earlier this week, Camilo Duran started in a front three alongside Kasper Hogh and Sebastian Tounekti.

Earlier in the week, there had been some reports in the Portuguese media that Benfica boss Marco Silva could make wholesale changes and field a B team for this match.

Those proved to be unfounded. Although Silva did rotate to an extent, there was still a strong spine to the Benfica team as they looked to build on their 2-0 win against AC Milan in the San Siro in their opening game.

A £23million signing from Shakhtar Donetsk in the summer, Ukrainian international Georgiy Sudakov operated in the No 10 position in Silva’s 4-2-3-1 system.

Benfica also spent £14m to take Joao Palhinha from Bayern Munich, the former Fulham and Tottenham midfielder anchoring the midfield alongside skipper Fredrik Aursnes.

The home side also had a further £30million worth of attacking talent on the wings in Belgium’s Dodi Lukebakio and Argentinian Gianluca Prestianni, as well as former Barcelona centre-back Clement Lenglet.

Perhaps the only blessing from Celtic’s point of view was the absence of Vangelis Pavlidis, the Greek striker who has fired 14 goals in 14 matches so far this season. Jhon Duran was preferred up front instead.

It would be Duran who was at the heart of it as Benfica came flying out of the traps and took the lead with only five minutes on the clock.

Celtic defender Murray took a wild swipe and kicked through the back of Duran’s leg, with the Montenegrin referee Nikola Dabanovic duly pointing to the spot.

With ice flowing through his veins, former Aston Villa striker Duran dusted himself down and dinked a cheeky panenka straight down the middle past Viljami Sinisalo.

O’Neill had spoken pre-match about a desire to see his team be competitive and have a go, despite the odds being stacked against them.

Hogh had a low shot saved by Anatoliy Trubin before a long shot from Mika Baur stung the palms of the Benfica keeper just moments later.

But it was rapidly turning into a horror show for Celtic. After getting off to the worst possible start, they conceded a second goal on 23 minutes.

Auston Trusty despairs as Benfica striker Jhon Duran scores his second goal

The outstanding Prestianni, a thorn in Celtic’s side all night down the left side of Benfica’s attack, cut in and clipped a simple cross in behind.

Having advanced forward from right-back, Alexander Bah was left totally unmarked and cushioned a finish beyond Sinisalo to double the home side’s lead.

Desperately seeking to gain some kind of foothold in the match, Celtic struck the woodwork twice in a matter of seconds.

Hogh should have scored when he met a Tounekti cross but his shot struck the post, with Camilo Duran then gathering the rebound and striking a combination of the bar and post.

The game was effectively over as a contest after just 36 minutes when Benfica scored a third, Duran holding off the attention of Trusty and firing low past Sinisalo.

Sinisalo, who had spoken pre-match about his surprise at being dropped a few weeks ago, should have done better. He was beaten far too easily at his near post.

Striker Kasper Hogh misses a chance during Celtic's defeat against Benfica

Ripped apart in the most brutal fashion once again in Europe, this was threatening to turn into another night of humiliation for Celtic against a Benfica side who had hardly broken sweat.

When they fell 3-0 behind to Rangers at Ibrox last month, Callum McGregor was seen gesturing to his team-mates and saying: ‘No more goals’.

The skipper, whose influence has steadily declined in these big games in recent times, was now involved in another painful exercise in damage limitation.

How many goals would Benfica feast on? On a night which saw one Duran in the Benfica team and another in Celtic’s, would the home side be Hungry Like the Wolf?

The second half had the distinct feel of the home side taking their foot off the gas knowing that the job was already complete.

Celtic pulled a goal back just after the hour when Duran got across his marker to head home from a Haissem Hassan cross.

That seemed to spark something of a wobble for the home side. Having been so impressive, Benfica totally lost their way for a period of 10 or 15 minutes.

Celtic almost pulled another goal back when Duran rattled the post after a good team move, albeit Andreas Schjelderup then did the same for Benfica only moments later.

O’Neill’s side were vastly improved in the second half, but any lingering doubts about the final outcome were finally extinguished when substitute Pavlidis rifled low beyond Sinisalo with just a couple of minutes left.

#803. Graeme Souness warns Derek McInnes that Rangers can no longer 'lose or draw some stupid games' after planting seed of doubt in Celtic's minds

Published: 20:34 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 20:47 BST, 15 October 2026

Graeme Souness has warned Rangers players to guard against complacency despite a massive turnaround in fortunes.

Derek McInnes’ men go into this weekend’s fixture at Dundee knowing that a seventh straight league win will see them go top of the Premiership and crank up the pressure on leaders Celtic ahead of their clash with Hearts on Sunday afternoon.

A perfect September has flipped the mood at Ibrox following a dismal start to the season that included defeat to Hibernian in McInnes’ first home league match in charge and embarrassing European exits at the hands of Jagiellonia Białystok and Jablonec.

However, former boss Souness insists the standards set in last month’s back-to-back victories over their Old Firm rivals must become the norm, not the exception, if the Light Blues are to contend for silverware this season.

In a wide-ranging interview with This Is Ibrox to promote his new book – My Rangers: How I Changed Scottish Football For Ever – Souness said: ‘We’ve had two really good games against Celtic and we’ve now planted a seed in their head that we’re better than them. But if we lose or draw some stupid games going forward, that seed will disappear.

‘We must continue in the same form, as if we’re playing Celtic every week, with the same attitude, the same willingness to do the hard yards, and being the same aggressive team we were [in those games].

Rangers boss Derek McInnes needs to keep pressure on Celtic, says Souness

Souness has been impressed by Rangers but says they can't afford to 'lose stupid games'

‘All of a sudden, we looked like a team of men and like we all know what we’re doing. We were first to everything and we were bullying Celtic. Please, do that every week.’

Souness reckons that maintaining those levels will be the biggest challenge the current squad will have to overcome, harking back to his own experiences of facing Manchester United during his Liverpool playing days in the 1980s.

‘We never, ever had an easy game against them,’ he added. ‘They’d beat us, we’d beat them. It was always very tight. But the difference between them and us was we could go to the smaller teams and turn them over for fun. There was no lapse in our attitude when we played them. But Manchester United, they would lose daft games. There was only one year they really challenged us and that was the year Ron Atkinson was in charge.

‘The message, if I was sitting with those [Rangers] players, is you have to be where you’ve been for the last two games against Celtic. Be aggressive, be first to everything, and let the other team know there’s nothing in this game for them.’

Souness led Rangers to three league titles as manager before Liverpool lured him back to Anfield in April 1991.

Reflecting now, he admits he didn’t fully appreciate the expectations that came with the job when he first took charge at Ibrox but is confident that McInnes won’t repeat his mistakes. ‘I made a schoolboy error in my first interview,’ said Souness. ‘I said: “I don’t care if we lose to Celtic every time as long as we win the league”. I quickly realised that that’s unacceptable. We have to win the league and beat them.

Rangers have had the upper hand on Celtic in two games this season

Rangers players celebrate with scorer Ryan Naderi after 1-0 win at Celtic Park

‘It’s an extremely pressurised job, managing Glasgow Rangers. But Derek knew that already. He’s played there under pressure. He knows the club. He knows how the west of Scotland is. There are fewer surprises for him than there were for me.

‘He’s already had to deal with some disappointments. We didn’t make a good start to the season, but he lived with that, he’s rallied the troops, and he’s got them performing.

‘But I keep coming back to it, all we have done is open the door. We now have to be like that every time we cross the white line.

‘Although we’ve turned an enormous corner, don’t be thinking the hard work’s done. The hard work’s still ahead.

‘Rangers players, every time they go out and play, are confronted by a team where it’s their cup final. Always remember that. No game starts easy, but you can make it easy: get a couple of goals, dominate, bully them. That’s what we have to be like.

‘When you’re playing for Rangers, you can’t pick and choose when you’re at 100 per cent. It has to be every single time, so your mentality has to be spot on.’

The full interview with Souness is available to watch now on the This Is Ibrox YouTube channel: youtube.com/thisisibrox

Lisandro Martinez on Thursday night apologised for his withering takedown of Manchester United’s hierarchy after ‘positive’ clear-the-air talks with director of football Jason Wilcox and other key figures.

A fuming Martinez publicly criticised Wilcox and United’s top executives after defeat to Atletico Madrid for not backing manager Michael Carrick in the summer transfer window and for not fronting up to criticism after a miserable start to the campaign.

Martinez looked to clarify his remarks with a statement on Instagram on Wednesday – the squad’s allocated day off following the 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid – before releasing a fresh statement after talks with Wilcox and the board.

He is also understood to have accepted a fine.

‘It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after the game,’ Martinez said.

‘Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity.

‘The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.’

Lisandro Martinez has released another statement after meeting with Man United chiefs

While Martinez has for the first time apologised for the timing of his remarks, made just moments after the match concluded in Spain on Tuesday, it is not clear whether he apologised privately for the nature of his blistering critique, particularly of Wilcox.

Club sources stressed that Martinez alone made the decision to apologise publicly for his comments. The matter, in the eyes of United’s hierarchy, is seen as closed.

‘Our club is at its best when we are all united, and I recognise that my words in that moment did not help with that,’ he added in his latest statement.

‘I know that every single person at Manchester United is doing everything possible to achieve our shared ambition: bringing the success that this club and its supporters deserve.

‘With this situation now behind us, we are fully focused on winning together.’

Carrick, who was also present in Thursday’s crunch meeting at Carrington, is going to need Martinez on Sunday when United travel to Elland Road to face Leeds United, not least with Noussair Mazraoui, Patrick Dorgu and Luke Shaw all already sidelined at the back.

Martinez’s long-term future is more uncertain, however. He is out of contract at the end of June, although United can extend it by another year.

If there is no resolution in the coming weeks, Martinez is free to negotiate with clubs outside of England for a pre-contract agreement.

United are unlikely to let a 28-year-old World Cup winner leave as a free agent five years after his £57million move from Ajax, but could trigger the extension so they can demand a transfer fee for him.

#805. Gareth Southgate suggests he will NEVER manage in the Premier League again - as former England boss admits he 'stopped enjoying' wins and hasn't been to a game in 18 months

Published: 20:13 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 20:14 BST, 15 October 2026

Gareth Southgate has ruled out a return to Premier League football with the former England manager revealing how he has not attended a single game in almost 18 months.

Southgate spent eight years in charge of his national team before resigning after the Euro 2024 final loss to Spain. However, the last match he attended was the 2025 Champions League final when Paris Saint-Germain thrashed Inter Milan 5-0, having also been at the 2025 FA Cup final to see Crystal Palace beat Manchester City 1-0.

Since then, the 56-year-old has not stepped inside a stadium and has hardly watched any football whatsoever, having seemingly fallen out of love with the game.

He has also admitted that he ‘did not even enjoy the wins’ towards the end of his time with England while discussing why a move into club management is not in the offing, despite being routinely linked with sides such as Manchester United.

‘I don’t see a scenario where I do that,’ Southgate said when asked whether he would consider a return to the Premier League on The Amol Rajan Connection podcast.

‘Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying (it). For a period, you know, the wins keep you going. By the end, I didn’t even enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes.

Gareth Southgate has suggested he will never manage in the Premier League again

‘I’ve hardly watched football (since leaving). I went to the Champions League final, the year after I left England, 2025, and I went to the FA Cup final to see my team (Crystal) Palace win their first trophy, but not been to a football ground since.’

Southgate has not managed at club level since a three-year spell at Middlesbrough from 2006. Since exiting the England national team in 2024, he has worked as part of UEFA’s Technical Observer Group in an advisory role, released a book called ‘Dear England: Lessons in Leadership’, and participated in some media work.

However, he has largely stayed away from the spotlight since stepping away from the international scene.

Southgate added: ‘I’ve had 37 years where my sense of self depended on, “Did I win? Did I win or lose on Saturday?” I’m not interested in survival, you know, just being a manager because it’s a good salary. Survival, that doesn’t excite me.

'One of the beauties with England was we could win, we could create history, we could break new ground. I’ve given a lot of my life to football. I’ve given every ounce I had. And I just fancy a different period of my life.’

Southgate was appointed England manager on a temporary basis in September 2016 following the resignation of Sam Allardyce, having previously coached the Under 21s. He took England to the final of two European Championships in 2020 and 2024 – losing to Italy and Spain respectively – and the 2018 World Cup semi-finals before stepping down.

#806. From mixing it with Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham at Dortmund, Bradley Fink has quickly found his stride at high-flying Dundee

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 18:52 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 19:05 BST, 15 October 2026

Not so long ago, Bradley Fink had stars in his eyes in more ways than one when he awoke each morning.

Signed by Borussia Dortmund in 2019 on the same day Giovanni Reyna put pen to paper, the forward’s early days saw him rub shoulders with Mats Hummels, who’d just returned to the club from Bayern Munich.

Jadon Sancho was already established in the first-team. Midway through Fink’s first season, Erling Haaland signed from RB Salzburg. Then, six months later, Jude Bellingham arrived from Birmingham City.

Having moved to Signal Iduna Park from Luzern as a 16-year-old, the Swiss never attempted to hide his light under a bushel.

‘It was my dream to run out at Luzern’s home stadium, but I think my chances of becoming professional are higher at Dortmund than they were at Luzern,’ he said.

‘My dream has now changed. My goal is to play for Dortmund in front of 80,000 spectators.’

Back then, Fink’s stated ambition looked eminently achievable. Having moved to Luzern from local side SC Cham as a nine-year-old, his scoring exploits at youth level were nothing short of ridiculous.

Bradley Fink scores in Dundee's victory over Motherwell in the Premiership last month

Fink strikes the post in the same game against the Steelmen

He managed 40 goals in 21 games for Luzern at under-16 level – a return which, unsurprisingly, helped his team win the double.

With seven goals in as many matches for Switzerland under-17s, he was one of the rising stars for his nation at that age group. When Puma shot a new advert for a range of trainers, he was the first name on the invitation list.

Before putting a three-year contract in front of him, Dortmund apparently scouted him 15 times. They were not alone.

‘We had inquiries from 16 other clubs,’ said the player’s father Thomas.

Signing for just £166,000 in compensation, Fink made short work of justifying Dortmund’s faith in him.

His debut season with the second team was a runaway success, 12 goals and four assists registered in 18 games, making him the league’s third highest scorer. He also made his debut for the under-19s in a UEFA Youth League game against Barcelona.

‘He is on the right track,’ noted Sebastian Geppert, Fink’s youth coach at the time.

‘He is technically savvy, has good control and can also pass the ball quickly.

‘He is a good guy with rough edges. There were days when we trained in the morning, at noon and in the evening and the boys were totally exhausted. As a result, we cancelled our early morning training, but Bradley preferred to train.’

In the fullness of time, this application would be sporadically rewarded by working with some of the best emerging players on the planet.

But the task of edging Haaland out of the team – three years Fink’s senior – was akin to splitting the atom.

Fink has quickly become a fans' favourite at Dens Park

There was assuredly no shame in failing to dislodge the Norwegian from his position as he sealed a move to Manchester City by tormenting defenders the length and breadth of Germany. A case of right place, wrong time – if ever there was one.

‘It was a very good time playing and training with the first team,’ reflected the Dundee forward ahead of Saturday’s match with Rangers.

‘Sadly, I never got my debut, but the experience of training with Haaland, Bellingham and all of them was very, very good.

‘But in the end it was a very great adventure. From that team we have loads of players that are playing football in higher leagues.’

Fink was different in style to the legendary Norwegian, relying more on his technique and nous than his strength. But there were still learnings to be taken from seeing him at work.

‘He doesn’t have 100 touches, but the touches he has he scores goals with,’ he offered.

When it became apparent that he faced mission impossible to elbow his way to the front of the strikers’ queue, Basel were the first club to recognise that Dortmund’s loss could be their gain.

Having persuaded the forward a return home on the basis that they’d grant him the openings he was denied in Germany, he signed a four-year deal there in 2022.

He did play under Sebastien Frei 25 times in the Swiss Super League in 2022-23, but with just five goals to his name, he wasn’t exactly the prolific marksman that many believed he’d be when he departed his homeland three years previously.

Unable to command a regular start, he moved for a season on loan to Grasshopper where he managed two goals in 31 league matches.

Fink found the net for Dundee at Tynecastle on league duty on September 6

His final season at Basel earned him a league winner’s medal yet just one goal in 16 league appearances.

Struggling to live up to expectations, the one-time golden boy of Swiss football agreed to a left-field move to League One Wycombe Wanderers in 2025.

If he hoped a change of environment would bring a change in fortunes, he was mistaken.

If it hadn’t been for bad luck at Adams Park, Fink would have had no luck at all.

He tore his quad muscle in the first week of pre-season. Having got himself ready for the league opener at Bradford, he did it again.

And by the time he was good to go again, Mike Dodds, the manager who’d signed him, had been sacked.

The upshot was that he immediately became a peripheral figure with just two starts in his 21 appearances last term which yielded two goals.

It was to be the misfortune of another, though, which finally opened the door to salvation at the start of this season.

The crucial ligament injury Simon Murray sustained against Aberdeen on August 15 compelled Steven Pressley to look for an alternative option up front.

Pressley felt the Swiss forward had ‘lost his way a little’ but knew there was a player of pedigree in there.

Facing a choice between sitting on the bench in Buckinghamshire or proving a point in the Scottish Premiership, Fink listened to what Pressley had to say and jumped at the opportunity.

The first impression the Dark Blues supporters had of him could not have been more favourable.

Signed only the day before the derby, he climbed off the bench to help ease Pressley’s side towards a famous 2-0 win at Tannadice.

His six appearances to date have been garlanded with goals against Hearts and Motherwell.

Just as impressive have been his link-up play and movement, traits he honed in his time mixing with football royalty at Dortmund.

Like the club whose jersey he’ll wear until next summer at least, Fink is a player who’s on the rise again. And at just 23, the zenith could still be some way off.

#807. Crystal Palace's John Textor nightmare: BOBBY MANZI reveals the blazing rows with Steve Parish, his crumbling football empire and why Lyon can't stand him either

Published: 02:00 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 17:26 BST, 15 October 2026

When the full-time whistle went at Wembley and Crystal Palace had defied all the odds to win the FA Cup, John Textor leaned over a row of Royal Box seats to embrace Steve Parish.

After Eberechi Eze's goal won them the first trophy in their 120-year history, the image depicted an ownership group that was united and jubilant. In reality, their relationship was anything but.

On Thursday, Palace will reopen old wounds when they travel to Lyon for the Textor Derby. The disgraced former owner of both clubs will be nowhere to be seen and that's probably for the best, given the acrimony towards him in both France and south London.

Without his cross-Channel multi-club network, Palace may well have been playing in the Europa League last season. Instead they were demoted by virtue of no two clubs being able to play in the same UEFA competition and Nottingham Forest - now Public Enemy No1 in Croydon - took Palace's place. And the animosity extends beyond the supporters.

Textor arrived at Palace in August 2021, acquiring the largest minority stake in the club for £87.5million before increasing his shareholding to 43 per cent three years later. Yet, despite his attempts, Textor failed to convert his equity into control. On several occasions, he tried to purchase a majority stake but was consistently blocked.

That irked him. Chairman Parish, the club's ultimate decision-maker despite owning significantly less of it than Textor, angered him. Textor deemed Parish risk-averse, while Parish viewed Textor as a risk to the club. But Parish had the measure of him, using the Missouri-born former competitive skateboarder's capital to pay off debt during Covid, develop the academy site and strengthen the playing squad without giving him decision-making power.

Former Crystal Palace director John Textor (left) had regular slanging matches with fellow part-owner Steve Parish (right)

Textor's ownership of Lyon meant that Palace were kicked out of the Europa League last season, as no two teams in the same competition can have the same controlling partner

Meanwhile, Textor wanted Palace to be the cornerstone of his multi-club ownership group, Eagle Football, which owned Lyon, Brazilian top-flight side Botafogo and the now-defunct RWD Molenbeek of Belgium. Given that Textor has since lost all the clubs amid financial mismanagement, Parish's wariness has been vindicated.

Textor wanted Parish to prioritise the playing squad and was aggrieved by ring-fencing cash for Selhurst Park's new Main Stand. Some believe Textor never supported the development, with the issue often prompting bust-ups.

Publicly, Parish and Textor mostly put on a united front, though Textor made some snide digs about the 'red Ferrari driving chairman' in an interview with talkSPORT. Behind the scenes, however, the pair never hid their dislike or the tension between them – and Textor eventually lost much of his interest in Palace after realising his sway was limited and he could not further his multi-club network ambitions.

The most disruptive period came during Textor's exit. He had been looking to sell for some time but the process was accelerated after the FA Cup win granted Palace entry into the Europa League for the following campaign, where the Lyon problem reared its head.

There was perhaps another reason for Textor's expediency. Lyon had problems of their own - the seven-times French champions were in the process of being kicked out of Ligue 1 by the French football authorities (DNCG).

But when Textor's money came in from selling his Palace stake to Woody Johnson, the former US Ambassador to the UK and owner of the NFL's New York Jets, they satisfied the DNCG's demands and were reinstated not just to the French top flight but also the Europa League.

So in the end, selling Palace and releasing them from the multi-club network resulted in Lyon taking their Europa League place. Palace were demoted to the Conference League - which they went on to win to again qualify for the Europa League - because Textor still had 'decisive influence' on the March 1, 2025 deadline for ownership conflicts to be resolved for the following season.

Palace fans had voiced their distrust of Textor long before the multi-club ownership issue hit them hard - with this banner in January 2023

Textor (centre) owned around 40 per cent of Palace from August 2021 to July 2025, when he sold his stake to New York Jets owner and former US Ambassador to the UK Woody Johnson

To this day, Textor is one of three parties Palace supporters blame for their expulsion, alongside Nottingham Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis and UEFA.

'F*** UEFA, f*** John Textor, f*** Marinakis' has become a staple chant at matches and will almost certainly be heard throughout the match at the Groupama Stadium on Thursday night.

Textor has both publicly and privately suggested that supporters are naive for blaming him. Of course, the Europa League demotion is the emotional source of their frustration. However, the Textor resentment originated in concerns over his ambition to put Eagle Football Holdings on the stock market and fears over whether he had suitable funding.

Having previously held stakes in four clubs, Textor now has none.

Palace and Lyon are under new management, Botafogo voted him off their board this summer a few months after the club were hit with a three-window transfer ban for non-payment of a transfer fee, and Molenbeek lost their Belgian football league licence in August over financial difficulties. At the top of it all, Eagle Football Holdings went into administration in March.

It should be said that Palace had not planned well enough for the possibility of playing European football. Had they done so, Textor's shares could have been placed in a blind trust before the deadline and the situation avoided. Whether Textor would have agreed to that while trying to sell up, though, is another matter.

Intriguingly, one Palace source defended Textor when speaking to Daily Mail Sport. The source argued that Textor was the driving force behind Palace appointing Oliver Glasner two years ago and that the investment he made helped to pay for the signings of Marc Guehi and Michael Olise, suggesting that none of Palace's three trophies in the last 18 months would have been possible without the American. That is an unpopular opinion among fans to say the least, though.

Even after his exit, there remained a tenuous link to the club. John Textor's son, Addison, was until this summer employed by Velocity Capital – an American private equity firm owned by minority Palace shareholder David Abrams. The firm invested more than £75m in leading football agency Unique Sports Group, which represents past and present Palace players Dean Henderson, Maxence Lacroix, Marc Guehi and Dwight McNeil.

Under Textor's ownership, Botafogo won the Copa Libertadores in 2024 but he was voted off the club's board in July this year

One source argued that Textor was the driving force behind Palace appointing Oliver Glasner, and as such none of Palace's three trophies in the last 18 months would have been possible

It was Textor who appointed now-Palace boss Pierre Sage as Lyon head coach in 2023. He led them to the French Cup final in his first season but was sacked the following January

Palace fans will use their trip to Lyon to lambast Textor once again and the home crowd is likely to join in. Although Lyon's involvement prevented Palace from competing in the Europa League, there is no bitterness between the two clubs – both equally disdain Textor.

Lyon endured persistent battles with the DNCG thanks to Textor building up debt, the provisional relegation last summer and being forced to sell key players because of their financial situation. Ironically, supporters also fumed over his decision to sack now-Palace boss Pierre Sage, a decision Textor admits he now regrets.

When Palace won the Conference League to qualify for the Europa League last season, they were almost destined to face Lyon.

This is the final chapter in their Textor debacle and, unless it's in their favourite chant, everyone at Palace will hope Thursday night is the last time he enters their thoughts.

Bournemouth appear to have this week softened their stance on selling Alex Scott in January, with the Cherries inviting a bidding war that they hope will include Liverpool.

Liverpool's interest in Alex Scott is genuine and Bournemouth have softened their stance on selling the midfielder in January

It was originally hoped he would return to training in either late September or mid-October but that date has been pushed back several times.

Giovanni Leoni has been out since suffering a cruciate ligament injury on debut over a year ago, but will have to wait at least another few weeks to return to first-team training

Dominik Szoboszlai remains hopeful of returning to action in the next week after missing the last two games through a hamstring injury – despite claims from Hungary that it is a serious issue.

The vice-captain sat in the stands for Sunday’s 3-0 defeat by Manchester City and then was not part of the squad against LASK – although he joined the team in travelling to Austria.

Rumours had suggested Szoboszlai’s injury might have been worse than Iraola’s initial verdict – he said it was just an ‘overload’ on international duty – and Hungarian media then claimed Szoboszlai would miss the next few matches.

But sources close to the vice-captain have played down any fears of the issue being a more serious problem. And then Szoboszlai himself, talking briefly to British reporters after Liverpool’s win at LASK, said ‘we will see’ when it comes to a return in the next week.

He will be given a chance at the very least to be part of the squad travelling to Brentford.

Sources close to Dominik Szoboszlai have played down any fears of the midfielder having a serious injury

There is a lot of buzz in the Liverpool fanbase around teenager Josh Abe, who went on the first team's pre-season tour of America – and many fans have asked Confidential when they can expect him to be fit from surgery on his shoulder.

It is understood he is still about a month away from returning to training.

Mixed zone diaries: s’il vous plait, Bradley?

If only I had not ditched French for German at GCSE! Well, my German's not up to much either, as I have proved repeatedly on this week’s trip to German-speaking Austria.

After the win over LASK, there was a cordial exchange with hat-trick hero Bradley Barcola where he was asked for a chat in English and declined, to which I – for some reason – said: ‘We can do the interview in French and I’ll get AI to translate it!’

I don’t… and he was soon saying his goodbyes as he left with the match-ball.

Barcola did not need to talk anyway, his facial expression said it all: he was euphoric to open his Liverpool account with a treble. Now can he do it on a cold, autumnal afternoon in Hounslow?

Bradley Barcola was in euphoric mood after opening his Liverpool account with a hat-trick against LASK

After starring in the Under-21 Euros in 2025, many might have expected Harvey Elliott to be a fully-fledged international by now. Instead, his prospects have nosedived.

But the recent international break was a chance for Elliott to reset, build fitness and confidence under new Valencia manager Javier Aguirre (who readers may remember from his touchline antics with Mexico at the World Cup).

Elliott changed Sunday's game against Racing Santander after coming on as a substitute and Aguirre said: ‘When I arrived, I saw the data for Dani Raba, Harvey Elliott, and Hugo Duro, and that they weren’t playing. I watched them train and thought, “These guys have to play”.’

Small steps but it appears the Liverpool loanee is heading in the right direction. Across the city of Valencia, meanwhile, Ifeanyi Ndukwe is making strides at Levante.

The defender, a star of pre-season who could not get a work permit and was forced to leave on loan, has featured in their last three La Liga matches – culminating in a last-gasp equaliser at home to Sevilla on Monday.

His emergence has helped his bid for a work permit in England.

Liverpool battled to a thrilling 4-2 victory in the UEFA Youth League on Wednesday afternoon on the outskirts of Linz, coming from two down to beat LASK.

The main man, as has often been the case this season, was young striker Will Wright, who scored a hat-trick and assisted Luca Eden for the other goal.

With Hugo Ekitike out for a bit longer yet and Liverpool having fitness issues in attack, Wright, 18, may soon be knocking on the first-team door.

Young striker Will Wright could be knocking on the first-team door after impressing regularly for Liverpool's youth teams

The week ahead: Iraola’s date with former right-hand man

One of the first people to text Iraola after the Champions League draw was made was Inigo Perez, the Villarreal boss who was the Basque’s No 2 at Rayo Vallecano.

Perez could not get the necessary work permit to join Iraola at Bournemouth so remained in Vallecas, where his side made the Conference League final only to lose to Crystal Palace.

He is now at Villarreal and has a similar style of play to Iraola. ‘Pressing is the best playmaker,’ he once said, and he has described his team as ‘ordered chaos’.

No doubt the pair will share a glass of red wine at Anfield on Tuesday.

#810. Jose Mourinho's mood darkens as he takes aim at 'shameful' LaLiga, 'strange' referees and even Real Madrid's own fans with pressure cranking up after another unconvincing display

By WILL GRIFFEE and MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER

Published: 16:00 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 16:54 BST, 15 October 2026

Jose Mourinho's mood at Real Madrid is darkening, with pressure beginning to tell on the 63-year-old.

The Portuguese watched his side rescue a victory against Roma on Wednesday night but the Spanish giants remain unconvincing and trail bitter rivals Barcelona by six points already in LaLiga.

Mourinho appears to be reverting to type, picking fights to deflect attention from his stuttering side, with LaLiga, referees and even his own booing supporters in the firing line on what Spanish press have branded his 'blacklist'.

Mourinho was furious with what he perceived as deliberately provocative timing from LaLiga's disciplinary committee, who released news of Vinicius Jr's hefty four-game ban for a hair-pull just two hours before the Brazilian took to the pitch in Rome.

Vinicius proceeded to have one of his worst 60 minutes of the season before being unceremoniously hooked by the manager and replaced by eventual match-winner Endrick.

Mourinho bristled at full-time: 'You're the journalist, but... can I ask you a question? Do you think it's normal that a player from a Spanish team, who has to play a match that's also important for Spanish football...

Jose Mourinho's 'blacklist' as described by Spanish press is a number of grievances

Mourinho was angered by the timing of news that Vinicius Jr had been given a four-match ban for a hair pull, with the decision announced hours before their Champions League match

'Do you think it's normal that two hours before a match, a player finds out he's been given a four-match suspension?

'You don't have to answer, but that's the question I'm asking. Do you think it's normal?'

LaLiga's disciplinary panel usually release punishments on a Wednesday afternoon and he used an unusual Portuguese expression to describe what he thought was an obvious move to enrage the club.

He said: 'Couldn’t they do it now (after the match)? Couldn’t they do it tomorrow morning (today)? We have to come by bus, and it’s almost as we arrive at the stadium that we find out Vinicius has a four-match suspension.

'In Portuguese there’s an expression, "a cat hiding with its tail sticking out".

'Well, it seems to me that now the cat isn’t hiding anymore. It’s out in full force. They do things without shame.

'You want to kill a player two hours before a match. It doesn’t seem normal to me; but at this point it seems normal, because at this point the cat isn’t hiding anymore.'

Mourinho wasn't finished there. His next gripe was with what he perceived as unfair scheduling with just 72 hours between matches in November before the international break.

He went on: 'At the very least, it shows a lack of respect. Playing in Athens on Wednesday night, arriving back in Madrid probably at five in the morning or something like that, and then playing in Valencia on Saturday, on a weekend preceding an international break, where it makes absolutely no sense to make you play in Valencia on Saturday, which is an extremely difficult match... It doesn't seem innocent to me.'

Vinicius Jr struggled against Roma with Mourinho claiming the suspension was an attempt to 'kill a player two hours before a match'

Mourinho took aim at LaLiga and its officiating in his post-match press conference after their dramatic Champions League win over Roma

'I don’t buy the same old excuses. I’ve been involved in football for 25 years. The excuses about ‘the TV’ — that "it was the TV that decided, it was the TV that chose Saturday for the match."

'I’m too old to swallow this. And this Vinicius story, finding out two hours before the match that he has a four-match suspension… It doesn’t deserve comment. Real Madrid fans aren’t stupid, and I’ll do everything I can to open people’s eyes.'

Only last week, he also took a swipe at the press, blaming the Spanish media for provoking Real fans into booing Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius this season.

'If there are whistles at the Bernabéu, for you it will be a great victory,' he said.

'This is one of your objectives! Obviously it is. You don't need to be Einstein to understand that the dynamic leads exactly to this... This is the objective. Whose? I prefer not to... not to talk about it.'

Mourinho had opted to skip his media duties at the weekend following Real Madrid's narrow 1-0 win over Villarreal.

Spanish outlet Marca reported that the 63-year-old was cautious not to make a comment that could result in a touchline ban.

Mourinho had hit out at officiating last month following Real Madrid's 2-1 loss to city rivals Atletico Madrid, where he labelled the appointment of referee Ortiz Arias as being 'very strange'.

The Real Madrid boss hit out at Arias' appointment by stating the referee has 'no international experience' and is not 'a great referee'.

Mourinho is seen complaining to referee Isidro Diaz de Mera at a game earlier this month

The criticism, which also included the appointment of the VAR officials, came as Mourinho held up photos of tackles made by Atletico Madrid players Cristian Romero and Kang-in Lee, which he believed warranted red cards.

Real Madrid fans have also felt the brunt of Mourinho's comments, with the Portuguese coach having questioned their booing of Vinicius Jr and Kylian Mbappe last month.

'In Portuguese, we have a proverb that says we only throw stones at the trees that have fruit,' Mourinho said.

'So what Vini has done here over recent years - how many CL has he won, how many goals has he scored, how many balls has he won? His achievements speak for themselves so he is the tree that has a lot of fruit on it and people want to get a piece of Vini.

'During this digital era where we have access to so many stats, we can tell that he is very close to getting to his best version.

'He [Mbappe] is the tree with a lot of fruit. Obviously a player who scores more than 40 goals for a team is never a problem.

'I saw Kylian giving it his all. He was defending like an animal, even when he had nothing left. His attitude is incredible. It is a joy for me to see a player like that.'

Mourinho's Real Madrid side are currently fourth in LaLiga after winning six and losing two of their opening eight league matches of the season.

His side are currently six points adrift of reigning champions Barcelona.

#812. Vinicius Jr's nightmare 24 hours: Real Madrid star fumes at being subbed early by Jose Mourinho against Roma - after four-game ban for hair-pull rules him out of El Clasico

Real Madrid star Vinicius Junior has endured a nightmare 24 hours after being hooked early against Roma - and being slapped with a four-match ban for a wild hair pull.

The winger was subbed by Jose Mourinho before the hour mark with Madrid 3-1 down at Roma in the Champions League - only to see his team-mates go on to thrive and win 4-3.

His frustrations were evident and he said: 'It’s only natural for me to be angry when I’m substituted, because I always want to play every minute, to be at my best and help the team, and today that wasn’t possible.'

He did acknowledge the positive impact of his replacement, 20-year-old Endrick, who scored his first goal of the season as Madrid completed a monumental comeback in the dying minutes.

The Brazilian will not have much of a chance to blow off steam, though, after he was hit with a ban for violent conduct after his outrageous hair pull during a recent 1-0 win over Villarreal.

And the Brazilian will miss the El Clasico against Barcelona next week as a result, with Real Madrid already playing catch-up in La Liga.

Vinicius Jr has been slapped with a four-match ban for this hair pull during Real Madrid's 1-0 win over Villarreal

'Someone from La Liga and the referees' association always comes to explain the rules, but never this specific point. It was a red card for me, simple as that... I've never been violent towards another player. I get hit quite a lot, yet the cards end up going to me.'

And he was fuming at his dismissal, with referee Isidro Díaz de Mera noting: 'after being sent off and still on the field, he continued to protest my decision loudly, heading towards the area where I was with an aggressive attitude.'

Vinicius Jr later posted a brief apology on Instagram, writing: 'Sorry to my team and my fans'.

But he also posted a series of clips of flashpoints from other matches where he believes players should have been sent off, but were not.

That post came with the caption: 'And the one who always sees yellow and red is Vinicius. A disgrace.'

Mourinho was highly irritated at the fact that they found out of his ban a couple of hours before the Roma game.

He told AS: 'Is it normal for a player to find out two hours before a match that he is going to be suspended for four games? There is no need to answer me. Is that normal? Could they not have announced the decision now or tomorrow morning? Did they have to do it while we were on our way to the stadium?

He protested against his dismissal and was condemned for his 'aggressive attitude'

'"In Portuguese we say: the cat is hiding but its tail is showing. It seems to me that the cat is no longer hiding now. The cat is acting freely, and there are things happening without shame. It is acting freely.

'Two hours before a match, a player at a Spanish club who contributed three points towards strengthening the standing of Spanish football, I do not see that as normal. But I am starting to consider it normal, because the cat is no longer hiding. What is the question?

'At the very least, it shows a lack of respect. Playing in Athens on Wednesday evening, arriving in Madrid at five in the morning, then playing on Saturday in Valencia, during a week before the international break, does not seem to me to be innocent.

'I do not believe the usual excuses, such as that the reason is television (broadcasting rights). I do not believe that. I have grown too old for that. As for the Vinicius story, and him finding out two hours before the match that he had been given a four-match suspension, Real Madrid fans are not stupid.'

The ban will only apply to domestic competitions, so he will miss fixtures against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia. The next La Liga match he will be available for is against Celta Vigo on November 22.

Madrid, being a rather argumentative club in these circumstances, may still appeal the suspension according to the Spanish press.

Manager Jose Mourinho held his tongue in his post-match press conference, saying: 'I’m not going to speak because I want to be on the bench against Sevilla and Barcelona.'

In any case, he will be allowed to play against RB Leipzig and AEK Athens in the Champions League during the period of the ban.

His domestic absence is a blow but the No7 has not been at his prolific best this term, only scoring once and creating three assists in eight games.

'He is going to emerge,' Mourinho told TNT Sports in a display of confidence. 'It is just a question of when.'

Oddly enough, Vinicius thought he had scored his second goal of the season against Villarreal, but after the referee was called over to the monitor, he was sent off for the hair pull during the build-up and his effort was chalked off.

Madrid sit fourth in La Liga, six points behind Barcelona, who have made a perfect start.

They found their mojo at Roma in the Champions League, coming from 3-1 behind to win 4-3 late on as the Italian hosts paid tribute to their former manager Mourinho with a tifo, making him visibly emotional.

#815. 'The first time I saw him play, I thought: "God exists"': Inside Estevao Willian's journey from Brazil to Stamford Bridge - KIERAN GILL is given exclusive access to intimate documentary which offers hint on teenager's future

Published: 12:05 BST, 15 October 2026 | Updated: 13:16 BST, 15 October 2026

Ivo Goncalves turns to Estevao Willian and gently rests his hand on the arm of his son. ‘A movie plays in our heads, everything we’ve been through to get here, and you get to a moment like this, and I want to have other moments just like it,’ he says.

It is a loving exchange, of a father telling his lad how proud he is of him, with his mother, Etienne Almeida, sitting and smiling on his other side on the sofa in their living room.

It follows a little reminiscing about the time Estevao scored in Chelsea’s 3-0 Champions League win over Barcelona; the night a star was born as the boy from Brazil upstaged Lamine Yamal at Stamford Bridge.

For Estevao, that game was the culmination of a long journey from Franca to Cruzeiro to Palmeiras to Chelsea, where he arrived aged 18. But there were a few who saw this coming.

Such as Gustavo Ferreira, the now-director of Santos FC who took him to Cruzeiro: ‘The first time I saw Estevao play, I thought, “God exists”. Our Under 20s coach, having watched Estevao train when he was still 13 or 14 years old, came into my office and said that if there was no physical component, Estevao at 13 would already be playing for Cruzeiro’s Under 20s.’

Such as Serginho Carioca, his youth coach: ‘Estevao, when he was six, used to play against kids who were eight or nine. He would always finish off the game, always stand out, and I had this problem – the parents asked me to take Estevao out because he always unbalanced the games.’

Chelsea wonderkid Estevao Willian offers a glimpse into his family life in a new as-yet-unreleased film called I Am Estevao

In the documentary, Estevao reminisces about his goal in a 3-0 win over Barcelona (pictured)

He also recalls meeting Cole Palmer for the first time when Palmeiras played Chelsea at the Club World Cup. 'I didn’t understand him much,' admits Estevao

Such as Joao Paulo, his academy director at Palmeiras: ‘The first time I saw him play, I said, “This is a great gem to be the best in the world... wow". I saw (Joaquin) Piquerez, who’s one of our captains and an experienced left back of ours. On the second or third day (of Estevao joining first-team training), he asked me, “Who’s this annoying, talented kid?”’

Such as Nike, who made him the youngest Brazilian to sign a sponsorship deal at the age of 10, with Francisco Godoy, Estevao's representative, explaining: ‘A huge global brand identifying his talent, for us, really confirmed that we were on the right path.’

It is all captured in a new documentary called I Am Estevao, to be available on the CFC+ video section on Chelsea’s website and seen by Confidential. Included are interviews with Joao Pedro, Thiago Silva, Andrey Santos, and, of course, Estevao himself.

He speaks Portuguese in the programme, though does confess: ‘I am very close with the Brazilians, but it is also very nice that they care about me. They tell me to speak English. They force me from time to time.’

Estevao produces printed pictures of his favourite moments in football, like the time he scored for Palmeiras after signing a pre-agreement with Chelsea aged 17. ‘This is me doing the (Cole) Palmer celebration,’ he says.

Estevao met Palmer after scoring against his future employers at the 2025 Club World Cup in Philadelphia. ‘I didn’t understand Palmer much,’ Estevao says of their chat after Chelsea defeated Palmeiras 2-1. ‘All I understood was “excited”, then someone came over who spoke Spanish or Portuguese. They translated. They were saying they were excited to see me, to welcome me at Chelsea. I believe it was a very important match in my life and it will be marked in my history.’

Estevao is now into his second season at Chelsea, though is trying to force his way into Xabi Alonso’s team. In their six Premier League fixtures this term, he has been an unused substitute once and introduced five times in the 83rd, 81st, 86th, 87th and 84th minutes.

Some will rightly say it is not a great deal of time for him to make a meaningful mark, with Chelsea fans hardly given a chance to sing their ‘Estevao, uh-huh, uh-huh, I like it’ chant to the tune of the 1975 hit That’s The Way (I Like It) by KC and the Sunshine Band.

Others may argue Alonso has elite players keeping this teenager out of the team, prioritises a 3-4-2-1 set-up which limits his opportunities, and gains all the information he needs from training.

Estevao has found minutes harder to come by under new Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso

He is yet to start a Premier League game this term, and was taken off at half-time against Leeds in the Carabao Cup

Either way, it has sparked talk back in Brazil of Estevao being concerned with where he stands at Chelsea.

The words of his father – ‘life in England, yes, I can say that I love England, I love England,’ says Ivo Goncalves – and of the son – ‘I see how much affection Chelsea fans have for me, I think this affection makes me feel at home, makes me love this club more,’ says Estevao – may ease the angst among supporters, even if the footage was not filmed recently.

Estevao is contracted to Chelsea until 2032, and, per sources, those inside Stamford Bridge are open to rewarding his patience with a new contract on improved terms.

His first standout season in the Premier League – from his man-of-the-match performance on his full debut away at West Ham to his stoppage-time winner against Liverpool – has not been forgotten internally. It would certainly lessen the noise externally.

‘That game was incredible, wasn’t it?’ Estevao’s mum says of Liverpool in the documentary.

Joao Pedro, the 25-year-old who has acted as a mentor to his compatriot, adds: ‘We’re here to help our kid. He really surprised me because there’s not much of an age difference between us. But compared to when I came here at 18 and him arriving now, I believe he’s further ahead than I was, mentally.’

What is fun to watch is the unseen footage of a young Estevao, with braces still shaping that big smile of his, making a mockery of older opponents.

We also see the moment when the now-19-year-old Brazilian had to nervously introduce himself to the Palmeiras squad: ‘My name is Estevao. Nice to meet you. I’m 16 years old, I am from Franca but live in Sao Paulo.’

'Compared to when I came here at 18, I believe he’s further ahead mentally,' says Estevao's compatriot and team-mate Joao Pedro (second right)

Estevao with his parents Ivo Goncalves and Etienne Almeida, and his younger sister Esther

Then came Chelsea. On that choice, at a time when every other European giant had declared their interest in acquiring him, Andre Cury, one of Estevao’s representatives from the Link Sports agency, explains: ‘When we met with Chelsea, Laurence (Stewart) and Paul (Winstanley), two very good people working there, told us that Estevao can play as a winger or No 10.’ Godoy, his other rep, adds: ‘Chelsea as a club had a plan for young players that stood out.'

Ivo Goncalves used to be a goalkeeper but, growing up, Estevao knew his father’s position was not for him. ‘Otherwise we would be in Franca still,’ the young Brazilian says of his home city.

His talents are indeed special, though Estevao cannot pinpoint a moment when he came to the realisation that he was a footballer in the making. ‘I didn’t realise; I was born with it,’ says Chelsea's terrific teenager.

CHELSEA WANT SCOTT… BUT IT'S A STEEP PRICE TAG

We can expect Chelsea to return for Alex Scott this January after receiving encouragement from Bournemouth, though his steep £100million-plus asking price could prove problematic.

Per sources, Chelsea made at least three offers for the 23-year-old midfielder in the summer with their highest bid worth £68m.

Chelsea are likely to return for Bournemouth's Alex Scott (left) in January though they may face competition from Liverpool

That provides an indication of their initial valuation and it is someway short of the one that has now been made public via Bournemouth sources. Scott is also eating into the final two years of his existing contract and currently sidelined by a muscular injury.

Scott’s former club Bristol City will be due an undisclosed sell-on fee if and when he is sold, and so the Championship side will be hoping for a bidding war, with Liverpool also interested.

Confidential is told Robert Sanchez’s move from Chelsea to Como is a 'dry' loan with no option or obligation to buy included. That means the Italian side will have to negotiate a price if they intend on keeping him permanently after this season.

Sanchez has been second choice to Jean Butez since joining, but Cesc Fabregas opted to start the 28-year-old in Wednesday’s Champions League trip to Feyenoord.

Como lost 3-2. It was an own goal from Sanchez which handed Feyenoord their third, though it was desperately unlucky, the way Anis Hadj Moussa’s deflected shot came back off the woodwork and hit Sanchez on the back of his heel as he was diving. He should not face criticism for that.

But he could be criticised for Feyenoord’s second as Hadj Moussa beat him at his near post. Chelsea fans would note it was scarily similar to the goal he conceded in their 3-2 opening-day win at Fulham back in August.

That, and the odd other mistake, convinced Alonso to bring in Emiliano Martinez as his new No 1 at Sanchez’s expense. But he could be back next summer and searching for a new home if he cannot convince Como to sign him after this loan.

Chelsea loan exile Robert Sanchez was given a rare opportunity by Como boss Cesc Fabregas against Feyenoord on Wednesday - but scored an own goal in a 3-2 defeat

A video circulating this week showed Palmer – not for the first time – walking in the street and surrounded by supporters after Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1.

He headed to his car with his girlfriend, Olivia Holder, and team-mate, Morgan Rogers, while they were also accompanied by a member of the club’s security staff.

As one source joked when we asked if there was an alternative solution to Palmer pounding the pavement in search of his ride after games at Stamford Bridge, Chelsea have no plans to dig an underground tunnel to allow for a much more private escape.

While it does represent a security risk for the club to have one of their stars out in the open, Chelsea are hamstrung by their stadium’s position and entry and exit points.

Fulham Road is closed 90 minutes before kick-off, and until 60 minutes after full-time. Stamford Bridge has an underground car park, and most players exit via there if they arrange for their ride to enter it early enough prior to the road closures.

That in itself has been a problem as fans have been known to wait for them to drive out of said car park and try to stop them for an autograph or selfie, which the players are advised to avoid doing in this congested area. It is not a case of footballers acting with arrogance; rather it is for safety reasons.

Palmer is one of those who prefers being picked up after games, which leaves him having to exit Stamford Bridge on foot with a security guard.

Cole Palmer leaving Stamford Bridge after Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1 🎥 @charliepatrick0 pic.twitter.com/LuqBE5aIhB

Former Chelsea director Marina Granovskaia attended her first game at Stamford Bridge in two years last weekend, taking in the win over Bournemouth with her 11-year-old son, Maxim.

It was previously noted that Granovskaia was interested in becoming a licensed football agent. However, she has yet to be added to the FA’s list of registered intermediaries.

Were she to re-enter the game, it could be complicated, given the FA and Premier League previously looked into Chelsea’s conduct when Granovskaia and Roman Abramovich were at the helm of the club
